papers.title: Neural Networks Based on Power Method and Inverse Power Method for Solving Linear Eigenvalue Problems
papers.abstract: In this article, we propose two kinds of neural networks inspired by power method and inverse power method to solve linear eigenvalue problems. These neural networks share similar ideas with traditional methods, in which the differential operator is realized by automatic differentiation. The eigenfunction of the eigenvalue problem is learned by the neural network and the iterative algorithms are implemented by optimizing the specially defined loss function. The largest positive eigenvalue, smallest eigenvalue and interior eigenvalues with the given prior knowledge can be solved efficiently. We examine the applicability and accuracy of our methods in the numerical experiments in one dimension, two dimensions and higher dimensions. Numerical results show that accurate eigenvalue and eigenfunction approximations can be obtained by our methods.
papers.summary: Two neural-network solvers for linear eigenvalue problems of differential operators are modeled on the classical power method and inverse power method. A neural network represents the eigenfunction, automatic differentiation applies the differential operator, and each iteration of the classical algorithm becomes the minimization of a specially defined loss function. The methods can find the largest positive eigenvalue, the smallest eigenvalue, and, given prior knowledge, interior eigenvalues. Numerical experiments in one, two, and higher dimensions show **accurate approximations of both eigenvalues and eigenfunctions**.

papers.title: Hear No Evil: Detecting Gradient Leakage by Malicious Servers in Federated Learning
papers.abstract:
Recent work has shown that gradient updates in federated learning (FL) can unintentionally reveal sensitive information about a client's local data. This risk becomes significantly greater when a malicious server manipulates the global model to provoke information-rich updates from clients. In this paper, we adopt a defender's perspective to provide the first comprehensive analysis of malicious gradient leakage attacks and the model manipulation techniques that enable them. Our investigation reveals a core trade-off: these attacks cannot be both highly effective in reconstructing private data and sufficiently stealthy to evade detection -- especially in realistic FL settings that incorporate common normalization techniques and federated averaging.
  Building on this insight, we argue that malicious gradient leakage attacks, while theoretically concerning, are inherently limited in practice and often detectable through basic monitoring. As a complementary contribution, we propose a simple, lightweight, and broadly applicable client-side detection mechanism that flags suspicious model updates before local training begins, despite the fact that such detection may not be strictly necessary in realistic FL settings. This mechanism further underscores the feasibility of defending against these attacks with minimal overhead, offering a deployable safeguard for privacy-conscious federated learning systems.
papers.summary: In federated learning (FL), a malicious server can manipulate the global model so that client gradient updates leak private training data. Taking the defender's side, the authors analyze these attacks and the model-manipulation techniques behind them. They find **a core trade-off: such attacks cannot be both highly effective at reconstructing data and stealthy enough to avoid detection**, especially in realistic setups with normalization layers and federated averaging. They also propose a lightweight client-side check that flags suspicious model updates before local training begins.

papers.title: Leaner Training, Lower Leakage: Revisiting Memorization in LLM Fine-Tuning with LoRA
papers.abstract:
Memorization in large language models (LLMs) makes them vulnerable to data extraction attacks. While pre-training memorization has been extensively studied, fewer works have explored its impact in fine-tuning, particularly for LoRA fine-tuning, a widely adopted parameter-efficient method.
  In this work, we re-examine memorization in fine-tuning and uncover a surprising divergence from prior findings across different fine-tuning strategies. Factors such as model scale and data duplication, which strongly influence memorization in pre-training and full fine-tuning, do not follow the same trend in LoRA fine-tuning. Using a more relaxed similarity-based memorization metric, we demonstrate that LoRA significantly reduces memorization risks compared to full fine-tuning, while still maintaining strong task performance.
papers.summary: Memorization in large language models (LLMs) exposes training data to extraction attacks, but it has been studied mostly in pre-training rather than fine-tuning. The authors revisit memorization under different fine-tuning strategies and find that factors which drive memorization in pre-training and full fine-tuning, such as model scale and data duplication, do not follow the same trends under `LoRA`. Using a relaxed, similarity-based memorization metric, they show that **`LoRA` significantly reduces memorization risk compared with full fine-tuning** while keeping strong task performance.

papers.title: A small HER2 reader for routine H&E slides: real-world deployment
papers.abstract: HER2 status decides who receives HER2-targeted therapy. Pathologists score HER2 protein by immunohistochemistry (IHC); equivocal IHC 2+ tumours, their hardest calls, wait for in situ hybridisation (ISH). We built a HER2 reader for routine H&E slides, owned end to end, as a baseline for pathologists. A 22M-parameter ViT-S/16 tile encoder was trained on public TCGA slides by self-supervision, distillation from H-optimus-0 and two rounds of JEPA refinement; five cross-validated attention-based slide classifiers average their probabilities; and an operating point is fixed on training data. Compared under one paired ten-seed protocol, readers on our encoder rank first of 7 on external validation from TCGA-BRCA to Yale-HER2 (AUC 0.812), level with readers on encoders 4 and 50 times larger. We also rebuilt PathBench's encoder benchmark on public cohorts; our replica reproduces its published order of reference encoders, and under it our encoder ranks first of 7 on TCGA-BRCA (0.689) and sits level with H-optimus-0 and Phikon on Yale-HER2 (0.897). On three external hospitals our deployed reader reaches AUC 0.82 on Yale-HER2 (about 0.81 with training slides balanced for tissue size), 0.75 on HEROHE and 0.63 on BCNB biopsies, and among HEROHE's 85 IHC 2+ cases it ranks ISH-amplified above non-amplified tumours at 0.76, best among our TCGA-trained readers. Per-laboratory score normalisation and a laboratory's own slides improve it further on a new site. Without a GPU our reader needs 5-6 s per slide. It serves as a research-use pre-read in a pathology platform, where it proposes a probability and a call beside IHC and helps prioritise ISH for equivocal cases. Weights, per-slide predictions and the data behind every figure are public at https://huggingface.co/cloudkites/her2-reader.
papers.summary: HER2 status decides whether breast cancer patients receive HER2-targeted therapy, and equivocal immunohistochemistry (IHC) 2+ cases need slower in situ hybridisation (ISH) testing. The authors built a HER2 predictor that works from routine H&E slides. It uses a 22M-parameter `ViT-S/16` tile encoder trained on public `TCGA` slides through self-supervision, distillation from `H-optimus-0`, and `JEPA` refinement, with an ensemble of five attention-based slide classifiers on top. The reader ranks first of seven on external validation (**AUC 0.812 on `Yale-HER2`**), level with encoders 4 to 50 times larger. It reaches AUC 0.75 on `HEROHE` and 0.63 on `BCNB` biopsies, runs in 5–6 seconds per slide without a GPU, and is deployed as a research-use pre-read in a pathology platform.

papers.title: Intervention-Conditioned Counterfactual Human Digital Twin Generator
papers.abstract: Chronic diseases evolve through long, heterogeneous trajectories shaped by interacting mediators, confounders, and treatment histories. Estimating long-term patient trajectories under alternative interventions is essential for in silico clinical trial design. However, most existing models overlook irregular visit intervals and cross-mediator dependencies, both of which are crucial for reliable long-term longitudinal prediction. Moreover, these models typically focus on outcome prediction rather than generating complete patient-state trajectories. To address these challenges, we propose CHDT, an intervention-conditioned Human Digital Twin generator under standard identification assumptions for multimodal longitudinal trajectory estimation. Its main empirical advantage arises from explicit modeling of irregular visit intervals, while cross-mediator refinement provides additional gains in selected intervention-conditioned settings. Across real-world ADNI and simulator-generated ALPACA cohorts, CHDT shows improved long-horizon patient-state fidelity relative to competing baselines. Ablation results indicate that irregular-time conditioning provides the primary empirical gain, and cross-mediator refinement provides additional improvements.
papers.summary: Simulating in silico clinical trials requires estimating long-term patient trajectories under different interventions, but most existing models ignore irregular visit intervals and dependencies between mediators, and they predict outcomes rather than full patient states. `CHDT` is an intervention-conditioned Human Digital Twin generator that produces multimodal longitudinal patient-state trajectories under standard causal identification assumptions. On the real-world `ADNI` cohort and the simulator-generated `ALPACA` cohort, it shows better long-horizon fidelity than baselines. Ablations show that **explicit modeling of irregular visit intervals provides most of the gain**, with cross-mediator refinement adding smaller improvements in some settings.

papers.title: Recycle only when you have to!
papers.abstract: AlphaFold 3-like models (e.g., Boltz, Protenix, etc.) have pushed the frontier of protein binder design. This architecture is used both for the generation of binder candidates (e.g., by hallucination or converting these models into backbone or full atom generative models) as well as for the screening of these candidates for valid binders. In this paper, we start from the observation that AlphaFold 3's confidence metrics (ipSAE, ipTM) as well as structural consistency metrics can be predicted directly from the trunk even at early recycling. Because our proposed predictor is cheap, differentiable, and available at every cycle, it can be used in two distinct ways: as a decision signal to wisely spend the recycling budget for screening and as an objective for hallucination-based design. We show that both applications lead to increased performance at significantly reduced computational cost.
papers.summary: AlphaFold 3-style models such as `Boltz` and `Protenix` are used both to generate protein binder candidates and to screen them, and both uses depend on costly recycling iterations. The authors observe that **the confidence metrics (`ipSAE`, `ipTM`) and structural-consistency metrics can be predicted directly from the trunk, even at early recycling steps**. Because this predictor is cheap, differentiable, and available at every cycle, it can decide where to spend the recycling budget during screening and serve as an objective for hallucination-based design. Both uses improve performance at significantly lower compute cost.

papers.title: VitisGP: Multi-Task Benchmark for Genotype to Phenotype Grapevine Prediction
papers.abstract: As climate change reshapes grape-growing conditions, predicting grapevine phenotypes from genomic variation is increasingly important for identifying and breeding cultivars suited to emerging environmental pressures. Existing research on the grapevine genotype-phenotype relationship using machine learning has often focused on individual traits, isolated regions, or a limited set of predictive models. We introduce VitisGP, a multi-phenotype curated dataset, integrating genome-wide SNP data with 26 heterogeneous phenotype prediction tasks spanning sommelier-curated aroma traits (N=11), botanical traits (N=14) and wine color---across 1,197 Vitis vinifera cultivars. We employ VitisGP to benchmark phenotype prediction, comparing machine-learning models with differing inductive biases---L2-regularized logistic regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, GBLUP and Transformer-based models, providing the first systematic comparison of this breadth on harmonized grapevine data. Across the benchmark, CatBoost achieves the strongest overall performance (macro-average AUROC=0.696 across 26 tasks), although model performance varies substantially across phenotype classes, with sensory and color traits showing stronger predictability than agronomic characteristics. VitisGP provides the community with a resource for investigating the genomic basis of phenotypic traits and screening grapevine diversity for climate-relevant characteristics.
papers.summary: Predicting grapevine traits from genomic variation can help breed cultivars suited to a changing climate, but prior machine-learning work has covered only single traits or a few models. `VitisGP` is a curated dataset that pairs genome-wide SNP data for 1,197 *Vitis vinifera* cultivars with 26 phenotype prediction tasks covering aroma, botanical traits, and wine color. Benchmarking logistic regression, `Random Forest`, `XGBoost`, `CatBoost`, `GBLUP`, and Transformer-based models shows that **`CatBoost` performs best overall, with a macro-average AUROC of 0.696**. Sensory and color traits are more predictable than agronomic ones.

papers.title: Dual-Corrected Stochastic Block Model ($\text{DC}^2\text{SBM}$): A Generalized Structure Detection Method for Attributed Networks
papers.abstract: Community detection in attributed networks is one of the core tasks of complex network analysis. The stochastic block model (SBM) and its variants are able to detect generalized network structures such as assortative, disassortative and mixed structures. However, existing generative methods either ignore node heterogeneity, or characterize node activity in the topological and attribute dimensions by one and the same factor, making it difficult to correctly model node activity when the two kinds of activity are decoupled. In this paper, we propose the Dual-Corrected Stochastic Block Model ($\text{DC}^2\text{SBM}$), which introduces independent correction factors---a topological degree factor and an attribute abundance factor---into the link-generation and attribute-generation channels, respectively, thereby effectively decoupling node activity from membership inference, and which further introduces a global scaling parameter to resolve the mismatch between the normalization constraints and the network scale. The model is inferred by the expectation--maximization (EM) algorithm, and the newly introduced factors cancel out completely in the posterior computation, so that no additional computational cost is incurred. Experiments on synthetic and real attributed networks show that DC^2SBM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in community detection accuracy, with an especially pronounced advantage when the topological signal is weak. The two correction factors can be recovered independently from their respective channels without cross-talk. Analytical as well as controlled experiments further demonstrate that modeling with a single shared factor fails when the two kinds of activity are decoupled---a regime that is prevalent in real networks---thereby validating the necessity of dual independent correction.
papers.summary: Stochastic block models (SBMs) for community detection in attributed networks either ignore node heterogeneity or use a single factor for a node's activity in both its links and its attributes, which fails when the two are decoupled. `DC²SBM` adds independent correction factors to the two channels, a topological degree factor for link generation and an attribute abundance factor for attribute generation, plus a global scaling parameter. It is fitted with expectation–maximization (EM), and the new factors cancel out of the posterior computation, so they add no computational cost. Experiments on synthetic and real networks show it outperforms state-of-the-art methods, **especially when the topological signal is weak**, and that single-factor models break down when the two kinds of activity are decoupled.

papers.title: Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations
papers.abstract: Calibrating a cosmological simulation is an expensive, high-dimensional parameter optimization task. Previous works employ Bayesian optimization for automation, which treats the simulator as a black box and precludes the incorporation of human domain knowledge or workflow into the selection policy. We propose AgenticTuner, an agentic calibration pipeline with a present-day large language model serving as the optimizer who proposes the next parameter trial. We show that these agents can achieve competitive calibration performance at a fraction of the CPU cost when they are given informal, human-readable priors (such as codebase, documentation, and heuristic guides that seasoned scientists may possess). We hope this work serves as an early step toward AI scientists that can carry out complex, long-horizon scientific tasks.
papers.summary: Calibrating cosmological simulations is an expensive, high-dimensional parameter search, and the usual Bayesian optimization treats the simulator as a black box, which leaves no way to use expert knowledge. `AgenticTuner` instead uses an LLM agent as the optimizer that proposes each next parameter trial. When given informal, human-readable priors such as the codebase, documentation, and heuristic guides, **the agents achieve competitive calibration at a fraction of the CPU cost**. The authors present this as an early step toward AI scientists that can carry out long-horizon scientific tasks.

papers.title: CausalGrade: Evidence-Guided Causal Graph Scoring with Jev
papers.abstract: Evaluating the structural quality of candidate causal graphs when the true causal structure is unknown is an important problem in applying causal discovery results. This paper proposes CausalGrade, a causal graph scoring method based on the probabilistic judgment model Jev. The method jointly provides Jev with evidence of association, conditional dependence, and directionality from observational data and edge probabilities produced by the causal discovery foundation model CDFM. Jev produces probabilistic judgments about direct causal edges, and a graph-level score is obtained by measuring the agreement between the adjacency structure of the graph under evaluation and these edge-level judgments. Across 300 synthetic datasets, the score exhibits a relatively strong negative correlation with structural error in all 20 combinations of four causal discovery algorithms and five variable counts, indicating that higher scores generally correspond to smaller structural errors. In 500 synthetic graph selection tasks, CausalGrade achieves a best-candidate hit rate of 54.4\%, exceeding the 48.4\% achieved by the Self-Compatibility metric \(\kappa_G\), further supporting its ability to discriminate the structural quality of graphs under evaluation.
papers.summary: Judging the quality of a candidate causal graph is hard when the true causal structure is unknown. `CausalGrade` gives the probabilistic judgment model `Jev` several kinds of evidence from observational data, namely association, conditional dependence, and directionality, along with edge probabilities from the causal discovery foundation model `CDFM`. `Jev` then judges each possible direct edge, and the graph's score measures how well its adjacency structure agrees with those judgments. Across 300 synthetic datasets, the score correlates negatively with structural error, and in 500 graph-selection tasks it picks the best candidate **54.4% of the time, versus 48.4% for the Self-Compatibility metric**.

papers.title: CalibCause: A Quality-Gated, Interpretable and Calibrated Deep Learning Framework for Diabetic Retinopathy Grading
papers.abstract: Most deep learning systems for diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading are evaluated on a single data source, with limited evidence of cross-site generalisation, uncertainty calibration, and interpretability. We propose CalibCause, a quality-gated mixture-of-experts framework that combines per-expert visual explanations, label-free image-quality conditioning, knowledge distillation, and calibrated confidence with deferral. We evaluated the framework using 51,310 fundus images from EyePACS, DDR, and APTOS 2019, with IDRiD and DeepDRiD for external testing. Evaluation included pooled testing, leave-one-environment-out experiments, paired bootstrap confidence intervals, and local grade-threshold adaptation. On the pooled test split, the label-free distilled student achieved quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.863 and accuracy of 0.865 with 27.8 million parameters, 52% fewer than its teacher. Across held-out environments, the label-free model achieved mean QWK of 0.741 compared with 0.743 for a plain ConvNeXt-Tiny baseline, while adversarial invariance did not improve cross-site grading accuracy. Refitting grade thresholds using 200 labelled images increased held-out EyePACS QWK from 0.533 to 0.621 for the label-free model. After vector scaling, expected calibration error ranged from 0.025 to 0.036 across CalibCause variants, and deferring the least confident 20% of images increased student accuracy from 0.865 to 0.923 on the remaining images. These findings demonstrate that quality-aware grading, interpretable expert routing, model compression, and calibrated deferral can be integrated without sacrificing cross-site performance relative to a plain baseline, although reliable deployment still requires local validation and adaptation.
papers.summary: Most deep learning systems for diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading are evaluated on a single data source, with little evidence of how they generalize across sites, how well calibrated they are, or how interpretable. `CalibCause` combines a quality-gated mixture of experts, per-expert visual explanations, label-free image-quality conditioning, knowledge distillation, and calibrated deferral. It was trained on 51,310 images from `EyePACS`, `DDR`, and `APTOS 2019` and tested externally on `IDRiD` and `DeepDRiD`. The distilled student reaches a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.863 with 52% fewer parameters than its teacher, but its cross-site performance only matches a plain `ConvNeXt-Tiny` baseline. **Deferring the least-confident 20% of images raises accuracy from 0.865 to 0.923**, and refitting grade thresholds on 200 local images improves results at a new site.

papers.title: Automatic Construction of Strong Simple Baselines
papers.abstract: To rigorously establish the value of a novel deep learning method, it must be compared against appropriate baselines. As deep learning has become increasingly common in the physical and life sciences, there have been numerous cases in which apparent progress has turned out to be an artifact of omitted or missing baselines. In this work, we investigate whether this problem can be mitigated by using large language models to automate the construction of baselines. We assemble 36 supervised classification and regression tasks from peer-reviewed studies in Nature, Science, and Cell-family journals that investigate novel deep learning methods for scientific applications. We then use a language model to construct simple baselines for each task. These automatically constructed baselines are strong, recovering a median of 95.5% (mean 85.7%) of the gap between a trivial predictor and the score of the deep learning model. The median simple baseline matches or exceeds the performance of the deep learning model in 12 studies. We further examine the variation across scientific domains and publication venues and we characterize the effects of test-time compute and access to different levels of study context. As human peer review has struggled to keep up with the rapidly increasing volume of research articles in recent years, our results suggest that automated baseline construction is a practical and scalable check on deep learning contributions in the physical and life sciences.
papers.summary: Apparent progress from deep learning in the sciences sometimes disappears once proper baselines are included, so the authors test whether LLMs can build those baselines automatically. They collect 36 supervised classification and regression tasks from deep learning papers in Nature, Science, and Cell-family journals and have a language model construct simple baselines for each. **The baselines recover a median of 95.5% of the gap between a trivial predictor and the published deep learning model, and match or beat it in 12 of the 36 studies.** The study also examines differences across domains and venues, and the effects of test-time compute and of how much study context the model receives.

papers.title: FGSM Attack Transferability from Simulation to Quantum Hardware in Network Intrusion Detection
papers.abstract: Quantum computers are now available through cloud platforms, and recent work has proposed using them to detect network intrusions. It is not yet clear how easily such systems can be attacked. We train a hybrid variational quantum classifier (VQC) on the Friday DDoS subset of CICIDS2017 and test it against two attacks: label flipping during training and FGSM evasion at prediction time. We run the tests in simulation and on IBM hardware, the Fez superconducting processor (Heron r2). We find that two models with similar accuracy can differ greatly in how easily they are attacked. A model that decides with little confidence loses half its detections to a very small change in the input, while a model trained to decide with more confidence needs a much larger change before it fails. Attacks built in simulation against the more confident model also work on real hardware, and the device classifies every unaltered attack sample correctly. Simulated device noise does not reduce accuracy, but it does reduce the model's confidence and makes attacks easier, so accuracy alone does not show how exposed a model is. Label flipping has no measurable effect until 15% of attack labels are changed. These results show that device noise should not be treated as a defense and that reported weaknesses in these classifiers depend partly on how they were trained.
papers.summary: Hybrid variational quantum classifiers (VQCs) have been proposed for network intrusion detection, but how easily they can be attacked is unclear. The authors train one on the `CICIDS2017` DDoS subset and test label-flipping and `FGSM` evasion attacks both in simulation and on IBM's Heron r2 Fez processor. Two models with similar accuracy differ greatly in robustness: a low-confidence model loses half its detections to tiny input changes. Attacks crafted in simulation transfer to real hardware, and **simulated device noise leaves accuracy intact while lowering confidence and making attacks easier**, so noise should not be treated as a defense. Label flipping has no measurable effect until 15% of attack labels are changed.

papers.title: The Geometry of Multitask Learning: Sharp Rates for Shared Subspace Estimation
papers.abstract: Learning a shared subspace in multitask learning is an important statistical problem, yet exact rates remain poorly understood in many of the formal settings considered in the literature. To address this gap, which arises from limitations of existing upper-bound techniques, we propose a general multitask lemma. The lemma provides sufficient conditions for fast subspace estimation in generic multitask settings, in the form of geometric conditions on the task regression functions and their estimators. We subsequently show that the multitask lemma yields sharp minimax rates---previously unknown---for linear regression and classification in the regimes considered, and rates matching up to logarithmic factors for additive-noise regression.
papers.summary: Exact statistical rates for learning a shared subspace across tasks in multitask learning are poorly understood, partly because existing upper-bound techniques are limited. The authors prove a general multitask lemma that gives geometric conditions on the task regression functions and their estimators under which the shared subspace can be estimated quickly. Applying the lemma yields **previously unknown sharp minimax rates for linear regression and classification** in the regimes studied, and rates that match up to logarithmic factors for additive-noise regression.

papers.title: PrivacyFlow: Privacy in AI Agents through Information Flow Analysis and Consequence-Aware Risk Management
papers.abstract: Autonomous LLM agents executing multi-step workflows over personal data often misalign with user privacy expectations and leak sensitive, out-of-context information. Although Contextual Integrity (CI) formalizes this problem, existing benchmarks and defenses rarely operationalize CI for realistic multi-step task sequences in evolving environments. In this work, we first introduce agentic PrivacyBench, a benchmark of 5873 tasks in 986 task sequences with dynamic environment updates and CI-grounded allow-sets for sensitive information. We also introduce PrivacyFlow, a defense that separates deliberative privacy planning (System 2) from task execution (System 1), treating each sharing decision as a structured risk-management problem. Before execution, PrivacyFlow traces the provenance and purpose of each planned data flow, models recipient background knowledge, and simulates what external actors could infer. This allows us to model the downstream consequences of disclosure, including inference attacks and context-dependent harms. It then weighs the remaining disclosure risk against task utility and executes a minimized plan, blocks it, or consults the user. Across six models, PrivacyFlow significantly reduces step-level privacy failures and raises the share of completed task sequences without a detected privacy violation by 22--55 percentage points. We further highlight a new privacy--utility--autonomy tradeoff: allowing PrivacyFlow to proactively prompt the user in case of uncertainty can increase authorized task completion at the cost of shifting decision effort back to the user. Our results suggest that proactive CI reasoning can substantially improve agentic privacy and motivate further study of this tradeoff.
papers.summary: Autonomous LLM agents that run multi-step workflows over personal data often leak sensitive information in contexts where sharing it is inappropriate, a problem formalized by Contextual Integrity (CI). The authors introduce agentic `PrivacyBench`, with 5,873 tasks in 986 task sequences whose environments change over time, and `PrivacyFlow`, a defense that separates deliberate privacy planning from task execution. Before acting, `PrivacyFlow` traces where each planned data flow comes from and what it is for, models what recipients already know and could infer, and then executes a minimized plan, blocks it, or asks the user. Across six models, it **raises the share of task sequences completed without a detected privacy violation by 22 to 55 percentage points**, and letting it ask the user under uncertainty reveals a trade-off between privacy, utility, and user effort.

papers.title: Characterizing LLM Agent Behaviors in Module Shadowing Environments
papers.abstract: LLM agents operating in untrusted workspaces face the risk of untrusted code execution during routine tasks, yet final reports and workspace states alone cannot reliably establish whether execution occurred. We introduce an evaluation framework that codes observation, reasoning, execution, and response behaviors from agent trajectories and aligns them with independent environmental records to reconstruct execution histories and verify final reports. We apply this framework to module shadowing, in which a local file is loaded in place of a trusted module during import, enabling untrusted code execution without adversarial prompts. Across 90 trials with 15 models, the payload executed in 51% of direct shadowing trials and 87% of indirect shadowing trials. Even explicit recognition of the shadowing mechanism did not ensure prevention, as the payload ran in 10 of the 29 trials with recorded recognition. These failures were often omitted from final reports, as 49 of the 62 triggered trials ended without mention of the security issue. Three reports even denied execution, including one from a trial in which independent logs recorded 19 payload executions. Final workspace states also obscured prior execution when agents deleted or overwrote the payload marker in 10 triggered trials. These findings demonstrate that combining behavioral coding with independent environmental auditing enables rigorous and transparent evaluation of agent safety.
papers.summary: LLM agents working in untrusted workspaces can execute untrusted code during routine tasks, and their final reports and the final workspace state cannot reliably show whether that happened. The authors build an evaluation framework that codes agent trajectories and checks them against independent environment logs. They apply it to module shadowing, where a local file is imported in place of a trusted module. Across 15 models, **the payload executed in 51% of direct and 87% of indirect shadowing trials**, and it still ran in 10 of the 29 trials where the agent explicitly recognized the mechanism. Agents usually omitted the issue from their final reports (49 of 62 triggered trials), and some denied execution outright, including one trial where the logs recorded 19 executions.

papers.title: MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection
papers.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used to automate vulnerability detection, but reliable detection is challenging because agents must distinguish subtle, security-relevant fixes from benign code variation. While underlying LLM capability has improved significantly, the accuracy of the agent still depends heavily on the harness: the code that defines the scaffolding around the LLM. Harnesses are typically fixed, and largely hand-written, limiting adaptation to evaluator feedback. Additionally, when harnesses are static, improvements on one dataset or model may not transfer to others. To address these challenges, we introduce MetaVul, a self-improving framework for harness discovery in vulnerability detection. Starting from a seed structured reasoning scaffold, MetaVul uses a workflow-based optimization loop to iteratively refine the harness using feedback from paired vulnerable and patched functions, while preserving the structured reasoning and verdict format. At each iteration, it searches over the history of prior harnesses, with access to their trajectories, logs, and metrics, and it returns a set of Pareto-optimal harnesses. We apply MetaVul to discover agent harnesses for various architectures. A validation set (202 pairs) is used for optimization, while an unseen dataset (430 pairs) is kept as the held-out set. We test whether harnesses learned from one model transfer to others not seen during optimization. Results on both frontier and small LLMs show that the optimized harnesses improve pairwise vulnerability detection up to 23.3 percentage points on the validation set and up to 25.8 points on the held-out set with a Pareto-frontier harness. Harnesses learned with one model also transfer to others. We show that harnesses optimized with one model transfer to another, improving held-out pairwise accuracy by 14.7 points without further optimization.
papers.summary: The accuracy of LLM agents at vulnerability detection depends heavily on the harness, the scaffolding code around the model, which is usually hand-written and fixed. `MetaVul` starts from a seed structured-reasoning harness and iteratively refines it using feedback from paired vulnerable and patched functions. At each step it searches over earlier harnesses along with their trajectories, logs, and metrics, and returns a set of Pareto-optimal harnesses. On both frontier and small LLMs, optimized harnesses improve pairwise detection accuracy by up to 23.3 points on validation data and **up to 25.8 points on a held-out set of 430 pairs**, and a harness optimized with one model improves another model's held-out accuracy by 14.7 points without further optimization.

papers.title: INLA for Adaptive UAV Sampling of Radio Environment Maps in IoT Networks: Prior Width Governs Accuracy and Calibration
papers.abstract: We study adaptive UAV sampling for radio environment map (REM) construction from non-Gaussian IoT observations. Integrated nested Laplace approximation(INLA) updates a Mat\'ern GMRF posterior, with waypoints selected by entropy pre-screening and Sherman--Morrison lookahead over the reachable set. We show that the likelihood-induced Skew-Normal correction has a sextic entropy effect, explaining its limited influence on waypoint selection. Across 19 retained ray-traced windows,Random and lawnmower sampling cost a median 18.0\% and 14.0\% more residual NMSE than posterior-informed sampling, equivalently reductions of 15.3\% and 12.3\% when referred to those baselines, while differences among informative rules remain unresolved. Widening the prior shadowing standard deviation from 6.0 to 10.025\,dB improves NMSE and credible-interval coverage, with monotone improvement over a 4--16\,dB sweep on this corpus and no observed turning point, although overconfidence persists. Online width estimation from the UAV's own counts yields about 6.5\,dB without recovering the gain. Across 30 measured LoRaWAN propagation windows paired with simulated counts and scored only on received cells, the margin over non-adaptive sampling reproduces, the training-derived width minimizes the tested interval score, and GP-UCB has nominally $3$--$5\%$ lower NMSE. The results show substantial, corpus-dependent sensitivity to prior specification, while fine differences among acquisition rules have limited or unresolved effects, the preferred width depends on the corpus, scored cells and model mismatch.
papers.summary: The authors study how a drone (UAV) should choose where to sample in order to build radio environment maps from non-Gaussian IoT signal observations. They use integrated nested Laplace approximation (INLA) to update a Matérn GMRF posterior, and choose waypoints with entropy pre-screening and a Sherman–Morrison lookahead. On ray-traced data, random and lawnmower sampling leave a median 18.0% and 14.0% more residual error than posterior-informed sampling, while the differences among informative selection rules remain unresolved. **Widening the prior shadowing standard deviation improves both accuracy and interval coverage** over a 4–16 dB sweep, and the results transfer to measured LoRaWAN data, showing that the prior specification matters more than the fine choice of acquisition rule.

papers.title: Li$^{2}$SAO: Lifting Light Singl-Rollout Asynchronous RL Optimization via Group-Relative Actor-Critic Bootstrapping
papers.abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) is becoming a mainstream paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), as it improves training efficiency by updating the model as rollouts arrive. Recent work argues that group-wise sampling in GRPO does not naturally fit asynchronous RL training because rollout lengths follow a long-tailed distribution, and proposes Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization (SAO) to improve stability and off-policy behavior, especially on agentic tasks. However, SAO relies on a closed-source value model obtained from scaling value pretraining. In this paper, we analyze GRPO and LiSAO, our lightweight reproduction of SAO without the pretrained value model, on single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic tasks. We find that GRPO outperforms LiSAO on reasoning tasks, while the reverse holds on agentic tasks. Since the value model of LiSAO is not yet well trained , LiSAO lags behind GRPO substantially in early training steps. To address this issue, we propose Li$^{2}$SAO, which Lifts Light Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization with group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping: while the critic is cold, a group-relative advantage trains the actor and a group-centered return trains the critic, after which training switches to single-rollout GAE. Experiments show that Li$^{2}$SAO catches up with or surpasses GRPO in early training and further raises the later performance ceiling. Code is available at https://github.com/jd-cc-coder/Li2SAO.
papers.summary: Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to post-train LLMs. Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization (`SAO`) was proposed as an alternative to group-sampled `GRPO`, but it relies on a closed-source pretrained value model. The authors reproduce it without that model as `LiSAO` and find that `GRPO` wins on single-turn reasoning while `LiSAO` wins on multi-turn agentic tasks, though `LiSAO` lags early while its value model is untrained. Their `Li²SAO` fixes this by using group-relative advantages to train the actor and group-centered returns to train the critic while the critic is cold, then switching to single-rollout `GAE`. Experiments show it **catches up with or surpasses `GRPO` early in training and raises the later performance ceiling**.

papers.title: Bayesian Distribution System State Estimation with Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Medium-voltage feeders have few real-time measurements, so distribution system state estimation (DSSE) rests on pseudo-measurements of the secondary substations, a prior in Bayesian terms. Weighted least squares keeps the power flow exact but reduces this prior to a mean and variance, while supervised deep learning estimators also learn the power flow and are tied to one measurement set. We propose PoSE (posterior sampling for state estimation), which keeps the Bayesian structure of DSSE and learns only what the distribution system operator does not know, namely the distribution of substation injections, modelled by a neural network trained with flow matching on historical data. The power flow equations, grid topology and measurements enter only at sampling, through a noise-aware Kalman-type correction. The neural network therefore never approximates the power flow, but every posterior sample is a physically consistent operating point, and one trained prior serves any measurement set, noise level and topology. On the IEEE 33-bus feeder, PoSE lowers the probabilistic injection error (CRPS) by 6.7-7.5% against a full-covariance Gaussian prior in all 12 tested settings. It provides reliable uncertainty: the 90% intervals contain the true injection almost exactly as often as exact posterior samples would, whereas those of supervised estimators contain it in only 37-78% of cases. On the 240-bus unbalanced three-phase Iowa feeder, it gives the lowest injection, voltage and branch-current errors of all estimators. A fast variant matches this accuracy at 0.2-0.6s per snapshot and, without retraining, beats Gaussian priors and retrained supervised estimators on seven reconfigured topologies.
papers.summary: Distribution system state estimation (DSSE) on medium-voltage feeders depends on pseudo-measurements, which act as a Bayesian prior, but weighted least squares reduces that prior to a mean and variance, and supervised deep learning estimators are tied to one measurement setup. `PoSE` uses flow matching to learn only the distribution of substation power injections from historical data, then brings in power flow equations, topology, and measurements at sampling time through a noise-aware Kalman-type correction, so every posterior sample is physically consistent. On the `IEEE 33-bus` feeder it lowers the probabilistic error (CRPS) by 6.7–7.5% against a Gaussian prior, and **its 90% intervals achieve near-exact coverage, whereas supervised estimators' intervals cover the true value only 37–78% of the time**. On the 240-bus Iowa feeder it gives the lowest errors of all estimators, and a fast variant handles reconfigured topologies without retraining.

papers.title: Don't Just Impute, Detect: Task-Aware Diffusion Pipelines for Edge Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) edge pipelines routinely lose contiguous blocks of multi-sensor data to network dropouts and hardware faults. The standard remedy is a disjointed "impute-then-detect" pipeline whose imputer is trained only for Mean Squared Error (MSE). Such an imputer fills a missing block with the most probable normal pattern: a partially observed anomaly is smoothed back toward normality, and boundary artifacts on normal data raise false alarms. We call this imputation bias and propose the Task-Aware Diffusion Refiner (TADR), a conditional diffusion refiner trained against the loss landscape of a frozen downstream detector. Because back-propagating through the sampling trajectory is intractable, the task-aware terms act on the one-step clean-window estimate that the noise prediction already yields, so training costs no more than plain diffusion training. Under strict Point-to-Point evaluation over five seeds with paired significance tests, TADR raises F1 by $0.338$ over the unrefined detector on SMD ($p = 0.0015$), and the anomaly enhancement objective alone contributes $0.463$ in ablation. We also characterise when the method helps: the gain tracks the continuous, mutually redundant channels available and the anomaly evidence the outage removes, and it is absent on telemetry datasets dominated by one-hot command channels and on PSM. At ten sampling steps TADR runs in $41.4$ ms per window on a single CPU core, sustaining about $24$ concurrent 1 Hz streams from a $4.03$ MB model. Code and per-seed results are available at https://github.com/int-park422/TADR.
papers.summary: Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) edge pipelines often lose contiguous blocks of sensor data, and the usual fix fills the gap with an imputer trained only for Mean Squared Error (MSE) before running anomaly detection. That imputer tends to smooth partially observed anomalies back toward normal and adds boundary artifacts that trigger false alarms. The proposed `Task-Aware Diffusion Refiner` (`TADR`) is a conditional diffusion model trained against the loss of a frozen downstream detector, applying task-aware terms to the one-step clean estimate so that training costs no more than ordinary diffusion training. On `SMD` it raises F1 by **0.338** over the unrefined detector, with no gain on `PSM` or on datasets dominated by one-hot command channels, and it runs in 41.4 ms per window on a single CPU core with a 4.03 MB model.

papers.title: Model-Agnostic Search for New Physics in the Presence of Imperfect Background by Smearing the Data
papers.abstract: In the search for new particles in high-energy physics, it is necessary to first define the signal region (SR) enriched in signal events, and then compare events in this region with the expected background distribution. While most existing search methods rely on prior domain knowledge of either the signal or the background, there has been less effort to relax both assumptions simultaneously, as methods that weaken one assumption typically rely on strong knowledge of the other. We propose Model-Agnostic Search with Smearing and Imperfect Background (MASSIB), a method that addresses this challenge by learning the density ratio of events relative to a misspecified background distribution using modern tools from machine learning, and defining the SR as the region with high density ratio. Recognizing that a naive application of this idea introduces significant bias in background estimation when interpolating from the control region to the SR, MASSIB mitigates this issue by introducing a "smeared" density ratio, which can be learned efficiently through data-level manipulation and used to define an SR that allows for accurate background estimation. By applying it to various types of simulated Large Hadron Collider (LHC) events with realistic background mismodeling, we demonstrate that MASSIB identifies a data-driven SR that achieves high signal concentration consistently across different types of signals while avoiding bias in background estimation. The method does this without making strong assumptions about either the signal or background distribution. We then show that this robustness extends to the validity and strong statistical power of the resulting hypothesis tests for signal detection, demonstrating the potential of this approach for future model-agnostic searches at the LHC.
papers.summary: Searches for new particles usually depend on prior knowledge of either the signal or the background, and methods that relax one assumption tend to lean heavily on the other. `MASSIB` (Model-Agnostic Search with Smearing and Imperfect Background) learns the density ratio of observed events relative to a misspecified background model and defines the signal region where that ratio is high. Because a naive version biases background estimation when interpolating from the control region, the method learns a "smeared" density ratio through data-level manipulation. On simulated Large Hadron Collider (LHC) events with realistic background mismodeling, it **finds signal-rich regions across several signal types without biasing the background estimate**, and the resulting hypothesis tests remain valid with strong statistical power.

papers.title: RiskyPy: Toward Model-Calibrated Prompt Generation for Joint Security and Functionality Evaluation of LLM-Generated Code
papers.abstract: Evaluating approaches that improve the security of LLM code generation requires datasets that jointly assess security and functionality and remain adapted to the capabilities of the models being studied. However, existing benchmarks are costly to produce and are generally not calibrated to a chosen range of model capabilities. We introduce RiskyPy, an automated pipeline that generates security-oriented code-generation datasets calibrated to model proficiency using functionality and vulnerability canaries. We instantiate RiskyPy for Python using domains covering 18 CWEs from the 2025 CWE Top 25, producing 101 prompts. Experiments on Qwen3-4B and Seed-Coder-8B show that the generated tasks remain functionally accessible, with 57-72% of prompts yielding functional code, while only 5-10% of generations are free of Bandit findings, leaving room for joint evaluation of security and functionality of security improvement approaches.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for the security of LLM-generated code are expensive to build and rarely matched to the capability of the models under study. `RiskyPy` is an automated pipeline that generates security-oriented coding prompts calibrated to model proficiency, using functionality and vulnerability canaries. A Python instance covering 18 weaknesses from the 2025 CWE Top 25 yields 101 prompts. On `Qwen3-4B` and `Seed-Coder-8B`, 57-72% of prompts produce functional code but **only 5-10% of generations are free of `Bandit` findings**, which leaves room to measure security and functionality together.

papers.title: Unsupervised Feature Selection Using Local Intrinsic Dimensionality -- Extended Version
papers.abstract: High dimensionality degrades both the efficiency and the effectiveness of learning algorithms, and in many applications no class labels are available to guide dimensionality reduction. This paper proposes LIDFS, an unsupervised feature selection method based on Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID). The method builds on the formal equivalence between LID and the indiscriminability of distance measures. The data matrix is transposed so that each feature is treated as a point, and the LID of each feature is estimated by maximum likelihood from the distances to its $k$ nearest neighboring features. Features with lower LID exhibit greater local discriminability and receive higher importance scores. A refinement step then retains one representative per feature neighborhood and demotes locally redundant features. The result is a complete ranking from which any number of features can be selected without rerunning the procedure. LIDFS does not use any information about labels or the number of classes, and runs in $\mathcal{O}(d^2 n)$ time for $n$ instances and $d$ features. LIDFS is compared with classic and state-of-the-art methods and a random baseline on 23 high-dimensional datasets, the classic benchmark collection. The evaluation uses classification accuracy and AUC with five downstream classifiers, as well as clustering accuracy and normalized mutual information, over both full and aggressive selection ranges. LIDFS ranks first in the supervised evaluations and first or tied second in the clustering-based evaluations. It belongs to the top statistical group together with methods that require the number of classes, and it runs faster than its closest competitor. Several recent methods, by contrast, fail to outperform the random baseline. A sensitivity analysis shows that small neighborhood sizes yield the best results.
papers.summary: `LIDFS` is an unsupervised feature selection method built on Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID). It transposes the data matrix so that each feature becomes a point, estimates each feature's LID by maximum likelihood from its k nearest neighboring features, scores lower-LID features as more discriminative, and then demotes locally redundant features. The method uses no label information, runs in O(d²n) time, and produces a full ranking. On 23 high-dimensional benchmark datasets, **it ranks first in the supervised evaluations** and first or tied second in the clustering evaluations, while several recent methods fail to beat a random baseline.

papers.title: Apriel Voice 27B Preview: An Open Model for Speech, Reasoning, and Tool Use
papers.abstract: A capable voice assistant must do more than recognize words; it must understand requests, reason over context, sustain conversations, and act through tools. We present Apriel Voice 27B Preview, an open speech-language model that unifies these capabilities within a shared reasoning backbone while retaining text and image input modalities. Built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint, Apriel Voice directly processes speech and generates both responses and tool calls without requiring a separate dialogue model. We introduce a two-stage training procedure to adapt the model to speech. The first stage establishes the speech interface, while the second jointly adapts the projector and backbone through supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and source-dependent cross-entropy and forward Kullback--Leibler divergence supervision. Automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues provide conversational training data, while local teacher serving, overlapping teacher and student computation, and fused full-vocabulary losses enable efficient online distillation. In thinking mode, Apriel Voice achieves a score of 98.90 on Big Bench Audio, 81.13 on Speech-BFCL, and a task success rate of 65.51% on $\tau$-Voice, with a mean latency of 1.91 seconds. It also achieves 51.27% English EVA accuracy and 74.13% experience pass@1. Finally, we deploy Apriel Voice 27B Preview on a custom serving platform to support interactive voice interactions.
papers.summary: `Apriel Voice 27B Preview` is an open speech-language model built on the `Gemma 4 26B-A4B` checkpoint. It processes speech directly and produces responses and tool calls without a separate dialogue model, while keeping text and image inputs. Training runs in two stages: the first establishes the speech interface, and the second jointly adapts the projector and backbone using supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and online distillation with forward Kullback-Leibler divergence, supported by automatically constructed speech dialogues and efficient teacher serving. In thinking mode it scores 98.90 on `Big Bench Audio`, 81.13 on `Speech-BFCL`, and **a 65.51% task success rate on `τ-Voice` at a mean latency of 1.91 seconds**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Voice assistants need to reason, hold a conversation, and call tools, not just transcribe speech. `Apriel Voice 27B Preview` adds a speech interface to the post-trained `Gemma 4 26B-A4B` mixture-of-experts model, so one backbone handles speech, text, and images and produces both replies and tool calls without a separate dialogue model.

- A frozen `Whisper large-v3-turbo` encoder feeds a projector of about 47.7M parameters (8-frame stacking plus a SwiGLU MLP); stage one trains only the projector on 18.17M transcription, translation, and continuation examples, and stage two also updates the backbone and its expert router.
- Stage two mixes supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and synthetic dialogues where user turns are voiced with TTS voice cloning; each data source gets its own blend of cross-entropy and full-vocabulary forward-KL distillation from a frozen copy of `Gemma`, and the run took about **3 days on 64 H100s**.
- In thinking mode the model scores **98.90 on `Big Bench Audio`** and **81.13 on `BFCL`**, with an **85.84 speech-reasoning average**, the best of the open two-stage models (speech fed straight into the language model rather than through a separate ASR step), but behind `Gemini 3.8` (90.75) and slightly behind a `Parakeet` + `Gemma4-26B` speech-recognition cascade (86.63).
- On agentic voice benchmarks it reaches **65.51% task success on `τ-Voice` at 1.91 s latency**, against 67.78% at 3.01 s for the cascade, and scores **51.27% `EVA-A` (accuracy) / 74.13% `EVA-X` (experience)**, the highest `EVA-X` among the systems compared.
- Text ability mostly holds (`MMLU-Pro` 85.27 → 84.42, `GPQA Diamond` 77.80 → 80.40), but non-thinking `τ²` drops **4.09 points**, six of nine image benchmarks score slightly lower, and `EVA` faithfulness is only **43.49%** compared with 66.33% for the cascade.

papers.title: Certified Behavioral Retention for Continual Adaptation with Held-Out Anchors
papers.abstract: Continual adaptation requires deciding not only how to update a model, but whether to commit an update without exceeding a declared budget for changes to protected behavior. We introduce Certified Anchor-Based Adaptation (CABA), a candidate-agnostic post-update gate that reserves historical observations from candidate optimization, compares old and candidate policies on frozen representations, and selects the largest tested interpolation coefficient whose worst-anchor forward KL divergence remains within budget. The finite check requires neither action labels nor complete trajectories. We develop a theory-led certification framework that separates measured anchor retention from conditional off-anchor guarantees. Under explicit representation-coverage and Lipschitz assumptions, an accepted update satisfies a uniform behavioral-divergence bound on protected support. The analysis gives regularity bounds for affine softmax heads, probabilistic coverage and compression guarantees, interpolation monotonicity conditions, grid-resolution bounds, and trajectory-level and sequential-composition guarantees. In a controlled UCI Human Activity Recognition study used as a non-stationary sensor-policy proxy, CABA reduces mean forgetting from 1.01 percent for unconstrained adaptation to 0.00 percent at budget epsilon = 0.05, while reducing final average accuracy from 93.04 percent to 88.48 percent. The experiment illustrates a retention-plasticity trade-off and does not establish foundation-model or robotic performance. CABA provides an auditable retention check for candidate generators exposing comparable policy distributions and a declared update path, while deployment also requires separate evidence of current-task utility.
papers.summary: Continual adaptation has to decide whether to commit a model update without exceeding a declared budget for changes to protected behavior. `Certified Anchor-Based Adaptation` (`CABA`) is a post-update gate that holds out historical observations as anchors and picks the largest tested interpolation between the old and candidate policies whose worst-anchor forward KL divergence stays within budget. The gate needs neither action labels nor full trajectories. Under coverage and Lipschitz assumptions, the theory gives behavioral-divergence bounds on protected support. On a `UCI Human Activity Recognition` proxy, **forgetting drops from 1.01% to 0.00%**, but final accuracy also falls from 93.04% to 88.48%, a retention-plasticity trade-off.

papers.title: Prevented is Not Protected: What Attack Success Rate Hides about RAG
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is vulnerable to knowledge poisoning, where adversaries manipulate retrieved evidence to influence model outputs. Existing defenses are primarily evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which obscures defense-induced failures and the mechanisms behind apparent attack prevention. To address this issue, this work introduces \textbf{Aligned RAG Evaluation}, a matched-query protocol that jointly examines clean and poisoned responses, with and without defense. By combining matched conditions analysis, LLM-judge endorsement, and retrieval dependence controls, the proposed framework distinguishes prevented from introduced failures, target mentions from LLM endorsement, and single-passage influence from evidence composition. Experiments on HotpotQA and Natural Questions reveal that existing defenses can introduce unexpected target-positive answers, although they can prevent some attacks, while evaluation criteria can also change defense rankings. Our findings expose critical blind spots in ASR-based evaluation and motivate a more comprehensive assessment of RAG poisoning defenses. The code and the evaluation artifact are available at https://github.com/chxhana/aligned-rag-eval.
papers.summary: Defenses against knowledge poisoning in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) are mostly judged by attack success rate (ASR), which hides failures that the defenses themselves cause. `Aligned RAG Evaluation` is a matched-query protocol that compares clean and poisoned responses with and without a defense, adding LLM-judge endorsement checks and retrieval-dependence controls. On `HotpotQA` and `Natural Questions`, **existing defenses prevent some attacks but also introduce new target-positive answers**, and changing the evaluation criteria can reorder the defense rankings.

papers.title: CLIC: Closed-Loop Intent Consistency for Securing LLM-Driven Control in Open RAN
papers.abstract: With the progressive capabilities of large language models (LLMs), researchers are finding ways to integrate them into the control loops of Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) to enable slicing and resource management through user intents. However, integration of LLMs in the O-RAN control loop via the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) makes the system vulnerable to \textit{runtime prompt injection threats}, which manipulate control decisions without violating interface authentication, and \textit{residual virtual prompt injection (VPI)} attacks that plant trigger mechanisms to silently steer the behaviour during fine-tuning. Existing studies address only the runtime threat and do not enforce consistency across the full control path, i.e. from the certified A1 intent, through the multi-step LLM trajectory, to the final E2 action. We propose a closed-loop intent-consistency layer (CLIC) that jointly mitigates both threats. The proposed CLIC defines a formal consistency score using a small quantized language model, which is deployed as a Non-RT rApp for model-integrity certification along with a Near-RT xApp for runtime enforcement. We implement CLIC on the OpenAI Cellular (OAIC) platform and evaluate it under domain-adapted JailbreakBench, AdvBench, and VPI workloads. The experimental results show that the proposed CLIC reduces the attack success rate from 0.92 to 0.29 and residual VPI attacks from 0.37 to 0.04, while improving isolation and fairness at slightly higher latency costs, i.e. approximately 27 ms.
papers.summary: Putting LLMs in the control loop of Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) systems exposes them to runtime prompt injection and to residual virtual prompt injection (VPI) backdoors planted during fine-tuning. `CLIC` is a closed-loop intent-consistency layer that uses a small quantized language model to compute a formal consistency score across the full path from the certified A1 intent, through the LLM's multi-step trajectory, to the final E2 action. It is deployed as a Non-RT rApp for model-integrity certification and a Near-RT xApp for runtime enforcement. On the `OAIC` platform with domain-adapted `JailbreakBench`, `AdvBench`, and VPI workloads, **attack success falls from 0.92 to 0.29** and residual VPI attacks from 0.37 to 0.04, at about 27 ms of added latency.

papers.title: Mage-VL-Cowork: A Full Training Recipe to Learn Hybrid Computer Use From Evolved Harnesses
papers.abstract: Effective computer-use agents (CUAs) should seamlessly combine visual GUI interaction with code and terminal execution within a single policy. We present Mage-VL-Cowork, a 4B hybrid CUA trained from a general multimodally aligned checkpoint through an end-to-end, progressive five-stage curriculum across midtraining, SFT, and RL. To power this curriculum at scale, Mage-CUA-Forge replaces per-task agent construction with reusable, skill-conditioned generation workflows and application-specific preparers, synthesizing 293,806 desktop and web tasks across 6,915 skills while reducing recurring per-task expenditure by 82.6%. Rather than directly distilling a default teacher, we evolve the teacher harness and instantiate specialized CUA harnesses to yield high-quality trajectories alongside stage-specific supervision. Mage-VL-Cowork-4B finally climbs to 66.0% on OSWorld-Verified through different training stages with more efficient reasoning cost, achieving state-of-the-art performance at its parameter size and pushing forward the frontier of on-device intelligence.
papers.summary: Computer-use agents (CUAs) should combine GUI interaction with code and terminal execution in a single policy. `Mage-VL-Cowork` is a 4B hybrid CUA trained from a multimodal checkpoint through a five-stage curriculum covering midtraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. Its data comes from `Mage-CUA-Forge`, which synthesizes 293,806 desktop and web tasks across 6,915 skills using reusable skill-conditioned workflows and cuts recurring per-task cost by 82.6%; trajectories come from evolved, specialized teacher harnesses rather than plain distillation. The model reaches **66.0% on `OSWorld-Verified`**, which the authors report as state of the art for its size.

papers.title: Combinatorial Residual Network: a decay-chain-aware classifier without explicit jet assignment
papers.abstract: Final states with several jets from the decays of heavy particles pose a combinatorial problem, since the jets must be assigned, at least implicitly, to their parent particles. We describe the Combinatorial Residual Network (CoReNet), a classifier that encodes the assumed decay chain of the final state in its architecture. CoReNet builds its event representation level by level along the decay hierarchy, evaluates every jet assignment hypothesis with weights shared across objects, and combines the hypotheses with learned weights using residual networks. The exchange symmetries of the decay are built into the construction, the size of the network does not depend on the number of hypotheses, and the network is trained with the classification loss alone, without generator-level jet assignments. The architecture was developed for the $b\bar{b}b\bar{b}$ final state and has been used in several CMS searches. On fast-simulation samples of Higgs boson pair production in the $b\bar{b}b\bar{b}$ final state against QCD multijet production, CoReNet with 1508 trainable parameters performs well above kinematic baselines and trains in minutes on a single GPU. Its hypothesis weights select the truth-matched jet pairing in most of the signal events in which it is defined, although no assignment target is used in training. Since only the encoded decay chain is specific to the final state, the construction carries over to other topologies, which we test with $HH \to b\bar{b}W^+W^-$ against semileptonic $t\bar{t}$. There, encoding the decay chain of the background as well as that of the signal further improves the classification, at a cost of about $10^3$ parameters. In both final states its performance is comparable to that of a state-of-the-art transformer-based network more than two orders of magnitude larger. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/cms-cmu/CoReNet.
papers.summary: Final states with several jets from heavy-particle decays force a classifier to assign jets to parent particles, at least implicitly. `CoReNet` (Combinatorial Residual Network) encodes the assumed decay chain in its architecture: it evaluates every jet-assignment hypothesis with shared weights and combines them with learned weights through residual networks, training on the classification loss alone. On Higgs boson pair production in the bbbb final state, a **1,508-parameter model performs comparably to a transformer more than two orders of magnitude larger** and recovers the true jet pairing in most signal events without any assignment target. The construction also carries over to the HH→bbWW final state, where encoding the background's decay chain improves results further.

papers.title: Safin-1.5: Safety-Native Architecture and Verifiable Reasoning for Recursive Safety Improvement
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) enables large language models to advance their capabilities through successive updates, but these updates can also introduce new risks and weaken existing safeguards. In line with the AI-45{\deg} Law, we pursue Safety RSI, in which safety develops as an intrinsic capability alongside general model capabilities through continual risk discovery and repair, while preserving utility and limiting over-refusal. We introduce Safin-1.5, a model built on a safety architecture and trained through recursive safety improvement, with an inference-time harness that extends its capabilities to formal reasoning. Our approach comprises three components: i) The safety architecture combines persistent safety states with hazardous-knowledge disentanglement. The former retains and selectively invokes safety knowledge, while the latter relocates targeted hazardous knowledge into removable experts, enabling its removal with minimal impact on general capabilities. ii) Recursive safety improvement establishes a discovery-evaluation-repair loop. The loop identifies new vulnerabilities and uses experimental feedback to develop repair strategies. It accepts updates only when they improve safety while preserving general capabilities and limiting over-refusal. iii) The formal reasoning harness combines the model's language understanding with symbolic inference and verification. Proof-obligation-guided semantic bridging recovers missing relations in formal representations, enabling symbolic solvers to construct checkable proofs under formalized premises and accepted semantic bridges. Experimental results demonstrate that Safin-1.5 achieves safety and reasoning performance, outperforming frontier models.
papers.summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) in language models can weaken safeguards with each update, so `Safin-1.5` aims to make safety improve alongside capability. Its architecture keeps persistent safety states and moves targeted hazardous knowledge into removable experts. A discovery-evaluation-repair loop accepts an update only if it improves safety while preserving general capability and limiting over-refusal. An inference-time harness pairs the model with symbolic solvers, using proof-obligation-guided semantic bridging to produce checkable proofs. The authors claim **it outperforms frontier models on safety and reasoning**, though the abstract gives no specific numbers.

papers.title: "Shall We Approve?" Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents increasingly rely on automated approvers to decide whether a proposed shell command may run. Existing approvers, from rule-based checkers to guardrail models and deployed permission classifiers, base their decisions on the text of the request and command. Yet a command's behavior depends on the code it invokes and the state of the workspace, and systems that observe file changes leave the assessment to the agent or a human after execution. We present Caper, a consequence-aware approval mechanism that pre-executes each command in a snapshotted sandbox, provides an independent approver with a bounded report of its observed effects, commits allowed commands, and rolls back blocked ones with a reason the agent can act on. Compared with six existing systems, Caper achieves the lowest harmful-outcome rate on SABER (6.7% versus at least 14.8%) and YoloFS-Ext, a benchmark we build in which harmful behavior is hidden inside invoked tools (7.8% versus at least 35.3%), while blocking 1.0% of the safe twins of the dangerous tasks in YoloFS-Ext.
papers.summary: Coding agents rely on automated approvers to decide whether a shell command may run, but current approvers judge only the text of the command, even though its real effect depends on the code it invokes and the state of the workspace. `Caper` pre-executes each command in a snapshotted sandbox and gives an independent approver a bounded report of the observed effects. Allowed commands are committed, and blocked ones are rolled back with a reason the agent can act on. Compared with six existing systems, it has the lowest harmful-outcome rate on `SABER` (6.7% versus at least 14.8%) and on the new `YoloFS-Ext` benchmark, where harm is hidden inside invoked tools (**7.8% versus at least 35.3%**), while blocking only 1.0% of safe twin tasks.

papers.title: AutoHebb: Self-Modifying Neural Networks that Zero-Shot Infer and Continually Learn
papers.abstract: Humans and animals have a unique capacity to generalize and learn in novel circumstances, including "0-shot" inference (ZI) and continual learning (CL) -- two powerful cognitive abilities. Despite this importance, efforts to model ZI and CL are seriously limited in several ways. First, existing models typically lack components critical to ZI and CL in the brain, namely, strong inductive biases (for ZI) and autonomous control of learning (for CL). Second, models can be less tractable to analysis if model components are overly complex (lacking simplicity), or too task-restricted if model components are overly bespoke (lacking expressivity). Here we introduce autonomous Hebbian networks ("AutoHebb"), a class of online learning feedforward neural networks that realize strong inductive biases and autonomously controlled learning, and are both simple and expressive. Unlike standard models that learn via externally controlled optimization (e.g. gradient descent), AutoHebb networks combine external feedback with internally generated activity to produce a global learning signal ('neuromodulator') fed back to the network. The neuromodulator in turn gates a biologically grounded local learning rule (3-factor Hebbian rule) that updates networks' plastic weights. Using meta-learning to search for fixed (non-plastic) weights, we find that AutoHebb networks (1) succeed on ZI tasks, (2) show emergent (untrained) ZI/CL abilities, (3) admit reverse-engineering into explicit algorithms, and (4) outperform modern learning models on ZI/CL tasks. Lastly, performance comparisons to related models implied an essential role for three model components: meta-learning, Hebbian plasticity, and autonomous control of learning. These findings indicate that AutoHebb may be useful in hypothesis generation, analysis, and discovery of biologically grounded forms of learning and generalization.
papers.summary: Models of zero-shot inference and continual learning usually lack two things the brain appears to rely on: strong inductive biases and autonomous control over when learning happens. `AutoHebb` networks are online feedforward networks that combine external feedback with internally generated activity into a global neuromodulator signal, which gates a local three-factor Hebbian learning rule on their plastic weights. The fixed weights are found by meta-learning. The resulting networks succeed on zero-shot tasks, show untrained continual-learning abilities, can be reverse-engineered into explicit algorithms, and **outperform modern learning models on zero-shot and continual-learning tasks**.

papers.title: More Rules, Longer Lists? Benchmarking Self-Evolving Agents on a Hidden-Rule Curriculum
papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents rewrite a persistent state from feedback, but it is largely untested whether this lets them learn a rule nobody told them. An agent can also pass by writing down each correction as an exception, and its list then grows with every new rule. We introduce CLR-Bench, a Curriculum of Latent Rules benchmark. Each chain adds one hidden rule per level on top of the earlier ones. A rule acts on an opaque label that stands for a named grouping published on the Web, such as the founding members of an airline alliance. The task gives one example value, practice feedback reveals one more member and one non-member, and the test checks unseen members and similar non-members. Probes certify that the base model knows the members of each grouping and does not guess it without feedback, and that the evidence identifies the grouping once labels are read as named groupings. An automated pipeline builds chains from a new data domain, and we release 20 chains over 10 domains. We evaluate six recent self-evolution methods. With the certifying model they barely learn. The best gain at most 5 points over a frozen agent and exclude only 6-12% of the unseen members from the count, fewer than the 20% reached by simply keeping the raw practice history. A fixed lesson that states the named-grouping convention lifts the same methods by 14.5 to 16.5 points. Their states hold the revealed member in 75-98% of cases and almost never the class name, and when practice exposes a member the list misses, they add that member to the list. With the stronger GPT-6-Sol, ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet learn from feedback alone. They reach 78% accuracy and solve 59-60% of the single cells, against 53% and 8% with the certifying model, and they surpass the raw history. CLR-Bench therefore measures how well an agent learns, and this ability differs across models.
papers.summary: `CLR-Bench` (Curriculum of Latent Rules) tests whether self-evolving agents can learn a hidden rule from feedback rather than just recording each correction as an exception.
