We develop a degree-resolved version of this nonlinear interaction picture and use the resulting block inventory to construct Specht Triple, a residual on unordered graph triples. On a synthetic structural benchmark with a frozen GIN backbone, Specht Triple reduces aggregate standardised test MSE by 11.05% relative to a parameter-matched Projector Control using the same irreducible projectors and complete linear equivariant space. The results support irreducible decomposition as an inductive bias for nonlinear higher-order equivariant processing.
papers.summary: Equivariant linear maps cannot mix non-isomorphic irreducible representations, but nonlinear activations can. The authors work out a degree-resolved version of this nonlinear interaction and use it to build `Specht Triple`, a residual module that operates on unordered triples of graph nodes. On a synthetic structural benchmark with a frozen `GIN` backbone, it **reduces standardized test MSE by 11.05%** compared with a parameter-matched control that uses the same projectors and linear equivariant space. The authors present this as evidence that irreducible decomposition is a useful inductive bias for nonlinear higher-order equivariant processing.

papers.title: Single-Annotation, Multi-Hypothesis Segmentation with Semantic-Spatial Residual Banks
papers.abstract: Multi-rater segmentation datasets show that a single image can admit several valid masks, yet most training sets expose only one annotation per image. We study single-annotation multi-hypothesis segmentation: each training image exposes one fixed mask, while the model must return a finite bank that covers held-out human annotations at test time. Our experiments reveal a representation tradeoff. Banks learned directly from images recover variations in local boundaries and extent but lose structural hypotheses, whereas frozen semantic features preserve structural grouping but underrepresent spatial variation. We introduce the Semantic-Spatial Residual Bank (SSRB), which freezes a semantic bank trained with balanced assignments and learns a residual from the image for each hypothesis. Across five medical endpoints, SSRB improves coverage of held-out masks at $K=8$ over a Probabilistic U-Net under the same one-mask constraint. On LIDC and LIDC-hard, it also produces substantially more distinct useful masks. On BSDS, it preserves the semantic bank's performance in grouping regions. Its advantage grows as more masks are returned, showing that residuals learned for corresponding heads improve coverage of local annotation variation while preserving how regions are grouped.
papers.summary: Many images admit several valid segmentation masks, yet most training sets provide only one annotation per image. The authors study how to train a model on single annotations that still outputs a bank of masks covering the range of human annotations at test time, and find a trade-off: banks learned from images capture boundary variation but lose structural hypotheses, while frozen semantic features keep structure but underrepresent spatial variation. The Semantic-Spatial Residual Bank (`SSRB`) freezes a semantic bank and learns a per-hypothesis spatial residual from the image. With eight hypotheses, it **improves coverage of held-out masks over a `Probabilistic U-Net`** across five medical endpoints, produces more distinct useful masks on `LIDC`, and preserves region grouping on `BSDS`.

papers.title: D2ML: Models for Direct-to-Biology Small Molecule Screening
papers.abstract: Direct-to-biology (D2B) screening enables rapid testing of newly synthesized molecules without purification. However, uncertain concentrations in crude mixtures and limited purified-compound measurements complicate the use of these data in machine learning. Here we show that models tailored to the structure of D2B data can improve prediction and guide the discovery of more potent and selective compounds. Our assay-aware models predict activity from single-point screens, relative potency across targets from crude dose-response assays, and absolute potency from purified-compound measurements. For crude assays, potency ratios between targets tested from the same well can retain selectivity information despite uncertain concentrations. A joint model that shares information across stages and balances their contributions to training improved predictions over separate neural networks. The largest gain was in crude dose-response selectivity prediction, where rank correlation increased from 0.27 to 0.40. In a separate experiment, independently trained models guided the selection of 84 new compounds to improve ROS1 potency while limiting activity against the anti-target TRKB. Synthesis and testing identified compounds that extended the measured Pareto front, achieving better combinations of potency and selectivity than those in the training data. The most selective new compound achieved a ROS1 IC50 of 14.7 nM and 233-fold selectivity over TRKB. By comparison, the most selective training compound had a ROS1 IC50 of 20.3 nM and 79-fold selectivity. ATLAS provides the experimental setting for this approach, supporting synthesis and screening of 1,000-10,000 model-selected compounds in two- to three-week cycles. Together, these results show how assay-aware learning can use the full D2B assay sequence to guide multi-objective molecular optimization.
papers.summary: Direct-to-biology (D2B) screening tests newly synthesized molecules without purifying them first, so concentrations in the crude mixtures are uncertain and purified measurements are scarce, which makes the data hard to use for machine learning. The authors build assay-aware models that predict activity from single-point screens, relative potency across targets from crude dose-response assays, and absolute potency from purified compounds, and they combine these stages in a joint model. The joint model beats separate neural networks, most clearly on crude dose-response selectivity, where rank correlation rose from 0.27 to 0.40. In a prospective run, the models chose 84 new compounds, and the most selective one reached a ROS1 IC50 of 14.7 nM with **233-fold selectivity over TRKB**, compared with 79-fold for the best training compound.

papers.title: LanG 2.0: Energy-Efficient Agentic AI for Semi-Automated Security Operations at Scale
papers.abstract: Security operations centers (SOCs) need to turn terabytes of alerts, logs and flows into trusted, affordable decisions to unveil hidden threats. We present LanG 2.0, an agentic system that detects threats, correlates evidence and writes rules, investigating whether small local models can replace frontier models affordably and safely when structural safeguards, not model accuracy, provide the guarantees. It incorporates entity-anchored correlation, human approval of rule changes and a tamper-evident ledger. Tests span eight flow datasets from five networks, real XDR alerts and multistage campaigns. Against its predecessor, campaign correlation precision rises from 18.75% to 51.81%, and rule acceptance from at most 60.00% to 98.33%. Against Claude Opus 5.5, scoring flows against each network's normal traffic detects attacks on unseen networks at 73.42% F1 without false positives, versus 58.10% with 49.00% false positives, for at least 650 times less energy. Finetuned models statistically match it on alert classification and rule writing for 5.6 to 59 times less energy. The work demonstrates LanG's practical scalability, processing 3.33 million records in 6.4 minutes, over 30 million hourly, and its safeguards resisted prompt injection, label poisoning and ledger tampering, so small local models can carry most SOC detection affordably and safely.
papers.summary: `LanG 2.0` is an agentic system for security operations centers (SOCs) that detects threats, correlates evidence and writes detection rules. It tests whether small local models can replace frontier models when structural safeguards provide the guarantees instead of model accuracy; those safeguards are entity-anchored correlation, human approval of rule changes and a tamper-evident ledger. Scoring network flows against each network's normal traffic detects attacks on unseen networks at 73.42% F1 with no false positives, while `Claude Opus 5.5` reaches 58.10% F1 with 49.00% false positives, and LanG uses **at least 650 times less energy**. Fine-tuned small models statistically match the frontier model on alert classification and rule writing, the system processes 3.33 million records in 6.4 minutes, and its safeguards resisted prompt injection, label poisoning and ledger tampering.

papers.title: bf16 Rounding Silently Discards Most RL Policy Updates: A Hidden Training-Inference Mismatch and an Unbiased One-Line Fix
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of language models keeps fp32 master weights in the optimizer and serves rollouts from a bf16 copy produced by round-to-nearest conversion. At the learning rates in common use, most per-step updates are smaller than half a bf16 spacing and the conversion discards them: on Qwen3-1.7B only 0.4-0.5% of served weights change per step, and the policy that generates the training data lags the optimizer by 50-150 steps. Existing mismatch corrections cannot see this lag because they compare two copies downstream of the same rounding. We propose Fair Cast: export the master with an unbiased rounding rule (stochastic rounding or error feedback) and compute the training loss on the served copy. The change is one line at the export call, adds no hyperparameters and costs 22-38 ms per export of 1.7B parameters. Across 25 matched seed-pairs on Qwen3-0.6B to 4B with AdamW and Muon, Fair Cast is ahead on 18, tied on 6 and behind on 1, with a mean gain of 6.1 points; on zebra puzzles it reaches 0.57 +/- 0.16 over four runs where round-to-nearest collapses to 0.33 +/- 0.10. It also makes the saved fp32 checkpoint agree with the served model, and it exposes the implicit lag of round-to-nearest as a regularizer that can be restored explicitly when a task needs it.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of language models keeps fp32 master weights in the optimizer but generates rollouts from a bf16 copy made by round-to-nearest conversion. At common learning rates most per-step updates are too small to survive that conversion: on `Qwen3-1.7B` **only 0.4-0.5% of served weights change per step**, so the policy generating training data lags the optimizer by 50-150 steps. The proposed `Fair Cast` exports weights with unbiased rounding (stochastic rounding or error feedback) and computes the loss on the served copy, a one-line change with no new hyperparameters. Across 25 matched seed-pairs on `Qwen3` models from 0.6B to 4B, using `AdamW` and `Muon`, it wins 18, ties 6 and loses 1, with a mean gain of 6.1 points.
papers.highlight_summary:
RL post-training keeps fp32 master weights in the optimizer but serves rollouts from a bf16 copy made by round-to-nearest conversion, which silently drops any update smaller than half a bf16 grid step. As a result the sampler lags the optimizer by 50–150 steps, and existing trainer-versus-sampler mismatch checks cannot see it. `Fair Cast` fixes this by exporting with an unbiased rounding rule (stochastic rounding or error feedback) and computing the training loss on the exact served copy.

- On `Qwen3-1.7B` at a learning rate of 1e-6, only **0.4–0.5% of served weights change per step**: the ratio frameworks check stays near |log ρ| ≈ 0.01 per token, while the never-formed master-versus-served ratio grows to **0.10–0.45**.
- Stochastic rounding makes the served weight equal the master in expectation, and gradients reach the master through a straight-through estimator; both halves are required, since unbiased export without training on the served copy collapsed (error feedback hit 0.00 accuracy in 4 of 4 long runs). The fix adds no hyperparameters and costs **22–38 ms per 1.7B-parameter export**.
- Across 25 matched seed-pairs on `Qwen3-0.6B` to `4B` with `AdamW` and `Muon`, `Fair Cast` is ahead on **18**, tied on 6 and behind on 1, with a **mean gain of +6.1 points**; on zebra puzzles it reaches **0.57 ± 0.16 versus 0.33 ± 0.10**, and on knights-and-knaves under `Muon` it scores **0.988 versus 0.907**.
- Under round-to-nearest, the saved fp32 checkpoint can score **up to 50 points below its own served model** (on `HumanEval+`), and fp16 exports inherit this drift; under `Fair Cast` the master and the served copy agree within 3 points.
- Removing the lag also removes an implicit regularizer: on list functions `Fair Cast` drops to 0.523 against 0.668 for round-to-nearest unless an explicit EMA export is added (α = 0.05 gives **0.707**). The experiments also stop at 4B parameters, use a single training implementation and include many single-seed runs, where the standard error is about 3 points.

papers.title: Where, When, and How Many Bits? Scaling Laws for SGD with Stochastic Rounding
papers.abstract: Low-precision training reduces computation but introduces additional rounding error. We theoretically study how stochastic rounding (SR) affects prediction risk as model size, training time, and precision change. We consider a two-layer linear network with a fixed random first layer, trained by mini-batch SGD on fresh Gaussian data with power-law spectra. At each SGD step, the features used in forward and backward computations are rounded independently. We prove matched upper and lower bounds on prediction error for the final model and for uniform parameter averaging, with general learning-rate and precision schedules chosen before training. For fixed precisions and constant learning rates with parameter averaging, we derive how the smallest prediction error decreases with compute, and we identify model sizes and training times that achieve this optimal-compute scaling. Rounding only the forward features preserves the compute scaling of exact arithmetic, while rounding backward features changes it. Averaging parameters can change which computation needs higher precision and when higher precision is useful. Our results also give bit requirements for a given accuracy tolerance and show how backward rounding can change learning-rate schedule design. At a fixed compute budget, lower precision can improve prediction when the benefit of a larger model or longer training outweighs the additional SR-induced error. Model simulations illustrate these tradeoffs, and experiments with an MLP and a small transformer examine rounding choices beyond the theoretical model.
papers.summary: The authors study theoretically how stochastic rounding (SR) in low-precision training affects prediction error as model size, training time and precision vary. Using a two-layer linear network with a fixed random first layer, trained by mini-batch SGD on Gaussian data with power-law spectra, they prove matching upper and lower bounds on prediction error and derive compute-optimal scaling. A key result is that **rounding only the forward features preserves the compute scaling of exact arithmetic, while rounding backward features changes it**. The analysis also gives bit requirements for a target accuracy and shows that, at a fixed compute budget, lower precision can help when a larger model or longer training outweighs the added rounding error; experiments with an MLP and a small transformer go beyond the theoretical model.

papers.title: BABA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Patient-Advocacy Agents
papers.abstract: An LLM agent that helps a patient get care must do two things. It must reach the correct outcome, and it must follow the necessary procedure. For example, the agent must get the patient's permission before it shares the patient's records. We introduce BABA-Bench, a benchmark of 47 interactive worlds. We built each world from a de-identified, real patient advocacy case that expert advocates reviewed. In each world, the agent must find hidden information and coordinate insurers, clinics, suppliers, pharmacies, and community organizations. The engine checks each action at the time the agent does it. It checks if the agent has permission, if the agent has evidence for the action, and if the action is prohibited. We evaluated 14 frontier models with three runs on each world, for a total of 1,974 runs. Agents often reached the correct outcome by an invalid route. Of the 921 runs that reached all required outcomes, 254 (28%) did not follow the necessary procedure. Claude Opus 5 reached all required outcomes in 81.6% of its runs, but only 52.5% of its runs passed all checks. When we gave two models a verified route, their pass rates increased from 29.8% to 91.5% and from 44.0% to 97.2%. For these models, the main problem is to find a route, not to execute it.
papers.summary: `BABA-Bench` evaluates LLM agents that advocate for patients. It consists of 47 interactive worlds built from de-identified real advocacy cases, in which agents must uncover hidden information and coordinate insurers, clinics, pharmacies and other organizations. The engine checks every action as it happens: whether the agent has permission, whether it has evidence for the action, and whether the action is prohibited. Across 14 frontier models and 1,974 runs, agents often reached the right outcome by an invalid route: **28% of runs that achieved all required outcomes broke procedure**, and `Claude Opus 5` achieved all outcomes in 81.6% of runs but passed all checks in only 52.5%. When two models were given a verified route, their pass rates jumped to 91.5% and 97.2%, which suggests the main difficulty is finding the route rather than executing it.

papers.title: EDU-Jev Training System-One Decision Models for Education
papers.abstract: Many automated decisions in education involve choosing from a fixed set of options: assigning a rubric score, checking whether an answer meets a marking criterion, or identifying the first wrong step in a solution. Generative language models are increasingly used to make these decisions, but their responses require parsing, longer outputs increase inference costs, and confidence expressed in words does not necessarily reflect the probability of being correct. We present EDU-Jev, a family of single-pass ("System One") decision models at 0.8B, 2B and 4B parameters. Given an assessment context and a question with predefined answer options, the model returns a probability distribution over those options without generating text. A pointer head scores a marker for each option, ensuring the predictions are restricted to the allowed choices. Training uses a single supervised stage with soft cross-entropy against the available target label distributions; calibration is assessed empirically. Across twelve education benchmarks, EDU-Jev 4B achieves an average accuracy of 67.6%, exceeding the strongest of five commercial decision APIs by 9.4 percentage points and the best open 4B decision model by 18.7 points. On four cross-domain education sets, it matches the strongest API, which remains ahead on general decision-making and reasoning tasks. The 2B model processes about 150 decisions per second on a single H100 GPU.
papers.summary: Many automated decisions in education, such as assigning a rubric score or finding the first wrong step in a solution, mean choosing from a fixed set of options. Generative models handle these poorly: their outputs need parsing, longer outputs cost more, and confidence stated in words is not well calibrated. `EDU-Jev` is a family of single-pass decision models at 0.8B, 2B and 4B parameters that use a pointer head to return a probability distribution over the allowed options without generating text, and it is trained with soft cross-entropy against target label distributions. Across twelve education benchmarks, `EDU-Jev 4B` averages 67.6% accuracy, **9.4 points above the best of five commercial decision APIs**, and the 2B model handles about 150 decisions per second on one H100 GPU.

papers.title: Optimization Techniques for Solving the Minimum Red--Blue Separating Set Problem with an Application to Human--AI Text Separation
papers.abstract: We study the so-called Minimum Red''Blue Separating Set Problem (MRBSSP) which arises from computational geometry. In particular, we propose a compact Set-Cover ILP formulation, safe preprocessing rules, a Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedure (GRASP), and two exact approaches: one is based on Logic-Based Benders Decomposition (LBBD) approach, and the second represents a novel Branch-and-Benders-Cut (BBC) approach. These two exact approaches are compared to ILP--alongside GRASP and the Variable Neighborhood Search (VNS) from literature. Experiments on 250 random graphs with up to 500 vertices reveal complementary strengths: ILP yields the best feasible solutions, LBBD provides the strongest lower bounds and smallest mean optimality gap, and BBC certifies optimality most frequently. We further introduce an NLP application distinguishing human- and AI-generated texts through vocabulary-based graph features. On 42 instances, BBC achieves the smallest mean optimality gap, certifying 16 optima, while GRASP outperforms VNS. Structural analysis of optimal vocabulary separators identifies 113 mandatory and 151 replaceable features across 272 tests, highlighting substantial variability among optimal solutions. Overall, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of complementary optimization strategies and the interpretability of optimal vocabulary-based discrimination.
papers.summary: The work tackles the Minimum Red-Blue Separating Set Problem (MRBSSP) from computational geometry. It proposes a compact set-cover ILP formulation, preprocessing rules, a GRASP heuristic, and two exact methods based on `Logic-Based Benders Decomposition` (LBBD) and a new `Branch-and-Benders-Cut` (BBC). On 250 random graphs the methods have complementary strengths: ILP finds the best feasible solutions, LBBD gives the strongest lower bounds, and **BBC certifies optimality most often**. In an application that separates human-written from AI-generated text using vocabulary-based graph features, BBC certifies 16 optima across 42 instances, and analysis of the optimal separators shows substantial variability among them.

papers.title: Payroll Fraud Detection in Synthetic HR/ERP Graphs: An Inductive Comparison of Rules, Path Features, and Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Payroll-fraud screening requires finding hidden employee--payee links while distinguishing suspicious relationships from legitimate ones. We formulate this problem as inductive link prediction and entity ranking on synthetic human-resources and enterprise resource planning (HR/ERP) graphs, with unseen organizations and a matched benign twin for every planted case. An original study on 24 held-out organizations and a prospectively frozen extension compare analyst rules, explicit path features and graph neural networks (GNNs). A tuned gradient-boosted model on chained-join features achieved the highest overall link average precision (AP; 0.823), above the GraIL-style GNN (0.663); its 4-hop AP was 0.646 versus 0.272. Thus, the observed multi-hop gain is not specific to GNNs. On a new synthetic cohort with 2.0% positive entities, chained-join boosting again led (AP 0.798); the relational entity GNN also exceeded record-aware rules (0.707 versus 0.504). At a 2% review budget, their precision was 0.695 versus 0.602. Under 40% failed identifier joins, the entity GNN ranked above chained-join boosting (AP 0.712 versus 0.683, descriptively). Structure-only auditing exposed a shortcut in the initial generator; matched twins reduced the audited twin-pool AUROC to 0.493--0.514. These results separate multi-hop candidate discovery, record-based discrimination and review prioritization within an explicit synthetic evaluation design. Code and data are available from the authors on request.
papers.summary: Payroll-fraud screening is framed as inductive link prediction and entity ranking on synthetic human-resources and enterprise resource planning (HR/ERP) graphs, with held-out organizations and a matched benign twin for every planted fraud case. Rules written by analysts, explicit path features and graph neural networks (GNNs) are compared. A tuned gradient-boosted model on chained-join features achieved the best link average precision, **0.823 versus 0.663 for a `GraIL`-style GNN**, which shows that the gain from multi-hop reasoning is not specific to GNNs. A relational entity GNN did pull ahead when 40% of identifier joins failed, and auditing the graph structure alone exposed a shortcut in the initial data generator that the matched twins removed.

papers.title: Stochastic and Noisy Oracles in Smooth Continuous Optimization
papers.abstract: We review models of inexact computational oracles in smooth continuous optimization and their implications for the convergence, computational complexity, and attainable accuracy of optimization algorithms. We adopt a framework in which zeroth-,first-, and second-order oracles are characterized by quantitative error bounds and may accept additional control parameters that influence both their accuracy and computational cost. We introduce deterministic and stochastic oracle models and illustrate their properties through a variety of examples, including finite-difference approximations, stochastic gradients, and randomized derivative estimators. Particular attention is given to the distinction between absolute and relative errors, bias and variance, and stochastic function evaluations with independent or coupled randomness. A central theme of the review is the use of common analytical tools to recover and compare convergence and complexity guarantees under different oracle models. For deterministic and stochastic first-order methods, we show how a general descent inequality leads to complexity bounds under various assumptions on the objective function and all proposed oracle models. In the stochastic setting, we develop bounds on expected stopping times and the accuracy that can be guaranteed under different oracle conditions. We also examine the total computational complexity of algorithms relying on specific oracle constructions and briefly review models of inexact second- order information and their use in optimization algorithms.
papers.summary: This review covers models of inexact zeroth-, first- and second-order oracles in smooth continuous optimization, including finite-difference approximations, stochastic gradients and randomized derivative estimators. It distinguishes absolute from relative errors, bias from variance, and independent from coupled randomness, and it treats oracle accuracy and cost as tunable through control parameters. The central theme is **a common set of analytical tools, built around a general descent inequality, that recovers and compares convergence and complexity guarantees across oracle models**. It also develops bounds on expected stopping times and attainable accuracy in the stochastic setting, and briefly reviews inexact second-order methods.

papers.title: CIRCE Divines LLM Task Complexity from Constraint Structure
papers.abstract:
Estimating whether a problem is too complex for a large language model (LLM) before the model attempts it can guide model routing, how to allocate test-time compute, and suggest the need for new tools to aid the agent. While existing estimators rely on the problem text, LLM-annotated task difficulty labels, or signals obtained after a model attempts to solve the problem, such as its hidden states, none explicitly leverage the constraint structure inherent in the problem: the variables to assign and how the constraints over them interact.
  We introduce CIRCE, which extracts a problem's structure by using a cheap LLM to construct a Constraint Intermediate Representation that deterministically compiles into the constraint graph. Across seven reasoning benchmarks (including SAT, logic, and math) and four LLMs, even a randomly initialized GNN encoder improves predictions of LLM response correctness, reducing negative log-likelihood from 0.465 to 0.423 and increasing AUROC from 0.691 to 0.727 relative to the strongest baseline for each metric.
papers.summary: Predicting whether a problem is too hard for a large language model (LLM) before it tries can guide model routing and how much test-time compute to spend. Existing estimators rely on the problem text, difficulty labels, or signals from after an attempt. `CIRCE` instead uses a cheap LLM to write a Constraint Intermediate Representation, which compiles deterministically into a constraint graph that a graph neural network encodes. Across seven reasoning benchmarks (including SAT, logic and math) and four LLMs, **even a randomly initialized GNN encoder improves correctness prediction**, raising AUROC from 0.691 to 0.727 over the strongest baseline.

papers.title: Verifying Text-to-SQL Queries under Changing Business Semantics
papers.abstract: In text-to-SQL and AI-agent analytics, successful SQL execution does not establish semantic correctness under changing business definitions. We study revalidation of fixed queries after changes to refund attribution, tax treatment, eligible populations and exchange-rate dates. An executable verification profile binds the requested revision and knowledge cutoff to legal counterexample data and exact monetary comparison. A preregistered confirmation on 32 newly authored revision families and two local producer bundles retains 192 query-definition cells: 144 nonconforming, 36 finite-suite agreeing and 12 unresolved. Of the nonconforming cells, 63 agree on the current snapshot. At an eight-ledger budget, obligation-guided checking detects 137 discrepancies versus 127 for generic ordering, a paired difference of 6.9 percentage points (family bootstrap 95% interval [2.1, 13.6]; exact family sign-flip p=0.0156). Every ledger arm rejects zero of the 36 agreeing cells. Current-obligation and equal-weight scoring match the guided result, identifying coverage rather than revision-specific priority as the observed source of benefit. Controlled assays, a natural-query pilot and repeated samples provide separate mechanism and robustness evidence. A legal discrepancy refutes conformance; agreement remains restricted to the recorded suite. The study establishes an auditable business-semantic revalidation profile within its authored schema and local-model scope.
papers.summary: In text-to-SQL and agent-driven analytics, a query that runs successfully can still be semantically wrong once business definitions change, for example in refund attribution, tax treatment or exchange-rate dates. The authors propose an executable verification profile that ties a requested definition revision to legal counterexample data and exact monetary comparison, and they test it in a preregistered study of 32 revision families. Of 192 query-definition cells, 144 were nonconforming, and 63 of those still agreed with the current data snapshot. With a budget of eight ledgers, **obligation-guided checking caught 137 discrepancies versus 127 for generic ordering**, with no false rejections; further analysis attributes the gain to coverage rather than revision-specific prioritization.

papers.title: QUAL: Quantile Alignment Improves Zero-Shot Time-Series Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) provide zero-shot forecasts for unseen series, but their accuracy varies across datasets. Combining several models can reduce this variability, yet zero-shot deployment provides no target labels for selecting or weighting them. We find that a model pool is useful not only as a final ensemble, but also as a probability reference for transforming each member forecast. Aligning quantiles through this pool-relative reference improves every member forecast in aggregate. Motivated by this finding, we propose QUAL (Quantile alignment), a simple label-free framework for improving and combining diverse TSFMs. QUAL first produces aligned member forecasts, then applies Huber aggregation and rearrangement to obtain a robust combined forecast without training or model modification. On GIFT-Eval, quantile alignment reduces average member MASE and CRPS by 7.4% and 9.8%. The full framework remains robust when weak forecasters enter a candidate pool whose quality cannot be verified in advance. Code is available at https://github.com/junhyeokkang/QUAL.
papers.summary: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast unseen series zero-shot, but their accuracy varies across datasets, and without target labels there is no way to choose or weight models. `QUAL` (Quantile alignment) uses a pool of models as a probability reference, aligning each member's quantiles to the pool and then combining the aligned forecasts with Huber aggregation and rearrangement. It needs no labels, training or model changes. On `GIFT-Eval`, **alignment alone reduces average member MASE and CRPS by 7.4% and 9.8%**, and the full framework stays robust when weak forecasters join the pool.

papers.title: MUON-RT Reusing the Teacher's Trajectory for Momentum-Free Muon for LLM Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Self-distillation methods for large language models with an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher already retain a history of student updates. Muon nevertheless stores a separate momentum buffer, increasing persistent training memory. We propose Muon with Reused Teacher (Muon-RT), which reuses the teacher-student displacement to eliminate momentum buffers for hidden weight matrices. We show that this displacement encodes an exponentially weighted history of applied updates and smooths temporally uncorrelated noise under a local model. Muon-RT removes its radial component, normalizes it spectrally, and mixes it with the current gradient after Newton-Schulz (NS) orthogonalization. Under explicit regularity and alignment assumptions, we establish linear contraction of an expected objective-gap bound toward a residual error level. With Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Muon-RT improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.6 points with 42% less persistent memory, and over momentum Muon by 5.4 points with 27% less persistent memory. With Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) on Olmo-3-7B-Instruct, it improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.0 points.
papers.summary: Self-distillation of large language models with an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher already keeps a history of student updates, yet the `Muon` optimizer stores its own momentum buffer on top of it. `Muon-RT` reuses the teacher-student displacement in place of that momentum: it removes the displacement's radial component, normalizes it spectrally, and mixes it with the orthogonalized gradient. The authors show this displacement acts as an exponentially weighted update history and prove convergence under stated assumptions. With self-distillation fine-tuning on `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct`, it beats `AdamW` by 2.6 points while using **42% less persistent memory**, and beats momentum Muon by 5.4 points while using 27% less.

papers.title: Differential rank preservation manifold learning
papers.abstract: Manifold learning methods like t-SNE and UMAP preserve local neighborhoods, but they do not preserve the ranking of the neighbors inside them. Two embeddings can return the same neighbor set while disagreeing on which point is closest. This loss of order degrades downstream applications that value the order in the embedding. We propose Smooth Rank t-SNE (SR-tSNE), which adds a differentiable rank term to the standard t-SNE loss. To enable efficient training, this term uses a sigmoid rank approximation to explicitly force a point's true high-dimensional neighbors to outrank unrelated intruders and retain their original order. We also introduce Ordinal DLP (O-DLP), an extension of the Degree of Locality Preservation (DLP) metric that credits a neighbor only when it returns at its original rank. Across eight benchmarks spanning image, text, speech, remote-sensing and single-cell data, SR-tSNE outperforms 12 baselines in rank preservation and neighborhood overlap. Ablation studies demonstrate our rank term alone boosts O-DLP by 5% to 28%, a gain not achievable using standard pairwise loss. This advantage transfers to downstream applications. SR-tSNE achieves the best label-transfer performance across seven vision datasets. For cell-type discovery across six single-cell datasets, it ranks first in 17 of 18 dataset-metric combinations, whether clustering resolution is selected with or without cell-type labels. In intraday trading, SR-tSNE achieves higher returns, lower risk, and lower turnover than the baselines. To our knowledge, SR-tSNE is the first t-SNE-family method with explicit order preservation.
papers.summary: Manifold learning methods like `t-SNE` and `UMAP` preserve which points are neighbors but not their order, so two embeddings can return the same neighbor set yet disagree on which point is closest. `SR-tSNE` adds a differentiable, sigmoid-approximated rank term to the t-SNE loss so that true neighbors outrank intruders and keep their original order, and the authors introduce an `O-DLP` metric that rewards exact rank recovery. Across eight benchmarks it beats 12 baselines on rank preservation, with **the rank term alone raising O-DLP by 5% to 28%**. The gains carry over to label transfer on vision datasets, cell-type discovery in single-cell data and an intraday trading task.

papers.title: Calibration of Large Model Quantization based on HiFloat4 Format
papers.abstract: Quantization of Large Language Models (LLMs) has be- coming increasingly important for reducing the computa- tional costs and resource requirements for practical deploy- ment.Growinginterestinthisareahasmotivatedthecommu- nity to move beyond 8-bit quantization towards 4-bit preci- sion, leading to the development of customized 4-bit formats such as MXFP4 and NVFP4. Recently, HiFloat4 (HiF4) has emerged as a competitive alternative which adopts a Block Floating-Point(BFP)formatwithathree-levelscalinghierar- chy, thereby achieving a significantly larger dynamic range. While quantization can substantially reduce memory usage and accelerate inference, it frequently introduces accuracy degradation. Calibration is therefore essential for narrowing theperformancegapbetweenlow-precisionquantizedmodels and their full-precision counterparts. Nevertheless, existing calibration methods are mainly designed and validated us- ing integer-precision formats, such as INT4, lacking support for HiF4 due to its hierarchical BFP structure. In this paper, weinvestigatethreecalibrationapproaches,namelyHiGPTQ, HiAutoRound, and HiFlatQuant, to further enhance model quantizationbasedontheHiF4format.Extensiveexperiments demonstratethatallthreeproposedapproachesimproveinfer- ence accuracy compared with direct HiF4 conversion, reduc- ing the gap between HiF4 and BF16 to less than 1% and out- performing the state-of-the-art NVFP4 format across various models and downstream tasks.
papers.summary: `HiFloat4` (HiF4) is a 4-bit block floating-point format for quantizing large language models (LLMs) that uses a three-level scaling hierarchy to get a larger dynamic range than `MXFP4` or `NVFP4`. Existing calibration methods target integer formats such as INT4 and do not support its hierarchical structure. The authors adapt three calibration methods to HiF4, producing `HiGPTQ`, `HiAutoRound` and `HiFlatQuant`. All three beat direct HiF4 conversion, **narrowing the gap to BF16 to under 1%** and outperforming `NVFP4` across a range of models and tasks.

papers.title: Predicting Human-Gain Curves under Local Proxy Optimization from Repeated Ratings
papers.abstract: Optimizing a proxy objective can improve human-perceived quality, but the resulting gain can vary with optimization strength. Average proxy-human correlation alone does not reveal how human-perceived quality changes as optimization strength increases. We propose PACE (Proxy Alignment and Curvature Expansion), a pre-optimization diagnostic that uses repeated human ratings to predict the human-gain curve induced by a fixed proxy. The method models proxy optimization as a KL-regularized exponential tilt. At KL radius $d$, the local gain is approximated by $A\sqrt{d}+Bd$, where $A$ measures first-order proxy-human alignment and $B$ captures the leading second-order correction along the proxy-optimization path. We estimate $A$ and $B$ from repeated human ratings on calibration items and test the resulting gain-curve prediction on held-out evaluation items. Across SummEval, analysis-eligible WMT MQM clusters, an OpenMEVA-MAGS ROC/WP repeated-rating slice, and a GPT-4o judge proxy experiment, PACE consistently reduces held-out gain-prediction error relative to $A$-only, zero-gain, and reliability-only baselines. With the same pre-pool information, it is competitive with flexible proxy-conditional calibration, and a LoRA-DPO experiment provides a modest bridge to actual optimization. Transfer experiments across datasets and evaluation slices show that source coefficients are useful priors, but target calibration further improves prediction. The resulting diagnostic is local and one-sided: it characterizes gentle optimization along the positive tilt branch of a fixed item pool.
papers.summary: Optimizing a proxy objective such as an automatic metric or LLM judge can improve human-perceived quality, but how much it helps depends on how hard the proxy is pushed, and the average proxy-human correlation does not reveal this. `PACE` (Proxy Alignment and Curvature Expansion) models proxy optimization as a KL-regularized exponential tilt and predicts the human gain at KL radius d as A√d + Bd, estimating both coefficients from repeated human ratings before any optimization. On `SummEval`, `WMT MQM`, `OpenMEVA-MAGS` and a `GPT-4o` judge experiment, **PACE consistently reduces held-out gain-prediction error** compared with baselines that use alignment alone, assume zero gain, or use reliability alone. The diagnostic is local and covers only gentle optimization on a fixed item pool.

papers.title: Language Models Show a "Women-Are-Wonderful" Effect in Blame Attribution That is Not Just Leniency
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the Women-Are-Wonderful (WaW) effect in language-model blame attribution: a favorable bias in which women receive more positive evaluations than men. Using 11,270 interpersonal conflicts from r/AmItheAsshole, we construct matched counterfactuals that vary the gender of the person being judged (the original poster) and the person affected (the counter-party). Across four language models, gender changes a minority of verdicts, but those changes consistently favor women. The effect is strongly role-dependent. Making the original poster a woman reduces the odds of blame by 9--52%, while making the counter-party a woman multiplies them by 2.7--9.2X. Counter-party WaW also varies across conflict types, strengthening in communication and relationship conflicts and weakening in family conflicts. Exploratory probes suggest that counter-party gender can shift judgments of sympathy, reasonableness, harm and protection. WaW is therefore not just leniency toward women being judged: models also judge conduct more harshly when it affects a woman.
papers.summary: The study tests whether language models show a "Women-Are-Wonderful" bias when assigning blame, using 11,270 conflicts from r/AmItheAsshole rewritten as matched counterfactuals that swap the gender of the person being judged and of the other party. Across four models, gender flips only a minority of verdicts, but those flips consistently favor women. The effect depends on role: making the poster a woman cuts the odds of blame by 9-52%, while **making the counter-party a woman multiplies the poster's odds of being blamed by 2.7-9.2x**. The bias is therefore not just leniency toward women being judged; models also judge conduct more harshly when it affects a woman.

papers.title: Confident Fools or Careful Searchers? A Behavioural Study of When LLMs Search Beyond Their Static Internal Memory
papers.abstract: Agentic LLM assistants must repeatedly decide whether to answer from memory or to call a tool such as web search. Unnecessary searches cost latency and money; missing ones yield confident but unsupported answers. Prior work mostly measures verbalised confidence or trains new adaptive-retrieval methods, and rarely audits the search decisions that deployed products actually make. We introduce a benchmark of 400 multiple-choice questions that combines widely known inside-knowledge (IK) questions, which should be answered directly, with outside-knowledge (OK) questions about facts from news published after the models' training cut-offs (to our knowledge), which should trigger search or, without tools, abstention. Each item offers an abstain option, and two action-level scores, NAS and KIS, reward searching on OK questions and restraint on IK questions. Across five commercial LLMs with and without their vendors' web search, GPT-5 mini and Grok 4 Fast search on over 90% of OK but only 1% of IK questions, whereas Mistral Small searches on just 20% of OK questions, often abstaining instead of using its tool; one product's search indicator proved unusable. Searching is partly triggered by explicit temporal cues: on uncued OK questions, the NAS of the two selective models falls from about 0.72 to 0.57--0.58. The scores thus measure the search triggering of specific products, not metacognition in a strict sense.
papers.summary: Agentic LLM assistants must decide whether to answer from memory or call a tool such as web search, yet the decisions deployed products actually make are rarely audited. The authors build a 400-question multiple-choice benchmark that mixes widely known facts with facts from news published after the models' training cut-offs, offers an abstain option on every item, and scores search decisions with two action-level metrics, `NAS` and `KIS`. Across five commercial LLMs, `GPT-5 mini` and `Grok 4 Fast` searched on over 90% of post-cutoff questions and only 1% of known ones, while **`Mistral Small` searched on just 20% of post-cutoff questions, often abstaining instead**. Searching is partly triggered by explicit temporal cues: without them, the selective models' NAS falls from about 0.72 to 0.57-0.58.

papers.title: When Should AI Agents Ask? Clarification Requests Under Limited Human Attention
papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly carry out delegated tasks in parallel, with one person overseeing several of them at once. In practice, an agent often lacks information its task requires, such as an unstated preference, constraint, or specification. It can ask the human to clarify, or it can search for the information itself, for example in past records, which takes time and effort and may fail. In this paper, we study how to coordinate these decisions across several agents that share one human with limited attention. We build a stylized model in which each agent can search, ask, or continue the parts of its task that do not depend on the missing information, and we formulate the problem as a dynamic program. We first show that whether an agent should ask depends on more than its own uncertainty: an agent with other work to do can be better off asking earlier, and which question the human should answer first depends on all waiting questions, so no ranking computed agent by agent is optimal. We then propose the Pairwise Coordination Policy (PCP), which uses exact one- and two-task problems to estimate how pairs of tasks delay each other when they share the human. Theoretically, PCP is exactly optimal when at most two requirements remain unresolved and costs at most twice the optimum when every unresolved requirement must be resolved by the human. We evaluate PCP on 864 synthetic cases and in a case study with LLM agents. On the synthetic benchmark, PCP's mean gap to optimal cost is 0.07%, and it reduces cost by an average of 18-31% relative to three standard rules for when to ask. In the LLM case study, agents completed every task correctly, and PCP achieved the lowest mean cost in all tested settings.
papers.summary: When one person oversees several AI agents running in parallel, each agent missing information must choose between asking the human, searching for the answer itself, or continuing the work that does not depend on it, and all agents share the human's limited attention. Formulating this as a dynamic program, the authors show that no ranking computed agent by agent is optimal, and that an agent with other work to do may be better off asking earlier. Their `Pairwise Coordination Policy` (PCP) uses exact one- and two-task solutions to estimate how tasks delay each other; it is provably optimal with at most two unresolved requirements and within twice the optimum when the human must resolve every requirement. On 864 synthetic cases, **PCP comes within 0.07% of optimal cost on average** and cuts cost by 18-31% versus standard rules for when to ask, and it achieved the lowest mean cost in every setting of an LLM-agent case study.

papers.title: One Verdict Is Not Enough: Regression Testing Learned World Models and Their Test Harnesses
papers.abstract: Learned world models ship as software components whose model versions, preprocessing, and test harnesses change between releases. Work on model updates already counts per-sample regressions, or negative flips, that an accuracy check hides. Two problems remain: a test can pass under one configuration and fail under another, and a harness fault can produce erroneous scores and wrong verdicts without a crash. We present TetraState, a regression-testing protocol for paired possible/impossible video tests. Each test runs under four fixed model-native configurations; its number of correct verdicts assigns one of four outcome classes. Inconclusive tests and failed executions are reported separately alongside the verdict rate. Revisions are compared by per-test outcome transitions, and the harness is versioned as part of the system under test. On all 506 IntPhys 2 Main tests and two heterogeneous systems, Cosmos 3 Nano and V-JEPA 2, two V-JEPA 2 harness revisions move modal accuracy by only 0.2 and 2.6 points yet change 11 and 214 test labels; in the second, accuracy rises although fewer tests are judged correctly, and 43 regressions keep the modal verdict, so a modal-verdict flip check misses them. These results outline a research agenda on configuration-level regression oracles for learned components.
papers.summary: Learned world models ship as software whose model versions, preprocessing and test harnesses change between releases, and a single accuracy number hides both configuration-dependent results and silent harness bugs. `TetraState` is a regression-testing protocol for paired possible/impossible video tests that runs each test under four configurations, sorts tests into outcome classes, reports inconclusive tests and failed runs separately, and versions the harness as part of the system under test. On the 506 `IntPhys 2` Main tests with `Cosmos 3 Nano` and `V-JEPA 2`, **two harness revisions moved modal accuracy by only 0.2 and 2.6 points yet changed 11 and 214 test labels**. In the second revision accuracy rose even though fewer tests were judged correctly, and 43 regressions would be missed by a check that only looks for flips in the modal verdict.

papers.title: When Disclosure Is Compulsory: Evaluating Ride-Hailing Rebalancing Policies with Self-Interested LLM Driver Agents
papers.abstract: The EU Platform Work Directive, to be transposed by December 2026, requires ride-hailing platforms to state in plain language the main parameters of their automated decisions and how a worker's behaviour affects them. Such rules are exactly what a large language model (LLM) can read, so drivers will be able to let one decide for them. We compare two main families of rebalancing policy once their rules are public: a reactive policy (R) that sends idle drivers to cover requests just lost, and an anticipatory policy (A) that plans moves on a demand forecast. Each driver is an LLM agent maximizing its own net income, given no rules (N) or the rules at the directive's level of detail (L). We test two LLMs, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Jev, which understand the rules equally well, in a three-zone model and in Manhattan. With the rules disclosed, drivers follow the platform more closely: in Manhattan, the share of relocation offers they decline falls from about four in five to one in four under both policies. Yet the effects differ by policy. For the platform, disclosure costs R 3.7% of its profit in Manhattan, as R now pays for moves drivers used to make for free, while A's profit is unchanged; the two policies, which tie on profit under full compliance, end 6.1% apart. For drivers, disclosure raises income in the small model under both policies and LLMs; for users, it raises the service rate there by 10 to 18 percentage points. In Manhattan, self-interested drivers also make A a win-win-win against full compliance, raising driver income, platform profit and service rate by 10 to 12% each. Rebalancing policies that perform equally well under full compliance can thus show opposite results under mandatory disclosure. The study offers a framework to evaluate such policies under the new requirement and is, to our knowledge, the first to do so with LLM agents.
papers.summary: The EU Platform Work Directive will require ride-hailing platforms to disclose the main parameters of their automated decisions in plain language, and drivers could hand those rules to an LLM to decide for them. The study simulates self-interested LLM driver agents (`Claude Haiku 5.5` and `Jev`) under a reactive and an anticipatory rebalancing policy, with and without disclosed rules, in a three-zone model and in Manhattan. Once the rules are disclosed, drivers comply far more often: in Manhattan, the share of relocation offers they decline drops from about four in five to one in four. The two policies diverge sharply, though. Disclosure costs the reactive policy 3.7% of platform profit, while the anticipatory policy becomes a win-win-win, **raising driver income, platform profit and service rate by 10 to 12% each** compared with full compliance.

papers.title: TalentRL: Strategy-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Hierarchical Skill Routing
papers.abstract: Natural-language skills enable large language model (LLM) agents to reuse procedures across tasks, yet most systems retrieve individual skills from a flat SkillBank without explicitly modeling the high-level strategy that governs their selection and use. We introduce TalentRL, a strategy-guided reinforcement learning framework for hierarchical routing over procedural memory. Coarse-grained talents represent recurring strategies for skill use, while fine-grained skills provide executable procedures. For each task, the policy model selects a talent that guides execution and softly prioritizes its associated skills during similarity-based retrieval. However, since task outcomes depend jointly on talent selection, retrieved skill context, and downstream execution, terminal rewards alone cannot isolate the contribution of the routing decision. TalentRL therefore trains talent routing with reward contrasts between rollouts of the same task under matched interventions on the talent-conditioned context, and optimizes downstream execution with group-relative advantages. Across seven open-domain and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, talent-aware supervised fine-tuning improves average success rate by 7.53%, 6.71%, and 9.21% over the corresponding zero-shot baselines for Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B, respectively. Reinforcement learning further improves these SFT checkpoints by 7.58% to 9.32%, and TalentRL achieves the highest average success rate among all compared methods on all three backbones. On the agentic benchmarks ALFWorld and WebShop, TalentRL achieves the highest ALFWorld success rate (99.3%) and the highest WebShop score (90.7) among all compared methods.
papers.summary: LLM agents that reuse natural-language skills usually retrieve them from a flat skill bank, with no explicit model of the high-level strategy that governs which skills to use. `TalentRL` adds a hierarchy: a policy first selects a coarse-grained talent (a recurring strategy), which then softly prioritizes its associated fine-grained skills during retrieval. Terminal rewards alone cannot isolate the effect of the routing decision, so routing is trained on reward contrasts between rollouts of the same task under matched interventions, while execution is trained with group-relative advantages. Reinforcement learning adds 7.58% to 9.32% on top of supervised fine-tuning across seven question-answering benchmarks and three 8B-scale backbones, and the method reaches **99.3% success on `ALFWorld`** and a score of 90.7 on `WebShop`.

papers.title: HyperRepair: Recovering Forgotten General Capabilities of Fine-Tuned Language Models
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning improves a language model's performance in a target domain but can weaken its general capabilities. Existing methods often face a trade-off between general capabilities and domain specialization, making it difficult to preserve both. We introduce HyperRepair, a framework for recovering general capabilities while retaining domain specialization at only inference cost. To make recovery generalizable across models sharing a pretrained backbone, HyperRepair learns a hypernetwork from repairs trained on source models. The hypernetwork uses activation fingerprints that summarize changes from the pretrained backbone to generate a tailored Repairing Side Net (RSN), whose prompt-conditioned gate applies corrections selectively. This enables recovery on models from unseen adaptation domains without target-domain examples or additional optimization. We evaluate HyperRpair across two model families, 12 LoRA adaptation datasets, and 15 general benchmarks. On the default split, HyperRepair achieves 93.4% of the base models' average general score while retaining 99.5% of the fine-tuned models' average domain score.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning a language model for a target domain often erodes its general capabilities. `HyperRepair` trains a hypernetwork on repairs learned for source models; given activation fingerprints that summarize how a fine-tuned model has drifted from its pretrained backbone, it generates a tailored Repairing Side Net (`RSN`) whose prompt-conditioned gate applies corrections selectively. This lets it repair models fine-tuned on unseen domains without target-domain data or extra optimization. Across two model families, 12 `LoRA` adaptation datasets and 15 general benchmarks, it recovers **93.4% of the base models' general score while keeping 99.5% of the fine-tuned domain score**.

papers.title: Counterfactual Pairwise Augmentation Improves Small Pointwise LLM Judges
papers.abstract: Agentic systems increasingly gate individual steps with a pointwise judge that scores a response against a criterion. Small language models are attractive for this role because they can be served and specialized efficiently. Such a judge must locate the criterion's decision boundary, but pointwise labels under-determine that boundary in fine-tuning: labeled responses to different queries differ along many dimensions at once, so they do not reveal which features decide the label. We introduce CPA (Counterfactual Pairwise Augmentation), which makes the deciding difference explicit in training. For each pointwise item, CPA synthesizes and audits a counterfactual response to the same query intended to carry the opposite label. It frames the accepted pair as a pairwise task asking which of the two responses satisfies the criterion. The judge is fine-tuned jointly on both pointwise and pairwise datasets and deployed in pointwise mode only. A second-order analysis shows when this should outperform the prevailing strategy of merging separately trained pointwise and pairwise experts: merging moves every parameter direction toward the pairwise expert by the same fraction, whereas joint training can hold the pointwise optimum wherever the pairwise loss is flat and absorb its curvature where it is sharp. This is the regime that CPA's same-source, counterfactually minimal pairwise view is designed to produce. On separate Qwen3-8B LoRA adapters for six binary criteria, CPA improves criterion-averaged pointwise macro-F1 by 2.5 points over pointwise-only training and outperforms model merging on all six criteria at every tested merge weight. It also surpasses the strongest zero-shot frontier judge we evaluate, Gemini 3.6 Flash, by 11.8 points.
papers.summary: Small pointwise LLM judges, which score one response against one criterion, are hard to fine-tune because the labeled examples differ in many ways at once and do not reveal which feature decides the label. Counterfactual Pairwise Augmentation (`CPA`) synthesizes and audits a counterfactual response to the same query that should carry the opposite label. It then trains the judge jointly on the original pointwise items and on pairwise questions asking which of the two responses satisfies the criterion, while deploying the judge only in pointwise mode. A second-order analysis explains why joint training should beat merging separately trained pointwise and pairwise experts. On `Qwen3-8B` `LoRA` judges for six criteria, `CPA` gains 2.5 macro-F1 points over pointwise-only training, beats merging at every tested weight, and **outperforms `Gemini 3.6 Flash` by 11.8 points**.

papers.title: Lineage Is Memory: Parent Inheritance and Feedback Disclosure in Short-Budget LLM-Guided Optimization
papers.abstract: Iterative language-model optimizers refine prompts and programs by evaluating a candidate, showing a proposer model a sample of failing cases, and keeping revisions that improve performance. Recent work attributes the limits of this loop to narrow single-round reflection, introducing full-set error clustering, targeted minibatches, or larger proposer models so the optimizer sees more failure modes per step. Yet every existing evaluation tests these mechanisms exclusively inside lineage-preserving search, where each revision edits a surviving parent, leaving the contribution of parent inheritance confounded with the breadth of per-round feedback. Across 1,750 pre-registered runs spanning nine prompt and program synthesis benchmarks, we separate parent inheritance from feedback disclosure under matched evaluation budgets. We find that greedy parent inheritance drives the vast majority of optimization progress, outperforming seed-reset resampling even when seed-reset proposals receive a clustered summary of all failures in every round or use a larger proposer model. While full-set error clustering and diverse failure selection improve single-step rewrites from the seed and accelerate the opening rounds of search, sequential parent inheritance rapidly closes this gap as solved error modes are retained in the candidate and filtered from subsequent failure lists. Moreover, decomposing token expenditure in GEPA reveals that proposer reflection accounts for only a small fraction of total cost whereas validation and minibatch gating consume nearly the entire budget, showing that greedy parent inheritance over raw failures captures the gains of complex reflective loops at a fraction of their compute.
papers.summary: Iterative LLM optimizers refine prompts and programs by showing a proposer model the cases a candidate fails. Recent work credits improvements to richer reflection, such as error clustering or larger proposers, but those mechanisms have only ever been tested inside search that edits a surviving parent candidate. Across 1,750 pre-registered runs on nine prompt and program synthesis benchmarks, the study separates parent inheritance from feedback breadth under matched budgets and finds that **greedy parent inheritance drives most optimization progress**, beating seed-reset resampling even when the reset proposals get clustered summaries of all failures or a larger proposer. Richer feedback speeds up only the opening rounds. A token breakdown of `GEPA` shows that validation and minibatch gating, not reflection, consume nearly the entire budget.

papers.title: Lifelong Learning of Scheduling Rules with Surrogate-assisted Genetic Programming for Dynamic Flexible Job Shop Scheduling
papers.abstract: Genetic programming (GP) has been widely used to learn scheduling rules for dynamic flexible job shop scheduling (DFJSS). However, trained rules tend to only generalise to tasks of similar scales and distributions, and when task characteristics change, learned rules often suffer significant performance degradation. Moreover, fine-tuning pre-trained rules on new tasks often leads to catastrophic forgetting, where prior knowledge is lost. This motivates the need for GP methods that can adapt to new tasks while preserving past knowledge, leading to a lifelong learning paradigm. However, lifelong learning in GP for DFJSS remains largely under-explored. To address this gap, this paper proposes a surrogate-assisted GP method for lifelong learning to handle sequential heterogeneous DFJSS tasks with job or batch arrivals. The framework includes three key components: an adaptive two-stage training strategy to balance plasticity and stability, a task-similarity-based weighting mechanism to regulate knowledge reuse, and an improved surrogate model with distance constraints to enhance estimation accuracy. Experimental results show that the proposed method effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting while maintaining strong adaptability, outperforming several compared methods and demonstrating the potential of lifelong GP in dynamic scheduling environments.
papers.summary: Scheduling rules learned by genetic programming (GP) for dynamic flexible job shop scheduling (DFJSS) generalize poorly when task scales or distributions change, and fine-tuning them on new tasks causes catastrophic forgetting. The proposed lifelong-learning method combines a surrogate-assisted GP with an adaptive two-stage training strategy that balances plasticity and stability, task-similarity weighting to regulate knowledge reuse, and a distance-constrained surrogate model that improves fitness estimates. On sequential heterogeneous tasks with job or batch arrivals, it **mitigates catastrophic forgetting while staying adaptable** and outperforms the compared methods.

papers.title: ARK: Avoiding Routing Collisions for KV Cache Transfer in Disaggregated LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Disaggregated LLM inference separates the prefill and decode phases across GPU pools, generating massive KV-cache transfers. Because these transfers last hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, they behave as mega elephant flows that dominate link bandwidth utilization. In this regime, stateless ECMP can perform poorly: hash collisions may overload one spine link while leaving others idle, stretching transfer times by seconds. Yet this same persistence makes coordination practical. Since these flows are long-lived, even lightweight one-to-all coordination can be amortized over their lifetime. We present ARK, a distributed elephant-flow path reservation mechanism. ARK coordinates senders to choose source ports whose hashes map concurrent flows onto distinct spines, without requiring switch changes or receiver-side packet reordering. Packet-level RDMA simulations show that ARK reduces mean and P95 FCT by up to 27.3% and 34.0% under moderate load, and further reduces mean TTFT by up to 12.9%.
papers.summary: In disaggregated LLM inference, prefill and decode run on separate GPU pools, and the KV-cache transfers between them become long-lived elephant flows. Under stateless ECMP routing, hash collisions can overload one spine link while others sit idle. `ARK` coordinates senders so that concurrent flows pick source ports whose hashes map them onto distinct spines, and it needs no switch changes or receiver-side reordering. In packet-level RDMA simulations under moderate load it cuts mean and P95 flow completion time by up to 27.3% and **34.0%**, and mean time-to-first-token by up to 12.9%.

papers.title: FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D
papers.abstract: To accelerate materials discovery, language models must be able to address problems at the research frontier. Yet textbook- and examination-derived benchmarks primarily assess established knowledge, leaving performance on frontier research problems largely untested. We introduce FrontierMat, a benchmark of 330 problems drawn from frontier academic and industrial research in fields including aerospace, semiconductors, embodied intelligence and nuclear fusion. Every problem is validated by leading experimentalists and industry experts in its field. Each problem presents a real study and asks the model to infer a withheld outcome or draw a conclusion from selected experimental evidence. Problems are annotated by functional domain, material system and the scale of the governing mechanism; 130 require cross-scale reasoning. The strongest general-purpose model scores only 53.7%, and on matched problems, cross-scale problems score 8.7 points below single-scale ones. Half of the problems are solved by at most one model, and models fail chiefly by endorsing what is plausible rather than what was observed. A domain-adaptation study with meta-weighted continued pretraining and scale-modular self-distillation raises an open-weight model from 36.7% to 55.4%, matching the strongest proprietary model, with improvements on public materials benchmarks and no decline in aggregate performance on general benchmarks. FrontierMat provides a testbed for measuring progress toward language models that support frontier materials R&D.
papers.summary: `FrontierMat` is a benchmark of 330 expert-validated problems drawn from frontier academic and industrial materials research in areas such as aerospace, semiconductors and nuclear fusion. Each problem asks a model to infer a withheld outcome or draw a conclusion from real experimental evidence, and 130 of them require reasoning across physical scales. **The strongest general-purpose model scores only 53.7%**, cross-scale problems score 8.7 points lower than matched single-scale ones, and models mostly fail by endorsing what is plausible rather than what was observed. Meta-weighted continued pretraining combined with scale-modular self-distillation lifts an open-weight model from 36.7% to 55.4%, matching the best proprietary model.

papers.title: LLM Detoxification via Transition-Aware Reward-Guided Representation Sampling
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate toxic content, motivating effective test-time detoxification. Existing representation steering methods often rely on static or coarse interventions and provide imprecise guidance because they inadequately model transitions between toxic and non-toxic generations. We propose Transition-Aware Reward-Guided Representation Sampling (TARGRS), a test-time framework that learns reward guidance over toxicity transitions in latent representation space. During exploration, progressive steering along the toxicity direction constructs trajectories from non-toxic to toxic states. Toxicity scores along these trajectories turn sparse annotations into dense, listwise supervision for a transition-aware token-level reward model. During inference, TARGRS uses this model to guide coarse-to-fine sampling along the opposite, non-toxic direction: coarse sampling identifies the intervention needed to reach non-toxic regions, and refinement selects a detoxified representation with minimal perturbation. Experiments on 10 LLMs across RealToxicityPrompts, BOLD, and AttaQ show that TARGRS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing toxicity by up to 69.38% on RealToxicityPrompts. TARGRS runs nearly as fast as the original LLM while preserving its core capabilities with minimal impact. By intervening in the language decoder space, TARGRS also extends to Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), reducing toxicity by up to 64.23% across 3 representative LVLMs.
papers.summary: Representation-steering methods for removing toxic output from LLMs at test time tend to use static, coarse interventions. Transition-Aware Reward-Guided Representation Sampling (`TARGRS`) progressively steers representations from non-toxic to toxic states and uses toxicity scores along those trajectories to train a dense, token-level reward model. At inference, this reward model guides coarse-to-fine sampling in the non-toxic direction, choosing the smallest perturbation that reaches a non-toxic region. Across 10 LLMs on `RealToxicityPrompts`, `BOLD` and `AttaQ`, it **reduces toxicity by up to 69.38%** at close to the original model's speed, and it cuts toxicity by up to 64.23% on three vision-language models.

papers.title: Adaptive Uncertainty Quantification on Simplicial Complexes with Conformalized Simplicial Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Simplicial neural networks (SNNs) are powerful tools for prediction tasks on higher-order relational datasets stored on simplicial complexes (SCs), a higher-order generalization of graphs. However, SNNs usually lack rigorous uncertainty quantification (UQ), limiting their usefulness in high-stakes scenarios. We propose conformalized SNN (CF-SNN), a framework that, given a simplicial-complex entity with m prediction targets, generates prediction sets for all m targets simultaneously. Under mild assumptions, CF-SNN guarantees that, for each target, the prediction set contains the true label with a user-specified nominal coverage probability, and the realized miscoverage proportion across all m targets is guaranteed to remain close to the nominal level with high probability. Extensive experiments across a wide range of SC prediction tasks demonstrate that CF-SNN is a flexible UQ framework that achieves user-specified coverage while producing informative prediction sets of small size.
papers.summary: Simplicial neural networks (SNNs) make predictions on simplicial complexes, a higher-order generalization of graphs, but lack rigorous uncertainty quantification. Conformalized SNN (`CF-SNN`) produces prediction sets for all m targets of a simplicial-complex entity at once. Under mild assumptions it **guarantees user-specified per-target coverage**, and the realized miscoverage across targets stays close to the nominal level with high probability. Experiments on a range of simplicial-complex prediction tasks show that it achieves the target coverage with small, informative prediction sets.

papers.title: ROSTrans: Empirically Benchmarking LLMs for ROS1-to-ROS2 Migration
papers.abstract: Although large language models have shown strong capabilities in domain-specific code generation, their performance in robotics software development, especially for the Robot Operating System (ROS), remains largely unexplored. ROS code generation presents distinctive challenges, including complex inter-node coordination, middleware configuration, and lifecycle semantics that go far beyond standard coding benchmarks, and many important correctness properties become observable only once migrated nodes are launched and communicate. We present ROSTrans, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on ROS1-to-ROS2 code migration, a representative and practically important setting for ROS code generation. ROSTrans comprises 108 scaffolded completion tasks drawn from a diverse set of 70+ open-source ROS1 repositories and organized into a hierarchical taxonomy assessing interface-level, behavioral-level and system-level correctness. For every task we establish an executable reference: a verified ROS2 implementation, a runtime test suite that launches the nodes and exercises their topics, services, actions and parameters, and a container ensuring reproducibility. Candidates are scored by injecting only their target files into an otherwise fixed copy of the reference package, so a candidate can neither supply nor weaken the tests it is judged by. Evaluating six frontier LLMs over five stochastic generations per task, we find pass@1 below 10.9%, and that 56.5% of all samples build successfully and then fail at runtime,and 32.0% fail runtime assertions on the migrated interfaces, a class of error no compile-only oracle can detect. Execution-guided repair further improves task success, reaching 49.1% and 47.2% for Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.5 after three rounds, respectively.
papers.summary: `ROSTrans` benchmarks LLMs on migrating Robot Operating System code from ROS1 to ROS2, where many correctness properties appear only once the nodes launch and communicate. It contains 108 scaffolded tasks from more than 70 open-source repositories. Each task comes with a verified ROS2 reference, a runtime test suite that exercises topics, services, actions and parameters, and a container; candidates are scored by injecting only their target files, so they cannot alter the tests. Across six frontier LLMs, **pass@1 stays below 10.9%**, and 56.5% of samples build successfully but then fail at runtime, a class of error that compile-only checks miss. Three rounds of execution-guided repair raise success to 49.1% for `Claude Opus 4.6` and 47.2% for `GPT-5.5`.

papers.title: ImplicitHop: Evaluating knowledge integration across context and memory
papers.abstract: The ability to integrate new information and deduce its consequences is central to learning, understanding, and reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Whether information arrives during training or in-context, models must not only store local facts, but propagate their long-range implications globally. To explore information integration in LLMs, we introduce two complementary natural language benchmarks for large-scale evaluation of deductive reasoning as a function of inference depth. The first is a formal graph benchmark enabling controlled evaluation over a wide range of graph topologies and integration tasks; the second is a knowledge composition benchmark grounded in real-world knowledge graphs. We use these benchmarks to compare knowledge integration from information encoded in context versus information encoded in model weights during pretraining, evaluating a set of open models implicitly, without chain of thought. We find that accuracy decays sharply with increased composition length for both pretrained and in-context knowledge. Information presented in-context, however, substantially outperforms deduction over information encoded in weights. These results quantify a fundamental limitation of current models with direct implications for prompt-based control of agent behavior and for continual learning strategies, and they provide a foundation for developing training, prompting, and integration methods that support deeper reasoning.
papers.summary: To measure how well LLMs propagate the long-range consequences of facts, `ImplicitHop` provides two benchmarks of deductive reasoning as a function of inference depth: a formal graph benchmark with controlled topologies, and a knowledge-composition benchmark grounded in real-world knowledge graphs.
