Open models are tested without chain of thought, on facts given either in context or learned in their weights during pretraining. **Accuracy decays sharply as composition length grows** in both settings, but deduction over in-context information is substantially better than deduction over knowledge stored in weights. The authors argue this limits prompt-based control of agents and has implications for continual learning.

papers.title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It exposes a context problem: an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents, and fills the window with unused passages. The missing layer is knowledge compilation: a configurable ingestion pipeline where LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk contains alone--navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis, and memory. Compilation is not a better retriever: under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. It is a supply layer. A navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs--the mechanism we measure--cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction; this implies a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, though substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and carries its own latency cost. Other artifacts--ontology, graph, wiki, timeline, mind map, memory--pay off in deployment (governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, continuity) where accuracy benchmarks cannot see them. We describe RAGFlow's pipeline and harness (open source at https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow), which turns the loop into five disciplined stations and keeps the context entering the model the smallest sufficient set; together they form an agent-native database: a store that hands the agent compiled, governed context instead of a ranked list of passages.
papers.summary: An agentic search harness using only `BM25` or grep with `MiniMax M3` already answers 85% of `BrowseComp-Plus` and 91% of `FRAMES`, so the authors argue the remaining problem in retrieval-augmented generation is context bloat, not accuracy. They propose knowledge compilation, an ingestion layer in which LLMs enrich documents with navigation trees, entity graphs, timelines and similar artifacts. These structures gave no measurable accuracy gain under a competent harness. However, a navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs **cuts query tokens by 38% on average**, and a decision gate reduces latency from 140 s to 30 s. The pipeline and harness are released as part of the open-source `RAGFlow`.

papers.title: CAP: Learning to Optimize from Sparse Observations of Related Tasks
papers.abstract: In experiment-driven black-box optimization, each evaluation can consume materials, equipment time, and other resources, limiting the number of experiments available for a new task. Records from completed related optimization campaigns could help, but learning a sequential query policy remains challenging when task-specific experience consists of only a few sparse histories. We propose CAP (Candidate Acquisition Policy), which models shared structure and task-specific variation in fixed historical records to sample interactive practice functions. On these functions, CAP learns a feedback-conditioned query policy aimed at final optimization performance under a fixed evaluation budget. At deployment, its parameters remain fixed while each new observation informs the next query. Across five synthetic task families spanning 6 and 20 dimensions and two engineering simulation benchmarks, BOPTEST and SU2, CAP attains the lowest median final-budget value among the reported methods on four synthetic families and both engineering benchmarks. These results indicate that sparse records from completed related tasks can support adaptive query decisions on new tasks, making more effective use of limited, costly experimental evaluations.
papers.summary: In experiment-driven black-box optimization each evaluation is expensive, and data from related past campaigns is often limited to a few sparse histories. Candidate Acquisition Policy (`CAP`) models the shared structure and task-specific variation in those records to generate practice functions, then learns a feedback-conditioned query policy on them aimed at the best final result within a fixed evaluation budget. At deployment its parameters stay fixed, and each new observation informs the next query. `CAP` attains **the lowest median final-budget value on four of five synthetic task families** and on both engineering simulation benchmarks, `BOPTEST` and `SU2`.

papers.title: S2TDR: Structured Multimodal Reconstruction for Sticker-Aware Dialogue Understanding
papers.abstract: Stickers are widely used in social media dialogues to express affect, stance, and intent beyond literal text. Their meanings are often non-literal and context-dependent, making them difficult to handle with generic visual fusion or standalone captioning. We propose Sticker-to-Text Dialogue Reconstruction (S2TDR), a structured multimodal reconstruction framework that converts sticker turns into contextually appropriate textual utterances. S2TDR decomposes sticker interpretation into visual cue extraction, affective-intent inference, and context-aware dialogue reconstruction, using OCR text only as an auxiliary cue when available. The reconstructed dialogue can then be consumed by existing text-based dialogue models. Experiments on sentiment analysis, intent recognition, and dialogue summarization show that S2TDR generally improves multiple downstream models over direct sticker integration methods. Further analyses on component ablations, OCR-empty stickers, and reconstruction quality indicate that structured reconstruction provides an interpretable and effective way to integrate sticker semantics into dialogue understanding.
papers.summary: Stickers in social-media dialogues carry non-literal, context-dependent meaning that generic visual fusion or standalone captioning handles poorly. Sticker-to-Text Dialogue Reconstruction (`S2TDR`) breaks sticker interpretation into visual cue extraction, affective-intent inference and context-aware reconstruction, then rewrites each sticker turn as a textual utterance, using OCR text only as an auxiliary cue. Existing text-only dialogue models can consume the reconstructed dialogue directly. Across sentiment analysis, intent recognition and dialogue summarization, it **generally improves multiple downstream models** over methods that integrate stickers directly.

papers.title: TraceSpec: Understanding and Improving Speculative Decoding for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents execute tasks through repeated model calls over evolving histories of reasoning, actions, and tool feedback. Aggregate speculative-decoding metrics merge these distinct decisions, providing limited guidance on where draft supervision is needed. We present TraceSpec, a framework connecting trajectory evaluation with adaptive draft training. It combines dynamic execution with fixed-prefix replay and introduces TraceSpec-Traj, a corpus of 10,000 training states and 2,500 test states spanning browsing and software engineering. Analysis of five speculative baselines reveals that aggregate acceptance can rise with context length while declining within matched late browsing actions. Workload and phase further distinguish these trends, motivating supervision guided by trajectory conditions. TraceSpec trains on intermediate assistant turns and allocates a fixed prediction budget using state-conditioned estimates of prefix-aware acceptance gaps. Across three target sizes and two temperatures, it improves replay throughput by 12.5% to 22.6% over its DSpark base. Qwen3-4B ablations show that adaptive allocation increases accepted length by 3.3% to 10.0% over fixed full-turn supervision, with additional comparisons substantiating the roles of state conditioning and consecutive-token agreement. The resulting evaluation resources, trajectory findings, and training strategy connect the analysis of agent execution to practical draft improvement.
papers.summary: Aggregate speculative-decoding metrics blur together the distinct decisions an LLM agent makes over a trajectory, so they give little guidance on where the draft model needs more training. `TraceSpec` pairs dynamic execution with fixed-prefix replay and releases `TraceSpec-Traj`, a set of 10,000 training and 2,500 test states from browsing and software-engineering tasks. Its analysis shows that aggregate acceptance can rise with context length even while it falls on matched late browsing actions. The method trains the draft model on intermediate assistant turns and allocates a fixed prediction budget according to state-conditioned estimates of acceptance gaps, **improving replay throughput by 12.5% to 22.6%** over its `DSpark` base.

papers.title: General Frequency Principle for Linear Approximation Classes
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study a general frequency principle under gradient descent training for the finite linear approximation classes. Under suitable assumptions, we prove that the learner amplitude relative to the target amplitude vanishes at high frequencies, uniformly throughout training. We also establish sufficient conditions for low-frequency priority, covering single-frequency targets trained separately and two frequency components trained in the same run. This general frequency principle does not imply that lower frequencies always converge faster. Instead, for two frequencies that satisfy certain comparison conditions, one component will take longer to learn than the other; and in common cases, the longer component has higher frequency. Numerical experiments with Legendre and trigonometric bases validate the theoretical results.
papers.summary: The frequency principle says that networks trained by gradient descent tend to fit low frequencies before high ones. This work studies a general version of it for finite linear approximation classes. Under suitable assumptions, the authors prove that the learner's amplitude relative to the target **vanishes at high frequencies uniformly throughout training**, and they give sufficient conditions for low-frequency priority. They also show that lower frequencies do not always converge faster; under certain comparison conditions one component takes longer, and in common cases that is the higher-frequency one. Experiments with Legendre and trigonometric bases confirm the theory.

papers.title: Researcher-in-the-Loop Evolutionary Discovery of Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Code Families
papers.abstract: LLM-guided program evolution can produce mathematical constructions, but validity, generality, and reproducibility require distinct evidence. We develop a researcher-in-the-loop discovery pipeline that combines program evolution, exact evaluation, mathematical generalization, certified nonexistence checks, and formal proof checking. We apply it to entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes (EAQECCs). Starting from tasks that did not specify a family formula, evolved programs produced finite qubit constructions whose structure researchers generalized to the family $[[n,1,n-1;n-q-1]]_q$ for prime powers $q\ge3$ at $n\ge2q+1$ and for $q=2$ at odd $n\ge5$. Lean checks the algebraic certificate underlying this family. Together with entanglement lifting, the family closes 54 gaps in archived EAQECC tables. The released evidence includes 115 verified code records, ten nonexistence results with checked DRAT proofs, family implementations, and preserved search programs for exact checks and seeded replay. In a controlled cohort of eight paired generation blocks, validation-selected iterative programs achieve success in 46.1% and 31.6% of held-out executions at unseen lengths $n=13,15$, compared with 19.5% and 3.1% for independently generated programs. In this setting, program evolution and researcher analysis turn finite computational discoveries into a proved family with independently checkable evidence.
papers.summary: LLM-guided program evolution can produce mathematical constructions, but establishing that they are valid and general requires separate evidence. The authors combine program evolution with exact evaluation, researcher-led generalization, certified nonexistence checks and `Lean` proof checking, and apply this pipeline to entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes. Evolved programs found finite constructions that researchers generalized into the proved family `[[n,1,n-1;n-q-1]]_q`, which, together with entanglement lifting, **closes 54 gaps in archived code tables**. In controlled comparisons, iteratively evolved programs succeed far more often than independently generated ones on unseen code lengths, for example 46.1% versus 19.5% at n=13.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for End-to-End Self-Driving
papers.abstract: End-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving models achieve strong planning performance but remain largely opaque, limiting observability and trust. We apply mechanistic interpretability to E2E driving by training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on the internal activations of a simple, single-camera end-to-end path planning model. Unsupervised clustering of SAE latents reveals interpretable structure aligned with route intent, vehicle speed, and braking behavior, recovering route intent with 98.3% accuracy without supervision. Through paired counterfactual image edits, we further show that specific SAE features are visually grounded and systematically respond to scene changes such as traffic light state and stop sign presence. Steering individual SAE latents produces predictable, monotonic changes in planner outputs including lateral displacement, curvature, and braking. Finally, we demonstrate a practical application of these representations: we build a lightweight adapter trained on SAE latents that reduces trajectory selection error by 3.44%, outperforming an equivalent adapter that omits SAE latents, confirming that the sparse representation captures useful information for interpretability. Code and visualizations are available at https://mgagvani.github.io/mechanistic-interpretability-for-e2e-driving/
papers.summary: End-to-end self-driving models plan well but are opaque. The authors train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on the internal activations of a simple single-camera path-planning model. Unsupervised clustering of the SAE latents reveals structure tied to route intent, speed and braking, **recovering route intent with 98.3% accuracy** without supervision. Counterfactual image edits show that individual features respond to visual cues such as traffic-light state and stop signs, and steering a single latent changes the planner's output predictably. A lightweight adapter trained on the SAE latents reduces trajectory selection error by 3.44%.

papers.title: When AI Investigators Cannot Trust Their Tools: Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification for Cyber Threat Investigation
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly triage security alerts by combining the outputs of several detection tools, implicitly treating those tools as trustworthy. Unlike prior work on conflicts between a model's knowledge and its context, we study conflicts among the tools themselves: what happens when this machine-generated evidence is conflicting or wrong. On the corrected CIC-IDS2017 dataset, four heterogeneous detectors emit labels and confidences that we corrupt under a threat model varying the number of corrupted tools, the persistence of the corruption, and the confidence attached to wrong outputs. Across open-weight LLMs from 3B to 14B parameters, unverified investigators are fragile: one corrupted detector out of four lowers naive accuracy to .50-.72, three lower every unverified investigator to .13 or less, and honest disagreement alone makes them abstain on up to 63% of flows. We propose Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification (CAV), built from established components: an equal-weight vote that ignores reported confidences, an evidence-conflict gate, and an independent nearest-neighbour trust check that tests the leading candidates. With its prompt frozen before testing, CAV-LLM improves on the naive investigator in every corrupted condition ($p < 0.001$), reaching .84-.88 with three corrupted detectors against at most .08, while calling the LLM on 0.4% of clean traffic. A fixed verification rule is as accurate or better unless most tools are corrupted. When we make the independent channel itself noisy, CAV inherits its errors: it stays ahead when two or more tools are corrupted, but adding the channel as an extra voter is better when at most one is. Verification thus moves trust from the tools to the check, which must be measured and protected in turn.
papers.summary: LLM agents that triage security alerts usually trust the outputs of the detection tools they combine. Using four detectors on the corrected `CIC-IDS2017` dataset, the authors corrupt tool outputs and find that unverified investigators built on 3B to 14B open-weight models are fragile: three corrupted detectors drive their accuracy to 0.13 or less. Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification (`CAV`) combines an equal-weight vote that ignores reported confidences, an evidence-conflict gate and an independent nearest-neighbour trust check. With three detectors corrupted, it **restores accuracy to 0.84 to 0.88** while calling the LLM on only 0.4% of clean traffic. If that independent check is itself noisy, `CAV` inherits its errors, so the trust problem moves to the check, which must be measured and protected in turn.

papers.title: Role-Aware Server Optimization for Multimodal Federated Learning with Missing Modalities
papers.abstract: Multimodal federated learning (MFL) trains a shared model by aggregating client updates without exchanging raw data. Under missing modalities, clients adapt active modality encoders and a shared prediction block (fusion and classifier) to different input subsets. This raises two server-side questions: which clients should contribute to each component, and how should their aggregates be incorporated across rounds? We observe that an absent-modality encoder can still adapt through missing-input handling. Availability- based aggregation can therefore omit its update while retaining jointly learned prediction-block updates. Contributor selection also shapes server momentum, a weighted history of aggregated updates. We observe that prediction-block momentum can improve or reduce performance depending on the encoder update policy. We therefore propose Role-Aware Server Optimization (RASO), which coordinates contributor selection with role-specific server updates. RASO selects contributors through prediction dependence and inclusion in local optimization, retains encoder momentum, and synchronizes the shared prediction block to its current aggregate. Experiments across datasets and fusion architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of RASO under missing modalities.
papers.summary: In multimodal federated learning (MFL), clients train a shared model without sharing raw data, but when some clients lack certain input modalities the server must decide which clients should update each model component and how to combine those updates across rounds. The authors observe that an encoder for a missing modality still changes through missing-input handling, and that server momentum on the shared prediction block can help or hurt depending on how encoders are updated. They propose `RASO` (Role-Aware Server Optimization), which picks contributors by their dependence on the prediction block and their participation in local optimization. It keeps momentum for encoders but **synchronizes the shared fusion-and-classifier block directly to its current aggregate**. Experiments across several datasets and fusion architectures show gains under missing modalities.

papers.title: Beyond CLIP: Calibrated (Few-Shot) Defect Detection With System One Decision Models
papers.abstract: Cameras and vision sensors are widely used for product and process inspection in manufacturing environments. Traditionally, this process required thousands of images of both nominal and defective products to train such models. Recent research shows that vision transformer (ViT) models, such as CLIP, can reduce this requirement to 50-100 images per nominal and defective class. However, collecting even 50 defective images can be difficult in high-yield or low-volume manufacturing processes. In this paper, we examine the utility of two recently proposed structured decision models (Jev and Clef-Flash) in applications using as few as k=2 reference images per class at inference. In the process, we provide three main contributions: (a) a framework for k-shot learning of these models for image classification/inspection applications; (b) an agentic approach for automatically refining the text descriptions that guide image classification in these decision models; and (c) an approach to calibrate the resulting defect probabilities to improve their reliability for inspection decisions. We test these contributions in five manufacturing case studies. Using two reference images per class, both Jev and Clef-Flash outperform CLIP's test accuracies with the same references (0.75-1.00 [Jev] and 0.71-0.99 [Clef-Flash] vs 0.67-0.84 [CLIP]). Furthermore, we show that our agentic refinement of text descriptions significantly improves accuracy across 6 of 8 model-application combinations, and our calibration approach reduces the Brier score in 13 of the 15 model-application configurations. To support the reproducibility of our work, we provide our replication code and have created the R "decisions" package for evaluating additional models. We also provide a publicly available web app that allows practitioners to inspect their own images with no code.
papers.summary: Visual defect inspection in manufacturing usually needs many defective examples, which are hard to collect in high-yield or low-volume production. The authors adapt two structured decision models, `Jev` and `Clef-Flash`, to k-shot inspection with as few as two reference images per class. They add an agentic loop that refines the text descriptions guiding classification, plus a calibration step for defect probabilities. Across five manufacturing case studies, **both models beat `CLIP` with two references per class (accuracies of 0.75–1.00 for `Jev` and 0.71–0.99 for `Clef-Flash`, versus 0.67–0.84 for `CLIP`)**, and calibration lowers the Brier score in 13 of 15 configurations; the authors also release an R package and a no-code web app.

papers.title: Shifting Focus by Reliability: Geometric Fusion Modulation for Robust RGB-T Detection
papers.abstract: RGB-thermal (RGB-T) object detectors combine visible and thermal imagery for robust detection, but signal corruption in either stream can substantially degrade accuracy. Restoration-based methods incur significant latency and do not consistently improve downstream accuracy, raising a more direct question: rather than restoring corrupted inputs, can we efficiently adapt the detector to their varying signal quality? Conventional PEFT offers an efficient route, but its input-independent corrections cannot track diverse test-time corruptions. Our controlled corruption sweeps show that corruption types have similar effects near clean conditions but diverge increasingly with severity, motivating corruption-aware, per-input adaptation. We therefore propose PG-FM (Prompt-Guided Feature Modulation), which adapts RGB-T object detectors to the estimated corruption type and severity of each modality. Under controlled RGB-T corruption simulations, PG-FM preserves clean-set performance, improves mAP50 by up to 20.8 points on FLIR and 19.9 points on KAIST, and transfers without retraining to unmodified, naturally acquired external RGB-T datasets.
papers.summary: RGB-thermal (RGB-T) object detectors lose accuracy when either the visible or the thermal stream is corrupted, and restoring the images first adds latency without reliably improving detection. Controlled sweeps show that different corruption types behave similarly when mild but diverge as severity grows, so fixed parameter-efficient fine-tuning cannot keep up. The proposed `PG-FM` (Prompt-Guided Feature Modulation) estimates the corruption type and severity of each modality for every input and modulates the detector's features to match. It keeps clean-data performance, **improves mAP50 by up to 20.8 points on `FLIR` and 19.9 points on `KAIST`** under simulated corruption, and transfers without retraining to naturally captured RGB-T datasets.

papers.title: From Evaluation to Evolution: Benchmarking Image Editing and Evolving Image Models
papers.abstract: Real-world image editing requires coordinating multiple visual transformations with content preservation and reference constraints, yet aggregate scores can readily obscure unmet local requirements. Effective evaluation must therefore identify local failures and translate them into priorities for subsequent model improvement. We introduce WeGenEditBench, comprising 2,740 evaluation instances and 148 task types across single-image, text-intensive, and multi-reference editing. Pre-generated checklists shared across models decompose each request into atomic requirements; item-level deductions and visual evidence are established first and then summarized into scores for edit execution, preservation, visual quality, and task-specific correctness. To support the experience-acquisition component of recursive self-improvement (RSI), we develop WeGenEvoStudio, a unified multi-agent harness for RSI-oriented learning that integrates model-conditioned failure diagnosis, retrieval-grounded data construction, supervised adaptation, and re-evaluation. Among 15 evaluated configurations, GPT-Image-2 leads single-image editing with an Overall score of 4.076, while Seedream-5.0-Pro leads text-intensive editing at 4.291. Evolution experiments across four generation and editing benchmarks demonstrate substantial targeted gains: on their report-selected Top-5 single-image targets, FLUX.2 [dev] improves Overall from 1.083 to 3.517, while Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 gains 13.2%. Together, our benchmark and harness provide a foundation for developing more reliable image models through interpretable evaluation and feedback-driven learning.
papers.summary: Aggregate scores for image editing can hide individual requirements a model failed to meet, so the authors build `WeGenEditBench`, a benchmark of 2,740 instances covering 148 task types across single-image, text-heavy, and multi-reference editing. It breaks each request into a checklist of atomic requirements and records item-level deductions with visual evidence before rolling them up into scores. `GPT-Image-2` leads single-image editing and `Seedream-5.0-Pro` leads text-intensive editing among 15 configurations. A companion multi-agent harness, `WeGenEvoStudio`, turns diagnosed failures into retrieved training data, fine-tunes the model, and re-evaluates it; on its targeted tasks **`FLUX.2 [dev]` rises from 1.083 to 3.517 Overall**.

papers.title: Beyond Scarcity: When Encoder Adaptation Is Worthwhile
papers.abstract: Long-tailed recognition often learns a shared representation before correcting the classifier for class imbalance. Once the classifier has been rebalanced, however, final accuracy does not reveal whether further encoder adaptation remains worthwhile. Standard imbalance benchmarks obscure this question because they jointly vary the number of distinct examples available to rare classes and the frequency with which those examples shape the representation. We introduce a controlled evaluation framework that separates unique support from representation allocation and estimates the incremental value of encoder updates through matched classifier-only and full-network continuations from a common corrected model. The framework combines stage-specific controls, multiple representation and adaptation objectives, whole-distribution metrics, and hierarchical inference over class assignments, support reconstructions, and optimization runs. Across the controlled study, the same low-support regime moves from one in which classifier-only training is adequate to one in which encoder adaptation yields a practically meaningful benefit solely as representation allocation becomes more imbalanced. The transition persists across classifier corrections, representation objectives, normalization and augmentation controls, and ImageNet-scale evaluation, while preserving frequent-class accuracy. Under the prespecified one-percentage-point operating margin, the two regimes are separated by simultaneous confidence bounds. These results show that benchmark construction can alter a post-correction training decision and that support size alone does not characterize the remaining value of representation adaptation.
papers.summary: In long-tailed recognition, a common recipe trains a shared encoder and then rebalances the classifier, but it is unclear when further updating the encoder still pays off. The authors argue that standard benchmarks confound two factors: how many distinct examples rare classes have, and how often those examples shape the representation. Their controlled evaluation framework separates these factors and compares matched classifier-only and full-network continuations from the same corrected model. With the number of rare-class examples held fixed, **encoder adaptation shifts from unnecessary to meaningfully beneficial purely as representation allocation becomes more imbalanced**. The effect persists across classifier corrections, training objectives, and an `ImageNet`-scale evaluation.

papers.title: Beyond Response Scoring: An AI-aware Cognitive Supervision Framework for Automated Mathematical Short Answer Grading
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved remarkable success in automated short answer grading (ASAG). However, current methods in ASAG struggle to comprehend, reason about and evaluate complex mathematical answers involving symbols and formulas. These score-only methods fail to generalize across diverse responses and skill states associated with identical scores. Moreover, they ignore the potential upward bias introduced by generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) usage in assessing students' performance and knowledge mastery. To address these limitations, we propose AICG (AI-aware Cognitive-supervised Grading), a two-branch multi-task framework. The first branch combines RoBERTa-based regression, ordinal, and classification heads for individual-answer grading. The second branch uses an expert-designed Q-matrix to associate responses with assessed skills and jointly predicts G-DINA-derived skill mastery and learning gain. Through the shared encoder, these skill-level targets provide cognitive supervision for answer grading beyond score labels. AICG further uses a Gen-AI detector, trained through supervised contrastive pretraining followed by linear classification, to estimate assistance probabilities and convert them into reliability weights, attenuating unreliable cognitive evidence during learning assessment. We conduct experiments on 49,402 instructor-graded responses spanning 19 academic semesters. Relative to RoBERTa regression, AICG reduces mean absolute error (MAE) by 50.3% and improves quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) from 0.798 to 0.927. Ablations identify Q-matrix-guided cognitive supervision as the primary source of improvement, while AI-aware weighting further reduces overall MAE by 4.2% over the unweighted cognitive model and consistently improves MAE and QWK across the four most recent post-Gen-AI semesters.
papers.summary: Automated short answer grading (ASAG) models struggle with mathematical answers full of symbols and formulas, and they ignore how help from generative AI can inflate apparent student mastery. `AICG` (AI-aware Cognitive-supervised Grading) pairs a `RoBERTa`-based grading branch with a second branch that predicts skill mastery and learning gain, using an expert-designed Q-matrix and the `G-DINA` cognitive diagnosis model. A generative-AI detector turns the estimated probability of AI assistance into reliability weights that down-weight suspect evidence. On 49,402 instructor-graded responses from 19 semesters, **`AICG` cuts mean absolute error by 50.3% relative to `RoBERTa` regression and raises quadratic weighted kappa from 0.798 to 0.927**, with the Q-matrix supervision accounting for most of the gain.

papers.title: A Positional Realizability Theory of Length Generalization in Single-Head Attention
papers.abstract: Why does length generalization (LG) depend so sharply on the positional encoding (PE)? Relative schemes extrapolate fixed offsets, absolute schemes fix positions, and neither handles growing offsets. We give a realizability theory for a deliberately controlled abstraction, a single positional-only attention head, that derives this well-documented empirical pattern and says precisely where it holds and breaks. The device is a simulation transfer operator $T_L$ that re-evaluates a selected length-$L_0$-realizing positional kernel on the longer grid, with a scalar $\alpha_L \in [0,1]$ read off before any training from $(\Phi, t_n)$ alone. Here $\alpha_L$ serves as the computable witness of that taxonomy's derivation, not as a stronger empirical predictor. Our results are a relative-head deep-row characterization for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer (Theorem 2), an absolute/relative duality that derives the pattern (Proposition 4), a learned-absolute underdetermination result, and a static expressivity bound; a sufficiency theorem (Theorem 1) bridges $\alpha_L$ to LG, and the general deterministic case is a precise open conjecture (correcting a tempting but invalid "outside-colspan" argument). Experiments confirm the structure: in the controlled single-head regime $\alpha_L$ exactly separates the taxonomy's generalizing and non-generalizing (PE, task) cells (2625 trained-model measurements; stable at vocab 64/d=128). Together, these results turn the received PE taxonomy into a positional-kernel transfer theorem, and identify the content and depth mechanisms that escape it. The theory concerns the positional channel alone: tasks whose targets depend on token content, including the standard length-generalization suite such as addition and sorting, fall outside Theorem 2.
papers.summary: Whether transformers generalize to sequences longer than those seen in training depends heavily on the positional encoding, and this work gives a formal account of why for a simplified setting: a single attention head that uses only positional information. The central device is a transfer operator that re-evaluates a positional kernel learned at the training length on a longer grid, along with a scalar `α_L` that can be computed before any training. Results include a characterization for relative encodings, a duality between absolute and relative schemes that derives the familiar empirical pattern, and an underdetermination result for learned absolute encodings. In 2,625 trained-model measurements, **`α_L` exactly separates the generalizing and non-generalizing combinations of encoding and task**, though content-dependent tasks such as addition and sorting fall outside the main theorem.

papers.title: Corroborative Learning: Mutual Enhancement through Task-Response Reconstruction
papers.abstract: In pattern analysis, models trained independently for the same task often develop complementary capabilities through differences in architecture, data, and optimization. Exploiting complementarity while retaining independent deployment is central to collaborative learning. Most methods establish transfer by reducing differences in predictions, relations, or representations between target and collaborator, although these differences also underlie complementarity. This creates a structural trade-off between reducing differences for knowledge exchange and preserving them for complementarity. We therefore propose Corroborative Learning (CL). Each model forms task-driven responses, with cross-group support from its collaborator. Source-excluded reconstruction of response increments from collaborator representations separates fitting and evaluation across disjoint groups and selectively constrains directions by cross-group reconstructability. The process requires no direct output or feature matching or additional inference dependency. Furthermore, with linear reconstruction and fixed collaborator representations, the loss equals a positive semidefinite directional regularizer, constraining less reconstructable directions more strongly. Signal and noise conditions characterize when directional shrinkage reduces response-estimation error. Across six language tasks, 24 models, and 36 pairs, CL improves over capacity-matched independent adaptation on every task, with positive gains across most directed model combinations. Pairwise comparisons show broad advantages over transfer and mutual-learning methods and different gains from complementarity across collaboration rules. Low-label language and vision results support cross-domain applicability. Task-relevant differences can support mutual enhancement without eliminating disagreement.
papers.summary: When independently trained models collaborate, methods that align their predictions or representations tend to erase the very differences that make them complementary. `Corroborative Learning` instead has each model reconstruct its task-driven response increments from its collaborator's representations, with fitting and evaluation done on disjoint data groups. This requires no output or feature matching and adds no dependency at inference time. In the linear case the loss reduces to a directional regularizer that constrains hard-to-reconstruct directions most strongly. Across six language tasks, 24 models, and 36 model pairs, **the method beats capacity-matched independent adaptation on every task**, and low-label vision results suggest it also works outside language.

papers.title: RTL-Interact: Training EDA-Interactive Models for Multi-Task RTL Design
papers.abstract: Large language models offer a promising route to register-transfer-level (RTL) design, but reliable implementations require checking and revision based on electronic design automation (EDA) tools' feedback. Existing RTL-specialized models often lack learned interaction with such EDA tools or rely on separate generation and repair components. We introduce RTL-Interact, a multi-task post-training framework that trains a single RTL-specialized model to generate RTL, construct task-appropriate EDA checks, and revise implementations using tool feedback. The framework combines automatically constructed multi-task demonstrations with staged supervision from chain-of-thought to tool-integrated reasoning. We further introduce Pattern-Aware Policy Optimization (PAPO) for multi-task reinforcement learning. PAPO augments Group Relative Policy Optimization with correctness-gated rewards that favor concise successful checking while rewarding effective revision, and uses task grouping to preserve coverage across objectives. On CVDP, RTL-Interact-32B achieves 48.7% weighted Pass@1 and 68.9% Pass@5, surpassing its teacher model, DeepSeek-V3.2, while RTL-Interact-8B achieves 44.9% weighted Pass@1. Additionally, we show that PAPO can reduce average tool calls by 63.8% while improving Pass@1. Both models also outperform all RTL-specialized baselines on VerilogEval v2 and RTLLM v2, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method.
papers.summary: Language models that write register-transfer-level (RTL) hardware code need to check and revise their output using feedback from electronic design automation (EDA) tools, yet existing RTL models rarely learn that interaction. `RTL-Interact` post-trains a single model to generate RTL, construct appropriate EDA checks, and repair its code from tool feedback. Training moves in stages from chain-of-thought to tool-integrated reasoning and ends with `PAPO`, a variant of `GRPO` with correctness-gated rewards and task grouping. **`RTL-Interact-32B` reaches 48.7% weighted Pass@1 on `CVDP`, surpassing its teacher `DeepSeek-V3.2`**, while `PAPO` cuts average tool calls by 63.8% and still improves accuracy. Both the 32B and 8B models beat RTL-specialized baselines on `VerilogEval v2` and `RTLLM v2`.

papers.title: Coarse3D: Controllable and Faithful Sparse Structure Generation for Image-to-3D
papers.abstract: Coarse-to-fine 3D-native generation relies heavily on the first-stage sparse structure, which determines the global orientation and overall geometry for subsequent refinement. However, existing coarse generators suffer from two key limitations: their orientation is difficult to control due to ambiguous semantic canonicalization, and their structures are often inconsistent with input images due to weak 2D-3D grounding. We propose Coarse3D, a sparse-structure generation model that produces orientation-controllable and structurally faithful voxel geometry from arbitrary unposed images. Coarse3D introduces three designs: a first-frame anchored canonical space that aligns generation with the first input view while preserving object-centric normalization; a dual-tower DiT that couples generation with auxiliary feed-forward reconstruction to learn spatially grounded features; and spatial-prior guided attention that regularizes cross-attention with pixel-to-voxel correspondence. Coarse3D can directly replace the coarse stage of existing pipelines. Experiments show that it substantially improves sparse structure quality and consistently enhances final 3D generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.summary: Coarse-to-fine 3D generators depend on a first-stage sparse voxel structure, but current coarse generators produce orientations that are hard to control and shapes that often disagree with the input images. `Coarse3D` anchors its canonical space to the first input view and uses a dual-tower diffusion transformer (DiT) that couples generation with auxiliary feed-forward reconstruction. It also adds attention guided by pixel-to-voxel correspondence. The model works with arbitrary unposed images and **can directly replace the coarse stage of existing pipelines**, improving both sparse-structure quality and final 3D generation to state-of-the-art levels.

papers.title: TRIDENT and SHAKTI: A Framework and Benchmark for Hindi AI-Text Detection
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly multilingual, distinguishing human-written from AI-generated text is essential for maintaining information integrity. However, research remains English-centric, with limited benchmarks for low-resource languages such as Hindi. To address this gap, we introduce SHAKTI, a large-scale Hindi benchmark covering four genres, eight LLM families, multiple prompting strategies, and adversarial transformations. We evaluate its quality through human annotation and analyze linguistic, grammatical, and sentiment-based differences between human- and AI-generated texts. Building on these findings, we propose TRIDENT, a round-trip translation-based detection framework with three variants: TRIDENT-S (static threshold), TRIDENT-D (dynamic threshold), and TRIDENT-C (logistic regression using multi-distance RTT features). TRIDENT leverages semantic consistency between original and round-trip translated texts to identify AI-generated content. Extensive experiments show that TRIDENT outperforms conventional and supervised baselines, with TRIDENT-S achieving the best overall performance. Further evaluations across seven languages, adversarial settings, and unseen LLMs demonstrate its multilingual applicability and robustness, while highlighting sensitivity to the translation model.
papers.summary: Research on detecting AI-generated text has focused on English, leaving low-resource languages such as Hindi with few benchmarks. `SHAKTI` is a large Hindi benchmark spanning four genres, eight LLM families, several prompting strategies, and adversarial transformations, with quality checked through human annotation. `TRIDENT` detects AI-written text by measuring how semantically consistent a passage stays after round-trip translation, and comes in static-threshold, dynamic-threshold, and logistic-regression variants. **The simple static-threshold variant, `TRIDENT-S`, performs best overall**, beating conventional and supervised baselines and holding up across seven languages, adversarial settings, and unseen LLMs, though results depend on the translation model.

papers.title: Experts Exhibit Structured Redundancy: Structure-Preserving Expert Pruning for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Sparse MoE mechanism significantly improves the trade-off between model capacity and inference efficiency. However, practical deployment still requires storing all experts, resulting in substantial memory overhead. We show that expert outputs in MoE layers exhibit structured redundancy. Across different models and task categories, the stable rank and entropy effective rank of expert outputs are consistently far below the nominal number of experts, while expert output distributions also exhibit fewer effective modes. Motivated by these observations, we reformulate expert pruning as a structure-preserving expert subset selection problem and efficiently optimize it via a greedy strategy, rather than only independently scoring and ranking individual experts or exhaustively searching over expert combinations. We propose two expert pruning methods under the unified structure-preserving framework: Projection Energy Expert Pruning (PEEP), which preserves the functional subspace by maximizing weighted projection energy, and Distributional Coverage Expert Pruning (DCEP), which preserves the distributional geometry by minimizing weighted coverage error. Both methods incorporate router-derived weights as priors, enabling them to jointly preserve the global structural relationships among experts while accounting for the local importance of individual experts. Experiments on DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate that, at the expert retention ratios of 75% and 50%, our methods outperform the state-of-the-art baselines on the majority of benchmarks and consistently achieve the best average performance across both general tasks and mathematical reasoning tasks.
papers.summary: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models are cheap to run per token, but every expert must still be stored in memory. The authors show that expert outputs are structurally redundant: **their effective rank is consistently far below the nominal number of experts**. They therefore frame pruning as selecting a subset of experts that preserves this structure, solved greedily. Two methods follow: `PEEP` preserves the functional subspace by maximizing projection energy, and `DCEP` preserves the shape of the output distribution by minimizing coverage error, with both using router-derived importance weights. At 75% and 50% expert retention on `DeepSeek-V2-Lite` and `Qwen3-30B-A3B`, they achieve the best average scores on general and math-reasoning benchmarks.

papers.title: Generative SDEs with Trainable Diffusion and Density-Based Losses
papers.abstract: We develop a divergence-kernel method for jointly optimizing neural SDE drift and diffusion fields and the initial Gaussian distribution, using losses that depend directly on the terminal density. In two- and eight-dimensional Gaussian-mixture experiments, we learn time-independent fields and obtain far fewer off-mode samples than score-based generators with similar parameter counts. The drift attracts samples toward the modes, while the diffusion helps disperse excess probability between them.
papers.summary: A divergence-kernel method jointly trains the drift field, the diffusion field, and the initial Gaussian of a neural stochastic differential equation (SDE), using losses defined directly on the density at the final time. In two- and eight-dimensional Gaussian-mixture experiments with time-independent fields, **the learned SDEs produce far fewer samples between modes than score-based generators of similar size**. The learned drift pulls samples toward the modes, while the learned diffusion disperses excess probability mass between them.

papers.title: A Unified Framework for Probability Estimation of Data-Dependent Events
papers.abstract:
We study the general problem of estimating $D(\dde(S))$, the probability that an unknown distribution $D$ assigns to an event determined by a sample $S$ of $n$ i.i.d.\ draws from $D$ through a known mapping $\dde$. The estimation algorithm knows $\dde$ and $S$ but does not have access to any additional samples from $D$. This formulation captures classical missing mass, the data-dependent targets of adaptive data analysis and post-selection inference, and the test error of a data-trained predictor, whose estimation was recently studied by \new{Gastpar et al.\ (2024a,b)}. Within this framework we examine the two classical approaches to estimation. The error of the empirical plug-in estimator is exactly a generalization gap, so generalization bounds transfer to it directly. The leave-one-out estimator, which recovers the Good--Turing estimator, is accurate for every mapping that is stable under the deletion of one sample point, including new structured examples such as neighborhoods of the sample and pierced sets.
  The main application of our framework is to error estimation for a predictor that combines a base classifier with memorized exceptions, a structure common in theory and in practice. For it, the test error is exactly the missing mass restricted to the error region of the base classifier, a region selected by the same sample. We formulate the general problem of \emph{adaptive missing mass estimation} to address such dependence and propose a natural hybrid estimator, the Good--Turing estimator restricted to the selected region. We show that the generalization of the base classifier alone does not guarantee the accuracy of this estimator, and derive two bounds on its error: the first one based on the VC dimension of possible error regions and another based on the mutual information of the selected region with the sample.
papers.summary: The authors study a general problem: estimating the probability that an unknown distribution assigns to an event that is itself chosen from the sample, with no fresh data available. The framework covers missing-mass estimation, adaptive data analysis, and estimating a trained predictor's test error. They show that the error of the plug-in estimator is exactly a generalization gap, and that the leave-one-out estimator, which recovers the `Good–Turing` estimator, is accurate whenever the event is stable to deleting one sample point. The main application is predictors that memorize exceptions on top of a base classifier, where **test error equals the missing mass inside a sample-selected error region**. For this case they introduce adaptive missing-mass estimation and bound its error using VC dimension and mutual information.

papers.title: MEMIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization
papers.abstract: Memory has become central to self-evolving LLM agents, which store and retrieve experience from past rollouts to guide future decisions. Existing systems represent this experience as free-form natural language and maintain it by rewriting, which fits tasks whose experience is narratable. However, in scientific discovery and optimization, experience is often a quantity measured by an oracle under a specific context. Rewriting it as text leaves no index for where a record should be, replaces a measurement with a description, and cannot express how interventions interact. To address this, we argue that agent memory for biomolecule optimization should instead be indexable, quantitative, and structured, and we introduce MEMIG. This memory construction framework realizes these three properties. In detail, MEMIG addresses each insight with a domain-grounded identifier and accumulates the quantitative effect measured by a property oracle, so that updates remain local and retrieval becomes an exact lookup. Next, MEMIG connects insights whose interventions are applied together and measures their epistasis by decomposing each evaluated set. Our results show that MEMIG improves performance in most settings across in silico antibody optimization tasks.
papers.summary: Self-improving LLM agents usually store past experience as free-form text that they rewrite over time, which suits narratable tasks but loses information in scientific optimization, where experience consists of measured quantities. `MEMIG` builds agent memory for biomolecule optimization that is indexable, quantitative, and structured. Each insight gets a domain-grounded identifier and accumulates the effect measured by a property oracle, so updates stay local and **retrieval becomes an exact lookup rather than a text search**. The memory also links interventions applied together and measures their epistasis, meaning how their effects interact. `MEMIG` improves results in most in-silico antibody optimization settings.

papers.title: Rome Wasn't Built in One Turn: Replay-Grounded Reward Signals for Long-Horizon Freeciv Agents
papers.abstract: Training language-model agents to play long-horizon strategy games is hard because deterministic feedback is sparse and often arrives only at the end of a game. In-game scores can offer dense signals, but they do not reliably predict future outcomes: in 8-68% of position pairs across eight strategy games, the higher-scoring position leads to the worse outcome. We term this phenomenon scoreboard traps. In Freeciv, an open-source turn-based empire-building game where several players manage units, cities, and diplomacy over hundreds of turns, we look into better reward signals for gameplay agents. To facilitate this, we build CivHarness, an open system that saves current game states, branches on different decisions, and replays the game to future turns to provide measurable long-horizon feedback from saved positions. We use CivHarness to train CivTelescope, an LLM Judge that predicts which one of two game positions will yield the better outcome. On scoreboard-trap pairs, CivTelescope is 1.3-2.0 times more accurate than off-the-shelf language models, and it generalizes to new game starts, later turns, and unseen rules. We then train a Freeciv gameplay agent with CivTelescope as a dense reward, and call this recipe CivMarshmallow. When used in the middle stage of the game where scoreboard traps are common, CivMarshmallow reaches an average training phase gain of 8.94 points, 77% more than the best baseline, the end-of-game reward. Over the full 120-turn game, CivMarshmallow uses a hybrid reward that starts from the scoreboard or the end-of-game reward and shifts to CivTelescope as the game advances; this hybrid reward scores highest among the rewards we compare.
papers.summary: Training language-model agents for long strategy games is difficult because reliable feedback arrives only at the end, and in-game scores are misleading: **in 8–68% of position pairs across eight games, the higher-scoring position leads to the worse outcome**, a failure the authors call scoreboard traps. For the open-source empire-building game Freeciv, they build `CivHarness`, which saves game states, branches on alternative decisions, and replays forward to measure long-horizon consequences. That data trains `CivTelescope`, an LLM judge that predicts which of two positions will end better and is 1.3–2.0 times more accurate than off-the-shelf models on trap pairs. Used as a dense reward, the recipe `CivMarshmallow` gains 77% more than the end-of-game reward baseline in mid-game training, and a hybrid reward that shifts toward the judge as the game advances scores highest over full games.

papers.title: From 1D Benchmarks to Complex 3D Geometries: Can Agents Reliably Specify Problems for Automated PDE Simulation?
papers.abstract: Turning an engineering request into a simulation requires consistent geometry, physics, boundary conditions, and numerical settings. Recent agent-assisted systems automate simulation setup, but successful execution alone does not establish whether the specification preserves the intended problem or correctly handles missing information. We study whether agents can reliably construct complete executable JSON specifications for automated geometry creation, meshing, PDE solving, and result export. Our workflow combines model extraction with deterministic scientific and capability checks, explicit clarification, and validated local patches that preserve unrelated accepted fields. We evaluate specification correctness, execution completion, and numerical verification separately. On 120 template-related requests, the full workflow achieves 98.3% correct first-turn specification and decision outcomes, compared with 92.5% for schema-assisted single shot and 82.5% for model-only: gains of 5.8 and 15.8 percentage points, respectively. It makes no false-ready decisions among the 42 requests requiring clarification or rejection. Component ablations identify contributions from scientific checks and conditional repair. Separate downstream studies cover 1D, 2D, and 3D steady and unsteady, linear and nonlinear problems, including flow and elasticity with complex three-dimensional wing geometries. A 30-case gallery demonstrates automated execution from retained JSON specifications, while 9 of 12 selected live user-to-results tests achieve joint specification, execution, export, and numerical-reference success (75.0%). These results support traceable, engineer-reviewed simulation assistance within the tested scope, while fresh-response regressions identify consistency as a priority for further improvement.
papers.summary: Agents can now automate simulation setup, but a run that executes successfully may still have quietly changed the intended problem or mishandled missing information. The authors study whether agents can produce complete executable JSON specifications covering geometry, meshing, partial differential equation (PDE) solving, and result export. Their workflow combines model extraction with deterministic scientific and capability checks, explicit clarification requests, and validated local patches. On 120 requests, **the full workflow gets 98.3% of first-turn specifications and decisions correct, versus 82.5% for the model alone**, with no false "ready" decisions among the 42 requests that needed clarification or rejection. In live end-to-end tests that include 3D wing geometries, 9 of 12 cases succeed fully.

papers.title: Coarse-Graining Optimal Transport for Rollout-Free Post-Training of Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Flow matching depends critically on the coupling used to pair source and target samples. Optimal transport (OT) couplings can reduce velocity conflict and straighten trajectories; but, in practice, challenges remain: the source comes from a continuous distribution, only a finite number of target samples data are accessible, and the neural network has finite capacity. For these reasons, making the coupling more OT-like may not consistently improve sampling quality, in particular in the low number-of-function-evaluation (NFE) regime. Motivated by this, we introduce ReCouple, a controllable framework that constructs coarse-grained OT couplings, to better understand rollout-free OT-based post-training. We also consider extensions of this basic framework: ReCouple+ extends this toward the continuous-source setting by increasing source resolution, converging to semi-discrete OT in the appropriate limit; and ReCouple++ further adds spatial regularization, motivated by the observation that straight trajectories need not correspond to spatially simple velocity fields. Empirical validation demonstrates the effectiveness of these methods, and it reveals an NFE-dependent interplay between coupling optimality, neural realizability, and generation quality.
papers.summary: Flow matching depends on how source and target samples are paired, and while optimal transport (OT) pairings can straighten trajectories, making the pairing more OT-like does not reliably improve samples when few function evaluations (NFE) are used. `ReCouple` builds controllable coarse-grained OT pairings for post-training without rollouts. `ReCouple+` raises source resolution toward semi-discrete OT, and `ReCouple++` adds spatial regularization, because straight trajectories need not imply simple velocity fields. Experiments show the methods are effective and reveal **an NFE-dependent trade-off between how optimal the pairing is, how easily a network can learn it, and generation quality**.

papers.title: ANGLER: Verifier-Grounded Benchmarking with an Adaptive Attacker for Web Agents
papers.abstract: Web agents are increasingly deployed to complete tasks autonomously on real websites, where adversarially injected content can induce them to perform unauthorized actions. Existing evaluations primarily use fixed attacks or focus on a single attack type, and evaluate attacks at the text level rather than through real state changes, thus underestimating how vulnerable agents are to diverse attacks. To address the gap, we introduce REEF, a benchmark of red-teaming executable environments with faithful verification for measuring the security vulnerabilities of web agents. REEF covers 9 verifier-grounded websites spanning travel, commerce, productivity, media, and communication, and pairs every authentic benign task with a malicious objective delivered through 5 attack types at both the user and the environment level. REEF's state-based verifiers provide the execution feedback that drives ANGLER, an adaptive near-miss-guided lure evolution framework for red-teaming. Rather than evaluating a fixed attack set, ANGLER uses outcomes from prior rollouts to guide LLM-based attack mutation and candidate selection, prioritizing near-miss seeds during refinement. Across 8 VLM-based web agents, ANGLER achieves an end-to-end attack success rate (ASR) of 20.36%, compared with 15.24% for the non-adaptive setting. Compared with attack-free execution on the same benign tasks, attacks generated by ANGLER reduce benign task success rate (BSR) from 61.9% to 44.4%.
papers.summary: Web agents acting on real sites can be manipulated by injected content, but existing evaluations rely on fixed attacks and judge success from text rather than from actual changes in site state. `REEF` is a benchmark of nine executable websites with state-based verifiers, pairing each benign task with a malicious goal delivered through five attack types at both the user and environment level. `ANGLER` uses verifier outcomes from earlier rollouts to guide LLM-driven attack mutation and prioritizes near-miss attempts during refinement. Across eight vision-language-model web agents, **`ANGLER` reaches a 20.36% end-to-end attack success rate versus 15.24% without adaptation**, and its attacks cut benign task success from 61.9% to 44.4%.

papers.title: SPT-Flow: One Integration, Many Futures in Continuous-Time World Models
papers.abstract: Continuous-time world models generate a latent trajectory through a single ODE integration, but adding stochastic conditioning does not ensure that the model uses it. In our teacher-forced baseline, posterior means vary by only about 1% of the prior scale, and matched and swapped latents yield indistinguishable reconstruction PSNR at the reported precision. We study a supervision-shortcut hypothesis: ground-truth intermediate states can reduce the need for trajectory-associated latent information. We introduce SPT-Flow, which samples one latent per trajectory and matches a free-running ODE rollout to demonstration states at multiple readout times. Re-anchoring experiments support the proposed mechanism. On LIBERO, with both models trained for 30k optimizer steps, SPT-Flow improves best-of-10 PSNR over our retrained ODEWorld baseline by 2.0 and 2.4 dB at the mid-trajectory and final frames and reduces mean LPIPS by 23%, with comparable per-sample inference cost. The rollout control recovers most of the accuracy gain; learned latent conditioning adds diversity and best-of-K gains while reducing mean sample accuracy relative to this control. The diagnostics support trajectory-associated latent utilization; semantic mode coverage under matched conditions in the robotic setting remains unverified.
papers.summary: Continuous-time world models generate a latent trajectory through one ordinary differential equation (ODE) integration, but the authors find that a teacher-forced baseline effectively ignores its stochastic latent: swapping latents leaves reconstructions unchanged. They hypothesize that supervising on ground-truth intermediate states removes the need for trajectory-level information. `SPT-Flow` samples one latent per trajectory and matches a free-running ODE rollout to demonstration states at several readout times. On `LIBERO`, **it improves best-of-10 PSNR by 2.0–2.4 dB over a retrained `ODEWorld` baseline and lowers mean LPIPS by 23%** at similar inference cost. Most of the accuracy gain comes from the rollout training itself, while the latent conditioning mainly adds sample diversity.

papers.title: AuditFL: A Contract-Backed Clearing Layer for Open Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) keeps raw data local, but most deployments still rely on a trusted coordinator for client admission, checkpoint distribution, update collection, aggregation, and rewards. This paper presents AuditFL, a contract-backed clearing layer for auditable FL in open settings. AuditFL keeps training and aggregation off chain, stores model artifacts in an assumed reliable off-chain artifact store, and records only content identifiers and economic state on chain. Clients reserve update tickets with deposits, publish update identifiers, and later claim refunds or rewards; the task coordinator publishes global checkpoints and finalizes rounds through deterministic settlement rules. The design does not remove the aggregator, but makes its on-chain round decisions attributable, replayable, auditable, and economically constrained. We implement AuditFL as both a deterministic state-machine prototype and a Solidity contract on a local Ethereum-compatible Anvil chain. On full MNIST with Dirichlet non-IID splits, 12 rounds, and up to 200 clients, AuditFL preserves the Plain FL learning trajectory while its overhead follows closed-form control-plane models. At 200 clients, the contract run issues 5,026 transactions, stores 2,413 off-chain artifacts (144.9 MiB), and consumes 829.7M EVM gas, dominated by per-client reserve and publish calls. Controlled dropout, invalid-update, and artifact-unavailability stress tests reduce inclusion nearly linearly but still finalize rounds, with final-accuracy changes remaining within a few tenths of an accuracy percentage point even under high injected failure rates.
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) keeps raw data local, but most deployments still depend on a trusted coordinator to admit clients, collect and aggregate updates, and pay rewards. `AuditFL` adds a smart-contract clearing layer: training, aggregation and model artifacts stay off chain, while content identifiers, deposits, refunds, rewards and round settlement are recorded on chain. The aggregator still exists, but its round decisions become attributable, replayable and economically constrained. On `MNIST` with non-IID splits and up to 200 clients on a local `Anvil` Ethereum-compatible chain, it matches the learning trajectory of plain FL, using **5,026 transactions and 829.7M gas at 200 clients**; under dropout, invalid-update and missing-artifact stress tests, rounds still finalize and final accuracy shifts by only a few tenths of a point.

papers.title: SciGraphSelect: Auditable Scientific Data Selection through Knowledge--Reasoning Graphs
papers.abstract: Scientific data selection is typically driven by relevance or utility scores, providing limited insight into why a document is retained. We introduce SciGraphSelect, a reference-grounded framework for auditable scientific data selection. SciGraphSelect organizes domain-specific knowledge, reusable reasoning operations, and reference-attested relations into a typed knowledge--reasoning graph, then scores candidate documents using concept coverage, relation and path co-support, and directional alignment. To avoid over-interpreting document embeddings, rich relational structure is preserved on the reference side while candidate-side evidence is treated conservatively without assuming relation entailment. By exposing the reference-grounded evidence behind each selection, SciGraphSelect brings traceability to the upstream construction of scientific training corpora and complements downstream scientific verification.
papers.summary: Scientific training data is usually selected with relevance or utility scores, which say little about why a document was kept. `SciGraphSelect` builds a typed knowledge–reasoning graph of domain concepts, reusable reasoning operations and relations attested by reference sources. Candidate documents are scored on concept coverage, support for relations and paths, and directional alignment, and the scoring deliberately does not assume that relations hold on the candidate side. The main claim is that **each selection decision comes with traceable, reference-grounded evidence**, which makes building scientific corpora auditable.

papers.title: Estimation of Quantum Umlaut Information
papers.abstract: Quantifying correlations is important for understanding how quantum states and channels support information processing. Quantum umlaut information $U$ connects such correlations to reliability in hypothesis testing and certain communication settings, but its known formulas require classical descriptions of the underlying states. To estimate correlations without these descriptions, we introduce measured quantum umlaut information $U^M$ by replacing Umegaki relative entropy with measured relative entropy. Its variational formulation leads to a quantum generative adversarial framework for estimating $U^M$ from measurement statistics of unknown bipartite states and classical-quantum channels. This framework optimizes reference states and measurements without reconstructing the target states or channel outputs. For classical-quantum channels, it also optimizes the input probabilities. We further analyze the relation between $U^M$ and $U$, deriving a state-dependent gap bound and characterizing equality for full-rank bipartite states. Numerical simulations show trained estimates close on average to independently computed numerical references for $U^M$ across the tested states and channels. These estimates could help assess how well quantum memories preserve correlations and how noise or drift affects input-output dependence in quantum transmitters and state-preparation devices.
papers.summary: Quantum umlaut information links correlations in quantum states and channels to reliability in hypothesis testing and some communication tasks, but the known formulas need classical descriptions of the states. The authors define a measured variant, `U^M`, by swapping Umegaki relative entropy for measured relative entropy. Its variational form gives a quantum generative adversarial framework that estimates `U^M` from measurement statistics alone, without reconstructing the states. They also derive a state-dependent bound on the gap between `U^M` and the original quantity and characterize when the two are equal for full-rank bipartite states; in simulations, **the trained estimates come close on average to independently computed reference values**.

papers.title: PsyInterviewee: Informational Invariance and Relational Adaptivity in Mental Health Interview Simulation
papers.abstract: LLM-based simulated interviewees support interviewer training and the evaluation of mental health interviewing systems. Existing studies have primarily focused on improving human-likeness through richer patient profiles and behavioral modeling. However, human-likeness alone does not establish their reliability. Reliable simulation requires preserving profile-grounded clinical facts (informational invariance) while adapting disclosure and interaction behavior to the interview (relational adaptivity). To this end, we introduce PsyInterviewee, which separates a protected truth channel from a dynamic interaction channel and verifies generated clinical claims against the profile. Specifically, asymmetric write permissions allow dialogue context to update disclosure and behavioral states without authorizing new clinical facts; these states guide what profile-supported information is revealed and how it is expressed. In an automated evaluation of interactions between LLM-based interviewers and interviewees, PsyInterviewee achieves higher scores than four representative baselines on most metrics across both axes, as assessed by two LLM judges. Ablations suggest that the two channels contribute to clinical grounding and response modulation, respectively.
papers.summary: LLM-simulated patients are used to train mental health interviewers and to evaluate interviewing systems, but sounding human does not make them reliable. `PsyInterviewee` separates a protected truth channel, which holds the clinical facts from the patient profile, from a dynamic interaction channel that controls what is disclosed and how. Asymmetric write permissions let the dialogue update disclosure and behavior states but never add new clinical facts, and generated clinical claims are checked against the profile. In automated LLM-to-LLM interviews scored by two LLM judges, it **outperforms four baselines on most metrics for both factual consistency and adaptive behavior**, and ablations tie each channel to one of these two properties.

papers.title: SAT-ACT: Learning CDCL Branching from Outcome-Derived Action Preferences
papers.abstract: Learning-based approaches have increasingly been explored for SAT solving, with particular attention to improving branching decisions in conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) solvers. These approaches derive branching guidance either from static structural properties of SAT formulas or from dynamic signals obtained through solver feedback and execution traces. However, these forms of supervision provide limited evidence about state-dependent branching effects, while different outcome measures may favor different branching choices. To address these limitations, we propose SAT-ACT, an outcome-derived learning framework for CDCL branching. We design three complementary outcome comparison criteria to extract action preferences from independent branching action rollouts initiated at the same solver state. The criteria identify preferences supported by the outcomes and leave comparisons unresolved when the evidence is insufficient or conflicting, instead of forcing an ordering using a predefined scalar metric. A state-conditioned network learns branching priorities from the extracted preferences and uses them to guide CDCL search directly without online action rollouts. We further introduce non-dominated heuristic action supervision, which retains the solver-selected action as a training target only when it remains non-dominated under these preferences. Solver-level experiments show that SAT-ACT consistently reduces CDCL search costs on three SAT families and improves PAR-2 on the SAT Competition benchmarks.
papers.summary: Learned branching heuristics for conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) SAT solvers are usually trained on static formula structure or on solver traces, and neither shows much about how a branching choice plays out from a specific solver state. `SAT-ACT` runs independent rollouts of different branching actions from the same solver state and compares their outcomes with three criteria, leaving a comparison unresolved when the evidence is weak or conflicting rather than forcing a ranking. A state-conditioned network learns branching priorities from these preferences and guides the solver without online rollouts; the solver's own choice is kept as a training target only if no other action beats it. The approach **consistently reduces search cost on three SAT families and improves PAR-2 on `SAT Competition` benchmarks**.

papers.title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 15.4 to 103.7 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.
papers.summary: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate contexts that are expensive to process and can bury the evidence that matters for the next decision, and external compressors that rewrite context into shorter text are lossy and may not match how the model itself represents the context. `Agentic Soft-Token Compression` (`ASTC`) is a training-free method for hybrid Gated Delta Network (`GDN`)–attention models: it uses the model's own recurrent state to decide what has already been absorbed, carries that forward as soft tokens, and keeps exact values as ordinary tokens. The shorter sequence cuts computation in later layers and produces reusable KV caches across the whole trajectory.
