On long-horizon tasks, `ASTC` **matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end attention pairs**, while trained compressors need 15.4 to 103.7 times more attention pairs per successful task.

papers.title: From Transcription to Reformulation: Defining and Benchmarking Grounded Generative Speech Recognition
papers.abstract: Speech language models have expanded automatic speech recognition (ASR) from transcription to general speech-to-text generation. Yet existing benchmarks still assume a single ground-truth transcript per utterance, an assumption that struggles when models produce readable, formatted, or structured outputs. In this work, we introduce Grounded Generative Speech Recognition (GSR), reformulating speech recognition as generating semantically grounded text instead of a single transcript. We define a grounded reformulation space that characterizes all valid textual realizations supported by the input speech, and establish a four-level hierarchy of reformulation capabilities, including literal transcription, canonical reformulation, semantic reformulation and speech-grounded structuring. Based on this formulation, we present GSR-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate generative speech recognition systems beyond exact transcript matching. GSR-Bench covers diverse scenarios including refined meeting transcription, cross-dialect translation, context-aware speech understanding, and robustness under silent or noisy acoustic conditions. To address the limitations of word-level evaluation metrics, we develop a multi-dimensional evaluation framework combining speech grounding assessment and LLM-based semantic judgment, whose reliability is validated through human preference studies. Extensive experiments across representative architectures, ranging from conventional ASR systems to end-to-end Speech-LLMs, reveal fundamental trade-offs between transcription fidelity and generative reformulation ability. Our analysis further identifies critical failure modes, including acoustic hallucination, unsupported generation, and instruction drift, providing insights into the design and evaluation of future grounded generative speech systems.
papers.summary: Speech language models now produce formatted, restructured or translated text from audio, but automatic speech recognition (ASR) benchmarks still assume a single correct transcript per utterance. The authors define Grounded Generative Speech Recognition (`GSR`), which covers every text output the speech supports, organized into four levels: literal transcription, canonical reformulation, semantic reformulation and speech-grounded structuring. They release `GSR-Bench`, which spans meeting transcription, cross-dialect translation, context-aware understanding and silent or noisy audio, and score it with a mix of speech-grounding checks and LLM-based semantic judgment validated against human preferences. Experiments from conventional ASR to end-to-end Speech-LLMs show **a basic trade-off between transcription fidelity and reformulation ability**, along with failure modes such as acoustic hallucination, unsupported generation and instruction drift.

papers.title: Self-Improvement with Auxiliary Rewards: Learning from Verified Traces and Evaluating Transfer
papers.abstract: Answer-level rewards cannot distinguish reasoning traces with equally correct outcomes. We study whether auxiliary trajectory preferences improve small-language-model self-improvement and transfer under limited supervision. We compare confidence-based (SC) and entropy-based metrics (UID-Conj.), which combines global entropy variation and local smoothness, through online reward augmentation and offline training on correct responses. Online experiments adapt Qwen3-1.7B on 30 AIME problems without reference answers; offline experiments use historical AIME problems. UID-Conj. improves the online macro-average across the adaptation benchmark and three transfer benchmarks by 2.08 percentage points over unmodified TTRL. The strongest evidence comes from offline weighted SFT: UID-Conj. exceeds uniform weighting on the same response pool by 1.93 points, with a paired prompt-bootstrap 95\% CI of [0.44, 3.44]. Benefits are task-dependent: SC rewards judged trace quality and instruction following, while UID-Conj. rewards yield stronger training outcomes in several settings. We find that auxiliary preferences can expose learning value among equally correct traces not captured during inference time, motivating their evaluation through downstream gains.
papers.summary: Rewards based only on the final answer cannot tell apart reasoning traces that are all correct. The study compares two auxiliary trace-level signals for self-improving small models: a confidence-based score (`SC`) and an entropy-based score (`UID-Conj.`) that combines global entropy variation with local smoothness. These are tested as online reward augmentation for `Qwen3-1.7B` on 30 `AIME` problems without reference answers, and as weights for offline fine-tuning on correct responses. `UID-Conj.` raises the online macro-average by 2.08 points over unmodified test-time reinforcement learning (`TTRL`), and in offline weighted fine-tuning it **beats uniform weighting by 1.93 points (95% CI 0.44 to 3.44)**; the benefits depend on the task, with `SC` tracking judged trace quality and instruction following more closely.

papers.title: Subliminal Reinforcement Learning: traits travel through a judge's scores
papers.abstract: Subliminal learning, the transfer of a model's trait through data with no semantic trace of it, has been shown for students trained on a teacher's text. Post-training relies on group relative policy optimization with a language-model judge, where the student learns only from its own outputs and one judge's scores. We show this suffices: a student writes invented syllables or numbers, a judge made to prefer one animal scores them, and the student's preference moves toward that animal relative to a run whose judge prefers another. Of 48 design cells, two fail the validity gate and 17 establish the trait at 5% false-discovery rate, numbers-only cells included; elsewhere, our account gives the reason. Removing only the reward difference between judges removes transfer. We establish the principle as a chain of four stages: the trait must show in the judge's scores, favour strings that move the student, accumulate and reach the answers. Judges with the same preference built from other data, or on another model, place it on other strings, and transfer is not detected. Carried unchanged to AI-safety dispositions, the chain holds: undesirable dispositions reach the student's answers, and stages measured before training anticipate where, helping to prevent part of this risk.
papers.summary: Subliminal learning, where a trait passes between models through data that carries no visible sign of it, had previously been shown only for students trained on a teacher's text. The authors show it also happens in group relative policy optimization (`GRPO`) with an LLM judge: a student writes invented syllables or numbers, a judge made to prefer a particular animal scores them, and **the student's own preference shifts toward that animal from the judge's scores alone**. 17 of 48 experimental settings show significant transfer, numbers-only settings included, and removing only the reward difference between judges removes the effect. They explain transfer as a four-stage chain, which also holds for undesirable AI-safety dispositions, and measurements taken before training predict where those dispositions will surface.
papers.highlight_summary:
GRPO students trained only on their own outputs, scored by a single LLM judge, can pick up that judge's hidden preferences even when the outputs carry no semantic trace of them. The paper shows this "subliminal" transfer happens with a standard RL recipe and breaks it into a four-stage chain: emission, absorption, transfer and behaviour. The chain explains both where transfer occurs and where it fails.

- **Setup:** students `Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct` and `Qwen3-1.7B` write lists of invented syllables or numbers, which a copy of their own base model scores after being made to favour one animal, either by system prompt or by fine-tuning. Each run is paired with a run under a judge favouring a second animal, so shared drift cancels out and only the trait difference remains.
- **Main result:** of 48 design cells, 2 fail the validity gate and **17 show transfer at a 5% false-discovery rate**, all in the judge's direction, including **6 in the numbers-only carrier**, which contains no letters of either animal name. The effects are small: a typical shift changes the two animal names' likelihood ratio by about **1.07×**, and the student's sampled answers change in only two cells.
- **Causal test:** splitting the reward into a shared part and a between-judge part, then training with the between-judge part removed, **eliminates transfer** (S₈₀ changes by −0.107 and −0.084 in the two cells tested). The policy still moves as far and stays as valid, even though the between-judge part is only a few percent of the reward's variance.
- **Mechanism:** the judge's trait shows up in surface statistics such as letter overlap with the animal name or number size. Transfer then depends on absorption, meaning whether those scores favour completions that move the student's preference margin; across eight fine-tuned judges, absorption correlates with transfer at **r = +0.65**. Judges from the other model family or at 8B still emit the trait, but their trait signal correlates at most 0.12 with the student's own judge's, and **no cross-model cell transfers**.
- **Safety extension:** with judges told to prefer rude, harsh or persuasive answers, a harsh-preferring judge moved `Qwen3-1.7B`'s self-descriptions toward harshness (**d = +0.95, q < 0.001**). Measurements taken before training predicted which cells would not transfer and which direction the others would start in. Limitations include implied-choice shifts of at most about 1 percentage point, small models, and two cells that transferred against the judge.

papers.title: rl_rob: A transparent, from-scratch Python library for teaching reinforcement learning from tabular methods to deep policy gradients
papers.abstract: rl_rob is an open-source Python library for teaching reinforcement learning. It implements the arc of a modern course, from tabular temporal-difference learning through linear function approximation to deep value-based and policy-gradient methods, with every algorithm written from first principles so that its update rule is visible in a few lines of code. All agents share one interface, so learners can compare methods directly across stages and trace a deep reinforcement learning update from the temporal-difference error to the weight change. The library supports teaching and assessment in which students implement, modify and explain update rules, rather than only produce working code.
papers.summary: `rl_rob` is an open-source Python library for teaching reinforcement learning. It follows the arc of a modern course, from tabular temporal-difference learning through linear function approximation to deep value-based and policy-gradient methods. Every algorithm is written from first principles so its update rule fits in a few lines, and **all agents share one interface**, so learners can compare methods directly and trace a deep RL update from the temporal-difference error to the weight change. It is meant for coursework where students implement, modify and explain update rules rather than only produce working code.

papers.title: ART of PIV: Agentic Real-Time Particle Image Velocimetry for Active Flow Control
papers.abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.
papers.summary: The accuracy of particle image velocimetry (PIV), which measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, depends on preprocessing, estimation and postprocessing choices that are usually tuned by experts and can degrade as flow conditions change. `ART of PIV` uses a learned agent to pick a pipeline configuration for each image pair from a library built for a given speed budget. Across cross-correlation, optical-flow and learning-based estimators, it **reduces average end-point error by 12.2–22.4% compared with the best single estimator at the same speed**, at up to 1000–4000 image pairs per second, and it lowers closed-loop control cost in simulation. In a physical water channel, a `DreamerV3` controller trained directly in the real world uses it to track a prescribed flow field behind a fluidic pinball.

papers.title: Erase the Injected Region: Multimodal Prompt-Injection Defense with On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Multimodal indirect prompt injection embeds malicious instructions in external media that also contains information needed for the user's task. Existing defenses can block the attack yet impair the model's use of that information, leaving a gap between attack defense and task preservation. We propose ERASE, an on-policy self-distillation method that constructs its reference by erasing the injected region in place. Modality-appropriate blank content replaces the injection while the surrounding media is preserved. A student reading attacked media learns from a frozen base model reading the erased view through full-distribution token-level feedback on its own rollouts. Across image, audio, and video on two model sizes, ERASE records near-zero observed attack success on the evaluated benchmark while retaining task utility close to the undefended clean-input level. On 3B audio, ERASE reaches 60.1% attacked-input accuracy compared with ARGUS's 33.1%, within 0.5 points of the undefended clean-input level. Experiments show that ERASE reduces injection dependence from 6.26 to 0.0095 on 3B audio while staying close to the base model on the erased input. Out-of-domain accuracy also stays near the base level. Our code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
papers.summary: Multimodal indirect prompt injection hides malicious instructions in images, audio or video that also contain information the user's task needs, and existing defenses often block the attack at the cost of that information. `ERASE` is an on-policy self-distillation method: the injected region is replaced with blank content suited to the modality, and a student model reading the attacked media learns, through full-distribution token-level feedback on its own outputs, to match a frozen base model reading the erased version. Across image, audio and video at two model sizes, it **reduces observed attack success to near zero while keeping task utility close to the undefended clean-input level**. On 3B audio it reaches 60.1% accuracy on attacked inputs, compared with 33.1% for `ARGUS`, and out-of-domain accuracy stays near the base model's.

papers.title: SERIAL-7: Deriving, Realizing, and Preserving Machine-Verifiable Outputs Across Representations
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly generate structured outputs consumed by programs and downstream systems, where semantic correctness alone does not guarantee reliable execution. We introduce SERIAL-7, a Korean-English benchmark built around an executable verification framework for machine-verifiable generation across seven representations. Using 177 validated canonical artifacts, SERIAL-7 separates semantic derivation (Derive), constrained artifact generation (Realize), and cross-representation preservation (Preserve). Its 43 atomic representation constraints are paired with executable checks over format, structure, and task-specific semantics, enabling progressively stricter verification from representation compliance to full artifact validity. Across ten models, REALIZE-L3 HSR ranges from 42.0% to 93.9%, while Full Compliance exposes additional artifact-level failures beyond correct final answers and valid representations. These results show that reliable structured generation requires explicit, executable verification of how artifacts are realized and preserved across representations.
papers.summary: LLM outputs consumed by programs must be correct and also execute reliably in their target format. `SERIAL-7` is a Korean–English benchmark of 177 validated artifacts across seven representations, which tests semantic derivation (`Derive`), constrained artifact generation (`Realize`) and preservation across representations (`Preserve`). It pairs 43 atomic constraints with executable checks on format, structure and task-specific semantics, so verification can tighten step by step from format compliance to full artifact validity. Across ten models, the strictest Realize score **ranges from 42.0% to 93.9%**, and full-compliance checks catch artifact-level failures even when the final answer and format are correct.

papers.title: GenDSR: Transferring Representations from Video Generation Models for Dynamic Spatial Reasoning
papers.abstract: Dynamic spatial reasoning is essential for connecting visual intelligence to thephysical world, yet remains challenging for vision-language models (VLMs), which must preserve scene state while tracking how spatial relations evolve over time. Meanwhile, video generation models (VGMs), trained to synthesize temporally coherent world dynamics, offer a rich source of spatiotemporal representations. We present GenDSR, a framework that transfers intermediate representations from VGM into VLM for dynamic spatial reasoning. Rather than treating a VGM feature as a monolithic prior, GenDSR constructs two complementary branches: a raw branch preserving holistic generative context and a delta branch emphasizing temporal variation. Task-conditioned tokenwise gates then fuse both signals and inject the result into the native visual representation. On DSR-Bench, GenDSR achieves 67.2%, surpassing the previous best result and establishing a new state of the art.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with dynamic spatial reasoning, which requires keeping track of a scene while following how spatial relations change over time. `GenDSR` takes intermediate features from a video generation model and splits them into a raw branch that keeps the full generative context and a delta branch that highlights temporal change. Task-conditioned per-token gates fuse the two branches and inject the result into the VLM's own visual representation. The method reaches **67.2% on `DSR-Bench`, a new state of the art**.

papers.title: Transferring Peptide-Target Interaction Patterns to Small Molecules by Joint Guidance for Diffusion and Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Generating small molecules to target protein-protein interactions (PPIs) remains one of the most challenging yet high-reward frontiers in drug discovery. Unlike traditional small-molecule drugs that bind to deep, well-defined pockets, PPI interfaces often comprise broad, shallow binding surfaces. A natural strategy is to leverage known peptide-target interactions, as peptide ligands provide rich interface-level constraints. However, a major algorithmic challenge is that rigid atom-level conditioning on peptide structures can over-constrain the generative space and exclude valid small-molecule solutions. To address this challenge, we present PIFT (Peptide InterFace Transfer), a novel framework that transfers peptide-target interaction patterns to small molecules through joint sampling-time guidance of masked discrete diffusion and continuous flow matching. PIFT first maps peptide-target and small-molecule-target interfaces into a shared, target-conditioned interaction space, capturing transferable interface information across molecular modalities. The resulting peptide-derived reference then jointly steers building-block logits and 3D coordinates toward peptide-compatible molecules while preserving a strong adapted molecular prior. Extensive experiments across diverse PPI targets show that the learned representation captures cross-modal interaction compatibility, while peptide guidance improves interface recovery and achieves strong docking performance and favorable molecular properties.
papers.summary: Designing small molecules against protein–protein interactions is hard because these interfaces are broad and shallow, and conditioning rigidly on atom-level peptide binder structures overconstrains generation. `PIFT` (Peptide InterFace Transfer) maps peptide–target and small-molecule–target interfaces into a shared, target-conditioned interaction space. A peptide-derived reference in that space then steers, at sampling time, both the building-block logits of a masked discrete diffusion model and the 3D coordinates of a flow-matching model, while keeping a strong molecular prior. Across diverse protein–protein interaction targets, **peptide guidance improves interface recovery and docking performance** while maintaining favorable molecular properties.

papers.title: With foundation-model features, aggregator complexity does not improve cross-hospital discrimination in gastric whole-slide image classification
papers.abstract: Whole-slide image classifiers are usually developed within one hospital and often go untested at unseen hospitals. We assembled 5,036 haematoxylin-and-eosin-stained gastric slides from five Korean hospitals, scanned at 20x and 40x, and compared multiple-instance learning aggregators under leave-one-hospital-out validation on frozen pathology foundation-model features. A hierarchical patch-region-slide graph aggregator (CHIME-MIL) with site alignment and two-scale fusion reached a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.837, above six conventional attention and transformer aggregators trained without these steps. Under a matched recipe it did not exceed attention-based pooling, and global max pooling given the same alignment and fusion was better (AUC 0.855, P = 0.0002). The alignment, which subtracts each hospital's mean feature vector without labels, onboarded a new hospital from ten unlabelled slides and cost 0.002 AUC without held-out-hospital data, but its accuracy gains were small and inconsistent. The model had low top-label calibration error (0.053) but under-confident malignancy probabilities, and removing its most-attended patches lowered the malignancy probability far more than removing random patches. With these features, more complex aggregators did not improve discrimination; what a deployable system adds is label-free onboarding, calibration checks and auditable evidence.
papers.summary: Using 5,036 gastric whole-slide images from five Korean hospitals, the authors compare multiple-instance learning aggregators on frozen pathology foundation-model features, holding out one hospital at a time. A hierarchical graph aggregator (`CHIME-MIL`) with site alignment and two-scale fusion reached a mean area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.837, but under a matched training recipe it did no better than attention pooling, and **simple global max pooling with the same alignment and fusion did better (AUC 0.855)**. The label-free alignment, which subtracts each hospital's mean feature vector, can onboard a new hospital from ten unlabelled slides, though its accuracy gains were small and inconsistent. The authors conclude that what a deployable system adds is label-free onboarding, calibration checks and auditable evidence, not a more complex aggregator.

papers.title: StrictPRMBench: A Replayable Evaluation Benchmark for Auditing Fixed-Score PRM Aggregation
papers.abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) score reasoning steps, but best-of-N selection also requires a rule that aggregates those scores. We study that rule as a separate evaluation object. StrictPRMBench fixes mathematical reasoning pools, scorer evidence, and the source trace of a deletion intervention, so that different reducers face the same recorded selection problem. Across seven scoring checkpoints and two benchmarks, the stored N=32 outcomes give higher deletion-induced selection instability for product than geometric mean (GM) in all 14 cells. The equal-cell difference is +0.0965; a shared-problem bootstrap, conditional on these checkpoints and frozen pools, gives a 95% interval of [0.0846,0.1086]. A pre-injection-defined sensitivity excludes replacement slots that are either reducer's clean winner and retains 4,459 of 4,622 cell-problem records. The retained difference is +0.0986 [0.0875,0.1098]. Effects are heterogeneous: the two Qwen cells have positive percentile-bootstrap intervals on retained support but two-sided exact paired p-values of 0.0625 and 0.0703. Clean-pool Qwen accuracy does not detect a product advantage, but this is not an equivalence result. We provide versioned outcome records, CPU reanalysis, and an explicit evidence-availability contract. The contribution is a diagnostic evaluation protocol and a reproducible audit of recorded selector behavior, not a new PRM, a universally optimal reducer, or evidence of deployment-wide harm. Raw-score replay and outcome-record reanalysis are distinguished: missing primary edited-score vectors limit independent evaluation of new reducers under the same stress.
papers.summary: Best-of-N selection with process reward models (PRMs) needs a rule for combining step scores into one score per answer, and the benchmark treats that rule as its own object of evaluation. `StrictPRMBench` freezes math reasoning pools, scorer outputs and a step-deletion intervention, so different aggregation rules face exactly the same selection problem. Across seven scoring checkpoints and two benchmarks at N=32, **the product rule is less stable under step deletion than the geometric mean in all 14 settings** (difference +0.0965, 95% interval 0.0846 to 0.1086), though the effect varies and is weaker for the `Qwen` checkpoints. The contribution is a reproducible audit protocol with versioned outcome records, not a new PRM or a claim that any one rule is best overall.

papers.title: Operon-S1: a fast decision controller for long-horizon biomedical agents
papers.abstract: Language-model agents now carry out long scientific work in biology, but their judgements about conventions, skills, errors, evidence and stopping are made inside the reasoning that does the work, where they cannot be measured, replaced or improved on their own. Here we present Operon-S1, a fast decision system, a System 1 for the agent, that separates judging from doing. A decision harness poses the agent's recurring judgements as closed questions at 13 decision points and acts only through fixed messages that never contain an answer, so any model that answers the questions can serve as the judge. Across seven life-science benchmarks, a local decision model took over these judgements in 0.6 s at the median for an in-loop request on CPU at no request cost, with no measurable change in the agent's score on five of six benchmarks, whereas the general language model that drives the agent, asked the same questions, accounted for 8.0% to 35.2% of task cost. Every decision is recorded with its consequence. Retraining on labels from task construction, verifiers or execution raised decision accuracy on every question in each of three trained versions, and a new version enters service only through a promotion gate. Task-level results in this study use the public checkpoint. The same closed decisions serve wet-laboratory protocol troubleshooting and the design of a germline target enrichment panel. Like the regulator of an operon, which switches genes on and off without making their products, Operon-S1 steers the agent without doing its work, and makes the agent's judgements a layer that can be measured, replaced and trained.
papers.summary: LLM agents doing long biomedical tasks make recurring judgments about conventions, skills, errors, evidence and when to stop inside the same reasoning that does the work, so those judgments cannot be measured or improved separately. `Operon-S1` moves them into a decision harness that poses closed questions at 13 decision points and responds only through fixed messages, so any model that can answer the questions can act as the judge. Across seven life-science benchmarks, **a local decision model answered these questions in 0.6 s (median) on CPU at no request cost, with no measurable change in agent score on five of six benchmarks**, whereas having the agent's main LLM answer the same questions accounted for 8.0–35.2% of task cost. Every decision is logged with its consequence, and retraining on labels from task construction, verifiers or execution improved decision accuracy, with each new version deployed only after passing a promotion gate.

papers.title: Quantile Propagation Planning for Budgeted Tail-Risk Evaluation
papers.abstract: Risk-aware planning must identify rare, costly outcomes using only a limited number of model evaluations. Monte Carlo rollouts spend this budget on noisy tail estimates, while planning from the mean can miss the tail entirely. We introduce quantile propagation planning (QPP), which propagates a small, fixed set of disturbance quantiles through the dynamics and integrates the resulting cost curve to evaluate both mean and tail risk. The method is exact at the propagated levels, converges as the quantile grid is refined, and admits a one-sided conservatism guarantee under stated structural conditions. In controlled overload and inventory tasks, QPP reduces realized tail cost and constraint violations relative to mean-rollout planning. On overload, it remains competitive with sampled evaluators that use substantially more trajectories. These results position QPP as a transparent, budget-controlled approach to tail-risk evaluation.
papers.summary: Risk-aware planning must find rare, costly outcomes with a limited budget of model evaluations; Monte Carlo rollouts give noisy tail estimates, and planning on the mean can miss the tail entirely. Quantile propagation planning (`QPP`) pushes a small fixed set of disturbance quantiles through the dynamics and integrates the resulting cost curve to estimate both mean and tail risk. It is exact at the propagated quantile levels, converges as the grid is refined, and is guaranteed to err on the conservative side under stated structural conditions. In overload and inventory tasks, **`QPP` lowers realized tail cost and constraint violations compared with mean-rollout planning** and remains competitive with sampling-based evaluators that use many more trajectories.

papers.title: Do Transaction Prices Reflect Visual Preference? A Diagnostic Study with Multimodal Language Models
papers.abstract: Existing visual preference evaluation relies on costly human annotations or preference reward models, whereas online marketplace transaction prices are readily available and reflect real purchasing behavior, offering potential low-cost supervision. However, transaction prices conflate visual preferences with non-visual factors such as provenance, demand, and competition, making aggregate accuracy insufficient to distinguish model errors, unreliable price signals, and protocol confounds. To address this identifiability challenge, we introduce MarketImage, a diagnostic framework that identifies when transaction prices reflect visual preferences, where they fail, and whether multimodal language models can recover human-supported visual preference signals. MarketImage comprises three components: (i) MarketImageArt, 266 six-image comparison sets with transaction prices and price-blind human rankings; (ii) MarketImageLens, a tie-preserving protocol that partitions 3,990 within-set image pairs into price-human agreement, conflict, and price-tie regions while separately auditing presentation-order effects; and (iii) MarketValuator, six elicitation methods spanning direct comparison, independent scoring, budget constraints, and multi-agent aggregation to evaluate signal recovery by static visual scorers and three multimodal language models. Experiments show that only 24.2% of image pairs have a non-tied price direction, of which 34.7% agree with the human majority. Within this region, HPSv2 leads at 66.4% Recoverable Accuracy; Qwen's budgeted and aggregated variants trail baselines, while GPT interface gains remain statistically unresolved. Thus, transaction prices encode recoverable visual preferences only under limited conditions and should be treated as uncertain proxies rather than ground truth.
papers.summary: Online marketplace transaction prices look like cheap supervision for visual preference, but they mix visual appeal with provenance, demand and competition. `MarketImage` is a diagnostic framework consisting of `MarketImageArt` (266 six-image sets with prices and price-blind human rankings), `MarketImageLens` (a protocol that sorts 3,990 image pairs by whether price and human judgment agree, conflict or tie, and checks for presentation-order effects), and `MarketValuator` (six elicitation methods for static scorers and three multimodal language models). Only 24.2% of pairs have a clear price direction, and **just 34.7% of those agree with the human majority**; in that region `HPSv2` leads with 66.4% recoverable accuracy, while the `Qwen` variants trail the baselines. The authors conclude that transaction prices should be treated as uncertain proxies for visual preference, not ground truth.

papers.title: LEAP: Efficient LLM Inference Scheduling with Generalizable Length Prediction
papers.abstract: Length-aware scheduling reduces request latency in LLM serving by prioritizing shorter requests. However, despite their large model sizes, length predictors can suffer degraded ranking performance under domain and task shifts, and adapting them can require costly retraining. Their prediction overhead can further offset the benefits of scheduling. To improve the generalization and efficiency of length-aware scheduling, we propose \textbf{LEAP}, a length prediction system with fast online adaptation and asynchronous CPU execution. LEAP reuses the serving model's prefill hidden states, which contain information about the output length, and extracts this signal through a linear readout. To adapt to substantial domain and task shifts, it updates the readout at test time through recursive least squares, using completed requests as supervision without gradient computation or historical-data replay. Prediction and updates run asynchronously on CPU, while prediction and initial batch ordering overlap the remaining GPU prefill. Across the evaluated cross-domain transfers, LEAP retains strong ranking performance, and online adaptation improves Spearman correlation by 64.7\% under a larger domain shift. Serving experiments show that LEAP reduces average per-token latency by 15.9--40.8\% compared with the evaluated length predictors, while achieving 1.9\% higher throughput with $30{,}569\times$ fewer predictor parameters than the strongest evaluated baseline.
papers.summary: Length-aware scheduling cuts latency in large language model (LLM) serving by running shorter requests first, but existing length predictors are large, rank requests poorly when the domain or task shifts, and add overhead of their own. `LEAP` predicts output length with a linear readout over the hidden states the serving model already computes during prefill. It adapts that readout at test time with recursive least squares, learning from completed requests without gradients or replaying past data. Prediction and updates run asynchronously on the CPU while GPU prefill continues. Online adaptation improves Spearman correlation by 64.7% under a larger domain shift, and in serving tests `LEAP` cuts average per-token latency by **15.9–40.8%** compared with the evaluated predictors while using 30,569 times fewer predictor parameters than the strongest baseline.

papers.title: Generated storm lifecycles fill the rare-event tail of short rainfall records
papers.abstract: Historically rare ''one-in-a-generation'' storms are occurring with unprecedented frequency, causing catastrophic damage and mounting casualties, and exposing the vulnerability of infrastructure designed around short observational records. To overcome the limitations of sparse data, we present StormGen, a generative machine-learning model that transforms an observed storm's initial hours into complete, physically plausible hourly rainfall lifecycles in minutes. Evaluated on a decade of southeast Texas rainfall, StormGen produced close counterparts for 4\5% of the most severe 2\% of storms--compared to just 3\% for stochastic storm transposition--and maintained spatial coherence over full 24-hour sequences. Crucially, from a single hour of initial rainfall, the model successfully reconstructed the specific lifecycle, spatial pattern, and extreme catchment totals of Hurricane Harvey itself, despite the event being entirely absent in training. Because storm timing alone can more than double peak flows, these complete generated scenarios provide a vital mechanism to stress-test flood protections against unprecedented extremes.
papers.summary: Flood infrastructure is designed around short rainfall records that rarely include the most extreme storms. `StormGen` is a generative model that takes the first hours of an observed storm and produces a complete, physically plausible hourly rainfall lifecycle in minutes. On a decade of southeast Texas rainfall, it produced close counterparts for far more of the most severe 2% of storms than stochastic storm transposition, which matched only 3%, and it stayed spatially coherent over full 24-hour sequences. From a single hour of initial rainfall it **reconstructed the lifecycle, spatial pattern, and extreme catchment totals of Hurricane Harvey**, even though Harvey was absent from training.

papers.title: What We Keep of What We Forget: Replacement Operators and Routing Semantics in Training-Free MoE Expert Pruning
papers.abstract: Training-free expert pruning makes two decisions: which experts to remove, and what the layer computes when its router still selects a removed expert. Published methods change both at once. Holding the mask fixed, we compare replacement operators from three families on OLMoE, DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight, with Granite as a fourth router, using paired, multiplicity-corrected tests. The largest effect is a choice usually left implicit: the survivors' gate scale. On routers trained without top-k renormalization, renormalizing the survivors' gates, a common implementation choice, costs 0.8-8.5 points and reverses whether rerouting beats MoNE's mean-output replacement; on two routers trained with renormalization, the trained scale wins at 50% pruning. We introduce the tilted novice, a closed-form low-rank map of the pruned expert's input whose rank-0 case is MoNE's constant. At 50% pruning it adds 1.2-1.8% parameters and gains 3.45 and 1.37 points over the constant on OLMoE and Moonlight, stable across calibration draws and largely unchanged by 4- and 3-bit quantization. No operator dominates: trained-scale rerouting is best on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and a partial copy of each pruned expert is statistically indistinguishable from the tilted novice on two models. Evaluation can change conclusions: at 25% pruning MoNE's constant keeps 92-97% of dense multiple-choice accuracy but only 5-65% of GSM8K and 0-17% of code scores, and the calibration domain moves the mask 4-9 times more than resampling. We propose a five-item reporting checklist.
papers.summary: Training-free expert pruning in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models makes two decisions: which experts to remove, and what the layer computes when the router still selects a removed expert. Published methods change both at once. Holding the pruning mask fixed, the authors compare replacement operators on `OLMoE`, `DeepSeek-V2-Lite`, `Moonlight`, and `Granite` using paired, multiplicity-corrected tests. The largest effect comes from an often-implicit choice: on routers trained without top-k renormalization, renormalizing the surviving experts' gates **costs 0.8–8.5 points** and can flip which method wins. A new closed-form low-rank operator, the `tilted novice`, gains up to 3.45 points over `MoNE`'s constant replacement, but no operator wins everywhere, and at 25% pruning multiple-choice accuracy hides large drops on `GSM8K` and code, which motivates a five-item reporting checklist.

papers.title: RECITE: Revising Eligibility Criteria Incorporating Textual Evidence
papers.abstract: Overly restrictive eligibility criteria contribute to widespread enrollment failure in clinical trials, yet published recommendations for how specific criteria should be broadened remain disconnected from trial design at scale. We introduce RECITE (Revising Eligibility Criteria Incorporating Textual Evidence), a framework for automated discovery, extraction, and implementation of evidence-based eligibility criteria revisions. RECITE uses protocol amendment documents from ClinicalTrials.gov to construct a dataset of 11,913 curated instances across 5,735 trials, each pairing original criteria with documentary evidence and target revisions. We benchmark fifteen LLM configurations under truncated-to-context-window and retrieval-augmented generation conditions, on a 3,116-instance sample under an LLM-as-judge protocol validated against ten domain experts (judge vs. human quadratic-weighted Cohen's $\kappa_{qw} = 0.694 \pm 0.096$). The best open-weight model, Gemma 2 9B, achieves $\kappa_{qw}$-aligned ordinal score $3.0 \pm 0.9$ on a 0--4 scale (normalized 0.742) and the best closed-weight model, GPT-4o, reaches $3.0 \pm 0.8$ (normalized 0.745). Using an agentic literature discovery system, we then identified 44 paper--trial matches across five publications providing trial-design and EC-modification evidence. Our findings suggest that existing clinical knowledge can be operationalized into actionable trial design recommendations.
papers.summary: Overly restrictive eligibility criteria cause many clinical trials to fail at enrollment, and published recommendations for broadening them are rarely applied to trial design. `RECITE` builds a dataset of 11,913 instances across 5,735 trials from `ClinicalTrials.gov` protocol amendments, each pairing the original criteria with supporting evidence and the target revision. Fifteen LLM configurations are benchmarked with full-context truncation and retrieval-augmented generation, scored by an LLM judge validated against ten domain experts. The best open-weight model, `Gemma 2 9B`, essentially **matches the best closed-weight model, `GPT-4o`**, with normalized scores of 0.742 and 0.745, and an agentic literature search found 44 paper–trial matches offering evidence for criteria changes.

papers.title: From the Zoo to the BULLPEN: Sample-Efficient LLM Profiling via Multi-Channel Model Embeddings
papers.abstract: Choosing among the hundreds of thousands of available large language models (LLMs) requires a thorough understanding of each candidate model's properties. In practice, each property is measured by its own benchmark suite, so profiling a model on many properties means paying for many separate evaluations. To address this, model embeddings compress each model into a fixed-length vector from which many properties can be predicted. Existing methods, such as EmbedLLM, build these vectors from correctness patterns and question features, and often need large probe batteries to do so. However, many behaviors that are important when choosing a model, such as its verbosity, safety and style, show up more in how it answers than in whether it is correct. We introduce BULLPEN (Behavioral Understanding of Large Language models via Profile ENcodings), a framework that extends EmbedLLM in three ways. First, BULLPEN organizes the downstream tasks that prior work uses and adds 20 task benchmarks we built on behavior, style and provenance. Second, it is the first framework to read a model's own answer text jointly with its correctness and the question text. Third, it encodes models from a few hundred questions instead of the full 24,118-question pool. Across 260 open-weight models, our answer-text encoder scores 0.48 +/- 0.10 on the new tasks against 0.35 +/- 0.10 for the best prior encoder. Our encoders that read answer text keep at least 91% of their full-pool skill from only 400 questions (1.3% of the inference compute of the full question pool), while a correctness-only baseline keeps 83% with the same 400 questions. Because these embeddings need only model outputs, they support behavioral auditing and low-cost profiling, and could extend to API-only models. Code and data: https://github.com/wcquesera/bullpen
papers.summary: Profiling a large language model (LLM) across many properties normally requires a separate benchmark for each one. Model embeddings such as `EmbedLLM` compress a model into a vector from which properties can be predicted, but they rely on correctness patterns and large probe sets. `BULLPEN` (Behavioral Understanding of Large Language models via Profile ENcodings) adds 20 benchmarks on behavior, style, and provenance, and encodes the model's own answer text together with correctness and question text. Across 260 open-weight models, its answer-text encoder scores 0.48 on the new tasks against 0.35 for the best prior encoder, and it **retains at least 91% of its full-pool skill from just 400 questions**, about 1.3% of the full question pool's inference compute.

papers.title: Ask on Demand: Targeted Peer Communication for Parallel Agentic Systems
papers.abstract: Parallel LLM agents tackle complex tasks by exploring multiple trajectories, yet useful discoveries remain isolated in individual execution histories. Existing sharing methods often select or summarize information before other agents' needs become clear, potentially overlooking details that become important later. We propose Ask on Demand (AOD), a communication framework that enables agents to seek targeted peer assistance when specific information needs arise. Upon an approved request, AOD retrieves relevant evidence from peer execution histories, selects a suitable peer, and generates a response tailored to the request. To determine when such assistance is worthwhile, we train a lightweight gate using paired team continuations, with supervision derived from final team outcomes and inference cost. Experiments on AppWorld and WebShop demonstrate that AOD consistently improves task performance over independent parallel execution while achieving lower inference cost than existing information-sharing baselines. These findings highlight the benefits of aligning peer communication with agents' evolving information needs to achieve more effective and efficient collaboration.
papers.summary: When LLM agents explore a task in parallel, useful discoveries stay locked in each agent's own execution history, and existing sharing methods pick what to share before anyone knows what will be needed. `Ask on Demand` (`AOD`) lets an agent request targeted help when a specific information need arises: it retrieves relevant evidence from peer histories, picks a suitable peer, and generates a response tailored to the request. A lightweight gate, trained on paired team continuations with supervision from final team outcomes and inference cost, decides when asking is worthwhile. On `AppWorld` and `WebShop`, `AOD` **outperforms independent parallel execution while costing less than existing information-sharing baselines**.

papers.title: Riemannian Optimization on Unknown Manifolds via Stochastic Proximal Refinement
papers.abstract: We study Riemannian optimization on an unknown manifold accessed only through feasible samples. The central challenge is to turn feasible samples into optimization steps, i.e., the samples are drawn from the unknown feasible manifold, but do not directly provide the tangent spaces, projections, or retractions required by classic Riemannian methods. Moreover, regions with low objective values may be sparsely represented in the data, so directly sampling from a distribution fitted to these observations can require many draws to find better feasible solutions. We introduce Proximal Refinement on Implicit Smooth Manifolds (PRISM), which turns feasible-sample access into an iterative optimization procedure by repeatedly sampling an objective-aware proximal distribution conditioned on the current iterate. Theoretically, we show that PRISM recovers the effect of Riemannian-gradient refinement, leading to provable objective descent, feasibility (manifold adherence), and convergence toward first-order stationarity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through synthetic experiments illustrating its geometric properties and applications to data-driven building control and diverse real world optimization tasks, highlighting its potential as a general framework for data-driven optimization across scientific and engineering domains.
papers.summary: Classic Riemannian optimization needs tangent spaces, projections, and retractions, which are unavailable when the feasible manifold is known only through samples. `PRISM` (Proximal Refinement on Implicit Smooth Manifolds) turns sample access into an iterative optimizer by repeatedly sampling from an objective-aware proximal distribution conditioned on the current iterate. The authors prove that this **recovers the effect of Riemannian-gradient refinement**, giving objective descent, adherence to the manifold, and convergence toward first-order stationarity. Experiments cover synthetic geometry tests, data-driven building control, and other real-world optimization tasks.

papers.title: Pinching Antennas for ISAC: Waveguide Architectures, Solutions, and Future Directions
papers.abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is a core design principle for sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems, yet fixed antenna geometry limits its performance. Pinching antenna systems (PASS) guide electromagnetic waves along dielectric waveguides and radiate them through position-adaptive antennas, allowing communication links and sensing observations to benefit from spatial reconfiguration. This article reviews PASS-enabled ISAC through single-waveguide, multi-waveguide, and segmented-waveguide architectures, comparing their feed structures, spatial degrees of freedom, operating protocols, and uplink/downlink support. We organize solution pathways around physics-consistent modeling, joint spatial-signal optimization, dynamic channel acquisition, and stable real-time control. A segmented waveguide-enabled pinching-antenna array (SWAN) case study demonstrates joint segment selection, antenna po?sitioning, and transmit beamforming using segment-hysteresis reinforcement learning. The results illustrate how waveguide loss and per-segment aperture gain create communication-sensing tradeoffs. We conclude with research directions in joint transmit?receive operation, measurement-calibrated digital twins, and trustworthy control.
papers.summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is central to sixth-generation (6G) wireless design but is limited by fixed antenna geometry. Pinching antenna systems (PASS) route signals along dielectric waveguides and radiate them through antennas whose positions can be adjusted. The article reviews single-, multi-, and segmented-waveguide PASS architectures for ISAC and organizes solution approaches around physics-consistent modeling, joint spatial-signal optimization, channel acquisition, and real-time control. A case study on a segmented waveguide array (`SWAN`) uses segment-hysteresis reinforcement learning to jointly choose segments, antenna positions, and beamforming, showing **how waveguide loss and per-segment aperture gain create communication-sensing tradeoffs**.

papers.title: From prediction error to sparse events: Biologically inspired signed-dyadic coding for Mandarin keyword spotting
papers.abstract: In continuous spiking keyword spotting, temporally correlated acoustic frames can repeatedly trigger memory access and neural computation at a dense input interface, even when hidden activity is sparse. Predictive processing and sensory adaptation suggest retaining predictable input locally and responding selectively to deviations. Inspired by this mechanism, we propose Predictive Signed-Dyadic Coding (PG). PG maintains a local prediction for each input channel and transmits an event only when the residual exceeds a learned threshold. Each event carries a sign and a finite power-of-two magnitude, and the receiver reconstructs it with fixed-point shifts and additions. In Mandarin keyword spotting, INPUT-PG reaches 90.00% accuracy while reducing mean SRAM reads by 33.87% and inference cycles by 32.77%. PG provides a hardware interface for research on low-power continuous speech processing and event-based sensory systems.
papers.summary: In continuous spiking keyword spotting, temporally correlated audio frames keep triggering memory accesses and computation at the input, even when hidden activity is sparse. Inspired by predictive processing in biology, `Predictive Signed-Dyadic Coding` (`PG`) keeps a local prediction for each input channel and sends an event only when the residual crosses a learned threshold. Each event carries a sign and a power-of-two magnitude, so the receiver can reconstruct it with fixed-point shifts and additions. On Mandarin keyword spotting, `INPUT-PG` reaches 90.00% accuracy while **reducing mean SRAM reads by 33.87%** and inference cycles by 32.77%.

papers.title: Online Evidence-Containment Prediction over Text Spans under Distinct Queries
papers.abstract: Evidence-grounded NLP systems often verify nested text regions sequentially, so verifying one region constrains others. We formalize this as Online Evidence-Containment Prediction (OECP): each candidate is predicted before exact verification and queried at most once. Span containment is exactly a triangular 2D product order, making OECP distinct-query online isotonic regression. With multiple admissible targets, worst-case regret is near-linear, $\widetilde{\Theta}(m_{\mathrm{eff}})$, in the effective scale given by endpoint-rank compression; a single fixed target, as in standard QA, admits an explicit polynomial-time learner with optimal $\Theta(\log m_{\mathrm{eff}})$ regret, run on real NQ episodes. On Natural Questions, containment yields a large deductive gain plus a smaller learned gain on unresolved candidates, reproduced across two backbones and DPR hierarchies. Expected Search-space Reduction (ESR) turns these probabilities into decisions, localizing evidence in fewer verifier calls on SciFact, ERASER, and DPR hierarchies; on DPR hierarchies under call budgets it outperforms four recent external selectors and raises fixed-reader F1 over learned and generator-greedy scheduling.
papers.summary: Evidence-grounded NLP systems often verify nested text spans one after another, so each verification result constrains the others. The authors formalize this as Online Evidence-Containment Prediction (OECP), show that span containment is a triangular 2D product order, and cast the problem as distinct-query online isotonic regression. With multiple admissible targets, worst-case regret grows nearly linearly, while a single fixed target, as in standard QA, admits a polynomial-time learner with **optimal logarithmic regret**. An Expected Search-space Reduction (`ESR`) policy turns the predictions into decisions, finding evidence in fewer verifier calls on `SciFact`, `ERASER`, and `DPR` hierarchies and beating four recent selectors under call budgets.

papers.title: Anomalies as Residuals: Cauchy Displacement Networks
papers.abstract: Neighbourhood-based detectors such as KNN, LOF and LUNAR remain among the most accurate methods for tabular anomaly detection, but they compare every query with the stored training set, so their inference cost and memory grow with the data and the data must be kept at deployment. We ask whether the neighbourhood geometry these detectors exploit can be compiled into a small network that scores a query with a single forward pass. We propose the Cauchy Displacement Network (CDN), which regresses each normal point onto the mean of its $k$ nearest training neighbours with a single-hidden-layer network of Cauchy activations and scores a query by the length of its predicted displacement. This displacement is an empirical mean-shift vector, whose fixed-radius population counterpart locally approximates a scaled gradient of the log density. We show that Cauchy units exactly represent the score fields of a structured family of Student-$t$ expert densities, and establish a constructive approximation bound for the corresponding population neighbourhood-mean map using a single-hidden-layer Cauchy network. We further show that the bounded network output guarantees asymptotically linear residual-score growth along every fixed direction. On 46 benchmark datasets against 28 baselines, CDN obtains the best mean rank under both AUC-ROC and AUC-PR, while scoring $10^4$ queries in a few milliseconds on a single CPU thread, up to three orders of magnitude faster than neighbourhood-based detectors, with a model whose size does not depend on the training set.
papers.summary: Neighbourhood-based anomaly detectors such as `KNN`, `LOF`, and `LUNAR` are among the most accurate on tabular data, but they must store the training set and compare every query against it. The `Cauchy Displacement Network` (`CDN`) compiles that neighbourhood geometry into a single-hidden-layer network with Cauchy activations that regresses each normal point onto the mean of its k nearest neighbours, then scores a query by the length of its predicted displacement. The authors connect this displacement to the gradient of the log density and prove representation and approximation results. Across 46 datasets and 28 baselines, `CDN` achieves the best mean rank on both AUC-ROC and AUC-PR while **scoring 10,000 queries in a few milliseconds on one CPU thread**, up to three orders of magnitude faster than neighbourhood methods.

papers.title: Comparative Evaluation of LLM-Based Review Paradigms for Academic Paper Quality Assessment
papers.abstract: Growing submission volumes have renewed interest in using large language models (LLMs) to support peer review. It remains unclear how such evaluation should be structured, how much the model matters, and whether LLM scores predict research impact. We evaluate five paradigms across three input representations and three LLMs on 232 stratified ICLR 2025 submissions. Direct absolute rating matches comparative ranking on rank correlation with human scores, yet compresses most predictions above the accept threshold, flagging almost none of the papers reviewers scored below it. A base-rate-matched recalibration control locates the cause: comparative ranking supplies placement, not better ordering, and after recalibration Direct Rating reaches higher agreement than Elo while making 24% as many API calls. Abstract-only input beats full-paper summarization, and model choice matters as much as paradigm choice. Replicating on all 11,513 scored submissions reproduces these patterns, shows absolute agreement depends on the evaluated set's score spread, and finds none beating an always-reject baseline in accuracy. Human scores track citations better than any paradigm, with one exception: Group Rating retains its citation correlation after controlling for human scores, and alone ranks within the accepted pool. Ranking quality alone cannot assess review quality; calibration, thresholds, model, and target outcome all matter.
papers.summary: Growing submission volumes have renewed interest in using large language models (LLMs) for peer review, but it is unclear how such evaluation should be structured. The authors compare five review paradigms, three input representations, and three LLMs on 232 stratified `ICLR 2025` submissions, then replicate on all 11,513 scored submissions. Direct absolute rating matches comparative ranking on rank correlation but places almost every paper above the accept threshold; after recalibration it agrees with humans better than `Elo` ranking while using 24% as many API calls. Abstract-only input beats full-paper summaries, model choice matters as much as paradigm, and **no paradigm beats an always-reject baseline in accuracy**.

papers.title: ProSearch: Benchmarking Multi-Constraint Protocol Retrieval in Experimental Science
papers.abstract: In AI for Science scenarios, experimental design and method reproduction require retrieving protocols that satisfy multiple interdependent constraints, yet existing benchmarks lack systematic evaluation of this capability. To address this gap, we introduce ProSearch, a benchmark for multi-constraint protocol retrieval in experimental science. ProSearch has three key features: (1) realism, with queries grounded in real experimental records and expert-defined templates; (2) complexity, with 60 experimental fields and their dependencies; and (3) diagnosticity, with 3-5 explicit constraints per query, including numerical and negation constraints. We construct ProSearch through LLM-based extraction, data-driven constraint selection, controlled query generation, and evidence-based relevance validation. The resulting benchmark contains 1,515 queries across six experimental science domains. We conduct extensive experiments on ProSearch with 19 representative retrievers and complementary analyses. The best-performing retriever achieves an average nDCG@10 of only 0.290, which improves to 0.474 with reranking. Structured diagnostic analysis shows that explicit constraint matching provides a strong ranking signal, while manual error analysis identifies joint constraint binding as a key bottleneck. ProSearch provides a testbed for systematically evaluating scientific retrieval systems.
papers.summary: Designing or reproducing experiments requires finding protocols that satisfy several interdependent constraints at once, and existing retrieval benchmarks do not test this. `ProSearch` contains 1,515 queries across six experimental-science domains, grounded in real experimental records, with 3–5 explicit constraints per query, including numerical and negation constraints. Across 19 retrievers, **the best reaches an average nDCG@10 of only 0.290**, rising to 0.474 with reranking. Error analysis identifies binding multiple constraints together as the key bottleneck.

papers.title: Cross-Interface Authorization for AI Computer-Use Agents
papers.abstract:
Computer-use agents act through graphical interfaces, command lines, APIs, scripts, and Model Context Protocol servers. A policy decision can be interface-invariant while its executable authorization is not: another route can bypass mediation, alter a security-relevant default, or commit after the authorized state has changed. We present a profile-bounded protocol for a fixed, versioned computer-use deployment. It enumerates effect-bearing routes and durable sinks, checks a route-to-sink enforcement cut, normalizes each concrete request to a canonical effect, issues a route-bound prepare ticket, and verifies the route, effect, grant, trace, profile, inventory, and authoritative state again at commit. A committed result requires an agreeing sink receipt. Under explicit assumptions, we prove profile-bounded refinement, matched-effect decision invariance, resistance to alternate-route laundering and declared cross-surface recomposition, commit-time state safety, and receipt-grounded outcomes.
  The reference profile registers 12 effect families, five interfaces, and 60 routes. Two structurally distinct runtime mappings produce 3,464 traces over 1,732 scenarios each: 960 commits, 2,312 denials, and 192 commits after re-preparation. An independent checker accepts every retained trace and pair and rejects 26/26 semantic regressions; coverage and normalizer suites reject 24/24 and 720/720 mutants; and 168/168 commit probes match their declared outcomes. A frozen-source audit passes 52 checks over 12 files from two independent hybrid runtimes and one public authorization substrate. Source-shaped adapter refinements commit 48/48 instrumented calls and reject 15/15 unbound cases. The resulting guarantees bind the declared profile and its effect semantics.
papers.summary: Computer-use agents can act through GUIs, command lines, APIs, scripts, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, so a policy enforced on one route can be bypassed through another, or the system's state can change between authorization and execution. The authors present a protocol for a fixed deployment profile that enumerates every effect-bearing route, normalizes each request to a canonical effect, issues route-bound tickets, and re-verifies state at commit time, accepting a result only with a matching sink receipt. They prove resistance to alternate-route laundering and to cross-surface recomposition, along with commit-time state safety. In a reference profile with 60 routes, an independent checker accepts every retained trace and **rejects all 26 injected semantic regressions**, and the mutation suites catch 744 of 744 mutants.

papers.title: Distilling Knowledge from Search: Decoder Model Factory for Quantum LDPC Codes
papers.abstract: We introduce GraphMP, a learning-based message-passing decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes that transfers without fine-tuning across code families, code sizes, physical error rates, and noise models. GraphMP uses local message passing to keep computation scalable as the decoding graph grows. Guided by its predictions, beam search progressively refines candidate error patterns, trading additional decoding time for lower logical error rates. We develop the decoder model factory as a paradigm for training successive models on experience generated by earlier models during decoding. Model-guided search supplies verified trajectories for knowledge distillation, folding computation spent on decoding into reusable training data. Repeated collection and distillation improve the decoder across generations and adapt its strategy as the noise changes. These results motivate a coupled quantum--classical architecture with two interacting cycles: rapid decoding protects quantum information, while slower learning renews the models from operating experience. The long-term vision is a scalable decoder model factory that produces high-performance, low-latency decoders and continually adapts them to evolving quantum hardware.
papers.summary: Decoders for quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes need to be fast, accurate, and able to adapt as hardware noise changes. `GraphMP` is a learned message-passing decoder that **transfers without fine-tuning across code families, sizes, error rates, and noise models**, and guides a beam search that trades extra decoding time for lower logical error rates. In the proposed decoder model factory, each model generation is trained by distilling verified search trajectories produced by the previous one, which improves the decoder over generations and adapts it as noise shifts.

papers.title: scAnyOmics: Foundation-Model Distillation for Any-to-Any Completion of Multi-omics Virtual Cells
papers.abstract: Recent advances in single-cell technologies have enabled the profiling of multiple molecular modalities, including transcriptomics, proteomics, and chromatin accessibility, providing a more comprehensive understanding of cellular states. However, integrating heterogeneous modalities and predicting missing molecular information remain challenging, particularly when paired measurements are limited. Here, we introduce scAnyOmics, a generative framework that distills knowledge from a frozen single-cell foundation model into a multimodal student model. scAnyOmics integrates scRNA-seq, protein-marker measurements, and scATAC-seq into a shared representation, enabling cross-modal prediction and reconstruction of missing modalities. We assembled 690,880 cells from six publicly available studies, covering both paired and partially paired multi-omics measurements, to systematically evaluate its predictive performance. We further evaluated scAnyOmics on held-out donor data, where it outperformed baseline methods across multiple evaluation metrics. Beyond cross-modal reconstruction, we explored its applications in cell-type annotation, perturbation-response prediction, and biological age estimation. Overall, scAnyOmics provides a unified framework for integrating incomplete single-cell multi-omics data and transferring pretrained biological knowledge, supporting the development of virtual cell models across diverse cellular contexts and experimental platforms.
papers.summary: Single-cell experiments can measure several molecular modalities, but paired measurements are scarce, which makes integrating them and predicting missing ones difficult. `scAnyOmics` distills knowledge from a frozen single-cell foundation model into a multimodal student that maps `scRNA-seq`, protein-marker, and `scATAC-seq` data into a shared representation for any-to-any completion. Evaluated on 690,880 cells from six studies, it **outperformed baselines on held-out donors** across multiple metrics. The authors also apply it to cell-type annotation, perturbation-response prediction, and biological age estimation.

papers.title: When Safety Checks Become Privacy Risks: A Privacy-Preserving Paradigm for LLM Agent Safety Auditing
papers.abstract: Large language model agents interact with online services through tool calls that may access private data or perform sensitive actions. Specialized providers can supply and maintain pre-execution safety auditing capabilities for agent operators. However, sending task descriptions, call arguments, and interaction histories to an external auditor may expose sensitive user information. In this work, we propose a paradigm for privacy-preserving safety auditing that separates delegated audit computation from plaintext access and execution authority. Grounded in a three-domain auditing model, the paradigm connects trusted representation construction, encrypted audit computation, and trusted decision and execution through explicit interfaces. These interfaces accommodate alternative representations and scorers, while encrypted computation protects audit inputs from a semi-honest auditor. We instantiate this paradigm in SealCall, a framework combining learned audit representations, CKKS-based encrypted similarity computation, and execution control bound to audited tool calls. Evaluated on 1,252 public binary candidates, SealCall achieves a mean F1 score of 0.840 under grouped nested evaluation, while preserving plaintext audit decisions in all measured cases. A representative configuration completes each encrypted scoring operation in 0.176 s.
papers.summary: Sending an LLM agent's task descriptions, tool-call arguments, and history to an external safety auditor can expose sensitive user data. The authors propose a privacy-preserving auditing approach that separates audit computation from plaintext access and execution authority across three trust domains, and instantiate it as `SealCall`. `SealCall` combines learned audit representations, `CKKS` homomorphically encrypted similarity scoring, and execution control bound to the audited tool call. On 1,252 public candidates it reaches a **mean F1 of 0.840**, reproduces the plaintext audit decision in every measured case, and takes 0.176 seconds per encrypted scoring operation in a representative configuration.

papers.title: DUGO: Dual-Scale Gaussian Memory for Online Temporal Action Localization in Egocentric Procedural Videos
papers.abstract: Online Temporal Action Localization (OnTAL) aims to detect and localize action instances from untrimmed streaming videos in real time. Unlike offline approaches, OnTAL models have no access to future frames and cannot go back and refine earlier predictions, which makes the task considerably harder given the strict real-time constraints and narrow temporal window available. Most existing OnTAL methods lean on either brief anchor-based context or a single-scale memory of past frames, which limits how well they can capture actions unfolding across multiple time scales or requiring long-range reasoning in Procedural Videos. To address these gaps, we present DUGO (Dual-Scale Encoding and Gaussian Memory Online), a new OnTAL framework that jointly models local motion dynamics and long-range temporal dependencies. At its core, DUGO uses a Dual-Scale Temporal Encoder, pairing depth-wise local representations with global self-attention so it can pick up both fine-grained temporal patterns and broader contextual cues. We also introduce a Gaussian Memory Bank, which represents action memory as stochastic, input-conditioned Gaussian prototypes, allowing for richer temporal memory through gated cross-attention applied at both the encoder and anchor-query stages. Extensive experiments on procedural egocentric datasets (EGTEA, EPIC-Kitchens-100) demonstrate that DUGO achieves state-of-the-art performance while also providing substantial improvements on non-egocentric benchmarks such as Muses. The project page is available at: https://aman554-eq.github.io/DUGO
papers.summary: Online temporal action localization (OnTAL) detects actions in streaming video without access to future frames, and existing methods rely on short context or single-scale memory that miss long procedural actions. `DUGO` pairs a dual-scale temporal encoder, combining depth-wise local features with global self-attention, with a memory bank of stochastic, input-conditioned Gaussian prototypes read through gated cross-attention. It **achieves state-of-the-art results** on the egocentric procedural datasets `EGTEA` and `EPIC-Kitchens-100` and also improves substantially on the non-egocentric `Muses` benchmark.

papers.title: Conditional Neural SDEs for Financial Time-Series Generation
papers.abstract: Conditional generation of time-series paths is a central problem in probabilistic modeling, where the goal is to simulate future trajectories that are both realistic and responsive to external context. It has direct applications in finance and economics. Neural stochastic differential equations provide a natural framework for this task by combining continuous-time stochastic dynamics with learnable drift and diffusion functions. However, directly modeling the target state can be unstable in conditional settings, especially when the target and conditioning variables have strong level dependence, limited training data, or different dimensions.We propose a residualanchor Neural SDE architecture that decomposes the target into a learned conditional anchor and a stochastic residual. The anchor captures the context-dependent baseline, while the Neural SDE (Stochastic Differential Equation) models the residual dynamics around this baseline. This separation reduces the burden on the stochastic dynamics and generalizes spread-based representations to more general conditioning settings.We evaluate the approach on real-world financial time series, including conditional interest-rate scenarios and a comparison with a time-series foundation model. The results show that the proposed model can generate plausible conditional paths, maintain competitive point accuracy, and provide calibrated uncertainty estimates.
papers.summary: Neural stochastic differential equations (SDEs) are a natural fit for generating future time-series paths conditioned on external context, but modeling the target directly is unstable when levels depend strongly on the conditioning variables or data is limited. The proposed residual-anchor architecture splits the target into a learned conditional anchor that captures the context-dependent baseline and a stochastic residual modeled by the Neural SDE. On real financial data, including conditional interest-rate scenarios and a comparison with a time-series foundation model, the model generates plausible paths with competitive point accuracy and **calibrated uncertainty estimates**.

papers.title: SACQ: Structure-Aware Codebook Quantization for Ultra-Low-Bit Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable capable robot behavior, but their large memory footprint limits deployment on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Weight quantization is a natural remedy, yet post-training quantization (PTQ) recipes inherited from large language models degrade when applied to VLAs at ultra-low precision. Existing low-bit PTQ methods often fail to explicitly account for the structure of downstream operations and allocate precision without considering its effect on the policy actions. We introduce SACQ, an ultra- low-bit weight-only vector-codebook quantization framework for VLAs. SACQ combines (1) structure-aware codebook fitting with role-specific quadratic metrics that reflect input statistics and downstream sensitivity; (2) action-aware mixed-bit allocation based on the increase in final-action error as individual layers are compressed; and (3) two-stage post-quantization refinement that reassigns codeword indices with second-order error compensation and calibrates codebooks and row-group scales against the decoded action. Using GR00T N1.7, SACQ achieves 93.85% average success across four LIBERO suites at 1.5 bits per language/action weight while reducing model memory by 4.83x. With INT8 activation quantization and low-precision attention, it retains 93.55% success while running 1.51x faster than BF16. On SimplER, SACQ further achieves 63.76% and 52.27% success under Visual Matching and Variant Aggregation at 2 bits per language/action weight, compared to 58.90% and 53.45% for BF16, respectively.
