papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are too memory-hungry for many robots, and post-training quantization (PTQ) recipes borrowed from LLMs degrade at ultra-low precision. `SACQ` is a weight-only vector-codebook quantizer that fits codebooks with structure-aware metrics, allocates bits per layer by how much each one increases final action error, and refines codewords and scales against the decoded action. On `GR00T N1.7`, it reaches **93.85% average success on `LIBERO` at 1.5 bits per weight with 4.83 times less memory**, and with INT8 activations it runs 1.51 times faster than BF16. On `SimplER` at 2 bits, it scores 63.76% on Visual Matching and 52.27% on Variant Aggregation, against 58.90% and 53.45% for BF16.

papers.title: Certifying Retraining Regret through Residual Structure
papers.abstract: We certify a fixed ridge predictor's regret against full-feature retraining over every continuous completion of an interval-valued table. Our main theorem gives verifiable original-row residual conditions for a uniform error bound independent of nuisance-feature scale and rank, with an asymptotically sharp leading constant and quantitative leakage stability. Full-rank constructions separate certification dimension from feature dimension, including examples requiring directions beyond the candidate. Observed-row anchors make the conditions computable, while exact row geometry and global search return valid upper bounds and feasible original-table witnesses. A finite-scale contraction and common-domain moment fallback implement the structural result. Four real-world tasks retain all model features and certify twenty rank-three instances to width $10^{-5}$. Their primary median widths improve over centered moments. Joint residual refinement additionally certifies all twenty new response-independent masks to the same precision within 76.21 seconds. For a concrete fixed-point predictor contract, pure energy certifies thirteen of fifteen stopping decisions in ten seconds, versus five for moments. Refinement certifies all fifteen within 91.68 seconds at the same objective threshold.
papers.summary: Gives a way to bound how much worse a fixed ridge regression predictor can be than a model fully retrained on all features, when some table entries are only known as intervals. The main theorem gives checkable conditions on the residuals of the original rows. These conditions yield a uniform error bound that does not depend on the scale or rank of nuisance features, and they are made computable through observed-row anchors and global search. On four real-world tasks the method certifies twenty rank-three instances to width 10^-5 and beats centered-moment baselines. A joint residual refinement **certifies all twenty new masks within 76.21 seconds**.

papers.title: CryoAtlas: A Large Curated Dataset and Unified Benchmark for Cryo-EM Atomic Model Building
papers.abstract: Deep learning has accelerated automated atomic model building from cryo-EM maps, yet progress remains limited by the lack of large, high-quality datasets and standardized evaluation benchmarks. We address this gap by introducing CryoAtlas, a rigorously curated dataset and unified benchmark for density-guided atomic model building of protein chains. By integrating and filtering EMDB and PDB entries (up to March 2026), CryoAtlas provides 17,809 map-model-sequence entries, including a curated 16,657-entry training split. From this resource, we construct a 618-target benchmark with a shared evaluation protocol that jointly assesses structural accuracy, model-to-map fit, and stereochemical validity. Using this framework, we benchmark state-of-the-art learning-based methods against Phenix and AlphaFold3, comprehensively analyzing the impact of map resolution, sequence length, protein category and sequence identity on modeling accuracy. As a case study, retraining the ModelAngelo CNN component on CryoAtlas improves performance on the benchmark. CryoAtlas provides an open, reproducible foundation for future cryo-EM atomic model building research. Project details and resource release updates are available at https://oulling.github.io/cryoatlas/.
papers.summary: Introduces `CryoAtlas`, a curated dataset and shared benchmark for building atomic protein models from cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) density maps. Progress in this area has been held back by the lack of large, clean training data and of standard evaluation. Built by filtering `EMDB` and `PDB` entries, the dataset has **17,809 map-model-sequence entries**. A 618-target benchmark scores structural accuracy, fit to the map, and stereochemical validity together. The authors compare learning-based methods against `Phenix` and `AlphaFold3` across resolution, sequence length, and protein category, and show that retraining the CNN component of `ModelAngelo` on the dataset improves its benchmark results.

papers.title: SparseGDN: Chunk Sparse in Linear Attention
papers.abstract: Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) offer linear-time sequence modeling, yet long-context prefill remains costly due to dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate state storage. We introduce SparseGDN, a hardware-aware framework that combines structured intra-chunk approximation with input-dependent recurrent-event selection while producing outputs for every token. A block-adjacent solver reduces local Delta-solve computation, while a dynamic selector allocates recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The GPU implementation materializes updates only for selected events and reconstructs token outputs using compact state snapshots and group-local interactions, reducing computation and memory traffic. We evaluate SparseGDN on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B across RULER tasks and context lengths from 4K to 128K. Retaining approximately 29% of recurrent events on average, SparseGDN achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including online selection overhead.
papers.summary: `Gated Delta Networks` (GDNs) model sequences in linear time, but long-context prefill is still expensive because of dense computation within chunks, recurrent state updates, and storage of intermediate states. `SparseGDN` approximates the computation inside each chunk and uses an input-dependent selector to decide which recurrent updates to compute, while still producing an output for every token. A GPU implementation materializes only the selected updates. On `Qwen3.5-4B` and `Qwen3.5-9B`, tested with `RULER` at context lengths from 4K to 128K, it keeps about 29% of recurrent events and reaches **1.50-1.94x prefill speedups in the GDN core** over native `FLA` kernels, with selection overhead included.

papers.title: A Unified XAI-NSAI Analytical Framework for Trustworthy IoT Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: The widespread deployment of Internet of Things (IoT) devices in critical environments makes anomaly detection essential for identifying abnormal behaviors and supporting timely investigation and response. However, accurate detection alone is insufficient. Practical IoT deployments must also provide explanations, incorporate domain knowledge and reasoning, operate under IoT constraints, and support human decision making. Although recently proposed approaches increasingly incorporate Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) or Neuro-Symbolic Artificial Intelligence (NSAI), XAI and NSAI methods are often considered independently. We argue that they should be considered together to better understand their complementary roles in supporting trustworthy IoT anomaly detection. To address this gap, we propose a unified analytical framework organized around five complementary dimensions. The framework provides a structured basis for characterizing existing approaches, identifying capability gaps and design trade-offs, and guiding the design of new anomaly detection systems for different IoT applications. We demonstrate the framework's analytical utility by applying it to three representative studies and illustrate its design utility through its application to a Medical IoT anomaly detection system.
papers.summary: Argues that Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) and Neuro-Symbolic Artificial Intelligence (NSAI) should be considered together when building trustworthy anomaly detection for Internet of Things (IoT) devices, instead of being treated separately. The authors propose an analytical framework with **five complementary dimensions** for describing existing approaches, finding capability gaps and trade-offs, and guiding new designs. They apply it to three representative studies and to the design of an anomaly detection system for medical IoT.

papers.title: Hybrid Computer Use: A Unified Programmatic, Semantic, and Visual Interface for General Agents
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents increasingly tackle tasks ranging from everyday desktop activities to long-horizon professional workflows. Yet interfaces centered on screenshots and mouse-and-keyboard actions can impose a human-interaction prior, requiring repeated screen interpretation while leaving the computer's semantic and programmatic capabilities underexposed. We argue for exposing these capabilities and letting models choose and combine them. We introduce Hybrid Computer Use (HCU), a unified interface for general agents that combines three complementary channels: programmatic interaction through code and command-line tools, semantic interaction through accessibility (AX), and visual interaction through graphical user interfaces (GUI). Our HCU supports efficient AX interaction and guards against stale-state actions during channel switching. A supplementary HCU skill guides agents in selecting and coordinating channels to use the unified interface effectively. Our designed AX tools return compact observations, execute actions in batches, and report their effects as AX diffs, so the model needs fewer round trips. On OSWorld 2.0, HCU achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores among the compared systems. Analyzing agent trajectories, we find that all evaluated models improve with HCU yet allocate work across the channels differently and consistently outperform compared baselines in terms of both efficiency and task success, highlighting the value of unified computer-use interfaces that allow flexible channel selection and combination.
papers.summary: Argues that computer-use agents limited to screenshots and mouse-and-keyboard actions inherit a human interaction pattern and miss the computer's programmatic and semantic interfaces. `Hybrid Computer Use` (HCU) gives agents one interface with three channels: code and command-line tools, the accessibility (AX) tree, and the graphical user interface (GUI). A supplementary skill helps agents choose and combine channels. The AX tools return compact observations, batch actions, and report their effects as diffs, which cuts round trips. HCU **achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores on `OSWorld 2.0`** among compared systems, and every evaluated model improved in both success and efficiency.

papers.title: BlindToChange: AI Agents Can Find Changes When Asked But Do They Look When Needed?
papers.abstract: Given that AI agents can search the web broadly and deeply in real time, it is tempting to conclude that their outputs account for recent world events. We show that this conclusion does not hold in practice. While agents can search and easily find recent changes, the correctness of their responses depends on whether they search and what they search for. Popular agentic search benchmarks like BrowseComp cannot expose failures wherein agents do not recognize their own assumptions that should be verified, since these benchmarks explicitly state what needs to be found. In contrast, many user requests state only the final information need (e.g., an itinerary for a trip), leaving the agent to discover relevant changes (e.g., the temporary closure of a museum) and account for their consequences. To highlight such gaps, we introduce BlindToChange, a benchmark that measures whether agents proactively discover recent events that affect their responses. Our benchmark comprises requests for recommendations where an obvious candidate is no longer applicable due to a recent real-world event. These events are drawn automatically from Wikidata, allowing BlindToChange to be periodically refreshed. Strikingly, we find a big gap -- as high as 27.5 points, even at high reasoning effort -- in systems' performance, when the recent event is not explicitly mentioned compared to when we ask about it directly. Analyzing search trajectories, we learn that more than half of the failures can be attributed to the fact that agents do not directly search to verify whether a relevant fact has changed. Our benchmark highlights, and tracks, a new axis of progress, wherein systems account for recent information that is not explicitly mentioned in the user request.
papers.summary: Shows that web-search agents often fail to account for recent real-world changes when a request does not mention them, even though they can find those changes easily when asked directly. `BlindToChange` is a benchmark of recommendation requests in which the obvious answer no longer applies because of a recent event, such as a temporarily closed museum. The events are drawn automatically from `Wikidata`, so the benchmark can be refreshed. Performance drops by **as much as 27.5 points** when the event is not mentioned, even at high reasoning effort. More than half of the failures come from agents never searching to check whether a relevant fact has changed.

papers.title: A prospective randomized study of patient-centered AI for clinical visit preparation
papers.abstract: Patients often arrive at brief, time-constrained clinical visits unsure of what to expect or ask, and millions of adults now turn to general-purpose AI chatbots to prepare beforehand. Yet whether conversational AI improves visit readiness remains unclear. We designed a large language model (LLM)-based visit preparation agent to guide patients before an appointment by gathering clinical context, setting visit expectations, providing relevant health information, building a prioritized list of questions for their clinician, and generating a summary. In a prospective consented randomized study in the Google Health app, 802 U.S. adults held 866 health-related conversations with the visit preparation agent (standard or concise variant) or a minimally prompted control chatbot built on the same LLM. The visit preparation agent significantly outperformed the control across blinded clinician evaluations and patient self-reports. In clinician reviews of completed sessions (n = 272), the agent achieved a 16.6% higher rate of comprehensive preparation (67.2% vs. 50.6%; P < 0.05) and an 8.5% higher rate of alignment with patients' health context (98.9% vs. 90.4%; P < 0.01), while maintaining high medical safety and appropriateness across all study arms. Patient post-surveys (n = 460) showed 16.8% higher visit preparedness (73.8% vs. 57.0%; P < 0.01), 14.3% higher confidence in knowing what to ask (81.4% vs. 67.1%; P < 0.01), and 12.0% higher overall satisfaction (74.0% vs. 62.0%; P < 0.05). Clinician and participant metrics were not significantly correlated, indicating that expert review and patient self-assessment capture complementary dimensions of patient-facing AI. These findings suggest that LLM chatbots can safely help patients prepare for clinical visits, with greater benefit when following a structured workflow, and motivate future studies on in-visit communication and clinical outcomes.
papers.summary: Tests whether a structured large language model (LLM) agent helps patients prepare for clinical visits. The agent gathers clinical context, sets expectations, and builds a prioritized list of questions for the clinician. In a prospective randomized study in the Google Health app, 802 U.S. adults used either the agent or a minimally prompted control chatbot built on the same LLM. In blinded clinician review, the agent produced comprehensive preparation more often (**67.2% vs. 50.6%**). Patients reported higher preparedness, confidence, and satisfaction, and safety stayed high in all study arms. Clinician ratings and patient ratings were not significantly correlated.

papers.title: From Representation to Readout: Mechanistic Analysis of Membership Signals in Language Models
papers.abstract: Membership inference aims to determine whether a particular example was included in a model's training data. Such membership signals are often broadly described as memorization, while the underlying mechanisms can involve both how information is represented internally and how it is accessed by the model to produce behaviors. We therefore present a mechanistic study of membership signals in large language models (LLMs). We introduce Decodable Information Score, Used Information Score, and Readout Accessibility Gap (DUG), a set of complementary measures that separately quantify membership information decodable from internal representations and the extent to which it is exposed through the model's readout. Across supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL)-based membership inference methods, membership-specific effects appear in both the amount of decodable information and readout under SFT, while under RL-based membership inference methods they appear primarily in readout. Activation patching further localizes this membership-specific effect to intermediate layers. To examine whether these findings extend to a more general RL setting, we further study reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) contamination, where the training reward is independent of the reference solution. In this setting, we find that behavioral changes can emerge without a corresponding increase in likelihood-based membership inference signals.
papers.summary: Separates two things that 'memorization' can mean in membership inference: how much training-set membership information is stored in a model's internal representations, and how much of it reaches the output. The proposed `DUG` measures (Decodable Information Score, Used Information Score, and Readout Accessibility Gap) quantify each part. Under supervised fine-tuning, membership effects appear in both what can be decoded and what is read out. Under reinforcement-learning-based methods they appear **mainly in readout**, and activation patching places the effect in intermediate layers. In contamination under reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), behavior can change without any rise in likelihood-based membership signals.

papers.title: Evidence-Guided Recovery for AI Agents with Ambiguous Tool Outcomes and Partial Execution
papers.abstract: Tool timeouts can leave AI agents facing ambiguous tool outcomes and partial execution: an action may have failed, committed or remained in flight while other workflow steps have already completed. We formulate evidence-guided task recovery over approved obligations, provider capabilities and states compatible with public evidence. A shared admissibility check handles key expiry, authorization timing, dependencies and residual effects; a terminal certificate separates actual goal satisfaction from publicly supported safe completion. The known-model implementation combines standard observation-contingent planning with a separately implemented effect-history adjudicator. In a finite study of 37 assignments, planning and three active controls each certify 28 completions; four saved synthetic fee units incur additional computation. A preregistered assignment-held-out comparison then evaluates planning advice against evidence prompting with two local model bundles. Across 58 paired units in 19 previously developed task families, advice certifies 30 completions versus 9, a 36.2-percentage-point difference (exact family sign-flip p=0.0078), using 272 proposals versus 399. All 116 trajectories pass independent replay. Both models exhibit a positive completion difference. The comparison measures the evaluated advice interface under a common shield; search-versus-rule advice requires a separate matched comparison. Unknown and handoff outcomes remain explicit, with guarantees tied to the declared provider capabilities rather than arbitrary third-party exactly-once execution.
papers.summary: Addresses agents left uncertain after a tool timeout, when an action may have failed, completed, or still be in progress while other workflow steps have already run. The approach plans task recovery over states consistent with the available evidence. A shared admissibility check covers key expiry, authorization timing, and dependencies, and a terminal certificate separates true goal satisfaction from completion that the evidence shows to be safe. In a preregistered comparison with two local model bundles, planning advice certified **30 completions versus 9** for evidence prompting across 58 paired units, while using fewer proposals. All 116 trajectories passed independent replay.

papers.title: When Everyone Can Build a Model: Mechanistic Inference in the Age of AI
papers.abstract: Modern deep learning and AI-assisted code generation are lowering the technical barrier to building mathematical models of biological systems that reproduce complex observations. This lets researchers with domain expertise build semi-mechanistic, hybrid models constrained by prior knowledge and augmented with learned structure without extensive training in modelling. However, easier construction does not make interpretation easier: predictive success of such so-called grey-box models does not establish that an inferred mechanism corresponds to the one that generated the data, and the learned component can absorb errors in the mechanistic part. Many biological modelling problems are underdetermined, so several, possibly infinitely many, models may reproduce the same data equally well. This ambiguity enters at two modelling choices: which variables can affect others, and which response function describes the underlying mechanism. For the first choice, causal inference provides a formal framework stating which causal relationships and intervention effects are identifiable from the data and available knowledge. For the second, ensemble analyses quantify the uncertainty and the range of behaviours still allowed by models that fit equally well. Together, they turn a single good fit into an explicit account of what is supported, what remains open, and which experiment would decide.
authors: Faculty of Mathematics and Natural Sciences
Ad\`ele H. Ribeiro (Causal and Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Life Sciences
Faculty of Mathematics and Natural Sciences
Faculty of Mathematics and Natural Sciences
papers.summary: A perspective piece arguing that deep learning and AI-assisted code generation make it easy to build hybrid 'grey-box' models of biological systems, but a good fit does not show that the inferred mechanism is the real one. Because many biological modeling problems are underdetermined, many models can fit the same data equally well, and the learned component can absorb errors in the mechanistic part. The authors recommend causal inference to decide which variables can affect others, and ensemble analyses to measure uncertainty about response functions. Used together, these turn a single fit into **an explicit account of what is supported and which experiment would settle what remains open**.

papers.title: Improving the Optimization Landscape of Matrix Completion with $\epsilon$-close Surrogates
papers.abstract: Non-convex optimization is central to machine learning and AI, yet unlike its convex counterpart, it still lacks a general and principled framework. In this work, we try to highlight the importance of combining noisy perturbations with over-parametrization mathematically under the classic setting of matrix completion (MC). Matrix completion is an important non-convex recovery problem in which only a subset of a matrix's entries is observed, and the remaining entries must be recovered using low-rank constraints. This problem is notoriously difficult because observations are limited. However, we show that by injecting $\epsilon$-level perturbations into the nullspace of the observation mask, we can construct noisy matrix sensing surrogates whose solutions remain $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)$-close to the ground truth with valid restricted isometry property (RIP) constants. The existence of RIP further enables powerful tensor frameworks to be applied with theoretical guarantees. This approach reflects a broader empirical trend in which stochasticity or noise improves the curvature of the optimization landscape, allowing over-parameterized (a.k.a large) models to better separate signal from noise. Assuming each matrix entry is observed independently, we establish quantitative recovery guarantees without explicit requirements on sampling rate or incoherence, and discuss how such assumptions can further strengthen our results.
papers.summary: Studies how noise combined with over-parameterization can improve non-convex optimization, using low-rank matrix completion as the setting. The authors inject epsilon-level perturbations into the null space of the observation mask. This produces noisy matrix sensing surrogates whose solutions stay **O(epsilon)-close to the ground truth** and that satisfy the restricted isometry property (RIP), so existing tensor-based guarantees apply. Assuming entries are observed independently, they prove recovery guarantees without explicit requirements on sampling rate or incoherence.

papers.title: NormDetect: Anchored Calibration for Low-False-Positive Detection of Machine-Generated Web Text
papers.abstract: Web platforms screen posts for text written by large language models, and every false flag hits a human writer. Detectors must therefore run at a very low false positive rate (FPR). Zero-shot detectors such as Binoculars score text with frozen language models, but invisible edits such as homoglyphs shatter tokenization and push machine text into the human range. Unicode normalization undoes these edits, yet the normalized score still misses half of the machine text at a strict FPR, under attacks that leave nothing to clean. We find that with the Falcon-7B scoring pair, heads on token statistics recall less than the normalized score at this FPR, and several flag too many human posts in some sections. We propose NormDetect, which anchors a learned per-section head to the normalized zero-shot score. A blend weight chosen on training folds under a human FPR cap combines the two scores, and one threshold is calibrated on human text only. On eight sections of the RAID benchmark with eleven attacks, NormDetect raises recall at a 0.1% calibrated FPR by 5.0 points over normalized Binoculars. Its human FPR bound stays at most 1% in every section, and no other detector within this bound recalls as much.
papers.summary: Targets detection of machine-generated web text at very low false positive rates, since every false flag lands on a human writer. Zero-shot detectors such as `Binoculars` can be fooled by invisible edits such as homoglyphs. Unicode normalization undoes those edits but still misses many machine texts under attacks that leave nothing to clean. `NormDetect` anchors a learned head for each section to the normalized zero-shot score, blends the two under a cap on human false positives, and calibrates one threshold on human text only. Across eight sections of `RAID` with eleven attacks, it **raises recall by 5.0 points at a 0.1% false positive rate** over normalized `Binoculars`.

papers.title: RetryRoute: Retry-Aware Model Routing for Agentic Image Editing Services
papers.abstract: Web agents increasingly edit images by calling open editing models in a critique-and-retry loop, and these models differ in cost by more than an order of magnitude. After every rejected edit, a service must decide whether to retry the same model, escalate to another or give up. Existing routers pick one model per request, and cascades escalate in a fixed order. However, both treat a retry as an independent draw. We identify sticky failures, meaning that a retry after a failure succeeds only 17-53% as often as a first try across six open models, three benchmarks and two judges. Based on this finding, we propose RetryRoute, a retry-aware router that estimates each model's chance of success given the request's failure history. It plans retries, escalations and abandonment over failure states and adds live queue waits to the cost, so the same plan becomes load-aware dispatch. At the main budget, RetryRoute's success under the in-loop judge exceeds the strongest of eleven prior baselines by 2.8 points on average over eight groups. On a GPU serving testbed it raises the share of edits delivered within the service-level objective by 5.0-6.3 points over the best prior baseline at every load.
papers.summary: Finds that in agentic image-editing loops, failures are 'sticky': **a retry after a failed edit succeeds only 17-53% as often as a first attempt**. This held across six open models, three benchmarks, and two judges, so treating retries as independent draws is misleading. `RetryRoute` estimates each model's chance of success given the request's failure history and plans whether to retry, escalate to another model, or stop. It also adds live queue waits to the cost so the plan accounts for load. It beats the strongest of eleven baselines by 2.8 points in success and delivers 5.0-6.3 points more edits within the service-level objective on a GPU serving testbed.

papers.title: When Links Mislead: Label-Free Structural Polarity for Zero-Shot Classification of Web Pages
papers.abstract: Web platforms such as digital libraries, online stores and university sites must classify new pages before anyone labels them. Large language models (LLMs) can label each page from its text, but these labels are noisy, and links could correct them only where linked pages share classes. Existing zero-shot methods ignore the links, or pull a page toward its neighbours as label propagation and graph neural networks (GNNs) do, which hurts where linked pages differ in class. Others weight propagation by an LLM-estimated homophily that costs extra calls and drifts across LLMs. We find that the sign with which links should enter a prediction, which we call structural polarity, is readable without true labels. It is the excess agreement of LLM labels and text-prototype predictions along links. We thus propose ZeroPolar, which gates one signed propagation step by this statistic. Training-free ZeroPolar mixes prototype scores with any number of LLM labels, and ZeroPolar-T denoises the labels with a text classifier once half of the pages carry one. With one GPT-4o label per page, ZeroPolar-T reaches the highest mean accuracy on eleven graphs (73.99%), 6.01 points above LLM-BP and significantly above all eighteen baselines we compare. With LLM labels on only 5% of the pages, training-free ZeroPolar leads a GNN trained on these labels by 10.80 points.
papers.summary: Tackles zero-shot classification of web pages, where large language model (LLM) labels are noisy and links help only when linked pages share classes. The authors show that whether links should pull a prediction toward or away from neighbors, which they call structural polarity, can be estimated without true labels. The estimate comes from how often LLM labels and text-prototype predictions agree along links. `ZeroPolar` uses this statistic to gate one signed propagation step. With one `GPT-4o` label per page, `ZeroPolar-T` reaches **73.99% mean accuracy on eleven graphs**, 6.01 points above `LLM-BP`.

papers.title: Spectral Haar Binarizer: Compact Boolean Contrast Representations for Hyperspectral Classification
papers.abstract: Tsetlin Machines offer an interpretable, hardware-friendly alternative to conventional machine learning models, but applying them to continuous hyperspectral measurements requires converting spectral signals into Boolean representations. Standard binarisation methods typically discretise each spectral band independently, potentially discarding important relationships between neighbouring wavelengths. In this paper, we introduce the Spectral Haar Binarizer (SHB), a contrast-based spectral representation method that constructs Boolean predicates from differences between selected spectral intervals. Inspired by Haar-like contrast features, the method uses an AdaBoost-style selection procedure to obtain a compact set of discriminative spectral predicates. We evaluate SHB on five heterogeneous hyperspectral datasets covering forensic blood detection, agricultural and urban remote sensing, and rainforest tree-species classification. Across binary and multiclass tasks, SHB consistently outperforms standard per-band binarisation strategies and provides the strongest or near-strongest results across classifiers. In binary tasks, TM-SHB achieves the best average performance, while RF-SHB is strongest in multiclass settings. Bayesian and rank-based analyses confirm that SHB's advantage is robust across datasets and not driven by isolated cases. The results show that representing continuous hyperspectral measurements is a central processing step for efficient classification. That contrast-based Boolean features provide an effective bridge between information-rich sensor measurements and compact, logic-based processing.
papers.summary: Tsetlin Machines are interpretable, hardware-friendly classifiers, but they need Boolean inputs, and standard binarization of hyperspectral data treats each spectral band separately. That loses relationships between neighboring wavelengths. The `Spectral Haar Binarizer` (SHB) instead builds Boolean predicates from contrasts between selected spectral intervals and picks a compact set with an AdaBoost-style procedure. Across five hyperspectral datasets, from forensic blood detection to tree-species classification, SHB **consistently outperforms per-band binarization**, and Bayesian and rank-based analyses support the result.

papers.title: EvoMCP: Co-evolving MCP agents and training data
papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning of Model Context Protocol (MCP) agents is typically conducted on a static data distribution, which fails to adapt to the student's evolving capabilities and leaves newly exposed weaknesses insufficiently addressed. To address these challenges, we propose \method, an agent--data mutual evolution framework that enables MCP agents to improve through a closed loop of task evolution, trajectory evolution, and supervised fine-tuning. Specifically, \method\ assesses the student's established capabilities and capability gaps from rollout feedback to identify learning targets. Task evolution then translates these targets into executable tasks by adapting the instructions and observable environment states of compatible verified seed tasks while keeping their verifiers aligned. To provide reliable and efficient demonstrations for these tasks, trajectory evolution uses reusable skills to recover failed teacher rollouts and refine successful ones. The resulting task--trajectory pairs are used to fine-tune the student, while accepted tasks seed subsequent evolution. To close the loop, we re-evaluate the updated student and use its feedback to guide the next round of data evolution. Experiments on Toolathlon, MCPMark, and MCP-Atlas demonstrate consistent improvements over the initial student, yielding absolute gains of 16.5\%, 10.2\%, and 12.6\%, respectively. Project page: https://github.com/xagao/EvoMCP.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning of Model Context Protocol (MCP) agents usually relies on a fixed dataset that does not adapt as the student model improves. `EvoMCP` closes the loop: it finds the student's capability gaps from rollout feedback and adapts verified seed tasks to target those gaps. Teacher trajectories are recovered or refined using reusable skills, and the student is fine-tuned and re-evaluated before the next round. The method gives absolute gains of **16.5% on `Toolathlon`**, 10.2% on `MCPMark`, and 12.6% on `MCP-Atlas` over the initial student.

papers.title: KV-Cache Patching: Tracing How and Where Fine-Tuned Behaviors Arise
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a language model changes how it responds, but where is this fine-tuned behavior instantiated? To better understand this, we evaluate whether the change in model behavior arises only during the generation of the answer tokens where the change manifests, or whether altered processing of previous tokens causes it via the attention mechanism. For this, we patch the KV cache from a LoRA fine-tuned model into the unmodified base model, and vice versa. Our results show that for some behaviors, like responding in German or emergent misalignment, patching the KV cache can indeed transfer them from the fine-tuned to the base model. Correspondingly, patching the KV cache from base to fine-tune can partially or fully remove fine-tuned behavior. Furthermore, we find that the effect of patching grows with how much of the KV cache is patched and concentrates at a few pivotal positions, with system-prompt and chat-template tokens having disproportionate influence.
papers.summary: Asks whether a fine-tuned behavior arises only while the model generates its answer, or whether it comes from altered processing of earlier tokens that reaches the answer through attention. The authors patch the KV cache from a LoRA fine-tuned model into the base model and the reverse. For behaviors such as responding in German and emergent misalignment, **patching the KV cache alone can transfer the behavior** to the base model, and patching in the opposite direction can partly or fully remove it. The effect grows with how much of the cache is patched and concentrates at a few key positions, especially system-prompt and chat-template tokens.

papers.title: KEEPER: Learning Control-Sufficient Textual Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Recursive textual memory can carry earlier errors into later updates, yet task performance alone does not establish memory reliability. We define self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims already present in the incoming memory. We present KEEPER, a comparative analysis of four auxiliary objectives along information-content and update-sensitivity axes within a shared recursive interface, examining how supervision targets relate to agent performance. Among evaluated conditions, reward-related prediction achieve the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, outperforming joint supervision. A claim-level analysis of one baseline trajectory documents error persistence despite corrective observations. Together, these analyses motivate evaluating error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.
papers.summary: Studies how long-horizon LLM agents that repeatedly rewrite a textual memory can carry earlier errors forward, which the authors call self-consistency bias. `KEEPER` compares four auxiliary training objectives for memory updates within a shared recursive interface. **Reward-related prediction gives the best task performance** both before and after offline reinforcement learning, and it outperforms joint supervision. A claim-level analysis shows errors persisting even after corrective observations, and the authors argue that error persistence should be evaluated alongside task success.

papers.title: Multi-Test Nation Bias Benchmarking of LLMs with Explicit Unbiased Baselines
papers.abstract: While prior work has highlighted that systematic nation-level bias in large language models (LLMs) can pose operational risks for international relations (IR) applications, many existing evaluations still lack a clearly specified unbiased reference (ground truth), limiting fully quantitative and cross-setting measurement. Using an expanded corpus of 722 official UN Security Council (UNSC) records, we measure nation-level bias with five complementary tests, thereby extending prior approaches to cover a broader set of bias expression channels: opinion ranking (WOW), association sorting (AK+-), vote simulation (PVS), opposition attribution (F-Oppose), and framing (Headliner). To enable grounded bias evaluation, we explicitly define an unbiased status for each test; in particular, for WOW and AK+- where ground truth is difficult to specify, we propose an action-based pseudo unbiased status derived from observable voting behavior to construct a quantifiable baseline. Benchmarking 4 LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.3-70B, Mistral-22B-Small, and Qwen3-30B) across the five permanent members of the UNSC, we find a test-agnostic macro-pattern: relative to the reference baselines defined for each test, model outputs lean toward the opposition (red) side for China and Russia and toward the supportive (blue) side for the U.K., the U.S., and France. These results underscore the need to audit IR-facing LLM deployments with grounded, multi-test benchmarks tied to explicit reference points.
papers.summary: Measures nation-level bias in large language models (LLMs) for international relations uses, using 722 UN Security Council records. The study applies five tests: opinion ranking, association sorting, vote simulation, opposition attribution, and framing. Each test has an explicitly defined unbiased baseline, built from observed voting behavior where ground truth is hard to specify. Across `GPT-4o-mini`, `Llama 3.3-70B`, `Mistral-22B-Small`, and `Qwen3-30B`, outputs consistently **lean toward the opposition side for China and Russia and the supportive side for the U.K., U.S., and France**.

papers.title: Sparse Text Diffusion under Dual Budgets: Context Connectivity and Expert Activation
papers.abstract: Long-context diffusion repeatedly pays for both token interaction and feed-forward computation. We formulate these costs as two separate budgets: the edges available to an attention graph and the experts activated for each token. This view connects local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming that sparsity alone preserves document-level information. We specify normalized masked attention, distinguish denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derive graph and compute bounds. A reported sparse-expert configuration, denoted DualBudget, is analyzed across scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction. All supplied table measurements are retained. The length study shows gains over the listed baselines through 16K, together with measurable degradation as length increases. Ablations reveal mixed changes across the three reported scores, while the cost record indicates a 20% reduction relative to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention. The analysis separates these observations from unmeasured claims about training speed, absorbing states, global coherence, and deployment memory.
papers.summary: Treats the cost of long-context text diffusion as two separate budgets: the edges in the attention graph and the number of experts activated per token. This view links local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation. The authors derive graph and compute bounds and analyze a sparse-expert configuration, `DualBudget`, on summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair tasks. It shows gains over the listed baselines up to 16K tokens, with degradation as length grows, and a **20% cost reduction relative to `DiffuSeq`** under an unspecified timing convention.

papers.title: PCD: Predictive Coding Dynamics for Irregularly Sampled Time Series
papers.abstract: Dynamic systems evolve continuously over time, whereas observations in real scenarios are often sparse, irregular, and asynchronous. Accurate prediction therefore requires inferring latent state evolution between observations, as future values depend on partially observed trajectories. We propose Predictive Coding Dynamics (PCD), a residual feedback mechanism for irregular continuous dynamic models. PCD maintains previous reconstructions, predicts observed entries from them, and incorporates masked signed residuals into state recognition through an energy penalty. The mechanism is implemented with ODE-RNN and Latent ODE, supporting event-based hidden updates and latent state recognition. Experiments on forecasting and trajectory recovery tasks show that PCD improves continuous dynamic backbones under sparse and irregular sampling. The results further indicate that predictive error feedback improves latent state estimation when observations constrain the current trajectory. These results suggest that PCD provides a residual feedback framework that jointly supports trajectory generation, observation consistency checking, and state refinement in continuous-time series modeling. The source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/PCD-for-paper-92F1/.
papers.summary: Real-world observations of continuous dynamic systems are often sparse, irregular, and asynchronous, so forecasting requires inferring how the hidden state evolves between observations. `Predictive Coding Dynamics` (`PCD`) adds a residual feedback mechanism that keeps previous reconstructions, predicts the observed entries from them, and feeds masked signed prediction errors back into state recognition through an energy penalty. It is implemented on top of `ODE-RNN` and `Latent ODE` backbones. Experiments on forecasting and trajectory recovery show that **predictive error feedback improves continuous dynamic backbones under sparse and irregular sampling**, especially when observations constrain the current trajectory.

papers.title: Specification-Guided Generation for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate structured outputs, but existing constrained-decoding methods mainly enforce syntax and cannot directly enforce satisfaction of a formal specification. We introduce a neuro-symbolic, specification-guided decoding framework that combines LLM generation with symbolic reasoning. At each step, the framework refines the decoding grammar by filtering out values that cannot be extended to an output satisfying the specification. We present a forward-only variant that guarantees specification satisfaction by construction, and a backtracking variant that revises earlier feasible choices when their downstream consequences leave only values that the LLM itself judges unsuitable. The framework is model-agnostic, requires no retraining, and builds on existing grammar-constrained decoding mechanisms. Experiments on configuration and constraint-solving benchmarks show that the forward-only variant reliably produces specification-compliant outputs while reducing repeated LLM inference compared with rejection sampling and incurring modest symbolic-reasoning overhead. The backtracking variant further reduces cases in which the model is forced to select values that it has itself judged unsuitable, thereby substantially improving adherence to the LLM's stated interpretation of the prompt.
papers.summary: Existing constrained-decoding methods for large language models (LLMs) enforce output syntax but cannot guarantee that the output satisfies a formal specification. The proposed neuro-symbolic decoding framework uses symbolic reasoning at each generation step to refine the decoding grammar, removing values that cannot be extended into a specification-satisfying output. A forward-only variant guarantees compliance by construction, and a backtracking variant revises earlier choices when their consequences leave only values the LLM itself judges unsuitable. On configuration and constraint-solving benchmarks, the forward-only variant **reliably produces specification-compliant outputs with less repeated LLM inference than rejection sampling**, requires no retraining, and works with any model.

papers.title: Infinite ResNets are Gaussian Mean ODEs
papers.abstract: Understanding the training dynamics of deep neural networks in large-scale limits is a question both of foundational and of practical importance. Prior works have obtained such descriptions through dynamical mean field theory (DMFT), yielding a system of non-Markovian dynamics that are challenging to analyze and that obscure the optimization structure of the original dynamics. In this paper, we obtain instead a simple description of the large-scale limit training dynamics for ResNets in standard shape scalings and in the $1/\text{depth}$ branch scaling that allows maximal (local) feature updates. For a model trained with gradient descent (GD) from a random initialization, the limit dynamics is simply GD on a Neural Mean ODE with Gaussian initial weights. Our analysis covers population or empirical risk GD in the joint limit of large width, depth and embedding, input, and output dimensions. We obtain approximation scaling laws that depend on the shape of the ResNet and the covariance spectrum of the data. We also illustrate the flexibility of our approach by discussing Mixture of Expert models, where likewise the limit admits an intuitive (nested) Mean ODE description.
papers.summary: Earlier descriptions of large-scale neural network training dynamics based on dynamical mean field theory (DMFT) produce non-Markovian equations that are hard to analyze and obscure the underlying optimization structure. The authors show that for ResNets under standard shape scalings, including the 1/depth branch scaling that allows maximal feature updates, **the infinite-size limit of gradient descent training is simply gradient descent on a `Neural Mean ODE` with Gaussian initial weights**. The analysis covers the joint limit of large width, depth, embedding, input, and output dimensions. It also yields approximation scaling laws that depend on network shape and the data covariance spectrum, and it extends to Mixture of Experts models as a nested Mean ODE.

papers.title: Enhancing Sentiment Classification on Small Datasets through Data Augmentation and Transfer Learning
papers.abstract: Small-scale sentiment classification often suffers from data scarcity, which limits the generalization ability of the models. This study evaluates and compares the effectiveness of three data augmentation strategies: Easy Data Augmentation (EDA), back-translation, and contextual token substitution (nlpaug-style), with both traditional machine learning classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest) and transformer-based models (BERT). We perform a comprehensive empirical comparison with low-resource sentiment datasets by summarizing the results of recent studies and performing targeted head-to-head experiments. Our findings indicate that all augmentation methods improve performance. Contextual augmentation yields the most consistent gains for BERT models, while EDA and back-translation provide greater benefits for traditional classifiers. These insights help guide the selection of data augmentation techniques tailored to model type and dataset size, filling a critical gap in research on data augmentation for sentiment classification on small datasets.
papers.summary: Sentiment classifiers trained on small datasets often generalize poorly because of data scarcity. The study compares three data augmentation strategies, `Easy Data Augmentation` (`EDA`), back-translation, and contextual token substitution, across `Logistic Regression`, `Random Forest`, and `BERT` classifiers, combining a summary of prior results with targeted head-to-head experiments. All augmentation methods improved performance, but **contextual augmentation gave the most consistent gains for `BERT`, while `EDA` and back-translation helped traditional classifiers more**.

papers.title: DAPS: Dependency-Aware Premise Selection for LLM Theorem Proving
papers.abstract: LLM-based theorem proving in Lean 4 has advanced rapidly, but provers are difficult to leverage newly contributed lemmas, because retrieval skews toward popular foundational lemmas, leaving the right premises buried among hundreds of thousands of candidates. Existing neural selectors rank candidates by semantic similarity, with three intrinsic limitations: frequency-skewed retrieval, isolated pairwise ranking, and degradation on out-of-distribution queries such as competition problems and informal language. Given that mathematics is structured by dependencies rather than similarities, we restore this signal to both the training data and the model. We curate two underused dependency resources. We conduct the first systematic mining of 53 Lean Blueprint projects, a previously untapped corpus of 3,805 manually curated informal+formal nodes that capture rare, research-level premises absent from Mathlib4. We further pair it with the extraction of comprehensive, typed, multi-level Mathlib4 dependencies. We then introduce DAPS, a dependency-aware premise selector with a structural neighborhood encoder, a group-level contrastive objective, and a Mathlib-then-Blueprint adaptation procedure. DAPS reaches mean Recall@32 of 89.25 on Mathlib4-Heldout (+11.41 over the strong selector LeanHammer), and maintains this lead on two out-of-distribution benchmarks. Further experiments demonstrate that DAPS premises improve theorem proving on miniF2F and IMO-ProofBench. Project page: https://daps-eth.github.io/.
papers.summary: LLM-based theorem provers for `Lean 4` struggle to use newly contributed lemmas because similarity-based premise retrieval is biased toward popular foundational lemmas and degrades on out-of-distribution queries. The authors mine 53 `Lean Blueprint` projects for 3,805 curated informal and formal nodes containing research-level premises absent from `Mathlib4`, and also extract typed, multi-level `Mathlib4` dependencies. Their selector, `DAPS`, combines a structural neighborhood encoder, a group-level contrastive objective, and a Mathlib-then-Blueprint adaptation procedure. It reaches **a mean Recall@32 of 89.25 on `Mathlib4-Heldout`, 11.41 points above `LeanHammer`**, keeps its lead on two out-of-distribution benchmarks, and improves theorem proving on `miniF2F` and `IMO-ProofBench`.

papers.title: FOCUS: First-Order Control Using Optimal Transport Supervision for Imitation from Observations
papers.abstract: Imitation learning from observations must recover behavior from state-only demonstrations without known temporal correspondence. Differentiable simulators provide pathwise policy gradients, but differentiating through long, contact-rich trajectories can make optimization unstable. We introduce FOCUS, which combines local optimal-transport alignment with short-horizon differentiable actor-critic learning. FOCUS matches agent rollout windows to multiple sampled expert segments using a soft best-of-$K$ objective that emphasizes locally compatible matches. The resulting transport-based costs provide differentiable imitation rewards, while a learned critic bootstraps value beyond the rollout horizon. FOCUS requires neither temporally aligned trajectories nor expert-aligned initialization or teacher forcing. Across contact-rich locomotion tasks in DFlex, including a musculoskeletal humanoid controlled by 152 muscle activations, FOCUS improves sample efficiency and training stability over adversarial imitation-from-observation methods and prior differentiable imitation baselines.
papers.summary: Imitation learning from observations has to recover behavior from state-only demonstrations that have no known temporal correspondence, and differentiating through long, contact-rich trajectories in differentiable simulators can make optimization unstable. `FOCUS` combines local optimal-transport alignment with short-horizon differentiable actor-critic learning: agent rollout windows are matched to multiple sampled expert segments through a soft best-of-K objective, and the resulting transport costs serve as differentiable rewards, with a learned critic bootstrapping value beyond the rollout horizon. It needs no temporally aligned trajectories, expert-aligned initialization, or teacher forcing. On contact-rich locomotion tasks in `DFlex`, including **a musculoskeletal humanoid driven by 152 muscle activations**, it improves sample efficiency and training stability over adversarial and prior differentiable imitation baselines.

papers.title: DeepWeave: Weaving Neural and Symbolic Evidence for ML-Based Network Intrusion Detection System
papers.abstract: Machine learning-based network intrusion detection systems can recognize complex traffic patterns, but often require substantial labelled attack data, degrade under deployment shift, and provide limited evidence for analysts. We present DeepWeave, a probabilistic neuro-symbolic Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS) that makes logic an integral part of detection. DeepWeave automatically constructs and validates interpretable rules, represents neural predictions as probabilistic predicates, and reconciles both evidence sources through explicit coupling policies over packet-, flow-, and hybrid-views. The resulting proofs provide intrinsic explanations for rule-supported alerts. Across multiple datasets, DeepWeave improves low-data detection, false-positive control, transferability, and robustness. With only 50 labelled packet observations per attack class, it improves macro-F1 from 0.632 to 0.924 and reduces the attack false-positive rate from 0.075 to 0.008 over the matched neural baseline. Its proofs are also more stable than post-hoc neural attributions, while batched inference keeps probabilistic reasoning practical. These results demonstrate label-efficient, adaptable, and inspectable neuro-symbolic intrusion detection.
papers.summary: Machine learning-based network intrusion detection systems (NIDS) usually need large amounts of labelled attack data, degrade when deployment conditions shift, and offer analysts little evidence for their alerts. `DeepWeave` is a probabilistic neuro-symbolic NIDS that automatically builds and validates interpretable rules, represents neural predictions as probabilistic predicates, and reconciles the two evidence sources through explicit coupling policies over packet, flow, and hybrid views, producing proofs that explain rule-supported alerts. With only 50 labelled packet observations per attack class, **it raises macro-F1 from 0.632 to 0.924 and cuts the attack false-positive rate from 0.075 to 0.008** compared with a matched neural baseline. Its proofs are also more stable than post-hoc neural attributions.

papers.title: Enhancing Knowledge Entity Relation Extraction in Abstracts and Full-text Content of Academic Articles Using Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of large pre-trained language models (LLMs) for knowledge entity relation extraction (KERE) from academic papers. Existing studies have examined individual types of LLM-based strategies and evaluated model performance using metrics such as precision and recall. To provide a broader evaluation, this study investigates multiple strategies, including closed-source LLM-based CoT prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, LLM-enhanced small pre-trained language models (SLMs), and SLM-enhanced closed-source LLMs. In addition, this study introduces two strategies, namely SLM-enhanced open-source LLMs and closed-source LLM-enhanced open-source LLMs. These strategies are evaluated from multiple perspectives, including metrics, their ability to mitigate errors observed in SLMs, and potential directions for model optimization. This study manually constructs two annotated datasets in the NLP domain, covering Abstract and Full-Text datasets. Experimental results show that the LoRA-adapted T5 model achieves the highest macro F1 scores of 0.7408 and 0.7013 on the Abstract and Full-Text datasets, respectively. SLMs also benefit from LLM-generated entity descriptions under the LLM-enhanced SLM strategy. Error analysis further reveals that the effectiveness of LLM-based strategies in mitigating SLM errors varies across error types. Based on the identified limitations and error patterns of these strategies, several optimization directions are proposed. In addition, combining strategies with different error patterns further improves KERE performance.
papers.summary: The study evaluates how well large language models (LLMs) handle knowledge entity relation extraction (KERE) from academic papers, comparing chain-of-thought prompting of closed-source LLMs, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, and several hybrid strategies that pair LLMs with small pre-trained language models (SLMs), two of which are new. The authors manually annotate two NLP-domain datasets, one built from abstracts and one from full text. **A LoRA-adapted `T5` model achieves the highest macro F1 scores, 0.7408 on abstracts and 0.7013 on full text**, and SLMs benefit from LLM-generated entity descriptions. Error analysis shows that LLM strategies fix different SLM error types to different degrees, and combining strategies with complementary error patterns improves results further.

papers.title: CEFR Level Assessment across Languages and Text Granularities
papers.abstract: Automatic assessment of textual CEFR levels is an important task in educational natural language processing. However, accurate CEFR level prediction remains challenging due to the naturally imbalanced distribution of CEFR levels and the ambiguous boundaries between adjacent levels. To address these challenges, we propose a unified training objective that combines focal loss with supervised contrastive learning. Focal loss mitigates class imbalance by emphasizing underrepresented and difficult examples, while supervised contrastive learning learns more discriminative representations by encouraging intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. We evaluate the proposed method on sentence- and document-level CEFR assessment in both monolingual and multilingual settings. Experimental results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms strong baselines across all settings, establishing new state-of-the-art performance on multiple CEFR assessment benchmarks.
papers.summary: Automatically assessing the CEFR proficiency level of a text is difficult because the levels are unevenly represented in data and the boundaries between adjacent levels are ambiguous. The authors propose a training objective that combines focal loss, which emphasizes underrepresented and difficult examples, with supervised contrastive learning, which pulls same-level representations together and pushes different levels apart. Evaluated on sentence-level and document-level assessment in monolingual and multilingual settings, **the method consistently outperforms strong baselines and sets new state-of-the-art results on multiple CEFR benchmarks**.

papers.title: Digital sovereignty in professional translation workflows: a case study of migrating from Windows to Linux
papers.abstract: This study examines digital sovereignty in professional translation through a screening of computer-assisted translation tools and translation management systems, and a case study of migrating a translator's workstation from Windows to Linux. The framework combines three principles - Control, Continuity and Exit - with three practical requirements: native Linux operation, independence from mandatory external services, and independent access to essential data and resources. Drawing on documentary evidence and the limited number of responses received from providers, the ecosystem screening distinguishes Linux accessibility from operational independence: browser-based platforms may remain dependent on provider-controlled infrastructure. The migration case demonstrates the feasibility of reconstructing one professional workflow around a locally operable Linux core, using LoopCAT, LibreOffice and locally run TranslateGemma, alongside tools for optical character recognition, communication, credential management and backup. Selected cloud services remained available where needed. The findings suggest that digital sovereignty depends on how workflow dependencies are organized, rather than on individual applications or operating systems. It does not require technological isolation, but meaningful control over essential components, continuity of work and practical exit options. The framework is tailored to the case examined here and may require adaptation to other professional workflows.
papers.summary: The study examines digital sovereignty for professional translators through a screening of computer-assisted translation tools and translation management systems, plus a case study of migrating one translator's workstation from Windows to Linux. It applies a framework of Control, Continuity, and Exit with three practical requirements: native Linux operation, independence from mandatory external services, and independent access to essential data. The migration rebuilt the workflow around a locally operable core of `LoopCAT`, `LibreOffice`, and a locally run `TranslateGemma`, while keeping selected cloud services where needed. The author concludes that **sovereignty depends on how workflow dependencies are organized rather than on any single application or operating system**, and notes that the framework may need adapting for other workflows.

papers.title: SCRBench: Beyond Equivalence Checking for Semantic Change Reasoning in Code
papers.abstract: Understanding how code changes affect program semantics is a core aspect of code reasoning in language models. It is commonly evaluated by asking whether two programs are semantically equivalent, but a yes/no answer does not reveal whether a model knows which code change caused a semantic difference, or which sequence of code changes produced the modified program. We study two tasks that ask these questions directly, diagnosing semantic change and reconstructing sequences of code changes, alongside detecting semantic equivalence. We build SCRBench, 67,658 Python program pairs generated by applying sequences of code changes that preserve or alter program semantics, and evaluate five language models on a stratified subset of 4,500 pairs. Detecting semantic equivalence exposes weaker models, whose accuracy declines as changes accumulate, but the strongest models remain near the ceiling. Diagnosing semantic change reveals weaknesses that equivalence accuracy hides: a model with 94.71% equivalence accuracy diagnoses only 54.44% of semantic changes. Reconstructing sequences of code changes is much harder: the best model reconstructs the exact sequence for only 39.27% of pairs, and no model exceeds 1.11% when five changes are applied. High equivalence accuracy therefore overestimates how well models reason about the semantic effects of code changes.
papers.summary: Code reasoning in language models is usually tested by asking whether two programs are semantically equivalent, but a yes/no answer does not show whether a model knows which change caused a difference. `SCRBench` contains 67,658 Python program pairs produced by sequences of semantics-preserving or semantics-altering edits, and it adds two tasks beyond equivalence detection: diagnosing which change altered semantics, and reconstructing the sequence of changes. Across five models, **a model with 94.71% equivalence accuracy diagnosed only 54.44% of semantic changes**. The best model reconstructed the exact change sequence for just 39.27% of pairs, and no model exceeded 1.11% when five changes were applied.

papers.title: ORION: An Outcome-Driven LLM Advisor for RL-Based Multi-Domain 6G Slice Placement
papers.abstract: Deploying 6G network slices across administrative domains requires an online decision for each arriving request: which domain hosts each virtual network function, how traffic crosses domain boundaries, and whether the slice is admitted. This joint decision problem is NP-hard under continuous arrivals. Experiments on a parametrized family of multi-domain topologies show that no fixed planning strategy dominates across all regimes: the performance ranking reverses between topology classes, and feasible placements exist for most rejected requests but remain undiscovered. These findings identify the plan layer as the decisive performance lever. We introduce ORION, a hierarchical orchestrator in which two LLM agents translate service intents into structured requests and generate abstract placement plans. A cooperative multi-agent RL coordinator selects the cross-domain partition, treating the plan as a persistent soft prior, while per-domain agents place the functions. ORION main contribution lies at the plan layer: an outcome-driven episodic memory that records, for each completed attempt, the network-condition profile, the proposed plan, and its verified feasibility outcome. The memory feeds verified successes and labelled failures back to the planner, thereby closing the adaptation loop using deployment feasibility rather than a scalar reward assigned to the planner's own proposals. To isolate the effect of the plan quality, we evaluate the planner on held-out topology families while keeping the downstream selection and execution mechanisms fixed. Under this controlled setting, the proposed memory improves admission by $4.6$--$11.5$ percentage points over the same planner without memory, while importance-based retention accounts for most of the improvement over a first-in-first-out store.
papers.summary: Placing 6G network slices across administrative domains requires an online, NP-hard decision for each arriving request, and experiments show that no fixed planning strategy works best across topology types. `ORION` is a hierarchical orchestrator in which two LLM agents translate service intents into structured requests and abstract placement plans, a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning coordinator chooses the cross-domain partition, and per-domain agents place the network functions. Its main contribution is an outcome-driven episodic memory that records network conditions, proposed plans, and verified feasibility outcomes, then feeds successes and labelled failures back to the planner. On held-out topology families, **the memory improves admission by 4.6 to 11.5 percentage points** over the same planner without memory, with importance-based retention accounting for most of the gain over a first-in-first-out store.

papers.title: Verify--Backtrack Loop: Structured Precondition Recovery for Long-Horizon Language Agents
papers.abstract: Language agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks in interactive environments, where actions often depend on latent preconditions. The core difficulty is not trajectory length but recovery: when a prerequisite is missing or an earlier decomposition fails, trying another plausible action rarely helps. ReAct and later reflection or adaptive-planning methods support local correction, but express recovery as free-form text, with no explicit control state linking the terminal goal, the active goal, and the failure source. We introduce the Verify--Backtrack Loop (VBL), a training-free extension of ReAct that turns precondition discovery and failure diagnosis into structured planning-state updates. VBL maintains the task decomposition as a bounded goal stack and, on goal activation, execution failure, or material state change, jointly verifies two horizons---whether the active goal contributes to the terminal goal and whether it is feasible in the current state. These dual-horizon judgments, combined with typed failure attribution, trigger explicit operations---Push, Pop, retry, or BacktrackTo the parent. We evaluate VBL with Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-V3.2 on AppWorld, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld. VBL improves over ReAct and reflection-based control on every backbone--benchmark pair. On the challenging AppWorld setting, it improves task success by up to 22.07 percentage points over ReAct. Ablations show that removing either verification or diagnosis degrades performance, in several settings below ReAct, confirming that the two mechanisms are complementary. These results show that reliable long-horizon interaction benefits from revising the planning state, not merely the next action.
papers.summary: Language agents on long-horizon tasks often fail at recovery: when a hidden prerequisite is missing or an earlier decomposition breaks, methods like `ReAct` and reflection-based approaches express correction only as free-form text. The `Verify--Backtrack Loop` (`VBL`) is a training-free extension of `ReAct` that keeps the task decomposition as a bounded goal stack, checks whether the active goal both serves the terminal goal and is feasible in the current state, and uses typed failure attribution to trigger explicit Push, Pop, retry, or BacktrackTo operations. Tested with `Qwen3.5-9B`, `GPT-4o`, and `DeepSeek-V3.2` on `AppWorld`, `ALFWorld`, and `ScienceWorld`, it beats `ReAct` and reflection baselines on every model-benchmark pair, with **gains of up to 22.07 percentage points in task success on `AppWorld`**. Ablations show that the verification and diagnosis components are complementary.

papers.title: Connectivity-Aware Client Selection in Decentralized Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) has emerged as a scalable alternative to centralized federated learning, removing the single point of failure and communication bottleneck at the server. However, most existing decentralized approaches rely on full-neighborhood broadcasting, where each client transmits its model update to all of its neighbors in each communication round. While effective, this results in significant communication overhead and high energy consumption. This paper applies spectral graph tools as lightweight client selection methods that leverage the graph topology by analyzing the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian over a fixed communication graph. Specifically, we exploit eigenvector embeddings and heat/diffusion kernel similarities to guide each client in selecting only a subset of structurally relevant neighbors, i.e., those that are most beneficial for the convergence of the federation process. This topology aware randomization matches or outperforms uniform neighborhood subsampling and approaches the accuracy of full broadcasting. The largest gains, about $3$ percentage points, emerge under strong data heterogeneity on larger, structurally rich graphs, while the total number of transmitted messages is reduced by $50\%$ compared to naive broadcasting.
papers.summary: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) removes the central server, but clients typically broadcast updates to every neighbor, which is costly in communication and energy. The authors use spectral properties of the communication graph's Laplacian, specifically eigenvector embeddings and heat or diffusion kernel similarities, so that each client sends updates only to a subset of structurally relevant neighbors. This topology-aware selection matches or beats uniform neighbor subsampling and approaches full-broadcast accuracy while **halving the total number of transmitted messages**, with gains of about 3 percentage points under strong data heterogeneity on larger graphs.

papers.title: BYOD: Build Your Own DLM - Efficient Autoregressive-to-Diffusion Language Model Conversion
papers.abstract: Unlike autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion language models (DLMs) permit parallel token updates, flexible generation, and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on costly pretraining or full-model fine-tuning. We present Build Your Own DLM (BYOD), a generalizable LoRA-only recipe for parameter-efficient AR-to-DLM conversion. Without architecture-specific tuning, BYOD induces diffusion generation in Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Ministral 8B; to our knowledge, this is the first reported AR-to-DLM conversion of a Mistral model. The adapters comprise 4.1-5.8% of final parameters while every base-model parameter remains frozen; each 25,000-iteration conversion needs at most 102.4M tokens, processed in 3.1-4.0 hours on one Google Colab GPU. All four models generate from fully masked sequences, use bidirectional context in a controlled attention test, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge. BYOD-Gemma is the strongest BYOD conversion on our nine-task evaluation, reaching 50.6% average accuracy compared with 51.9% for LLaDA 8B Instruct in the same harness. Open-generation quality at low network function evaluation (NFE) budgets remains the principal limitation: BYOD perplexity is 8.3-11.1 versus 4.1 for LLaDA and 2.2-3.0 for the AR parents when generating 128 tokens in 64 steps. To enable further experimentation and inspection, we provide a standalone training and evaluation implementation and interactive demos for all four conversions. BYOD thus provides a practical route for extending diffusion generation to other existing model families while identifying the gap that efficient conversion must next close.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) allow parallel token updates and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on expensive pretraining or full-model fine-tuning. `Build Your Own DLM` (`BYOD`) is a LoRA-only recipe that converts autoregressive models into DLMs while keeping all base parameters frozen, using adapters that make up 4.1 to 5.8% of the final parameters and at most 102.4M tokens per conversion. It converts `Gemma 2 9B`, `Llama 3.1 8B`, `Qwen2.5 7B`, and `Ministral 8B`, **each in 3.1 to 4.0 hours on a single Google Colab GPU**, and the best conversion reaches 50.6% average accuracy across nine tasks against 51.9% for `LLaDA 8B Instruct`. The main limitation is open-ended generation quality at low step budgets, where perplexity is 8.3 to 11.1 compared with 4.1 for `LLaDA`.

papers.title: Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B: Adapting a 2.6B Hybrid Model to Tajik Tool Calling, and What Continued Pretraining Takes Away
papers.abstract: We release Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B, a Tajik adaptation of the 2.6B-parameter hybrid model LFM2.5-2.6B-Base, built for tool calling in Tajik on modest hardware. The recipe has two stages: LoRA continued pretraining (CPT) on 1,485,319 cleaned Tajik web documents for 3 epochs, then one epoch of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a mix of machine-translated Tajik tool calls, English tool calls kept as replay, and Tajik instructions. On a 174-item tool-calling test set built from BFCL v3 and machine-translated to Tajik, strict full-call accuracy on Tajik prompts rises from 20.69 for the base model to 64.14 (paired difference +43.45 points, 95% interval +35.2 to +51.7); a lenient parser that also accepts the base model's own call formats puts the base at 31.72. English shows no detectable change (76.55 and 77.24). Every CPT checkpoint scores zero: CPT removes the native tool-call format and, as the lenient re-scoring shows, part of the skill itself. Outside tool calling, accuracy on a Tajik knowledge benchmark rises from 28.0 to 35.0, Belebele Tajik shows no significant change, and English MMLU falls from 60.8 to 52.5. The model is not a general Tajik assistant. It almost never declines when no tool fits (6.9% correct on Tajik, against 31.0% for the base under the lenient parser), it is weak at multi-turn calls, and its calls should be checked before they are executed. We describe the data, the training settings and every evaluation in enough detail to repeat them.
