papers.summary: The authors release a Tajik adaptation of the 2.6B-parameter hybrid model `LFM2.5-2.6B-Base`, built for tool calling on modest hardware through LoRA continued pretraining on about 1.5 million Tajik web documents followed by supervised fine-tuning on translated Tajik tool calls, English tool-call replay, and Tajik instructions. On a Tajik translation of 174 `BFCL v3` items, **strict tool-call accuracy rises from 20.69 to 64.14**, while English tool calling is unchanged. Every continued-pretraining checkpoint scores zero, because that stage erases the native tool-call format and part of the underlying skill. English `MMLU` drops from 60.8 to 52.5, and the model rarely declines when no tool fits, so the authors advise checking its calls before executing them.

papers.title: Reliability-Weighted Direct Preference Optimization: Penalized Weights for Robust Preference Learning
papers.abstract:
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) treats every reported comparison as correct, yet preference data contain
  reversed, tied or otherwise noisy comparisons. RW-DPO gives each comparison an unknown reliability weight
  $w_i\in[0,1]$ that enters the likelihood linearly -- DPO is $w\equiv1$, a reversed comparison $w_i=0$ -- and estimates
  the weights jointly with the policy under a minimax-concave penalty on $-\log w_i$. The penalty keeps every
  comparison the model agrees with at exactly $w_i=1$ and acts only on those it contradicts, through closed-form weight
  updates at negligible cost over DPO. We prove that recovering all flipped comparisons from a single annotation per
  comparison requires margins of order $\log n$. Furthermore, in a linear-index model, starting from an initial fit
  pointing in the correct direction, our estimator jointly consistently recovers the preference direction and weights,
  as well as identifies the flipped comparisons above this margin scale, even when a fixed fraction of comparisons is
  flipped. In simulations RW-DPO has the lowest average estimation error among DPO, noise-rate corrections and recent
  robust methods, with far more precise flags than recent label-correction methods. In DPO fine-tuning of a language
  model with 10-30% flipped labels, its win rate does not fall as the flip rate grows and exceeds that of DPO trained on
  clean labels, matching the strongest recent method with corrections concentrated on the flipped labels.
papers.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (`DPO`) treats every preference comparison as correct, even though real preference data contains reversed, tied, or noisy pairs. `RW-DPO` gives each comparison a reliability weight between 0 and 1 and estimates the weights jointly with the policy under a minimax-concave penalty, so comparisons the model agrees with keep full weight and the closed-form updates add negligible cost. The authors prove that recovering flipped labels from a single annotation needs margins on the order of log n, and they establish consistent recovery in a linear-index model. When fine-tuning a language model with 10 to 30% flipped labels, **its win rate does not drop as the flip rate rises and exceeds that of `DPO` trained on clean labels**.

papers.title: PDE-Residual-Informed Kriging
papers.abstract: Physics-informed Gaussian process (GP) methods provide a probabilistic framework for PDE solving. Existing approaches incorporate PDE information in different ways: pointwise conditioning uses the governing equation only at finitely many selected locations, globally constrained GPs restrict the admissible functions to satisfy the PDE exactly, and residual-penalized methods control the PDE mismatch over the whole domain through an additional penalty weight. What is still missing is a GP formulation that directly incorporates global PDE-residual information of the entire domain into its covariance structure, while retaining model flexibility and standard GP conditioning without a separate residual-weight parameter. To solve this issue, this study proposes PDE-residual-informed Kriging (PRIK) based on a PDE-residual kernel. The PDE-residual kernel is constructed by equipping a kernel-section space with an inner product defined by the $L^{2}$ inner product of PDE residuals. This construction makes PRIK yield the posterior mean with minimum integrated squared PDE residual. It also provides direct statistical interpretations: the variance-scale estimate equals the normalized PDE-residual energy (i.e., the integrated squared PDE residual of the posterior mean divided by the number of labeled observations), and the profile likelihood balances this residual energy against model complexity. Under the stated regularity and stability conditions, we establish $H^{2}$-quasi-optimality and convergence rates for the posterior mean, together with a nonasymptotic bound for its PDE-residual norm. We further show that the normalized posterior kernel converges to a variational Green-type kernel and derive a uniform nonasymptotic contraction bound for the posterior variance. Numerical studies provide empirical evidence consistent with the theory and demonstrate the PDE-solving capability of PRIK.
papers.summary: Physics-informed Gaussian process (GP) methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) enforce the equation at selected points, constrain admissible functions exactly, or add a separately weighted residual penalty, but none build the global PDE residual directly into the covariance. `PDE-residual-informed Kriging` (`PRIK`) constructs a kernel whose inner product is the L2 inner product of PDE residuals, so **the posterior mean minimizes the integrated squared PDE residual** without needing a residual-weight parameter. The authors prove H2 quasi-optimality, convergence rates, and nonasymptotic bounds on the residual norm and posterior variance, and numerical studies are consistent with the theory.

papers.title: Patch-Based Deep Kernel Learning for Data Assimilation and Bias Correction with Extremely Sparse Observations
papers.abstract: Data Assimilation (DA) reconstructs the state of a spatio-temporal system by combining sensor observations with the output of a numerical model. Since model states are high-dimensional while observations cover only a small fraction of the domain, DA is a challenging large-scale estimation problem, central to weather forecasting and oceanography. Classical variational methods such as 3D-Var rely on a hand-crafted background error covariance that assumes unbiased errors, and therefore cannot capture state-dependent correlations or systematic model biases. Moreover, their cost grows with the size of the domain. Deep learning (DL) methods can perform DA and bias correction (BC) non-linearly, but typically offer limited interpretability and no calibrated uncertainty estimates. We propose a hybrid framework that couples a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a learnable-kernel Gaussian Process (GP) to jointly perform DA and BC from extremely sparse observations. The model is trained end-to-end by maximizing the marginal log-likelihood, learns a data-driven covariance over the whole grid, and provides both the Maximum A Posteriori analysis and its uncertainty by design. A patch-based strategy reduces the $O(N^3)$ training cost of exact GPs over $N$ grid points to $O(N)$ for a fixed patch size. Inference remains exact and only requires solving a linear system whose $O(m^3)$ cost depends on the number of observations $m \ll N$, not on the domain. The learned covariance can also replace the hand-crafted one in 3D-Var, improving its accuracy without changing the variational formulation. Experiments on sea surface temperature and salinity, with both synthetic and real, extremely sparse in-situ observations, show that the framework outperforms 3D-Var, a classical GP and a competing DL model, while reducing inference time by more than 98% with respect to 3D-Var.
papers.summary: Data assimilation (DA) reconstructs the state of systems like the ocean from sparse sensors and a numerical model, but classical methods such as `3D-Var` rely on hand-crafted, unbiased error covariances and scale poorly, while deep learning methods lack calibrated uncertainty. The authors couple a convolutional neural network with a learnable-kernel Gaussian process, trained end-to-end by marginal likelihood, to jointly perform DA and bias correction and return both an analysis and its uncertainty. A patch-based strategy reduces training cost from cubic to linear in grid size, and the learned covariance can also replace the hand-crafted one inside `3D-Var`. On sea surface temperature and salinity with extremely sparse in-situ observations, it outperforms `3D-Var`, a classical GP, and a competing deep learning model while **cutting inference time by more than 98% relative to `3D-Var`**.

papers.title: Underdamped Stochastic Optimal Transport with Landauer boundary conditions: machine learning and analytical solution
papers.abstract: Finding optimal transport protocols for underdamped stochastic processes is a difficult yet important problem in control theory. In this paper we develop a direct method, based on machine learning, to find the optimal solution of the problem in the presence of non-linear boundary conditions, including those modelling the Landauer bit-erasure problem. The dynamics is steered from a single-peak to a double-peak distribution in position space, by only acting on a controllable external potential. The problem is highly non-linear, and analytical solutions are not available in general. We benchmark our numerical results with a perturbative expansion, which is expected to hold in a suitable overdamped limit.
papers.summary: Finding optimal transport protocols for underdamped stochastic processes is a hard control problem, especially with the nonlinear boundary conditions that model Landauer bit erasure. The authors develop a direct machine learning method that steers a particle distribution from a single peak to a double peak in position space by controlling only an external potential. Because analytical solutions are generally unavailable, **they benchmark the learned protocols against a perturbative expansion** that is expected to hold in a suitable overdamped limit.

papers.title: Real Computation or Merely Naming? A Pre-Registered Mechanism Audit of 25 Cognitive-Architecture Modules in an LLM-Based Agent System
papers.abstract: Agent systems built on local large language models are increasingly marketed through the vocabulary of cognitive architecture: modules named global workspace, theory of mind, causal reasoning, or active inference are listed as features, and the presence of the name is taken as the presence of the mechanism. We ask the prior question -- does the named computation actually happen -- and contribute a transferable verification method for the claim-implementation gap: a four-question static audit protocol with line-number evidence and call-chain tracing, demonstrated on two systems. We audit a system claiming 25 cognitive mechanisms, pre-register falsifiable predictions for 11 modules and execute the interventions, replicate the protocol on the IIT-phi core of a second, independent system with its own pre-committed falsification criteria, and run two repair experiments as positive controls. In 18 of 25 modules the computed value never reaches any production output; three idle-wiring shapes new to the dead-code and code-smell literatures emerge (connected-but-never-called, called-but-inert, called-but-content-blind). Of 61 frozen criteria across 12 interventions, 53 were confirmed, two partially adjudicated, five falsified, one adjudication-ambiguous. Repairs raised planner task success from 0.028 to 1.000 and cut state-controller error by 52%. Module names and module computations must be audited as independent claims; the protocol and the five-class failure taxonomy are reusable for the claim-implementation gap at two-system, case-level depth.
papers.summary: Agent systems built on local large language models (LLMs) often advertise cognitive-architecture modules such as global workspace, theory of mind, or active inference, and the authors test whether the named computation actually runs. They introduce a four-question static audit protocol that uses line-number evidence and call-chain tracing. They apply it to a system that claims 25 cognitive mechanisms, pre-register falsifiable predictions for 11 of its modules, and replicate the protocol on the `IIT-phi` core of a second, independent system. In **18 of 25 modules the computed value never reaches any production output**, and the audit identifies three new idle-wiring patterns: connected-but-never-called, called-but-inert, and called-but-content-blind. Of 61 pre-registered criteria, 53 were confirmed, and repairing the modules raised planner task success from 0.028 to 1.000.

papers.title: VLA Policies Do Not Know When Not to Act: Unintended Task Execution and Start Suppression
papers.abstract: A robot should act only on an instruction from a person or on an intent that the robot explicitly represents and generates. Unintended actions taken without such an instruction can cause risk or inconvenience to people and the environment. We examine how recent vision-language-action (VLA) policies respond when the instruction is missing or meaningless. We apply a paired protocol with empty, neutral, nonsense, infeasible, and wrong-task instructions to six model checkpoints in LIBERO-Goal simulation. Holding the initial state fixed and varying only the instruction, we ask three questions: whether the robot starts to move, which task it completes, and what the instruction determines. Even when the instruction was empty, the robot started moving in every episode with all six checkpoints, and with five of them it often completed a task that the instruction had not specified. On two GR00T checkpoints, the instruction determined which task was executed but not whether the robot started moving; the robot moved even on infeasible instructions. We then tested three methods for suppressing the start: prepending "if no task is given do not move" to the instruction; a gate that holds the robot when the first action chunk for the given instruction nearly equals that for an empty instruction; and fine-tuning the policy to hold still on non-task inputs. The prefix stopped the robot in none of the six checkpoints, and the gate held it on non-task inputs in five of the six checkpoints. The fine-tuned policy never completed a task on non-task inputs, but it did not reliably keep the robot still, and it failed to suppress the start on infeasible instructions.
papers.summary: Robots should act only when given an instruction, so the authors test how vision-language-action (VLA) policies behave when the instruction is empty, neutral, nonsense, infeasible, or names the wrong task. Across six checkpoints in `LIBERO-Goal` simulation, **the robot started moving in every episode even with an empty instruction**, and five checkpoints often completed a task nobody asked for. On two `GR00T` checkpoints, the instruction decided which task was executed but not whether the robot moved. Of three fixes tested, a "do not move" prompt prefix never worked. A gate that compares the first action chunk with the one produced for an empty instruction held the robot still in five of six checkpoints, and fine-tuning prevented unwanted task completion but did not reliably keep the robot still.

papers.title: What Should LLMs Forget: Reinforcement Unlearning of Knowledge Associations
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire extensive factual knowledge during pre-training, which may include sensitive, private, or copyrighted information, motivating the development of unlearning methods that selectively remove specific knowledge while preserving general capabilities. However, existing approaches typically optimize entire responses without explicitly identifying the knowledge to be forgotten, resulting in coarse and uncontrolled forgetting. To address this, we revisit the forgetting target of LLM unlearning and introduce Knowledge Association (KA), which characterizes the association between a query context and its target knowledge and is instantiated by the corresponding conditional predictive distribution, as the fundamental target of forgetting. Based on KA, we propose Knowledge Association Reinforcement Unlearning (KARU), a unified reinforcement learning framework that suppresses forgotten knowledge associations while preserving retained ones. Specifically, KARU derives complementary mechanisms from the KA-based formulation: token-level reward construction for finer-grained forgetting supervision, distribution-level regularization for precise knowledge suppression, and proximity-aware retain sampling to mitigate collateral degradation. Experiments across diverse LLMs on representative benchmarks demonstrate that KARU consistently improves forgetting effectiveness over existing baselines while maintaining comparable retention performance and general utility.
papers.summary: Unlearning methods for large language models (LLMs) aim to remove sensitive, private, or copyrighted knowledge, but they usually optimize whole responses without pinpointing what should be forgotten, so forgetting is coarse and hard to control. The authors define Knowledge Association (KA), the conditional predictive distribution linking a query context to its target knowledge, as the thing to forget. They build `KARU`, a reinforcement learning framework that combines token-level rewards, distribution-level regularization, and proximity-aware sampling of retained data. Across several LLMs and standard benchmarks, `KARU` **consistently forgets more effectively than existing baselines while keeping comparable retention and general utility**.

papers.title: Attention Maps Know When to Think: Training-Free Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought for Reasoning Segmentation
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has become a standard reasoning strategy in Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), showing strong performance in complex vision-language tasks such as reasoning segmentation. However, our analysis reveals that indiscriminate CoT usage can lead to degraded performance by inducing unnecessary reasoning, a phenomenon we term overthinking. In reasoning segmentation, overthinking often leads to misalignment between the query's intent and visual grounding. To address this, we propose Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought (DA-CoT), a training-free adaptive framework that selectively triggers CoT based on the input's intrinsic difficulty. We find that the entropy of the model's attention maps reliably reflects task difficulty: low entropy indicates confident, localized grounding, while high entropy suggests uncertainty and potential benefit from CoT. DA-CoT uses this entropy signal to determine whether to apply CoT prompting. Additionally, we introduce a Bidirectional Rethinking mechanism that enables the model to automatically flip its reasoning decision when the initial output fails, enhancing robustness by recovering from failures induced by overthinking and underthinking. DA-CoT demonstrates its effectiveness by achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Reasoning Segmentation benchmarks while significantly improving inference efficiency.
papers.summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can hurt reasoning segmentation through "overthinking", where unnecessary reasoning pulls visual grounding away from what the query intends. `DA-CoT` is a training-free method that applies CoT only when the input looks difficult, using **the entropy of the model's attention maps as a difficulty signal**: low entropy indicates confident grounding and high entropy indicates uncertainty. A Bidirectional Rethinking mechanism reverses the decision to reason or not when the first output fails. The authors report state-of-the-art results on reasoning segmentation benchmarks along with faster inference.

papers.title: What Carries Architectural Signal? A Code-to-Architecture Mapping Study
papers.abstract:
Code-to-architecture mapping assigns source files to modules of a reference architecture. Representations of implementation artifacts can capture code text, dependencies, and directory organization, but predictive gains alone do not establish the contribution of additional graph processing. Dependencies may already be encoded in these representations, while directories may closely match the reference decomposition. We investigate how artifact representations and graph context affect mapping on ten Java, C, and C++ systems with a limited labeling budget. We compare lexical, structural, and contextual file representations and assess each predictor with and without dependency neighbors. Using a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT), we compare file-level graphs extended with member nodes summarizing each file's program elements, folder nodes, or both, alongside a variant encoding folder paths directly in file representations. We compare folder-aware predictions with a directory rule using the same labeled files.
  Representations encoding dependency information outperform lexical representations on most systems. Additional neighbor aggregation can improve mapping, depending on the predictor and aggregation direction. Folder-aware variants yield the largest and most consistent gains across the evaluated HGT configurations. However, the directory rule achieves per-system median accuracy of 89-100%, and adding folder information does not consistently improve predictions for files the rule misclassifies. Member nodes provide no consistent improvement over file-level graphs. These findings support assessing what file representations and directory organization already provide before attributing improvements to graph neural networks.
papers.summary: Code-to-architecture mapping assigns source files to the modules of a reference architecture, and the authors ask which signals actually drive accurate mapping. Using ten Java, C, and C++ systems with a limited labeling budget, they compare lexical, structural, and contextual file representations, with and without dependency neighbors, and test a `Heterogeneous Graph Transformer` (HGT) extended with member and folder nodes. Representations that encode dependencies beat lexical ones on most systems, and folder-aware variants give the largest gains. However, **a simple directory rule alone reaches a per-system median accuracy of 89–100%**, and adding folder information does not reliably fix the files that rule gets wrong. The authors recommend checking what representations and directory layout already provide before crediting improvements to graph neural networks.

papers.title: GRIT: Gradient Masking for Visually Misgrounded Tokens in Text-Rich Reasoning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has recently been extended to vision-language models (VLMs), yet its effectiveness remains limited for text-rich reasoning tasks. We highlight a key factor contributing to this limitation: models frequently arrive at correct final answers despite misperceiving visual information during intermediate steps. We define this phenomenon as Correct-but-Visually-Misgrounded Reasoning (CVMR). Because standard RLVR rewards only final-answer correctness, it fails to differentiate between properly grounded and misgrounded reasoning, reinforcing both equally. Through token-level analysis, we reveal that CVMR tokens exhibit distinct attention patterns that differ systematically from well-grounded ones. Based on this observation, we propose GRIT, a training framework that incorporates visual grounding into RLVR to mitigate the impact of CVMR. Furthermore, to address the lack of text-rich reasoning benchmarks that allow for systematic evaluation across text length and reasoning depth, we introduce GRIT-Bench. Experiments demonstrate that GRIT significantly improves both reasoning accuracy and grounding fidelity over existing RLVR methods.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for vision-language models (VLMs) rewards only the final answer. As a result, it also reinforces Correct-but-Visually-Misgrounded Reasoning (CVMR), where the model reaches the right answer despite misreading visual content along the way. A token-level analysis shows that misgrounded tokens have distinctive attention patterns, and `GRIT` uses these patterns to mask their gradients during RLVR training. The authors also release `GRIT-Bench`, a text-rich reasoning benchmark that varies text length and reasoning depth. `GRIT` **improves both reasoning accuracy and grounding fidelity** over existing RLVR methods.

papers.title: Co$^2$ODE: Conditionally Coarse-Grained Model Discovery for Rewiring in Biochemical Networks
papers.abstract: Biochemical networks propagate the signals that regulate cellular behaviour, and which routes carry them depends on cellular context: a shift in context rewires the network's effective dynamics. Mechanistic simulators are misspecified here because the effective dynamics emerge from an interaction structure that is only partially known. Model discovery instead learns the dynamics from data, but sparse, correlated measurements poorly identify a full network model. What matters is narrower: the portion the context rewires. We introduce conditionally coarse-grained ODEs (Co$^2$ODE), which model that portion as a sparse neural or symbolic ODE: a conditional mask selects the markers carrying the rewiring, and a variational autoencoder compresses the remaining markers into a learnt closure term. On single-cell phosphoproteomic data spanning 30 cancer-relevant overexpressions, Co$^2$ODE compresses a 30-marker panel into a 10-dimensional state while matching the predictive accuracy of a neural ODE fit to the full panel. The closure absorbs what the mask drops, hence the accuracy is insensitive to which markers are kept. Adding a prior score to the loss shifts the selected markers at no cost in fit, indicating the data are not interventional enough to identify the underlying biology.
papers.summary: When cellular context changes, biochemical signaling networks rewire, but sparse and correlated measurements are not enough to identify a full network model from data. `Co²ODE` models only the rewired portion as a sparse neural or symbolic ordinary differential equation (ODE): a conditional mask selects the relevant markers, and a variational autoencoder compresses the rest into a learned closure term. On single-cell phosphoproteomic data covering 30 cancer-relevant overexpressions, it **compresses a 30-marker panel into a 10-dimensional state while matching the predictive accuracy of a full-panel neural ODE**. Accuracy barely depends on which markers are kept, which the authors take as a sign that the data are not interventional enough to identify the underlying biology.

papers.title: Chance-Constrained Inspection Viewpoint Sequencing for On-Orbit Servicing via Safe Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Autonomous inspection of a target spacecraft is typically the initial step in on-orbit servicing. Planning close-proximity observation viewpoints involves a complex combinatorial problem constrained by coverage, fuel, and safety considerations. This paper models the viewpoint selection as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) and applies Proximal Policy Optimization with Lagrangian relaxation to solve it. The system combines a high-level planner, which sequences camera viewpoints on an observation sphere around the target, with a low-level model that assesses each transfer using the Clohessy--Wiltshire (CW) equations for relative motion. The deterministic constraints on single-impulse reachability and $\Delta v$ cap are enforced directly on the action set. Safety margins are affected by navigation and manoeuvre errors, making the actual clearance stochastic. To address this, a chance constraint on the realised trajectory is implemented, with a Lagrangian multiplier governed by PID control to adapt the penalty during training. The approach is tested on a Galileo-class navigation satellite in medium Earth orbit, modelled as a point cloud where visibility from each viewpoint considers field-of-view and line-of-sight occlusion. Across various risk budgets, the trained policy maintains the keep-out violation rate within the specified limit, achieving coverage close to its maximum and staying within the mission $\Delta v$ budget. Compared to the usual practice of applying a fixed margin to the keep-out radius and planning deterministically, the chance-constrained policy attains less than half the violation rate at comparable coverage. This makes the collision risk an explicit design parameter, eliminating the need for re-tuning per case. The learned policy selects a viewpoint without the repeated Monte Carlo risk estimates required by a greedy, chance-constrained planner at every decision point.
papers.summary: Inspecting a target spacecraft before on-orbit servicing requires choosing a sequence of close-range camera viewpoints that balances coverage, fuel, and collision safety. The authors frame the problem as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) and solve it with `Proximal Policy Optimization` (PPO) using Lagrangian relaxation, where a PID controller adapts the multiplier on a chance constraint for the realized trajectory's clearance. Relative motion between viewpoints is evaluated with the Clohessy–Wiltshire equations. Tested on a Galileo-class satellite, the policy keeps keep-out violations within the specified risk budget at near-maximum coverage, with **less than half the violation rate of the standard fixed-margin deterministic approach**.

papers.title: A Constructive Orbit-Based Theory of Learnability
papers.abstract: We develop a finite-dimensional orbit framework for constructing data-adapted dictionaries, sparse realizations, and predictive extensions. The method uses wrapped weighted shifts to generate orbit dictionaries and local interpolation maps from independent orbit representatives, turning the learning problem into three explicit tasks: scaffold discovery, sparse realization on the discovered dictionary, and prediction through learned sparse coordinates. We introduce CCDS as the main constructive ingredient: a deviation-controlled sparse realization procedure that recovers MP/OMP-type behavior at the minimal-deviation boundary while allowing feasible interior paths with prescribed residual geometry that is inaccessible to MP/OMP. We prove generic orbit independence, exact block interpolation with norm control, observable bounds on sparse approximation distortion, sparse realization guarantees on selected supports, and fixed-path stability under admissible perturbations of the block interpolants. These results connect sparse approximation, interpolation, and finite-dimensional operator dynamics through the construction and analysis of data-induced orbit dictionaries. Experiments on synthetic geometry, controlled realization tests, and standard classification benchmarks show that selected orbit scaffolds have substantially better matched-rank projection behavior than random orbit or unstructured alternatives, that CCDS attains near-zero realization error at the minimal-deviation boundary, and that predictors trained from the sparse CCDS certificates give competitive performance.
papers.summary: The authors develop a finite-dimensional framework that builds data-adapted dictionaries from orbits generated by wrapped weighted shifts. This splits learning into three steps: discovering a scaffold, finding a sparse realization on it, and predicting from the learned sparse coordinates. The main tool, `CCDS`, is a deviation-controlled sparse realization procedure that reproduces matching-pursuit-style (`MP`/`OMP`) behavior at one boundary while allowing residual geometries those methods cannot reach. The authors prove orbit independence, interpolation, and stability guarantees. In experiments, **selected orbit scaffolds project substantially better than random or unstructured alternatives**, and predictors trained on `CCDS` outputs are competitive on standard classification benchmarks.

papers.title: Risk-Sensitive Mission Planning for Multi-Target On-Orbit Inspection via Distributional Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Multi-target on-orbit servicing missions require planning tools that can adapt to evolving operational conditions while accounting for the outcome variability inherent to safety-critical spaceflight. This paper presents an adaptive planning approach for multi-target servicing campaigns in low Earth orbit and applies it to inspection missions flown by a low-thrust servicer. The approach is based on Distributional Reinforcement Learning, which learns the full distribution of mission returns and thereby supports explicit risk-sensitive decision-making at each planning step. Specifically, a Quantile-Regression Deep Q-Network (QR-DQN) agent selects which target to inspect next by jointly considering the expectation and the variance of the predicted return through a mean-variance criterion. The mission environment models circular orbits with a spread in inclination and uses Edelbaum's combined-manoeuvre low-thrust transfer estimates. The observation comprises the orbital elements, the visit history, the observed risk state of each target and the remaining mission-time budget. The risk state of each target changes stochastically during the campaign, making the outcome of an inspection uncertain and creating operationally meaningful distinctions between risk-neutral and risk-averse planning strategies. Because the mission-time budget generally admits only a subset of the candidate targets, the planner must also select which targets to inspect. Numerical experiments on scenarios with five target satellites show that one risk-aversion weight moves the policy across a range of mean return and return variance, over an unchanged environment and reward. Risk-averse agents reduce the variance of the episodic return by approximately one half relative to risk-neutral agents and lower the probability of a mission loss, at a cost in mean return. To validate the learned policies, the efficient frontier, which gives the highest mean return attainable at each level of return variance, is computed exactly by enumerating the admissible visit orders. At equal variance, the learned policies lie close to this frontier in mean return, and the risk-averse policies have a lower probability of a mission loss than the frontier policies.
papers.summary: Missions that service several satellites in low Earth orbit must decide which targets to inspect under uncertain and changing risk conditions. A Quantile-Regression Deep Q-Network (`QR-DQN`), a distributional reinforcement learning agent, selects the next target using a mean-variance criterion, while low-thrust transfers are estimated with Edelbaum's approximation. In five-target scenarios, a single risk-aversion weight moves the policy along a range of mean and variance trade-offs, and **risk-averse agents roughly halve return variance** and lower the probability of mission loss, at some cost in mean return. Checked against an exactly enumerated efficient frontier, the learned policies come close to optimal mean return at equal variance.

papers.title: On the Generation Order in GFlowNets
papers.abstract: Sampling from discrete distributions specified by unnormalised probability functions is a classical statistical problem. GFlowNets address this problem by constructing objects sequentially, adding one discrete component at a time in either a predefined or a learned order. The choice of order determines which conditional distributions the neural network must learn, some of which may be easier to learn than others. Yet whether existing GFlowNet algorithms discover interpretable generation orders and make use of them during training remains unexplored. We introduce controlled problems where generation order is experimentally shown to affect convergence and standard GFlowNet training struggles to discover useful orders. To address this difficulty, we develop Learning-Order GFlowNet, a training recipe that learns interpretable generation orders without order annotations and improves convergence on these problems. Finally, we investigate gradient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) as a possible explanation for order emergence: orders associated with faster convergence exhibit higher SNR at comparable validation loss, suggesting both a mechanism favouring their emergence and an SNR-based characterisation of a good generation order.
papers.summary: GFlowNets sample discrete objects by building them one component at a time, and the order in which components are added determines which conditional distributions the network has to learn. The authors design controlled problems where generation order affects convergence and show that standard GFlowNet training struggles to discover useful orders. Their `Learning-Order GFlowNet` training recipe **learns interpretable generation orders without order annotations and converges faster**. They also find that orders linked to faster convergence have a higher gradient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) at comparable validation loss, which suggests both why such orders emerge and a way to characterize good ones.

papers.title: Enhancing Medical Lesion Segmentation via Several Simple Modules
papers.abstract: This work introduces three lightweight enhancement modules for medical lesion segmentation to improve clinical applicability, particularly under data-scarce and computationally constrained environments. Current mainstream methods struggle with the lack of high-quality annotations for rare pathologies, which often leads to severe morphological distortions during inference, despite achieving seemingly ideal DSC scores. Furthermore, the isolated development of individual segmentation tasks restricts cross-domain methodological innovation, underscoring the need for leveraging shared knowledge across different lesions within the same anatomical region. However, constrained access to historical data and annotations hinders efficient knowledge extraction and triggers catastrophic forgetting when adapting to new classes. To address these challenges, we first propose DT-Morph Combined Loss with continuous spatial pooling to optimize differentiable topological structures and boundary continuity. Second, we introduce 3D Group Prompt, which extracts domain-universal knowledge via curated volumetric image-mask alignment prompts together with text prompts built on SAT baseline. Finally, we replace conventional output layers with Many-to-One Conditional Segmentation Head equipped with synonym-resolved routing, which brings negligible computational cost and enables fast incremental learning for new categories without sacrificing performance on old tasks. Ablation studies on abdominal and extra-abdominal datasets covering both organ and lesion segmentation verify the efficacy of our modules.
papers.summary: Medical lesion segmentation suffers from scarce annotations for rare pathologies, morphological distortions that good Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) scores can hide, and catastrophic forgetting when new classes are added. The authors propose three lightweight modules built on the `SAT` baseline: a `DT-Morph Combined Loss` that targets topological structure and boundary continuity, a `3D Group Prompt` that pairs volumetric image-mask prompts with text prompts to share knowledge across lesion types, and a `Many-to-One Conditional Segmentation Head` with synonym-resolved routing. The head **enables fast incremental learning of new categories at negligible compute cost without degrading old tasks**. Ablations on abdominal and extra-abdominal organ and lesion datasets support each module.

papers.title: $\nabla$Mimic: Ultra-Efficient Humanoid Control with Differentiable Simulation
papers.abstract:
Robot policy learning is dominated by zeroth-order methods such as PPO, which treat the simulator as a black box and pay for it with enormous sample counts. First-order policy learning differentiates through the dynamics, but on contact-rich whole-body control it has rarely worked: its gradients explode. A recent world-model method showed that derivative information can make humanoid motion tracking far more efficient, using surrogate gradients of a learned model. We show that exact gradients of the simulator itself do better, once two obstacles are removed. Exact gradients contain rare unbounded samples, because contact dynamics is not differentiable everywhere and its derivative diverges near some events; and they are expensive, because the simulator's adjoint has to replay the contact solve.
  $
abla$Mimic bounds these samples with median-relative per-sample gradient clipping at every step of the backward pass, and reuses each costly simulated window by multistep regression onto gradient-derived action targets, which bounds every action target independently of the gradient scale. NablaEngine, a differentiable GPU simulation engine for the Unitree G1, removes the cost: it computes MuJoCo's full contact dynamics with fused per-world kernels and the adjoint of a whole control step as a single megakernel, with analytic gradients that match float64 finite differences, $11.5	imes$ faster than the available MuJoCo Warp adjoint.
  On whole-body tracking of all 40 LAFAN1 clips with one policy on one GPU, $
abla$Mimic reaches the score reported by the state-of-the-art world-model method, 0.82, in 20 minutes instead of 1.2 h, and 0.874 in 1.8 h. SHAC, the standard first-order baseline, stops on exploding gradients within minutes. We release NablaEngine and $
abla$Mimic as open-source infrastructure for first-order humanoid policy learning.
papers.summary: Robot policy learning is dominated by sample-hungry zeroth-order methods such as `PPO`, while first-order methods that differentiate through the simulator usually fail on contact-rich whole-body control because their gradients explode. `∇Mimic` clips each gradient sample relative to the median at every step of the backward pass and reuses expensive simulated windows by regressing onto gradient-derived action targets. It runs on `NablaEngine`, a differentiable GPU simulator for the Unitree G1 whose analytic gradients match float64 finite differences and run 11.5× faster than the `MuJoCo Warp` adjoint. Tracking all 40 `LAFAN1` motion clips with one policy on one GPU, it **matches the state-of-the-art world-model score of 0.82 in 20 minutes instead of 1.2 hours** and reaches 0.874 in 1.8 hours, while the first-order baseline `SHAC` diverges. Both tools are released as open source.

papers.title: When Steering Shifts Discourse: Identifying and Intervening on Discourse-Level Changes due to Activation Steering in LLMs
papers.abstract: Activation steering is an inference-time technique used to control or modify the behavior, tone, or safety properties of a large language model (LLM) without retraining the model's weights or editing its input prompt, but simply by adding a vector to its residual-stream activations. However, activation steering also changes the generated text in unintended ways, unrelated to intended behavior change, that are not well understood. Prior work has measured these changes only through coarse signals such as perplexity. In this work, we show that steering systematically produces significant changes in discourse dimensions of the generated text, such as its formality, use of evidence, and ambiguity. We present a way of countering this by adding a second, complementary vector that targets the affected discourse dimension. This intervention restores about 78% of the unintended discourse changes while preserving the intended steering behavior in about 93% of the generations.
papers.summary: Activation steering changes a large language model's (LLM's) behavior at inference time by adding a vector to its residual-stream activations, but its side effects on the generated text have mostly been measured with coarse signals such as perplexity. The authors show that steering systematically shifts discourse dimensions of the output, such as formality, use of evidence, and ambiguity. To counter this, they add a second, complementary steering vector that targets the affected discourse dimension. This **restores about 78% of the unintended discourse changes while keeping the intended steering effect in about 93% of generations**.

papers.title: Breaking Information Islands in Sparse Tuning via Small-World Connectivity
papers.abstract: Sparse tuning is widely used to adapt large language models due to its parameter efficiency. However, its effectiveness depends not only on the number of trainable parameters, but also on the feature-interaction topology of the sparse update's structural support. Limited or uneven connectivity in this support may isolate subsets of feature dimensions, forming information islands that restrict direct task-specific interactions through the trainable update. To address this issue, we propose Small-World Induced Fine-Tuning (SWIFT), a sparse tuning framework inspired by small-world connectivity. SWIFT combines block-diagonal sparse updates for local feature mixing with a fixed deterministic scattering permutation that routes the mixed outputs across feature groups without additional trainable parameters. We further show theoretically that certain random sparse-update models and block-diagonal updates can exhibit information islands, whereas a sufficiently scattering permutation guarantees positive block-level expansion when the trainable block-diagonal factor consists of equal-sized, structurally dense square blocks. Extensive experiments on commonsense reasoning, natural language generation, and image classification demonstrate that SWIFT outperforms the evaluated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) baselines on average and can match or surpass full fine-tuning. Implementation is available at https://github.com/xianchaoguan/SWIFT
papers.summary: In sparse fine-tuning of large language models, poorly connected update patterns can leave groups of feature dimensions isolated as "information islands" that cannot interact through the trainable update. Inspired by small-world networks, `SWIFT` combines block-diagonal sparse updates for local mixing with a fixed scattering permutation that routes outputs across feature groups without adding trainable parameters. The authors prove that some random and block-diagonal sparse updates form islands, while a sufficiently scattering permutation guarantees cross-block connectivity. On commonsense reasoning, natural language generation, and image classification, `SWIFT` **beats the evaluated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) baselines on average and can match or exceed full fine-tuning**.

papers.title: Radial Kernel Attention for Long-Range Modeling in Polymer Machine Learning Force Fields
papers.abstract: We introduce Radial Kernel Attention (RKA) for long-range modeling in polymer machine learning force fields. Local neighbor graphs constrain communication across polymer chains and their surrounding environments, while explicit all-pair attention incurs quadratic cost. RKA maps atomic distances from the cluster centroid to learned radial features and combines their overlap with content-dependent queries and keys. Factorized aggregation and readout enable global feature exchange at linear cost in atom count for fixed feature dimensions. We insert the invariant scalar update between EquiformerV3 local blocks and obtain conservative forces by differentiating the total energy, including its radial coordinate dependence. We evaluate energy and force prediction for finite polymer-derived clusters in OPoly26. Our models are trained on the official training split for 12 epochs and evaluated directly after training on the complete official validation split. A matched 5M comparison shows that RKA reduces per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%, respectively. The 20M RKA model is compared with UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1 on the same validation structures. The 20M model attains a total-energy MAE of 15.81 meV and a force MAE of 2.619 meV/angstrom; its per-atom energy MAE is 0.1182 meV/atom. RKA provides a compact global communication pathway that improves energy and force prediction on the evaluated polymer-derived clusters.
papers.summary: Machine learning force fields for polymers need long-range interactions, but local neighbor graphs limit communication across chains and full all-pair attention scales quadratically. Radial Kernel Attention (`RKA`) maps each atom's distance from the cluster centroid to learned radial features and combines them with content-dependent queries and keys, giving global feature exchange at linear cost; it is inserted between `EquiformerV3` local blocks. On polymer-derived clusters from `OPoly26`, a matched 5M-parameter comparison shows that **`RKA` cuts per-atom energy error by 67.4% and force error by 36.3%**. A 20M-parameter model is also evaluated against `UMA-S-1.2` on the same validation structures.

papers.title: OT-CAL: Optimal-Transport-Guided Adaptive Sample Selection for Efficient Visual Learning
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks for image recognition are typically trained using mini-batches, with a forward pass to compute predictions and losses followed by a more computationally expensive backward pass to update model parameters. However, not all training samples contribute equally to learning, suggesting that computation can be reduced by performing backward passes only on informative samples. The challenge is that sample informativeness changes throughout training: difficult samples may be valuable early on, improving samples become important later, and class diversity becomes increasingly relevant toward the end. Existing methods often rely on fixed selection rules or computationally expensive per-sample gradient calculations. We propose OT-CAL, an adaptive data selection method that automatically adjusts its sampling preferences during training. OT-CAL represents each sample using five informativeness features, including difficulty, learnability, and uncertainty. A curriculum vector describes the currently preferred sample characteristics, and optimal-transport-based matching assigns selection weights according to how closely samples match this target. The curriculum vector is then updated using the selected samples, forming a feedback loop that adapts without a manually defined schedule. Experiments on three standard visual learning benchmarks show that, when selecting 50% of each mini-batch, OT-CAL improves performance by 1.3--2.1 points over AdaSelection while achieving 1.18--1.24 times faster training than full-data training.
papers.summary: Image-recognition training can save compute by running backward passes only on informative samples, but what makes a sample informative shifts over the course of training. `OT-CAL` describes each sample with five features, including difficulty, learnability, and uncertainty. It assigns selection weights by optimal-transport matching against a curriculum vector, which is then updated from the selected samples, so the curriculum adapts without a hand-designed schedule. Selecting 50% of each mini-batch on three visual benchmarks, it **improves accuracy by 1.3–2.1 points over `AdaSelection` while training 1.18–1.24× faster than full-data training**.

papers.title: When the Past Shapes Action: Understanding Embodied Memory
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative foundation models have expanded the capabilities of embodied AI, enabling increasingly general navigation, manipulation, and long-horizon task execution. However, effective interaction with dynamic environments requires more than only strong perception and reasoning: agents must act with partial knowledge and retain, retrieve, and update information from past observations, actions, and experiences. This survey examines embodied memory as a mechanism for preserving decision-relevant information beyond the current observation. We organize existing approaches along two complementary dimensions: six fundamental memory requirements, spanning world-state persistence, task progress, belief maintenance, and experiential learning; and eight architectural categories, including recurrent states, fast weights, visual and symbolic representations, spatial memory, and experience-based systems. We analyze their capabilities and limitations, and examine how existing benchmarks evaluate memory-dependent behavior, distinguishing genuine use of historical information from general task performance. Finally, we identify open challenges in selecting relevant experiences, maintaining consistent beliefs in changing environments, and consolidating knowledge across episodes. Our analysis provides a framework for understanding memory as an essential component of reliable, adaptive, and lifelong-horizon embodied intelligence.
papers.summary: Embodied agents that navigate and manipulate in dynamic environments must keep, retrieve, and update information beyond the current observation. This survey organizes embodied memory along **six memory requirements**, including world-state persistence, task progress, belief maintenance, and experiential learning, and eight architectural categories such as recurrent states, fast weights, symbolic and spatial memory, and experience-based systems. It also examines whether existing benchmarks actually test the use of past information rather than overall task performance. Open challenges it highlights include selecting relevant experiences, keeping beliefs consistent as environments change, and consolidating knowledge across episodes.

papers.title: Does Reasoning Make Language Models Agree?
papers.abstract: Language models face two opposing concerns: monoculture, in which models err in correlated ways, and multiplicity, in which equally accurate models make conflicting decisions. The rise of reasoning models has complicated this debate: On the one hand, reasoning may increase model agreement if models anchor on the same salient features or follow similar reasoning paths. On the other hand, stochastic reasoning traces may introduce additional branch points leading to more diverse predictions. We resolve this tension by distinguishing reasoning as an intervention from reasoning as an observed behavior. We compare agreement under controlled changes in reasoning effort with agreement across observed reasoning lengths, measuring both against the agreement expected from model accuracy. Across nine models from two developers and three classification tasks, enabling reasoning increases agreement between models evaluated on the same individuals. Yet the individuals who elicit longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models. Both patterns persist after accounting for differences in accuracy. Asking models to reason more thus promotes agreement, while observing them reason longer signals disagreement.
papers.summary: Language models can fail through monoculture, where they make correlated errors, or through multiplicity, where equally accurate models disagree, and it is unclear which way reasoning pushes them. The authors separate reasoning as an intervention, meaning controlled changes in reasoning effort, from reasoning as an observed behavior, meaning trace length, and compare agreement against the level expected from accuracy alone. Across nine models from two developers and three classification tasks, **turning on reasoning increases agreement between models, yet individuals who elicit longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models**. Both effects hold after accounting for accuracy.

papers.title: From WSIs to Bulk, Spatial and Single-Cell Transcriptomics via Multi-Scale Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution of gene expression is key to studying complex diseases like cancer. While Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) and Single-Cell Transcriptomics (scT) provide high-resolution insights, they remain expensive and scarce. In contrast, standard histopathology Whole-Slide Images (WSIs) paired with bulk RNA sequencing are widely available. This work introduces a Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network (GNN) capable of simultaneously predicting bulk, spatial, and single-cell transcriptomics directly from WSIs. By extracting morphological features using a Pathology Foundation Model (PFM) (UNI2-h) and constructing spatial graphs at both patch and cell levels, the model learns the hierarchical relationships within the tissue. The network is trained on a combined dataset of The Cancer Genome Atlas Program (TCGA), Visium, and Xenium samples across lung, kidney, and breast tissues. A hybrid training strategy is employed, leveraging direct supervision alongside weakly supervised consistency losses to ensure predictions align across biological scales. Results show the model accurately predicts gene expression at the slide level and moderately at the patch level (strongest on Xenium), and achieves moderate correlation at the challenging single-cell level. Furthermore, downstream tasks explore the clinical relevance of these predictions, demonstrating their utility in survival analysis, spatial hazard mapping, and tumor classification via molecular signatures.
papers.summary: Spatial and single-cell transcriptomics are expensive and scarce, while standard histopathology whole-slide images (WSIs) paired with bulk RNA sequencing are widely available. The authors build a multi-scale graph neural network (GNN) on features from the `UNI2-h` pathology foundation model, with spatial graphs at both patch and cell level, that **predicts bulk, spatial, and single-cell gene expression directly from WSIs**. It is trained on `TCGA`, `Visium`, and `Xenium` lung, kidney, and breast samples using direct supervision plus consistency losses across scales. Predictions are accurate at slide level, moderate at patch level (strongest on `Xenium`), and moderately correlated at single-cell level, and they prove useful for survival analysis and tumor classification.

papers.title: From fleet trajectories to single-cell promises: hierarchically weighted conformal prediction for battery SOH monitoring
papers.abstract: Interval predictions from conformal prediction are usually read as "90% coverage", but on nested battery data that number promises the fleet average, not the individual cell. We measure the gap on 124 public LFP cells under a preregistered three-tier reporting protocol (fleet, batch, cell): pooled coverage looks healthy (0.875-0.906 across splits) while the worst cell is covered 0.1-2% of the time, with exact binomial tests against the nominal level. We then repair part of the gap with a hierarchically weighted conformal engine whose weights consume only side information frozen at prediction time - signature features, batch labels, cycle indices - and never touch residuals. The preregistered repair criterion passes: 10th-percentile cell coverage moves 0.750 to 0.830 (53% of the gap), the worst cell 0.642 to 0.694, with zero deferrals and a flat sensitivity spectrum. What the engine does not repair is localized rather than left open: under protocol drift the frozen weights harm monotonically on the SOH scale (the absolute scale is reported in full), a structural dead end we report instead of tuning away; and repair capacity is bounded by calibration-pool battery diversity, measured on both datasets. On a cross-chemistry external set the calibrated intervals collapse (0.286), while the within-domain skeleton replicates (pooled 0.933, worst cell 0.686). The deliverable is a reporting protocol - three tiers of promise anchored to measured regimes, worst-cell statistics, deferral share - that makes per-cell interval claims auditable before deployment.
papers.summary: Conformal prediction intervals are usually described as giving "90% coverage", but on nested battery data that figure is a fleet average and says little about any individual cell. On 124 public lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells, the authors use a preregistered reporting protocol at three tiers (fleet, batch and cell) and find that pooled coverage looks healthy at 0.875–0.906 while **the worst cell is covered only 0.1–2% of the time**. A hierarchically weighted conformal method closes about 53% of the gap at the 10th-percentile cell, using only side information fixed at prediction time such as signature features, batch labels and cycle indices. The authors also report where the method fails: under protocol drift, and on a set with a different battery chemistry, where coverage collapses to 0.286. They propose the three-tier protocol as a way to make per-cell state-of-health (SOH) interval claims auditable before deployment.

papers.title: TSBPO: Tree-Structured Branching for Policy Optimization in Interactive Language Agents
papers.abstract: Training interactive language agents from terminal outcomes poses three coupled problems: which task and state continuations to sample, how to assign delayed feedback to decisions, and how to aggregate token losses for multi-token actions. We present TSBPO, a tree-structured sampling-to-update paradigm that addresses these problems within one training loop. A likelihood-fitted Root/Branch allocator uses retained task and state evidence to target continuations likely to produce contrasting terminal outcomes under fixed rollout budgets. On the resulting replayed physical trees, trajectory advantages compare immediate sibling segments, while observation-group step advantages compare outcomes at matched task/observation states. The actor then sums clipped token surrogates over each complete response and normalizes across active turns, avoiding response-length averaging in the policy-gradient term. With a Qwen2.5-1.5B actor, fixed checkpoints obtain 97.79% seen and 96.64% unseen stochastic success on ALFWorld and an 81.07% per-episode success rate over six stochastic episodes for each of the 500 WebShop test goals. A WebShop step-term ablation yields 75.93% at the same update-100 evaluation; an ALFWorld aggregation comparison shows higher observed command validity with complete-turn weighting. These results support the evaluated training configuration on two interactive benchmarks.
papers.summary: Training interactive language agents only from end-of-episode outcomes raises three linked problems: which continuations to sample, how to assign delayed credit to individual decisions, and how to aggregate token losses over actions that span many tokens. `TSBPO` addresses all three in one training loop. An allocator targets continuations likely to produce contrasting outcomes within a fixed rollout budget. Advantages are computed by comparing sibling branches in replayed trajectory trees and outcomes at matched observation states, and token losses are summed over each complete response rather than averaged by response length. With a `Qwen2.5-1.5B` actor, the method reaches **97.79% seen and 96.64% unseen success on `ALFWorld`** and 81.07% per-episode success on `WebShop`.

papers.title: Precision--Recall Trade-off on the Inference Level for LLMs in Grammatical Error Correction
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been adopted for Grammatical Error Correction (GEC), achieving strong performance via both full fine-tuning and prompt-based approaches. As probabilistic sequence models, LLMs expose inference-time parameters that directly modify token generation behavior; however, their potential for controlling GEC-specific trade-offs has not been systematically studied. In this work, we investigate decoding strategies for grammatical error correction. We show that the repetition penalty parameter enables controllable adjustment of the precision--recall trade-off at inference time, without modifying the model architecture, training procedure, or prompt. Through experiments on standard GEC benchmarks, we demonstrate that repetition-penalty-based decoding enables inference-time control of the precision--recall balance, conceptually related to methods previously proposed for sequence-to-sequence GEC models, such as Align-and-Predict Decoding (APD), while remaining simple and broadly applicable to existing LLMs that expose inference-time decoding penalties.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are now widely used for grammatical error correction (GEC), but how their inference-time decoding parameters affect GEC-specific trade-offs has not been studied systematically. The authors show that **the repetition penalty can steer the precision–recall balance at inference time**, with no change to the model, its training or the prompt. Experiments on standard GEC benchmarks show this control is conceptually similar to `Align-and-Predict Decoding` (`APD`) for sequence-to-sequence models, while being simpler and applicable to any LLM that exposes decoding penalties.

papers.title: GraphNIAH: A Benchmark for Long-Context Reasoning over Real-World Graphs
papers.abstract: The needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) benchmark was introduced as a test for measuring a model's ability to find small relevant facts within a very large body of input text. However, existing NIAH benchmarks each suffer from one or more of the following limitations: (1) reliance on synthetic data, so their evaluations may not generalize to real-world settings; (2) reuse of previously published datasets, leading to the risk of benchmark contamination; (3) dependence on manual annotation, which requires human effort to create and update data and is prone to future benchmark contamination; and (4) unrealistic simplification of long-context multi-hop reasoning where each next step is trivial given previous steps, while real-world reasoning often requires planning over multiple possible proof paths. To address these limitations, we introduce \Benchmark, a dynamic benchmark built from real citation relationships among scientific papers published after the evaluated models' knowledge cutoff date, which utilizes real-world information while ensuring no benchmark contamination. The fully automated benchmark construction pipeline samples representative subgraphs of the citation graph formed by these papers and converts each subgraph into a long-context QA example with a verifiable answer. We use GraphNIAH to evaluate eight LLMs from the GPT-5.6, Gemini-3, and Qwen3.5 families. We find that accuracy falls as questions require longer reasoning paths: at question depths of 16 and 32, the GPT-5.6 and Qwen3.5 models answer YES/NO questions no better than random guessing, mostly by answering NO; four of the eight models answer no counting example correctly, and the others model get worse as the subgraph size increases. These findings suggest that current LLMs often stop searching the citation relationships in their context before they reach the answer, even though every fact they need is in the context.
papers.summary: Existing needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) benchmarks rely on synthetic or reused data, need manual annotation, or reduce multi-hop reasoning to trivial chains. `GraphNIAH` addresses these issues by automatically sampling subgraphs from real citation graphs of papers published after the evaluated models' knowledge cutoff, then converting each subgraph into a long-context question with a verifiable answer, which avoids contamination. In tests of eight LLMs from the `GPT-5.6`, `Gemini-3` and `Qwen3.5` families, accuracy falls as reasoning paths get longer: **at question depths of 16 and 32, the `GPT-5.6` and `Qwen3.5` models answer yes/no questions no better than random guessing**, mostly answering no. Four models got no counting questions right. The authors conclude that models often stop searching their context before reaching the answer, even though every needed fact is present.

papers.title: Advancing Clinical Trial Outcome Prediction with Domain-Specific Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Clinical trial failures are a major barrier to efficient drug development, incurring substantial costs and delaying patient access to effective therapies. Structured approaches such as the Hierarchical Interaction Network (HINT) predict trial outcomes by explicitly modelling interactions between drugs, diseases and protocols, but make limited use of the free text in trial registrations. We evaluate two domain-specific language models, BioBERT (108M parameters) and BioMistral (7B parameters), for phase-level outcome prediction on the TOP benchmark (12,477 trials), representing each trial as text built from ten ClinicalTrials.gov fields. We compare fine-tuning (full fine-tuning for BioBERT, low-rank adaptation for BioMistral) with probing, in which the pretrained model is frozen and only a lightweight classifier is trained on its embeddings. On the held-out test set of each phase, all four language-model variants achieved higher ROC-AUC (0.613--0.772) and PR-AUC (0.649--0.901) than the published HINT results, corresponding to relative PR-AUC gains of 10--20\%. F1 differences were small and mixed, and no model, including HINT, clearly exceeded the F1 of a trivial classifier that predicts success for every trial. Under the configurations tested, probing performed comparably to fine-tuning: fine-tuned models scored highest on ROC-AUC and PR-AUC in Phases I and II, and frozen BioMistral embeddings in Phase III (ROC-AUC 0.772; PR-AUC 0.901), although most differences between variants were below 0.03 and were not tested for significance. These results suggest that pretrained biomedical representations already encode signal relevant to trial outcome, and that probing is a computationally cheaper alternative to fine-tuning for this task.
papers.summary: Clinical trial failures are costly, and structured predictors such as the Hierarchical Interaction Network (`HINT`) make little use of the free text in trial registrations. The authors represent each trial in the `TOP` benchmark (12,477 trials) as text built from ten ClinicalTrials.gov fields. They then compare fine-tuning and frozen-embedding probing for `BioBERT` (108M parameters) and `BioMistral` (7B parameters, adapted with low-rank adaptation, LoRA). **All four variants beat published `HINT` results on ROC-AUC and PR-AUC, with relative PR-AUC gains of 10–20%**, though no model, including `HINT`, clearly beat a trivial always-success classifier on F1. Probing performed comparably to fine-tuning, making it a cheaper option for this task.

papers.title: Hierarchical Residuals: A Minimalist Decoupling of Residual Width from Compute Width
papers.abstract: Residual connections underpin Transformers, but they implicitly tie the residual width carried through depth to the compute width used inside each layer. We introduce Hierarchical Residuals (HiRes), a minimalist architectural change that decouples these dimensions, widening the residual state while keeping per-layer compute width fixed. HiRes groups layers into blocks: standard d-dimensional PreNorm layers operate inside each block, while a wider D-dimensional PostNorm outer residual connects blocks. Learned read/write projections bridge the two spaces at block boundaries, leaving individual Transformer layers unchanged. Across different model sizes and depths, HiRes consistently outperforms vanilla residual addition, with fitted scaling laws indicating a 1.30-fold improvement in FLOPs efficiency. On OLMoE-1B-7B pretraining for 500B tokens, HiRes achieves 0.0208 lower training loss and 1.14-point higher downstream accuracy. HiRes is also competitive with other residual expansion methods such as VWN, mHC and AttnRes with less activation memory and I/O costs. Built from only dense projections and normalizations, it requires neither specialized kernels nor infrastructure-level optimizations. HiRes thus exposes residual width as a practical scaling variable using only standard operators.
papers.summary: In Transformers, residual connections tie the width of the residual stream carried through depth to the compute width used inside each layer. Hierarchical Residuals (`HiRes`) separates the two. Layers are grouped into blocks that use standard narrow PreNorm layers, while a wider PostNorm outer residual connects the blocks through learned read and write projections. Fitted scaling laws show **about a 1.30× improvement in FLOPs efficiency** over vanilla residuals. On `OLMoE-1B-7B` pretrained for 500B tokens, `HiRes` gives 0.0208 lower loss and 1.14 points higher downstream accuracy. It matches other residual-expansion methods such as `VWN`, `mHC` and `AttnRes` with less activation memory and needs no specialized kernels.

papers.title: Simple Features Beat Most AI Control Monitors
papers.abstract: AI control relies on monitors to catch a capable model that sabotages its work. These monitors are evaluated on their ability to differentiate honest from backdoored code. We show that on a standard evaluation dataset, simple features beat most monitors without ever running the code, outranking 20 of 24 open-weight models prompted as monitors. The dataset gives its labels away in two ways. People wrote the honest solutions and older language models the backdoors, so the style of the code reveals the class. Additionally, problems that LLMs can backdoor have different characteristics, so basic facts about the problem reveal it too. Swapping one class at a time for code by Claude Sonnet 5 shows that these features reward a contrast between authors, since human code against Sonnet 5's backdoors is easier to separate than the original pairs, 0.95 against 0.79. One in seven backdoors in the standard test set fails our validity checks, which distorts comparisons between attackers. A Sonnet 5 monitor appears to catch 77% of the older models' backdoors but 37% of Sonnet 5's, and 78% against 61% once both are verified. We do not show that published monitors rely on these shortcuts, but our findings suggest that a high score on such a dataset is not by itself evidence of sabotage detection. We release the rebuilt dataset and checks.
papers.summary: AI control research evaluates monitors by how well they separate honest code from backdoored code. On a standard evaluation dataset, **simple features that never run the code outrank 20 of 24 open-weight models prompted as monitors**. The dataset leaks its labels in two ways: humans wrote the honest solutions while older LLMs wrote the backdoors, and problems that LLMs can backdoor differ in measurable ways. One in seven test backdoors also fails validity checks. A `Claude Sonnet 5` monitor appears to catch 77% of older models' backdoors but only 37% of its own, a gap that narrows to 78% versus 61% once both sets are verified. The authors release a rebuilt dataset and their validity checks.

papers.title: UpLoop: Training Looped Transformers via Upcycling at No Extra Pretraining Compute
papers.abstract: Looped language models can strengthen reasoning through repeated computation with shared weights, increasing execution depth without adding independent parameters. However, each additional pass increases training floating-point operations (FLOPs), making these gains more expensive to obtain. To address this cost, we propose UpLoop, a pretraining schedule that uses upcycling to train looped Transformers while exactly matching a standard dense baseline in final parameter count, total training tokens, and training FLOPs. Specifically, UpLoop begins with a shallow Transformer, progressively grows its depth by copying learned layers, and uses the computation saved early to support repeated execution of a shared middle block later in training. Experiments across model scales show improvements in language modeling and downstream performance, with the average score across 22 downstream tasks increasing from 22.99 to 27.52 at 1.3B parameters. These gains also extend to mathematical reasoning after supervised fine-tuning.
papers.summary: Looped Transformers reuse shared weights across repeated passes to strengthen reasoning, but each extra pass adds training compute. `UpLoop` is a pretraining schedule that starts with a shallow model, grows its depth by copying learned layers (upcycling), and spends the compute saved early on looping a shared middle block later. The result exactly matches a dense baseline in parameter count, training tokens and training FLOPs. At 1.3B parameters, **the average score across 22 downstream tasks rises from 22.99 to 27.52**, and the gains carry over to mathematical reasoning after supervised fine-tuning.
papers.highlight_summary:
Looped Transformers reuse a shared block to add execution depth without adding parameters, but every extra pass costs more training compute. `UpLoop` covers that cost by training shallow models first, growing them by copying layers, and spending the compute saved early on looping a shared middle block late in training, so it matches a dense baseline's parameter count, training tokens, and training FLOPs.

- The schedule has four stages with execution depths of L/4, L/2, L, and then L + (r−1)m: each growth step copies layer weights and their Adam optimizer states, and the final stage runs a 4-layer middle block twice (L=16, giving 20 executed layers from 16 unique ones).
- On `FineWeb-Edu` with `OLMo 2` architectures from 370M to 1.3B parameters, all at matched budgets, `UpLoop` raises the 22-task downstream average at 1.3B from **22.99 to 27.52**, with the largest gains on variable-assignment reasoning (`VarAssign-math` goes from **58.1% to 91.1%**).
- Held-out NLL improves at every scale by about **0.035** (2.43 to 2.40 at 1.3B), and after `GSM8K` fine-tuning, zero-shot accuracy at 1.3B rises from **8.72% to 12.05%**.
- In 370M ablations, `UpLoop` (NLL 2.74) beats looping from scratch and looping from a dense checkpoint (both 2.76) even though those use 1.20× and 1.11× the FLOPs, and it ties a 438M-parameter 20-layer dense model that needs 1.20× the compute.
- The compute matching applies only to training: the looped model needs about **1.2× the inference FLOPs** of the baseline, the experiments stop at 1.3B parameters, each configuration was trained with a single seed, and the strategy ablations were run only at 370M.

papers.title: Leveraging Quantum Measurement Randomness for Shot-Efficient Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: In quantum computing, the readout always carries finite-shot sampling noise. Suppressing this noise through repeated measurements raises the cost of a quantum neural network (QNN). Meanwhile, a stochastic diffusion sampler deliberately adds randomness at each reverse (generation) step. This paper turns the measurement noise from a liability into a resource. Specifically, we use the noise quantum measurement produces anyway to replace part of the noise the sampler would otherwise inject. We characterize the measurement error as multinomial sampling noise propagated through a trainable linear readout. To connect the circuit's Born probabilities to the denoising task, we further formulate the diffusion process on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane mapped to the probability simplex. Therefore, we can employ a compensation noise to match the mean and covariance of the shot-noise-free linear update under some minimum shot conditions. Solving this condition for the shot count gives a state-dependent adaptive budget. For the denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM), this budget increases as the sampler becomes more deterministic.
