On an eight-dimensional Gaussian mixture, the schedule achieves comparable generation quality with $303$ shots per sample against a high-shot reference of $1.6\times10^{6}$, about $5300\times$ fewer. Latent diffusion experiments on MNIST further validate the proposed mechanism for generation in a learned latent space.
papers.summary: Reading out a quantum neural network always carries finite-shot sampling noise, and suppressing that noise requires many repeated measurements. The authors instead use the measurement noise as part of the randomness that a stochastic diffusion sampler injects at each reverse step. They model the noise as multinomial sampling through a linear readout and run the diffusion on a bounded hyperplane mapped to the probability simplex. A matching condition then yields a state-dependent adaptive shot budget. On an eight-dimensional Gaussian mixture, the method matches the generation quality of a 1.6 million-shot reference using **303 shots per sample, about 5,300× fewer**, and latent diffusion experiments on `MNIST` further support the approach.

papers.title: From Training Exposure to Membership Evidence: A Controlled Study of OLMo 2
papers.abstract: Whether a language model was trained on a document matters for copyright, privacy, and benchmark contamination. Yet most membership-inference (MI) evaluations on language models collect members and non-members after the fact, so success may reflect distribution shift and failure is inconclusive. We re-ran OLMo 2 1B's official 50-billion-token mid-training stage, replacing selected training chunks with documents from 7,814 pairs matched on domain and difficulty. For each pair, a coin flip determined which document was inserted and which was held out. The run released by the Allen Institute for AI (AI2) from the same seed saw identical data everywhere else and serves as the counterfactual. One exposure raises a previously unseen document's likelihood on average but rarely identifies it. Using the counterfactual as reference, the reference ratio has an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.767 but, with one threshold across domains, catches 3.8% of members at a 1% false-positive rate (FPR). In contrast, 13 matched pairs give a paired test 80% power at the 5% level to detect training on a collection, given same-domain non-members and a close reference. A reference trained with another seed recovers 92% of the counterfactual's AUC advantage over chance, whereas reference-free attacks stay within 0.07 of chance when pooled over domains. The full official post-training recipe, re-run on both models, leaves 89% of the average effect. Even with a closely matched reference, substantial document-level variability limits individual membership inference. We will release the checkpoints, per-token log-probabilities, and the evaluation documents; the code is available at https://github.com/ali-bana/OLMo-Twin.
papers.summary: Most membership-inference (MI) evaluations on language models gather members and non-members after the fact, which confounds results with distribution shift. The authors re-ran `OLMo 2 1B`'s 50-billion-token mid-training stage with documents from 7,814 matched pairs inserted by coin flip, using the official run from the same seed as a counterfactual. A single exposure raises a document's likelihood on average but rarely identifies it: the counterfactual reference ratio reaches an AUC of 0.767 yet **catches only 3.8% of members at a 1% false-positive rate**. By contrast, just 13 matched pairs give a paired test 80% power to detect training on a collection. Reference-free attacks stay near chance, and the effect largely survives post-training.

papers.title: Leakage-Controlled Structure-Preserving Augmentation and Template-Aware Evaluation for Bangla Symptom-Based Disease Prediction
papers.abstract: Bangla symptom-based disease prediction is commonly evaluated on a small, imbalanced structured benchmark containing many profiles that differ by only one or two symptoms. We test whether train-only asymmetric Bernoulli perturbation improves classification using 725 unique profiles spanning 85 diseases and 172 binary symptoms. Experiments use ten repeated real-profile holdouts and parent-grouped inner cross-validation. The 2 x 2 design separates augmentation from hyperparameter tuning, with exact duplication, random oversampling, class weighting, and SMOTEN as balancing controls. For Bernoulli Naive Bayes (BNB), the gain over tuned raw training does not withstand Holm correction, although BNB attains the highest mean accuracy (97.50%). The boosted-tree models benefit substantially: XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost improve by 18.10, 28.45, and 10.09 percentage points, respectively. A Hamming-distance audit places 91.0% of standard held-out profiles within one symptom bit of the training data. Accuracy decreases on a same-disease 1-bit-purged challenge; nevertheless, XGBoost and LightGBM retain large augmentation gains. We also evaluate robustness to missing and spurious symptoms and the faithfulness of BNB explanations. Overall, Bernoulli perturbation is useful for some model families, but benchmark accuracy should be interpreted together with template proximity.
papers.summary: Bangla symptom-based disease prediction is usually evaluated on a small, imbalanced benchmark in which many profiles differ by only one or two symptoms. Using 725 unique profiles, the authors test train-only asymmetric Bernoulli perturbation as data augmentation, with repeated holdouts and balancing controls such as `SMOTEN`. `Bernoulli Naive Bayes` gains no significant benefit, but **`XGBoost`, `LightGBM` and `CatBoost` improve by 18.10, 28.45 and 10.09 percentage points**. A Hamming-distance audit finds that 91% of held-out profiles lie within one symptom bit of the training data, so the authors recommend reading benchmark accuracy alongside how close test profiles are to training templates.

papers.title: Locality-Controlled Out-of-Distribution Guidance for Robust Regulatory DNA Sequence Design
papers.abstract: Designing regulatory DNA sequences for targeted gene-expression control is an important challenge. Recent approaches frame this task as property-conditioned generation, where diffusion models trained on natural sequences are guided toward high predicted activity through reward-based fine-tuning or sampling-time guidance. We show that single-reward evaluation can obscure reward-hacking behavior. By decomposing evaluation into property, novelty, and plausibility, we identify an empirically underexplored region of the evaluation space in which all three objectives are satisfied, but no existing baseline succeeds. We postulate that this gap arises because prior methods treat guidance primarily as a matter of magnitude. In regulatory DNA, however, sequence grammar is spatially nonuniform: motif positions are sensitive to perturbation, while background regions allow more exploration. We therefore propose LOCOGEN by reformulating guidance as a problem of locality. LOCOGEN learns an invariant motif mask through sequence-level invariance learning to protect motif positions, while applying OOD damping only to background positions. It operates at sampling time on a frozen diffusion backbone, without retraining the backbone. Across HepG2, K562, and SK-N-SH, LOCOGEN reaches this previously underexplored region of the property-novelty-plausibility space. Code is available at https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/LocoGen.
papers.summary: Diffusion models for designing regulatory DNA are usually guided toward high predicted activity, but evaluating them on a single reward can hide reward hacking. When evaluation is split into property, novelty and plausibility, **no existing baseline reaches the region where all three are satisfied**. `LOCOGEN` treats guidance as a question of where to intervene rather than how strongly. It learns an invariant mask that protects motif positions and applies out-of-distribution damping only to background positions, at sampling time on a frozen diffusion backbone. Across the `HepG2`, `K562` and `SK-N-SH` cell lines, it reaches the previously unmet region of that space.

papers.title: Task Vectors Can Be Linearly Decomposed into Interpretable and Controllable Components
papers.abstract: Task Vectors (TVs) provide a compact way to steer large language models, but they are typically treated as atomized directions merely extracted from hidden states, leaving their internal functional structure poorly understood. Motivated by prior work that decomposes in-context learning into Task Recognition (TR) and Task Learning (TL), we ask whether a single TV can likewise be decomposed into functionally meaningful components. We formulate a TR/TL-based decomposition from candidate-label unembeddings, separating each TV into TR, TL, and residual components, and try to optimize the TR and TL coefficients using Bayesian optimization for more effective intervention. We evaluate this formulation across multiple model families, classification tasks, and both instruction- and demonstration-based TVs. Across these settings, TR/TL-based optimization identifies intervention directions that outperform the original TVs. Although optimization over random directions can also improve performance, TR/TL-based search yields more reliable gains, particularly for instruction-based TVs. Moreover, isolated interventions on the decomposed components produce distinct logit-level effects that are consistent with their intended functional roles. Together, these results suggest that TVs are not monolithic steering directions, but can be decomposed into functionally meaningful components that support both interpretation and control.
papers.summary: Task vectors are compact directions extracted from hidden states and used to steer LLMs, but their internal structure is poorly understood. Building on prior work that splits in-context learning into task recognition and task learning, the authors use candidate-label unembeddings to decompose each task vector into recognition, learning and residual components. They then tune the component coefficients with Bayesian optimization. Across model families, classification tasks, and both instruction-based and demonstration-based task vectors, **the optimized decompositions outperform the original task vectors**, and do so more reliably than optimizing over random directions. Intervening on each component separately produces distinct logit-level effects consistent with its intended role.

papers.title: Do LLMs Know When They Are Wrong About Molecules? In-Context Property Prediction with Self-Reported Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are used in many domains, but molecular property prediction with them is still little explored. In this work we evaluate the capability of 7 frontier LLMs to predict molecular properties together with a self-reported uncertainty from in-context examples, and compare them with classical baselines trained on the same molecules. We use 4 datasets and screen each for contamination of the training data of the LLMs: three are clean, and the fourth, ESOL, is memorised by most of the models and serves as a comparison. On the clean datasets every LLM improves with the context, at 30 examples the most accurate one beats every baseline. The requested reasoning effort changes accuracy little. The self-reported uncertainty ranks the prediction errors weakly, with Spearman rank correlations of up to 0.46, about the level reached by the uncertainties of the baselines. Combining uncertainty and prediction, on lipophilicity the most certain half of the best LLM is the most accurate at small context sizes; on BACE and antiviral, and on lipophilicity at large context sizes, the best LLMs are on par with the best baseline. On the contaminated ESOL dataset the LLMs show no improvement with the context size, as expected for a memorised dataset, and their stated uncertainty is smaller on the molecules whose value they recall.
papers.summary: The authors evaluate seven frontier LLMs on predicting molecular properties from in-context examples while also reporting their own uncertainty, and compare them with classical baselines trained on the same molecules. On three datasets screened as uncontaminated, every LLM improves as more examples are added, and **at 30 examples the most accurate LLM beats every baseline**. The self-reported uncertainty ranks errors only weakly, with Spearman correlations of up to 0.46, which is comparable to the baselines' uncertainties. On the memorized `ESOL` dataset, the models do not improve with more context and report lower uncertainty on molecules whose values they recall.

papers.title: Latent-Lens: Visual Perception in Small Language Models Through Latent Communication
papers.abstract: Bridging independent vision-language models (VLMs) and small language models (SLMs) in a modular multi-agent system typically forces them to exchange information as discrete text, which creates a lossy bottleneck for spatial and fine-grained details. This constraint is especially acute for SLMs, whose limited capacity makes them more reliant on the quality of the input signal. Recent latent-communication methods exchange states between language models. How a VLM can pass visual information to a separately pretrained text-only SLM though remains unexplored. We propose \textbf{Latent-Lens}, a lightweight codec that bridges the representation gap between a frozen VLM and a frozen SLM directly in latent space, enabling them to communicate purely through hidden states. The codec consists of a domain encoder that projects hidden states from the VLM into the SLM's embedding space, and an attention decoder formalised as a LoRA that teaches the SLM to attend to these visual prefixes, while training only ${\sim}1.6$M parameters (0.2\% of the combined model size). On visual question answering (CLEVR, GQA), Latent-Lens achieves $81.0\pm7.9$\% and $65.4\pm5.4$\%, compared with $58.3\pm5.7$\% and $61.8\pm1.0$\% for text communication with the same LoRA budget (+30.2--69.8pp relative to frozen text communication), while on image captioning (Flickr8k) it improves over the same baseline by +16.5 (+18.8 frozen). We also evaluate Latent-Lens with TinyLlama-1.1B and InternVL2-1B, which use different architectures, vocabularies, and hidden dimensions.
papers.summary: Modular systems that pair a vision-language model (VLM) with a small language model (SLM) usually pass information between them as text, which loses spatial and fine-grained detail. `Latent-Lens` is a lightweight codec that lets a frozen VLM and a frozen SLM communicate through hidden states. A domain encoder projects VLM states into the SLM's embedding space, and a LoRA-based attention decoder teaches the SLM to use them, with only about 1.6M trainable parameters. On visual question answering, **it reaches 81.0% on `CLEVR` versus 58.3% for text communication at the same LoRA budget**, plus gains on `GQA` and `Flickr8k` captioning. It also works across mismatched architectures such as `TinyLlama-1.1B` and `InternVL2-1B`.

papers.title: Multimodal In-Context Learning with Explicit Rule Induction
papers.abstract: A central challenge in multimodal in-context learning (MICL) arises from tasks that are ill-defined without context and require uncovering the underlying rules from demonstrations. Existing methods predominantly treat MICL as direct input-output mapping, overlooking the importance of explicitly inducing and reasoning over such rules, limiting both performance and interpretability. We propose ERIM, Explicit Rule-Induction for Multimodal In-Context Learning, a unified framework that enhances MICL by explicitly inducing the latent rules governing demonstration samples. Leveraging the reasoning ability of multi-modal large language model (MLLM), ERIM constructs rule-centric MICL datasets, introduces explicit supervision for rule induction, and fine-tunes MLLM to perform explicit rule-induction via a two-stage training strategy that combines mixed cold-start supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments show consistent performance improvements across diverse MICL settings and demonstrate that correctly inducing underlying rules directly leads to stronger and more stable performance.
papers.summary: Some multimodal in-context learning (MICL) tasks are ill-defined until the model works out the rule behind the demonstrations, yet most methods treat MICL as direct input-to-output mapping. `ERIM` (Explicit Rule-Induction for Multimodal In-Context Learning) uses a multimodal LLM to build rule-centric training data. It then fine-tunes the model to state the underlying rule explicitly, in two stages: mixed cold-start supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. Experiments show consistent gains across diverse MICL settings, and **correctly induced rules lead directly to stronger and more stable performance**.

papers.title: Stepwise-Querying: Distilling Reasoning without Access to Teacher Chain-of-Thought
papers.abstract: Reasoning distillation is widely used to transfer the reasoning capabilities of large language models to smaller students through teacher-generated supervision. In the black-box setting, however, teachers may expose only final answers and brief solutions, leaving intermediate calculations and validity conditions unavailable and thus limiting the reasoning supervision available for distillation. We propose Stepwise Querying, which elicits step-specific explanations without requiring access to the teacher's internal chain-of-thought (CoT) traces. Independent queries to the same teacher request intermediate derivations, validity checks, and corrections for individual steps, the assembled solutions are then used for standard supervised fine-tuning. Across two teachers, two students, and four mathematics and code benchmarks, our method achieves the highest score in 14 of 16 comparisons with three baselines. We further introduce Stepwise Explanation Information Gain (SEIG), a diagnostic based on the log-ratio of a frozen student's probabilities of correct step completion under stepwise and global explanations. Analyses on GSM8K show that incorrect-answer trajectories can remain useful when they preserve valid intermediate reasoning, while further decomposition yields limited additional gains.
papers.summary: Black-box teacher models often expose only final answers or brief solutions, which limits the reasoning supervision available for distilling them into smaller students. Stepwise Querying sends independent queries to the same teacher asking for intermediate derivations, validity checks and corrections for individual steps, then assembles the answers into data for standard supervised fine-tuning. Across two teachers, two students, and four math and code benchmarks, **the method scores highest in 14 of 16 comparisons against three baselines**. A new diagnostic, Stepwise Explanation Information Gain (`SEIG`), shows on `GSM8K` that trajectories with wrong final answers can still be useful when their intermediate steps are valid.

papers.title: Clinical-Protocol-Aware Cyber Resilience for Connected Clinical Technologies Under AI-Enabled Adversarial Conditions
papers.abstract: Healthcare increasingly relies on connected medical devices, clinical information systems, cloud services, and distributed-care technologies, creating cybersecurity risks across clinical workflows. AI-enabled capabilities can accelerate vulnerability discovery and attack-path analysis, increasing the need to limit compromise propagation. This paper proposes a clinical-protocol-aware cyber-resilience framework based on bounded clinical micro-networks and controlled interconnections. The framework integrates clinical factors into cybersecurity design, management, and evaluation, covering prevention, containment, and incident response. A parameterized Monte Carlo simulation distinguishes technical cyber exposure from modeled clinical consequence. Experiments investigate architectural connectivity, adversarial capability, security controls, protocol dependency, risk alignment, communication directionality, lifecycle integration, and response timing. Under the simulation assumptions, connected architecture increases mean cyber exposure by 56.3% relative to segmented architecture, while combined prevention and containment reduce exposure by 60.1% relative to no controls. Increasing protocol dependency raises the modeled clinical-impact index from 1.021 to 7.567 without changing mean cyber exposure, demonstrating that technical exposure and clinical consequence can diverge. Risk-alignment experiments further indicate higher modeled clinical impact when greater technical risk corresponds to greater clinical significance. The findings support comparative architectural analysis, not calibrated estimates of real-world cyber risk, control effectiveness, or patient harm. The framework provides a clinical-context-aware approach to security-boundary design, control prioritization, and coordinated containment in connected healthcare environments.
papers.summary: Connected medical devices and clinical systems widen the attack surface in healthcare, and AI-enabled attackers can speed up vulnerability discovery. The authors propose a cyber-resilience framework built on bounded clinical micro-networks with controlled interconnections. They evaluate it with a parameterized Monte Carlo simulation that separates technical cyber exposure from modeled clinical consequence. In simulation, connected architectures raise mean exposure by 56.3% compared with segmented ones, and combined prevention and containment cut exposure by 60.1%. **Higher protocol dependency raises the clinical-impact index from 1.021 to 7.567 without changing cyber exposure.** The authors state that the results support comparing architectures, not calibrated estimates of real-world risk.

papers.title: Peeling the Matryoshka: Extracting Ontological Structure from Retrieval Embeddings
papers.abstract: Taxonomy construction is essential for knowledge-intensive NLP yet remains costly: clustering-based methods (i) need careful per-corpus tuning and yield unstable hierarchies, while LLM-based pipelines (ii) depend on expensive task-specific training that does not transfer across domains. We report an empirical finding that bears on both: in Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) embeddings, where each leading prefix is itself a usable, coarser vector, prefix length aligns with the coarse-to-fine granularity of gold taxonomies; shuffled- and reverse-dimension controls isolate the alignment to the learned early prefix dimensions. The pattern holds across three architecturally distinct MRL models. To test whether this regularity is usable, we introduce PEEL (Peeling Embeddings to Extract Latent ontologies): a minimal probe over these frozen embeddings, trained once with an order-embedding objective that represents hierarchy as vector containment; a minimum spanning arborescence then decodes taxonomic DAGs. Using only a concept vocabulary (no documents), PEEL recovers taxonomic DAGs with high structural fidelity on two OLLM benchmarks, transferring to a new domain with no target-edge supervision. The end-to-end OLLM pipeline, which jointly discovers concepts and induces structure from document corpora, is reported as a cross-task reference. Pre-trained retrieval embeddings encode a decodable granularity gradient; a minimal probe renders it as explicit parent-child (is-a) structure.
papers.summary: Building taxonomies is costly: clustering methods need per-corpus tuning, and LLM-based pipelines need task-specific training that does not transfer across domains. The authors find that in Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) embeddings, **the length of the embedding prefix aligns with the coarse-to-fine granularity of gold taxonomies**, a pattern that holds across three MRL models and disappears under shuffled-dimension controls. `PEEL` exploits this with a minimal order-embedding probe over frozen embeddings and decodes parent-child graphs with a minimum spanning arborescence. Using only a concept vocabulary, it recovers taxonomies with high structural fidelity on two `OLLM` benchmarks and transfers to a new domain without target supervision.

papers.title: Different Models, Shared Failures: Auditing Frozen-Encoder Pools for Medical Segmentation
papers.abstract: Average segmentation accuracy and model count do not reveal whether models fail on the same cases. We present CoFailMed, an audit of correlated failures in pretrained-encoder pools for medical segmentation. Across five 2D tasks, we evaluate 11 public pretrained encoders (a controlled sample, not a census) using frozen features and separately trained $1\times 1$ readouts with four seeds per encoder. Shared-checkpoint pairs have the highest mean per-case Dice correlation. An expanded 17-encoder analysis shows that distinct checkpoints within the same encoder family remain more correlated than cross-family pairs. At the pooled 33rd-percentile Dice threshold, four-member pools drawn from distinct encoders have mean effective sizes of 1.56-2.92, estimated from failure correlations in pools with enough failures and passes per member. In the primary pool, richer readouts and fine-tuning narrow the Dice-correlation gap between pairs sharing a checkpoint (or the DINOv2-B/S release) and all other pairs. Yet dependence between different encoders can increase, and fine-tuning does not consistently increase effective pool size at 33rd-percentile thresholds recomputed for each training recipe. A smaller between-group gap can coexist with greater dependence. Pool evaluation should therefore report absolute dependence and threshold-specific effective size alongside accuracy and nominal pool size. The CoFailMed release provides aligned per-case traces, analysis scripts and study code to reproduce the central audit results.
papers.summary: Average accuracy and model count do not show whether models in a pool fail on the same cases. `CoFailMed` audits correlated failures across 11 public pretrained encoders on five 2D medical segmentation tasks, using frozen features with simple readouts, plus an expanded 17-encoder analysis. Encoders from the same family remain more correlated than encoders from different families. **Four-member pools of distinct encoders have effective sizes of only 1.56–2.92**, and fine-tuning does not consistently increase effective pool size. The authors recommend reporting absolute dependence and effective pool size alongside accuracy.

papers.title: Implicit Assumptions About Tasks in Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Continual learning is the study of how a model accumulates knowledge from data received over time, rather than all at once. In practice, this is typically achieved by dividing a dataset into tasks and presenting them sequentially. Explanations of the resulting measurements take into account factors such as the similarity between segments, the rate at which the data changes and the order of presentation. Each of these factors can be defined in terms of the underlying data, the partition imposed on it, or the learner that encounters it. These levels do not necessarily coincide, and it is usually left implicit which level a reported quantity refers to. We separate these and identify which properties acquire a value at each level. In controlled teacher--student experiments, we demonstrate that partitioning the same underlying trajectory at different levels of granularity, changing the order of presentation, and varying the similarity structure of the underlying data all result in different measured outcomes. We review representative benchmarks to determine which of these properties are stated. Where the underlying data cannot be inspected, as in foundation models built on undisclosed pre-training corpora, its properties are inherited by the model's initial state, and the training applied on top of it can be described.
papers.summary: Continual learning research usually splits a dataset into tasks and presents them in sequence, then explains results through factors like task similarity, rate of change, and presentation order. The authors point out that each factor can be defined at three levels: the underlying data, the partition imposed on it, or the learner. Papers rarely say which level a reported quantity refers to. In controlled teacher-student experiments, they show that **re-partitioning the same underlying trajectory at different granularities, reordering it, or changing its similarity structure all change the measured outcomes**. They also review common benchmarks to see which of these properties are actually reported. For foundation models whose pre-training data is undisclosed, they argue that the data's properties carry over into the model's initial state, so only the training applied on top can be described.

papers.title: Whose Values, Which Contexts, and What Signals? Grounding Cultural Value Alignment with Re3Culture
papers.abstract: Cultural value alignment requires not only model optimization but also a well-specified target grounded in real-human evidence. Yet how such targets should be grounded in human data remains largely unexplored, raising three fundamental questions: (1) whose values should be represented? (2) where should cultural values be observed? and (3) what signals reveal underlying values? We investigate these questions through Re3Culture, a large-scale dataset linking (i) Representative communities: 700+ human participants across four cultures recruited through cultural-affiliation screening and demographic-aware sampling; (ii) Realistic scenario: culturally sensitive scenarios selected by community members, e.g., family and kinship; and (iii) Revealed value signals: 1,400+ value surveys, 20,000+ topic-grounded behavioral principles and explicit value priorities with responses for 6,000+ situated questions. Our analysis shows why these choices matter for defining the target, with three implications. First, estimating cultural values requires both community affiliation and broad internal coverage. Substituting other cultures or restricting subgroup coverage shifts value estimates. LLM simulations also disproportionately reflect particular subgroups. Second, values must be observed in concrete, community-guided situations. Abstract questionnaire profiles weakly recover situated priorities, and communities differ in which scenarios they identify as culturally value-revealing. Third, value priorities should be elicited explicitly, not learned from response preferences or bottom-line answers alone. Preferences conflate value agreement with other response-level qualities, and similar answers can be derived from different value priorities. By addressing these requirements, Re3Culture provides the first human-grounded resource that explicitly informs target definition for cultural value alignment.
papers.summary: Aligning models with cultural values requires a well-defined target grounded in real human evidence, and this work asks whose values to represent, in which contexts to observe them, and which signals reveal them. The authors build `Re3Culture`, a dataset from 700+ screened participants across four cultures, with community-chosen scenarios such as family and kinship, 1,400+ value surveys, 20,000+ behavioral principles, and explicit value priorities for 6,000+ situated questions. Their analysis shows that substituting other cultures or narrowing subgroup coverage shifts value estimates, and that LLM simulations disproportionately reflect particular subgroups. They also find that abstract questionnaire profiles poorly recover situated priorities, and that **value priorities must be elicited explicitly, because preference data conflates value agreement with other qualities of a response**.

papers.title: Accurate and Auditable ECG Classification via Visibility Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Physicians read electrocardiograms (ECGs) from waveform shape and timing, yet accurate deep-learning classifiers rarely show which waveform regions drive their predictions. We introduce LYNX-ECG, a graph neural network that represents each heartbeat as a sparse visibility graph of timestamped turning points. On CODE-Test, LYNX-ECG reaches a macro F1 score of 0.889, outperforming five baselines including the ECGFounder foundation model, while its graphs need about 14% of the storage of graphs built from every sample. Because each node maps to a specific ECG time, we can delete clinically defined waveform regions and alter beat timing to audit predictions. For conduction disorders, the clinically expected region was the strongest evidence in more than 90% of correct predictions. Bradycardia and tachycardia calls follow heart rate with conduction intervals held fixed, and atrial fibrillation calls vanish when beat-to-beat variation is removed. Sparse visibility graphs thus pair accurate ECG classification with clinically grounded, testable explanations.
papers.summary: Deep-learning electrocardiogram (ECG) classifiers are accurate but rarely show which parts of the waveform drive their predictions. `LYNX-ECG` is a graph neural network that represents each heartbeat as a sparse visibility graph of timestamped turning points, so every node maps to a specific moment in the signal. On `CODE-Test` it reaches **a macro F1 of 0.889**, beating five baselines including the `ECGFounder` foundation model, while needing about 14% of the storage of graphs built from every sample. Deleting clinically defined waveform regions and altering beat timing shows that the predictions follow clinical logic. For example, the expected region was the strongest evidence in over 90% of correct conduction-disorder predictions, and atrial fibrillation calls disappear when beat-to-beat variation is removed.

papers.title: On-device Detection of Wearer-induced NLOS on Chest-worn UWB Tags: Machine Learning, Link Indicators, or Both?
papers.abstract: Ultra-wideband (UWB) enables high-accuracy distance estimation (ranging), but performance degrades in non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions. When UWB tags are worn, the human body inevitably causes a wearer-induced NLOS (WNLOS), yielding significant errors; still, despite its relevance, WNLOS remains understudied. Moreover, WNLOS detection typically must occur on-device at the tag, requiring classification accuracy to be balanced against tight runtime and energy constraints often hard to meet with machine learning (ML) -- the dominating NLOS classification approach. Meanwhile, UWB radio link indicators (LI) offer a faster and lightweight alternative that has rarely been explored. We study existing on-device ML and LI classifiers when applied to WNLOS, and propose novel hybrid ones exploiting their complementarity. We focus on chest-worn tags and analyze 21 classifiers on a dataset of 1.5 million samples across channels, PHY settings, environments, subjects, and orientations. Results show that while all of them achieve good classification accuracy, relative performance, including ranging errors due to misclassification, depends heavily on channel and PHY configuration. Runtime and energy efficiency also vary dramatically; some techniques offer marginal accuracy gains while consuming up to 39.6x more energy. Therefore, we also introduce a recommender tool to identify optimal classifiers under user-defined constraints, publicly released with our dataset.
papers.summary: When ultra-wideband (UWB) ranging tags are worn on the chest, the wearer's body blocks the signal and causes large distance errors, a condition called wearer-induced non-line-of-sight (WNLOS) that must be detected on the tag under tight energy and runtime limits. The authors compare 21 on-device classifiers on a dataset of 1.5 million samples: machine learning (ML) models, lightweight radio link indicator (LI) methods, and new hybrids that combine the two. All of them classify reasonably well, but their relative performance depends heavily on the channel and physical-layer configuration, and **some techniques gain only marginal accuracy while using up to 39.6x more energy**. The dataset is released together with a recommender tool that picks a classifier under user-defined constraints.

papers.title: Towards Out-of-Distribution Uncertainty Quantification for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials via Pre-Training
papers.abstract: Informative uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for the practical deployment of machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), as it provides insight into their reliability across chemical space. Although numerous post-hoc uncertainty estimation methods for MLIPs have recently been proposed, most have been trained in low-data regimes, restricting their applicability to narrow domains of interest. Inspired by the emergence of foundational MLIPs, we propose pre-training uncertainty estimators on large, diverse datasets to enable broader applicability. We pre-train several UQ models on large materials science datasets to quantify the uncertainty of different MLIPs, and evaluate their performance on both in-distribution and out-of-domain (OOD) adsorption-energy predictions. We find that pre-trained uncertainty estimators provide viable zero-shot uncertainty estimates across multiple datasets, while fine-tuning consistently yields positive correlations between predicted uncertainty and prediction error, even on the most challenging datasets. These results lay the groundwork for foundational UQ models for MLIPs, ultimately facilitating their deployment in practical settings by providing users with a priori information about model reliability and applicability.
papers.summary: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) need reliable uncertainty quantification (UQ) to be used safely across chemical space, but most post-hoc uncertainty estimators are trained on small, narrow datasets. Taking a cue from foundational MLIPs, the authors pre-train several UQ models on large materials-science datasets and evaluate them on in-distribution and out-of-domain adsorption-energy predictions. The pre-trained estimators give usable zero-shot uncertainty estimates across several datasets, and **fine-tuning consistently produces positive correlation between predicted uncertainty and actual error, even on the hardest datasets**.

papers.title: What Standard Evaluations Hide About Detectors of Hijacked LLM Agents: Rare Attacks, Unseen Tools and Benchmark Transfer
papers.abstract: Detectors can flag hijacked large language model (LLM) agents from the traces of the tools they call. In the eleven evaluations we audited, attacks or anomalies make up 16% to 86% of the test samples, no evaluation varies that share, and six report no test on data from a second benchmark or source. We ask what such evaluations hide. On the AgentDrift and AgentDojo benchmarks we test trained detectors that read tool identities, behavior, call sequences, step embeddings or text, and a released LLM action monitor, AlignmentCheck, with thresholds fixed on training data or set by the monitor's released decision rule. First, at a 2% attack rate a detector with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.879 reaches a precision of 0.076, and the mix of negatives alone moves that precision between 0.039 and 0.117. Second, as tool coverage, the share of test tool calls whose tool was seen in training, falls, detector rankings cross near 50% coverage and reverse below it, because unseen tools map to inputs that training never reached. Dropout on tool inputs largely removes the reversal. Third, no detector trained on AgentDrift ranks AgentDojo traces better than chance (AUROC 0.47 to 0.52), including one that reaches 0.996 within AgentDojo. The monitor, trained on neither, reaches 0.930, but with its open backbone its released decision rule would still mostly raise false alerts at a 2% attack rate (precision 0.096). We turn these findings into a checklist for evaluating trace detectors.
papers.summary: Detectors that flag hijacked large language model (LLM) agents from their tool-call traces are usually evaluated with high, fixed attack rates and little cross-benchmark testing: the eleven audited evaluations have 16% to 86% attacks, and six never test on data from a second source. Testing trained detectors and the `AlignmentCheck` monitor on `AgentDrift` and `AgentDojo`, the authors show that at a 2% attack rate a detector with an area under the ROC curve (AUROC) of 0.879 has a precision of only 0.076. As the share of tools seen during training falls below about 50%, detector rankings reverse; dropout on tool inputs largely removes this reversal. Most strikingly, **no detector trained on `AgentDrift` beats chance on `AgentDojo` (AUROC 0.47 to 0.52)**, including one that scores 0.996 within `AgentDojo`. The monitor reaches 0.930 AUROC there but would still mostly raise false alerts at realistic attack rates. The findings are condensed into a checklist for evaluating trace detectors.

papers.title: Backpropagation-free Deep Learning for Time-Series Classification
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks for time series classification (TSC) are trained almost exclusively by error backpropagation, which imposes update locking and the weight-transport problem. Backpropagation-free learning rules such as Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA), Direct Random Target Projection (DRTP), and the diffusion-inspired NoProp relax these constraints but have been evaluated almost exclusively on 2D image benchmarks. We adapt these three learners to univariate TSC with 1D convolutional architectures and present the first systematic study of them across 112 datasets from the UCR time series archive, with one hyperparameter-optimized configuration per method. The optimized learners reach mean F1 scores of 0.76 to 0.79, below ROCKET (0.83) and InceptionTime (0.84). We propose an analysis framework that relates the per-dataset gap to InceptionTime to dataset properties and tests convolutional feature learning by replacing the flatten readout with global average pooling, measured as a difference-in-differences (DD) against a backpropagation control on the identical architecture. Intra-class temporal variability is the dataset property most consistently associated with the gap for all three learners (partial Spearman $\rho$ from $0.28$ to $0.40$). Pooling harms DFA and DRTP more than backpropagation (DD $-0.025$ and $-0.055$), consistent with near-random convolutional features, whereas NoProp tolerates pooling as backpropagation does (DD $+0.013$). Relative to backpropagation on the same architectures, DRTP reduces training floating-point operations (FLOPs) by 33% and trains faster only on series longer than about 700 time steps, DFA yields no computational reduction, and NoProp reduces peak memory by 38% at the cost of 48% longer training.
papers.summary: Backpropagation-free learning rules such as `Direct Feedback Alignment` (DFA), `Direct Random Target Projection` (DRTP), and the diffusion-inspired `NoProp` avoid update locking and the weight-transport problem, but have mostly been tested on 2D images. The authors adapt them to univariate time-series classification with 1D convolutional networks and evaluate them on 112 datasets from the `UCR` archive. The optimized learners reach **mean F1 scores of 0.76 to 0.79, below `ROCKET` (0.83) and `InceptionTime` (0.84)**, and the gap tracks how much series vary in timing within a class. A pooling ablation suggests DFA and DRTP learn near-random convolutional features while `NoProp` does not. On compute, DRTP cuts training operations by 33%, DFA saves nothing, and `NoProp` lowers peak memory by 38% but trains 48% longer.

papers.title: Exploring Bad Minima in Transfer Learning
papers.abstract: Transfer learning is a highly successful learning paradigm in deep learning which leverages knowledge from one task and applies it to another. Despite its success, the necessary conditions for knowledge transfer are unclear and require further research. In this dissertation, our aim is to understand transferability a little better by answering the following question: Does good generalization on a source task necessarily imply transferability to a related target task? We hypothesize the answer is negative, and attempt to find counterexamples via adversarial attacks on the transfer learning procedure. Over three types of adversarial attacks, our empirical results show a strong relationship between generalization on the source task and transferability. These results do not rule out generalization on the source task as a sufficient condition for successful transfer.
papers.summary: This dissertation asks whether good generalization on a source task guarantees that a model will transfer well to a related target task. The author hypothesizes that it does not and looks for counterexamples by mounting three types of adversarial attacks on the transfer-learning procedure. Contrary to the hypothesis, **the experiments show a strong relationship between source-task generalization and transferability**, so the results leave open the possibility that good source generalization is a sufficient condition for successful transfer.

papers.title: Continual Reinforcement Learning Is an Integration Problem
papers.abstract: This paper presents an opinionated set of ten desiderata intended to inform the design and evaluation of reinforcement-learning agents that learn continually throughout a continuing lifetime. We use these desiderata to examine a representative selection of existing approaches. Progress on individual desiderata is valuable, but the longer-term aim should be to integrate all ten within a single agent. To our knowledge, no published evaluation has yet provided evidence for such an integration. Likewise, the representative benchmarks we review probe different parts of this target, but separate evaluations do not establish that the corresponding properties coexist within one agent throughout a continuing lifetime. As a secondary contribution, we therefore present a compact persistent-world scenario as a playable companion to the desiderata and outline a proposed benchmark that examines a broad range of associated behavioral capabilities together within one such lifetime.
papers.summary: This position paper proposes ten desiderata for reinforcement-learning agents that keep learning throughout a single continuing lifetime, and uses them to examine a representative set of existing approaches and benchmarks. The authors argue that progress on individual desiderata is not enough, and that **no published evaluation yet shows all ten properties coexisting in one agent**. As a secondary contribution, they provide a small playable persistent-world scenario to accompany the desiderata and outline a benchmark that would test many of these capabilities together within one lifetime.

papers.title: RECAST: REconstruction of Chain-of-Thought via Auditable Structured Traces
papers.abstract: Large closed-source reasoning models expose only their final answers. The intermediate reasoning that produces those answers is hidden behind API surfaces, tool-call policies, and safety filters. Existing chain-of-thought (CoT) extraction methods assume a side channel: a visible reasoning field, a scratchpad carried through tool calls, or a signed/encrypted reasoning block. We reproduce three representative state-of-the-art extraction methods and find that, on Claude-Sonnet-5.5 accessed through the standard chat-completions interface, all three return zero CoT tokens. The failure is structural rather than a bug: the reasoning field is absent, named tool selection is rejected, free-text scratchpad arguments are filtered, and no replayable reasoning block is exposed. We therefore take a different route. We present RECAST, a reconstruction-based framework that conditions a decoder on the question and the target model's final answer, reconstructs a first-person structured rationale, cleans it, and builds SFT-ready data. To the best of our knowledge, RECAST is the first system to reconstruct CoT from frontier closed models such as Claude-Sonnet-5.5, GPT-6.1, and Gemini 3 without using hidden reasoning channels. We instantiate RECAST on Claude-Sonnet-5.5 and additionally obtain successful qualitative reconstructions on GPT-6.1 and Gemini 3 with the same answer-only protocol. The system is open-source and packaged as an agent skill: one prompt deploys it and runs the complete pipeline to produce SFT-ready CoT data. This preprint describes the system, its threat model, and a controlled artifact validation; it does not claim large-scale benchmark improvements.
papers.summary: Closed reasoning models typically expose only their final answers, and the authors find that **three reproduced state-of-the-art chain-of-thought (CoT) extraction methods return zero reasoning tokens on `Claude-Sonnet-5.5`** through the standard chat-completions interface, because the side channels they depend on are absent or filtered. `RECAST` takes a different route: instead of extracting hidden reasoning, it conditions a decoder on the question and the target model's final answer to reconstruct a first-person structured rationale, then cleans it into supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data. The pipeline is demonstrated on `Claude-Sonnet-5.5`, with qualitative reconstructions on `GPT-6.1` and `Gemini 3`, and is released open-source as an agent skill that runs end to end from a single prompt. The preprint covers the system, its threat model, and a controlled artifact validation, and explicitly does not claim large-scale benchmark gains.

papers.title: DIFFNAS: Predictor-Free Neural Architecture Search via Diffusion Model and Zero-Cost Evaluation
papers.abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has advanced the automated design of deep networks, but remains computationally expensive due to reliance on model training or performance predictors. We introduce DIFFNAS, a predictor-free NAS framework that leverages a discrete graph diffusion model guided by zero-cost performance proxies. Unlike prior diffusion-based NAS methods that require learned performance predictors, DIFFNAS conditions the generative process on training-free metrics such as MeCo and SWAP, enabling efficient architecture search with minimal computational overhead. Experiments on NAS-Bench-201 show that DIFFNAS finds the optimal architectures for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (94.37% and 73.51%) without a pretrained predictor, while reducing search cost by up to 17.5x compared to DiffusionNAG. On the MobileNetV3 search space, its accuracy is lower than that of DiffusionNAG. These results highlight the promise of diffusion models combined with zero-cost proxies for scalable and effective architecture search.
papers.summary: Neural architecture search (NAS) is expensive because it relies on training candidate models or learning performance predictors. `DIFFNAS` instead guides a discrete graph diffusion model with training-free zero-cost proxies such as `MeCo` and `SWAP`, so it needs no learned predictor. On `NAS-Bench-201` it finds the optimal architectures for `CIFAR-10` and `CIFAR-100` (94.37% and 73.51%) while **cutting search cost by up to 17.5x compared with `DiffusionNAG`**. On the `MobileNetV3` search space, however, its accuracy falls below `DiffusionNAG`.

papers.title: ElTab: Elastically Looped Tabular Transformers
papers.abstract: Tabular transformer models such as TabPFN achieve strong predictive performance but incur substantial inference costs, making them difficult to deploy in resource-constrained settings. While looped transformers reduce parameter count through weight sharing, they can lose significant predictive power when stopped early. To address this challenge, we introduce the Elastically Looped Tabular Transformer (ElTab), a single model trained to operate across different computational budgets through supervision at randomly sampled early exits. Across 30 OpenML classification datasets, a single ElTab model matches six depth-specific looped models while cutting training cost by more than half, and matches a 12-layer TabPFN-style baseline with 25% fewer inference FLOPs. These results show that elastic-depth training yields a single model that adapts to the deployment budget at hand, offering a favorable trade-off among predictive performance, storage, and computational cost.
papers.summary: Tabular transformers such as `TabPFN` predict well but are costly at inference time, and looped transformers, which save parameters by sharing weights across layers, lose accuracy when stopped early. `ElTab` (Elastically Looped Tabular Transformer) trains a single looped model with supervision at randomly sampled early exits, so it can run at whatever depth the compute budget allows. Across 30 `OpenML` classification datasets, one `ElTab` model matches six depth-specific looped models at less than half their combined training cost, and **matches a 12-layer `TabPFN`-style baseline with 25% fewer inference FLOPs**.

papers.title: Trainable Vector Quantization for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Vector Quantization (VQ) is a rapidly evolving technique for compressing Large Language Model (LLM) weights, reducing memory usage, and speeding up inference. However, extreme compression deteriorates model performance, which is challenging to recover due to the discrete nature of VQ parameters. Existing methods employ training-free approaches that are limited to layer-wise reconstruction loss minimization. To address this limitation, we propose TVQ, a novel method that leverages straight-through estimation to enable gradient descent-based optimization of vector-quantized LLMs. By reformulating VQ LLM optimization with trainable latent weights, TVQ enables arbitrary objective minimization. We constitute our approach by applying TVQ in a block-wise knowledge distillation paradigm, which balances quality and training efficiency, and propose several practical solutions to accelerate training. In experiments on modern LLMs, we demonstrate that TVQ is compatible with modern VQ schemes. As a result, TVQ achieves state-of-the-art quality in low-bit post-training quantization settings with a modest training budget and straightforward PyTorch implementation. For instance, TVQ achieves near-lossless 2-bit quantization for LLaMA2-70B with only 1% accuracy drop on popular Question-Answering benchmarks.
papers.summary: Vector quantization (VQ) compresses large language model (LLM) weights to cut memory and speed up inference. At extreme compression, however, quality drops, and the discrete codebook parameters are hard to optimize beyond layer-wise reconstruction. `TVQ` uses straight-through estimation with trainable latent weights so that vector-quantized LLMs can be optimized by gradient descent toward any objective, and applies this through block-wise knowledge distillation with several speedups. It works with modern VQ schemes and reaches state-of-the-art quality for low-bit post-training quantization on a modest training budget with a straightforward PyTorch implementation. Notably, it achieves **near-lossless 2-bit quantization of `LLaMA2-70B`, losing only about 1% accuracy on common question-answering benchmarks**.

papers.title: Overcoming the Representational Limitations of Amplitude Encoding for Quantum Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) offer a framework for learning functions from classical data, but their expressive power depends critically on how inputs are encoded into quantum states. Angle encoding can require resources that scale with the number of features, whereas amplitude encoding represents $d$ features using only $\mathcal{O}(\log_2 d)$ qubits. This compactness comes at a representational cost: normalization makes conventional amplitude encoding invariant to nonzero real rescaling of the input, up to an unobservable global phase. We show that this invariance induces an exact, architecture-independent restriction on the resulting hypothesis class. No downstream quantum circuit can distinguish inputs differing by nonzero real scaling. We develop a general condition under which deterministic preprocessing can remove this ambiguity and show that nonlinearity alone is insufficient. Based on this analysis, we introduce a fixed nonlinear feature map that provably distinguishes all real inputs under subsequent amplitude encoding, without adding trainable parameters and while retaining logarithmic qubit scaling. We evaluate the resulting QNN on three canonical classification benchmarks and a nonlinear synthetic dataset against conventional amplitude and angle encoding, as well as a classical neural network. Across these tasks, the proposed encoding consistently improves classification accuracy over both quantum encoding baselines by 21$-$44 %. Our results establish normalization-induced scale invariance as a concrete representational bottleneck of amplitude encoding and demonstrate that it can be removed while preserving a compact quantum representation, marking a step toward quantum models capable of capturing arbitrary relationships in classical data.
papers.summary: Amplitude encoding lets quantum neural networks (QNNs) represent d features with only O(log d) qubits, but its normalization step makes it blind to any nonzero real rescaling of the input. The authors prove this is an exact, architecture-independent limit: no downstream quantum circuit can tell scaled inputs apart, and adding nonlinearity alone does not fix it. They give a general condition under which deterministic preprocessing removes the ambiguity, and build a fixed nonlinear feature map that provably distinguishes all real inputs while keeping logarithmic qubit scaling and adding no trainable parameters. On three standard classification benchmarks and a synthetic dataset, **the new encoding improves accuracy over both conventional amplitude and angle encoding by 21-44%**.

papers.title: ReuScope: Auditing Data Reuse and Evaluation Sensitivity in Capsule Vision 2024
papers.abstract: We develop ReuScope, a protocol for auditing data reuse and evaluation sensitivity, using Capsule Vision 2024 as a case study. It combines measurements of data relationships with two comparisons: changing the evaluation population while holding predictions fixed, and changing training data while holding evaluation fixed. Byte-identical files cross the public training-validation boundary, and all 41 Kvasir-Capsule recordings that contribute frames occur in both partitions. Shared source recordings establish cross-split overlap; missing cross-recording patient identifiers prevent counting unique shared patients. Across ten paired seeds, removing all training rows attributed to Kvasir-Capsule, plus five rows from other sources flagged as near-matches to it, lowers public-validation balanced accuracy from 82.5% to 61.2%. Evaluating the same fitted models on the validation rows of the other sources reverses the comparison: removal improves balanced accuracy by 1.38 percentage points. The public-validation drop measures sensitivity to source removal, not an amount of leakage-induced inflation. Matched controls show that sample size and class counts alone do not explain the observed score differences. An exploratory experiment removes the training neighbors of validation frames that have close training matches, or equally many distant training rows, and yields a difference-in-differences estimate, relative to matched unflagged frames, of -0.355 percentage points in true-class probability; the paired-t interval for accuracy spans zero. The resulting procedure distinguishes observed reuse from conditional performance sensitivity and specifies the population, class support and uncertainty unit for each conclusion.
papers.summary: `ReuScope` is a protocol for auditing data reuse and evaluation sensitivity, demonstrated on the `Capsule Vision 2024` endoscopy challenge. The audit finds byte-identical files on both sides of the public training-validation split, and all 41 contributing `Kvasir-Capsule` recordings appear in both partitions. Removing the `Kvasir-Capsule`-attributed training rows **drops public-validation balanced accuracy from 82.5% to 61.2%**, yet slightly improves accuracy on the other sources' validation data. The authors stress that this drop measures sensitivity to removing a source, not the amount of leakage-induced inflation. The protocol requires each conclusion to state its population, class support, and unit of uncertainty.

papers.title: Dynamical Memory Transformer: Selective Recurrent Memories with Constant Cost Attention
papers.abstract: Transformers retain an explicit history of the sequence, allowing attention to directly retrieve past representations. However, the size of the KV-Cache and the cost of a new token increase with the context length. State Space Models compress the past into a fixed-size recurrent state, at the cost of reduced addressability. We present the Dynamical Memory Transformer (DMT), a hybrid architecture that separates sequence encoding from information reading. The encoder uses several memory units, each implemented by a dynamical system with a complex diagonal recurrent matrix. An input-dependent leak rate controls their updates. The decoder then uses attention to read and combine their outputs, without going through the token history. The formulation of the recurrence allows an associative scan with O(T ) total work and O(log T ) parallel depth, with fixed dimensions. During autoregressive inference, the recurrent states and the convolution cache remain fixed in size. We compare DMT with Mamba and Transformer on cognitive and language modeling tasks, and show its strengths and limitations: DMT achieves the best results on several cognitive tasks and language modeling performance close to that of Transformer, but remains behind Mamba in language modeling. On selective copy, DMT also shows stronger length extrapolation than Mamba and Transformer. These results demonstrate that parallel dynamical memory units are a promising mechanism for retaining and using information over sequences.
papers.summary: Transformers keep an explicit history of past tokens, so their key-value cache and per-token cost grow with context length. State space models compress the past into a fixed-size state but make it harder to address specific past information. The `Dynamical Memory Transformer` (`DMT`) is a hybrid in which several memory units, each a dynamical system with a complex diagonal recurrence and an input-dependent leak rate, encode the sequence. An attention decoder then reads these memories instead of the token history, so inference state stays fixed in size and training parallelizes through an associative scan. Compared with `Mamba` and a Transformer, `DMT` is best on several cognitive tasks and close to the Transformer on language modeling, but still behind `Mamba` there. It also **extrapolates to longer sequences better than both on selective copy**.

papers.title: Iterated Integrals as Lexical Fingerprints: Path Signature Embeddings for Lexical Similarity
papers.abstract: While sentence embeddings are primarily designed for semantic generalization, their latent geometry implicitly encodes surface-level lexical properties, a relationship that remains poorly understood. Shallow pooling methods discard word order, while deep Transformer models obscure these lexical alignments behind computational complexity and uninterpretable spaces. We propose constructing sentence embeddings via the path signature of Word2Vec trajectories, leveraging the iterated integrals of rough path theory to create representations that explicitly capture sequential and lexical structure in a geometrically tractable manner. Through extensive ablations spanning Word2Vec dimensions, signature depths, and PCA compression, we correlate embedding distances against five lexical string metrics: Levenshtein, Jaro-Winkler, word Jaccard, phoneme Levenshtein, and character TF-IDF. We reveal that while average pooling almost entirely fails to capture character-level edit distances, path signatures strongly align with them, with depth 2 signatures optimally balancing character and word-level sensitivities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the critical lexical variance is concentrated in a highly compact PCA subspace, and unlike pooling, signatures structurally preserve and quantify word order. These findings establish path signatures not as semantic generalizers, but as rigorous mathematical lenses that explicitly encode discrete lexical structures and word order, offering an interpretable alternative to opaque deep learning for lexical tracking.
papers.summary: Sentence embeddings implicitly encode surface-level lexical properties, but average pooling discards word order and deep Transformer embeddings are hard to interpret. The authors build sentence embeddings from the path signature of `Word2Vec` word trajectories, using iterated integrals from rough path theory, and compare embedding distances against five lexical string metrics, including Levenshtein, Jaro-Winkler, and word Jaccard. **Average pooling almost entirely fails to capture character-level edit distance, while path signatures align strongly with it**, with depth-2 signatures best balancing character- and word-level sensitivity. Signatures also preserve word order, and the relevant lexical variance sits in a compact PCA subspace.

papers.title: SimXAI: A Simple Drop-in Layer Increases Interaction Quality and Understanding in Conversational XAI
papers.abstract: Conversational explainable AI (ConvXAI) agents often use GUS-style architectures with separate modules for intent recognition, dialogue management, and template-based response generation. While faithful to the underlying XAI methods, these pipelines are hard to adapt and often struggle with context-dependent follow-up questions. We present SimXAI, a lightweight LLM-centric conversational layer that replaces these modules with a single tool-calling LLM that bridges access to existing XAI resources. Rather than a standalone agent, SimXAI serves as a modular interface that enables conversational access to external XAI resources. We further introduce an evaluation suite for single- and multi-turn parsing, faithfulness, and contextualization. Across existing and new datasets, SimXAI achieves strong function-selection accuracy and high faithfulness while better handling context-dependent requests. In a user study replacing only the conversational layer of TalkToModel, a representative GUS-based agent, users completed tasks more accurately and in fewer turn. Overall, SimXAI improves GUS-based design while preserving faithfulness and improving conversational quality.
papers.summary: Conversational explainable AI (ConvXAI) agents often use pipelines with separate modules for intent recognition, dialogue management, and template responses, which are hard to adapt and struggle with context-dependent follow-up questions. `SimXAI` replaces these modules with a single tool-calling LLM layer that connects to existing XAI resources, and the authors pair it with an evaluation suite for single- and multi-turn parsing, faithfulness, and contextualization. It achieves strong function-selection accuracy and high faithfulness while handling context-dependent requests better. In a user study that swapped only the conversational layer of `TalkToModel`, **users completed tasks more accurately and in fewer turns**.

papers.title: Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents
papers.abstract: Video director agents orchestrate multistage production to realize users' creative visions. Emerging research on their self-evolution advances screenplay planning effectively. However, the mutual reinforcement between directing and user interaction remains largely overlooked. Improved interaction clarifies user intent and informs workflow refinement, while more reliable execution shifts collaboration from troubleshooting to creative decisions. To this end, we introduce LIT (Learning to Interact and DirecT), a framework comprises a director agent, a simulated user, and a meta engineer. Simulated user assigns creative tasks to probe the director's weaknesses, while the meta engineer uses the task traces to revise the director's interaction and production strategy. Although this approach can address discovered interaction and production issues, it still relies on passive attribution by the meta agent. This limits its ability to adapt to broader user interaction patterns and production techniques. To solve this problem, we equip LIT with a co-evolution paradigm. The meta agent proactively learns external knowledge, thereby improving its ability to discover problems and propose solutions. The meta agent, simulated user, and director together form an evolutionary closed loop, collaboratively enhances the system's directing and interaction capabilities. Across the Test and OOD Test splits, LIT improves production and Interaction scores by 19.1% and 32.0%, respectively, relative to the initial pipeline. Controlled ablations reveal the correlation between improvements in production and interaction, where the co-evolution mechanism further encourage directing skill and interaction mode exploration.
papers.summary: Video director agents coordinate multistage video production from a user's creative brief. Prior work on self-improvement has focused on screenplay planning and largely ignored how directing and user interaction can improve each other. `LIT` (Learning to Interact and Direct) pairs a director agent with a simulated user, which assigns tasks designed to expose weaknesses, and a meta engineer, which revises the director's interaction and production strategies based on the task traces. A co-evolution loop has the meta agent proactively learn external knowledge so it can find problems and propose fixes, rather than only attributing failures after the fact. Across test and out-of-distribution splits, **`LIT` improves production scores by 19.1% and interaction scores by 32.0%** over the initial pipeline, and ablations show the two kinds of improvement are correlated.

papers.title: AI evaluators favor job applications written by certain AI models, independent of candidate quality
papers.abstract: Job applicants increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to write cover letters, while employers deploy LLMs to screen them. In this all-AI setting, we ask whether the \emph{choice of model} affects hiring outcomes independently of candidate qualifications. We introduce a multi-model auditing framework pairing eleven LLM writer agents with nine API-hosted evaluator agents across ten job descriptions and fifty candidates per job. Four findings emerge. First, we identify a generative preference hierarchy: a consistent global ranking of writer models by evaluator acceptance, in which locally hosted models are systematically disadvantaged regardless of their license, compounded by self-preference bias where evaluators favour their own outputs. Second, evaluator models differ substantially in how much bias they introduce based on applicants' tool choice, offering actionable guidance for fairer screening design. Third, this hierarchy has measurable competitive consequences: in the most adverse pairing, approximately two (1.8) out of twenty-five qualified candidates are filtered out purely due to model mismatch. Fourth, a common mechanism explains the patterns above: writer preference and self-preference trace to a combination of how much each writer leans on specific stylistic cues and how strongly evaluators, often unanimously, reward or penalise those same cues. A further check finds little evidence that an unmeasured "writer fingerprint" remains once these same features are accounted for. We discuss implications for algorithmic fairness in employment, regulation of AI-assisted screening, and the design of auditing frameworks that can be reapplied as the model landscape evolves.
papers.summary: As applicants use LLMs to write cover letters and employers use LLMs to screen them, the authors ask whether the choice of writing model affects hiring outcomes regardless of candidate quality. Their auditing framework pairs eleven writer models with nine API-hosted evaluator models across ten jobs and fifty candidates per job. They find a consistent ranking of writer models, with **locally hosted models systematically disadvantaged regardless of license**, and evaluators also favor their own outputs. In the worst pairing, about 1.8 of every 25 qualified candidates are filtered out purely because of model mismatch. Both the writer ranking and the self-preference trace back to stylistic cues that writers lean on and that evaluators, often unanimously, reward or penalize.

papers.title: Fuzzy selective state model for forecasting the dynamics of consumer preferences
papers.abstract: We consider forecasting the dynamics of consumer preferences of retail chain customers. A customer's preference is described by a triangular fuzzy number. The evolution of the preference over time is governed by a Mamba-type selective state space model whose hidden state is a triangular number, with computations carried out in M.G.~Matveev's two-component algebra of fuzzy numbers. The recurrence parameters are computed from crisp features, while the fuzzy part of the model remains linear with non-negative coefficients. We show that the state then always remains a proper triangular number and is a convex combination of past observations, so that the fuzziness of the forecast does not accumulate over time and the algebraic computations coincide with Zadeh's extension principle. On a synthetic example with competitor promotions and customer switching, a lightweight 107-parameter model reaches a mean absolute error of the forecast centre of 0.154 versus 0.163 for the constant-inertia evolution operator and 0.179 for the naive forecast, matches a crisp model of the same architecture and additionally provides a linguistically interpretable estimate of forecast vagueness. We also show how the linguistic readout of the forecast can be used to detect a permanent switch of a customer to a competitor.
papers.summary: The authors forecast how retail customers' preferences change over time, representing each preference as a triangular fuzzy number. They use a `Mamba`-type selective state space model whose hidden state is a triangular number, computed in Matveev's two-component algebra of fuzzy numbers, with recurrence parameters derived from crisp features. They prove that the state always stays a proper triangular number formed as a convex combination of past observations, so forecast vagueness does not accumulate. On a synthetic scenario with competitor promotions, a **107-parameter model reaches a mean absolute error of 0.154**, compared with 0.163 for a constant-inertia operator and 0.179 for a naive forecast, and its linguistic readout can flag customers who have switched permanently to a competitor.

papers.title: Text as an Index for Zero-Shot Cross-Domain Knowledge Tracing
papers.abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) predicts a student's next response from their history. New platforms often have question texts but no response logs for training, motivating zero-shot cross-domain KT. Existing transfer and cold-start methods use question semantics, but cross-platform semantic discrepancies limit transferability. We propose TIZSKT, which separates behavioral sequence modeling from domain-local historical evidence construction and uses text as an index rather than a directly transferable predictive representation. The Mastery-Dynamics Encoder learns correctness dynamics without question identifiers or text embeddings. Domain-Local Question Addressing builds fixed question addresses using a frozen text encoder and an unsupervised per-domain projection. The Text-Addressing Kernel uses these addresses to aggregate the current student's previous outcomes into a question-specific historical correctness summary. Cross-Segment Continuation retains access to earlier responses without extending the behavioral encoder's input sequence. Evidence-Volume Read-Out preserves the total kernel mass discarded by normalization and combines its log-compressed value with the behavioral state and historical correctness summary to predict the next response. All trainable parameters are learned from source domains; target inference uses public question texts and the current student's observed history without target-domain training. Leave-one-domain-out experiments on three public datasets show that TIZSKT achieves the highest mean AUC and accuracy among evaluated baselines on all target domains. Ablations confirm the contributions of text addressing and cross-segment continuation.
papers.summary: Knowledge tracing (KT) predicts a student's next answer from their history, but new learning platforms often have question texts and no response logs to train on. `TIZSKT` treats question text as an index for retrieving the student's own past outcomes on similar questions, rather than as a representation that transfers directly across platforms. A behavioral encoder learns correctness dynamics without question identifiers, while a frozen text encoder with a per-domain projection builds question addresses that a kernel uses to summarize relevant past correctness. In leave-one-domain-out experiments on three public datasets, it **achieves the highest mean AUC and accuracy on every target domain** without any target-domain training.

papers.title: How Much Can Tool Calls Reveal About You? Privacy Leakage from Tool-Call Traces
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents interact with external tools through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), producing tool-call traces that may expose behavioral signals about users. In this work, we systematically study the risk of user-profile inference from MCP tool-call traces, where observers infer user attributes from protocol-valid tool interactions without access to user conversations. We introduce PrivacyTrace, a benchmark containing 1,000 synthetic user profiles and 4,000 agent trajectories across four domains, generated with real MCP tools from 25 servers. Experiments with four mainstream LLM attackers show that tool-call traces enable a 26.25% attack success rate for profile inference, compared with 17.97% from prior-based guessing. Further analysis reveals that tool arguments and returned results provide the main trace-grounded evidence, while linking traces across sessions further amplifies profiling risk. These findings demonstrate that MCP tool-call traces can act as effective behavioral side channels for user profiling, motivating the development of privacy-aware mechanisms for agent-tool interactions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/AI45Lab/PrivacyTrace.
papers.summary: LLM-based agents call external tools through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (`MCP`), and the resulting tool-call traces can reveal personal attributes even to an observer who never sees the user's conversations. The authors build `PrivacyTrace`, a benchmark of 1,000 synthetic user profiles and 4,000 agent trajectories across four domains, generated with real tools from 25 MCP servers. Using four mainstream LLMs as attackers, tool-call traces give a **26.25% profile-inference success rate versus 17.97% for prior-based guessing**.
