Tool arguments and returned results carry most of the evidence, and linking traces across sessions increases the profiling risk further.

papers.title: Learning Nonlocal Interactions in Large-Scale Heterogeneous Metamaterials through Scientific Machine Learning
papers.abstract: In multiscale systems, nonlocal interactions among spatially distributed constituents can unlock collective, potentially emergent behavior irreducible to individual constituent responses. Beyond characterization, nonlocality in multiscale systems is increasingly viewed as a design element across fracture mechanics, wave physics, and disordered systems. Existing nonlocality theories provide rigorous descriptions and mechanistic insight, but often require prescribed analytic forms, range, symmetries, or periodicity. Machine learning offers a data-driven route to learn interactions, yet principled approaches that tie the network design to physical theory remain nascent. Here we present domain-decomposition attention neural operator (DANO), which learns configuration-dependent interactions in heterogeneous systems governed by linear field equations from field data alone. Through a case study in large-scale optical metasurfaces, we demonstrate DANO's full-field prediction under geometric heterogeneity and across drive conditions, small-to-large domain transfer, and multifunctional inverse design, with learned interactions validated through physics-based interrogation. As an AI-for-Science tool, it supports interaction discovery and scalable, customizable design of nonlocal multiscale systems, including virtual-reality optics.
papers.summary: Nonlocal interactions among the components of multiscale materials produce collective behavior, but existing theories usually require prescribed analytic forms, interaction ranges, or periodicity. The domain-decomposition attention neural operator (`DANO`) learns configuration-dependent interactions from field data alone, for heterogeneous systems governed by linear field equations. In a case study on large-scale optical metasurfaces, it predicts full fields under geometric variation and different drive conditions, **transfers from small to large domains**, and supports multifunctional inverse design. The learned interactions are checked against physics-based tests.

papers.title: On-Chain Behavioral Signatures for Classifying Centralized Exchange Addresses on Ethereum Using Proof-of-Reserves
papers.abstract: Centralized exchanges (CEXs) are key gateways between traditional finance and digital asset markets, yet identifying their blockchain addresses remains challenging. Existing approaches often rely on opaque attribution labels or treat exchanges as secondary classification targets, leaving generalization to unseen exchanges insufficiently examined. This study develops a classification framework using Proof-of-Reserves (PoR) disclosures, with 3,033,857 Ethereum addresses from 15 CEXs and five Non-CEX categories. We derive 58 on-chain behavioral features and evaluate LightGBM against logistic regression (LR) under a leave-one-exchange-out protocol. Across five lookback windows (30-730 days), LightGBM consistently outperformed LR, with macro PR-AUC increasing from 0.6611 to 0.9594 using the selected 17 features, compared with 0.7697 for LR at 730 days. Robustness checks showed comparable performance when feature selection and hyperparameter optimization were repeated across splits and held-out exchanges, while exchange-balanced reweighting improved macro PR-AUC. SHAP analysis and feature-group ablation identified gas behavior, ERC-20 token activity, and internal transactions as key predictive signals in the constructed dataset. These findings support interpretable CEX address screening for blockchain monitoring, while the released feature dataset enables reproducible follow-up research.
papers.summary: The authors classify Ethereum addresses belonging to centralized exchanges (CEXs), using Proof-of-Reserves (PoR) disclosures as ground truth for 3,033,857 addresses from 15 exchanges and five non-exchange categories. They derive 58 on-chain behavioral features and compare `LightGBM` with logistic regression, holding out one entire exchange at a time to test generalization to unseen exchanges. With 17 selected features and a 730-day lookback, **`LightGBM` reaches a macro PR-AUC of 0.9594 versus 0.7697 for logistic regression**. `SHAP` analysis points to gas usage, ERC-20 token activity, and internal transactions as the strongest signals, and the feature dataset is released.

papers.title: Automated Keyword Generation Using LLMs in a High-Volume Data Virtualization Service
papers.abstract: In modern data infrastructure, a data virtualization service (DVS) allows users to create many versions of source datasets for different processing tasks. For example, a multivariate or multi-modality dataset can be used for different machine learning tasks (e.g., classification, detection, segmentation, forecasting, and so on). Data selection, participation, integration, and preprocessing in different tasks result in many virtual datasets [Khan et al., SSC 2026]. Meanwhile, different users need to discover existing virtual datasets frequently and easily to avoid duplicate efforts. To enable an effective search engine in a DVS, it is desirable to automatically generate keywords for each virtual dataset. In this work, we present a solution for generating keywords for virtual datasets using large language models (LLMs). We propose five strategies for selecting different collections of text data for processing by the LLMs. We applied the five strategies to virtual datasets created in five application case studies with different source datasets. We conducted experiments with three LLM generators and two embedding techniques. The experiments show that the performances of the five strategies depend on the quality of the text descriptions. The results help us adopt a multi-strategy implementation of a new keyword generation service (KGS) as part of an extended DVS. The work demonstrates that the capability of automated keyword generation is indispensable for a high-volume DVS that is dataset-rich and frequently accessed.
papers.summary: A data virtualization service (DVS) lets users create many derived versions of source datasets, so finding existing virtual datasets requires good search keywords. The authors generate these keywords with LLMs and compare five strategies for choosing which text to feed the model, across five application case studies, three LLM generators, and two embedding techniques. They find that **which strategy works best depends on the quality of the available text descriptions**, which led them to build a multi-strategy keyword generation service into an extended DVS.

papers.title: On k-nearest-neighbor regression in metric spaces
papers.abstract: We study mean squared consistency of k-nearest-neighbor regression for metric space valued features. For a fixed feature distribution mu with atomless distance distributions, we describe how neighbor selection redistributes probability through the density of a uniformly chosen neighbor of an independent query. This gives separate conditions for the approximation error and the conditional response variance, and weakens Stone's domination condition when stronger response moments are available. In particular, when k_n tends to infinity and k_n/n tends to zero, a uniform L2(mu) bound on the selection densities suffices under a finite fourth response moment. We give a corresponding condition in terms of neighborhoods of fixed population mass and recover the Euclidean density bound. Finite global Nagata dimension gives Stone's domination. While sigma-finite Nagata dimensionality is known to ensure universal consistency of k-NN classification in complete separable spaces, we show that this is not the case for mean squared consistency with unbounded responses: we construct a space in this class on which one fixed noiseless response with all finite moments has diverging mean squared error.
papers.summary: The paper studies when k-nearest-neighbor regression is mean-squared consistent when features live in a general metric space. By analyzing how neighbor selection redistributes probability through the density of a uniformly chosen neighbor of a query point, the authors give separate conditions for approximation error and response variance, and weaken Stone's classical domination condition when the responses have higher moments. As a counterexample, they **construct a space with sigma-finite Nagata dimension where a noiseless response with all finite moments has diverging mean squared error**, even though that class of spaces guarantees universal consistency for k-NN classification.

papers.title: General-purpose foundation models surpass specialized ones on chemical property prediction tasks
papers.abstract: Foundation models (FMs) learn reusable representations from large collections of unlabeled data. In chemistry the corresponding data mainly consists of molecular structures, which are abundant, whereas experimental measurements are scarce. Chemical FMs such as ChemBERTa and MoLFormer were therefore trained on diverse molecular structures to enable fine-tuning on small experimental datasets (less than 100 datapoints in most realistic scenarios) and subsequent property prediction. At the same time, general-purpose FMs such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were trained on virtually all publicly available data, including knowledge of the humankind on molecular properties and laws governing them. Here we compare accuracies of chemical and general-purpose FMs on tasks from various areas of chemistry. Strikingly, general-purpose GPT-6 Astra outperforms the currently eligible chemical FMs on five physicochemical and quantum-chemical regression tasks when only 60 experimental datapoints are available. Only when provided 10x datapoints do the best chemical FMs reach performance of GPT-6 Astra: on 1,000 and 10,000 points they show performance on par with Astra on 60 and 1,000 points, respectively. Thus, counterintuitively, frontier general-purpose FMs are better suited for guiding chemical research in data-scarce areas than specialized chemical FMs, suggesting that learning relevant primitives (e.g. chemical structures) does not substitute training on relevant humankind knowledge.
papers.summary: Chemical foundation models such as `ChemBERTa` and `MoLFormer` are pretrained on molecular structures so they can be fine-tuned on the small experimental datasets typical in chemistry. The authors compare them against general-purpose models such as `GPT-6 Astra` and `Claude Opus 5.5` on property-prediction tasks across several areas of chemistry. With only 60 experimental datapoints, **`GPT-6 Astra` outperforms the chemical models on five physicochemical and quantum-chemical regression tasks**, and the best chemical models need roughly ten times more data to match it. The authors conclude that learning structural primitives does not replace training on accumulated human knowledge about molecular properties.

papers.title: Using Machine Learning to Measure Self-Efficacy Belief Through Learners' Interaction Traces in Technology-Enhanced Learning
papers.abstract: Self-efficacy beliefs play a critical role in learners' performance, academic choices, and, more broadly, in their future career trajectories. As Technology-Enhanced Learning (TEL) environments have demonstrated strong potential for supporting both performance and motivation, investigating self-efficacy within such environments is of particular interest, especially for implementing remedial practices as early as possible to support learners' self-efficacy beliefs. Our research aims to develop a system capable of detecting low self-efficacy based on learners' interaction traces while they solve exercises in a TEL system. In this paper, we present initial results and future perspectives on a detection approach based on data mining and machine learning techniques to identify features indicative of low self-efficacy beliefs. Because the detection of learners' self-efficacy beliefs through their use of TEL systems remains largely unexplored, this work is exploratory in nature. To this end, we conducted an experiment across two universities to collect interaction traces and self-reported measures of self-efficacy. We then developed a machine learning pipeline comprising multiple classification models, enabling us to highlight the importance of closely monitoring of learners' self-efficacy beliefs for improved prediction performance, given their highly dynamic nature during learning.
papers.summary: The goal is to detect learners with low self-efficacy, meaning low belief in their own ability, from their interaction traces while they solve exercises in a technology-enhanced learning (TEL) system, so that support can come early. The authors collected interaction logs and self-reported self-efficacy measures in an experiment at two universities, then built a machine learning pipeline with several classifiers. These exploratory results indicate that **frequent monitoring of self-efficacy improves prediction**, because the belief changes a lot during learning.

papers.title: ReX-GG: a LLM Ensemble Pipeline for Relation-extraction and Graph Generation
papers.abstract: Current LLM ensemble frameworks focus on multi-step setups with additional modules for answer ranking, often opting for token and span analysis rather than structured outputs, leading to heavyweight architectures with potential fail states along the pipeline. Faster, lighter solutions are more vulnerable to hallucination propagation and can lack output control in more complex pipelines. This paper proposes a customisable, lightweight ensemble workflow of coordinated Large Language Models that leverages JSON-structured outputs and anonymous peer-review ranking to mitigate hallucinatory outputs and single-model failure points. The pipeline is demonstrated on a relation extraction task applied to popular science articles in English, targeting four ontologically-grounded relation types (strong causation, weak causation, contrastive, and compositional), with semantic node canonicalisation and interactive, colour-coded HTML causal graphs as the final output. Performance is evaluated through an anonymous user study, achieving an average perceived accuracy of 0.778 against a human-annotated gold standard. The modular architecture supports flexible deployment across both API-based and in-house LLM setups, and the full framework is released under an open license to foster reproducibility and collaborative research.
papers.summary: `ReX-GG` is a lightweight ensemble of coordinated LLMs for extracting relations from text and building graphs. It uses JSON-structured outputs and anonymous peer-review ranking among the models to reduce hallucinations and avoid depending on any single model. Applied to English popular-science articles, it extracts four relation types (strong causation, weak causation, contrastive, and compositional), merges equivalent nodes, and produces interactive, color-coded HTML causal graphs. In an anonymous user study against a human-annotated gold standard, it reaches an **average perceived accuracy of 0.778**, and the framework works with both API-based and in-house LLMs.

papers.title: Statistical Foundations of Reinforcement Learning: A Non-Asymptotic Perspective
papers.abstract:
Reinforcement learning (RL) embodies a foundational paradigm for sequential decision-making in the face of uncertainty. The rapid growth of model complexity in emerging applications has significantly amplified the challenges of achieving data-efficient RL, particularly in sample-starved scenarios where data collection may be costly, time-consuming, or even high-stakes. Consequently, understanding and improving the data efficiency of RL algorithms has become a central problem of both fundamental theoretical interest and practical importance.
  Despite decades of research, the statistical underpinnings of RL remained remarkably underdeveloped until relatively recently, particularly in the finite-sample regimes most relevant to modern practice. Over the past few years, there has been a surge of activity advancing the frontiers of non-asymptotic statistical RL theory, drawing on ideas from high-dimensional statistics and probability, information theory, and statistical learning theory. In this monograph, we present a non-asymptotic treatment for RL based on tabular Markov decision processes, focusing on three canonical sampling mechanisms --- RL with a generative model, online RL, and offline RL --- together with two algorithmic paradigms: model-based and model-free approaches. Centered around non-asymptotic sample complexity analysis, our treatment emphasizes minimax-optimal algorithm design, particularly methods that attain statistical optimality without significant burn-in costs, as well as sharp statistical characterizations of several widely used RL algorithms. Whenever possible, we provide largely self-contained analyses together with intuitive explanations. We also briefly discuss several extensions, such as robust RL, competitive multi-agent RL, federated RL, uncertainty quantification, and RL from human feedback.
papers.summary: This monograph gives a non-asymptotic, finite-sample statistical treatment of reinforcement learning (RL) on tabular Markov decision processes. It covers three ways of collecting data (a generative model, online RL, and offline RL) and both model-based and model-free algorithms. The focus is sample complexity, with an emphasis on **minimax-optimal algorithms that avoid large burn-in costs** and sharp analyses of widely used methods, presented with largely self-contained proofs and intuitive explanations. It also briefly covers robust RL, competitive multi-agent RL, federated RL, uncertainty quantification, and RL from human feedback.

papers.title: Completeness and Cost of Retrieval Structures for Multi-Tool Requests in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: An agent that must call several tools to fulfill a request fails when the tool retriever omits any one of them, yet tool retrievers are mostly built and evaluated on queries requiring a single tool. We compare representatives of six retrieval structures (flat lexical and dense retrieval, LLM query decomposition, LLM-navigated hierarchies, server-then-tool matching, dependency graphs, and trained set-level retrievers) across two multi-tool testbeds: 345 AppWorld queries with expert dependency labels and 103 MCP-Bench tasks over 257 MCP tools. We measure completeness@k, the share of queries whose entire required tool set appears in the top k, alongside the LLM calls, tokens, and latency that each structure incurs at retrieval time. A motivating analysis on all 7,961 ToolRet queries shows that aggregate completeness mixes two regimes: completeness at 10 is .58 to .67 on single-target queries and .08 to .17 on queries with four or more targets, and the ordering of retrievers on single-target queries reverses on multi-target ones. Across the two testbeds, none of the compared structures that is untrained on the testbed and makes at most one LLM call per query completes more than 10% of AppWorld queries at k = 16. The two structures that do better incur different costs: a set-level retriever trained on 75 to 90 in-domain queries reaches .33 on AppWorld and .58 on MCP-Bench with no LLM calls, while an LLM-navigated hierarchy reaches .30 and .40 with a median of 31 to 38 LLM calls and about five minutes per query. Their failure modes also differ: the trained retriever mostly ranks the missing tools just below the cutoff, whereas the hierarchy finds the target API and stops before collecting its prerequisites. In a downstream check with the official AppWorld agent, tasks with a complete retrieved set succeeded 21 of 21 times, whereas incomplete ones succeeded 2 of 39 times.
papers.summary: An agent that needs several tools fails if the tool retriever misses even one of them, yet tool retrievers are mostly evaluated on single-tool queries. The authors compare six retrieval structures, from flat lexical and dense retrieval to LLM-navigated hierarchies, dependency graphs, and trained set-level retrievers, on `AppWorld` and `MCP-Bench`. They measure completeness@k, the share of queries whose entire required tool set appears in the top k results, together with LLM calls, tokens, and latency. No untrained structure that uses at most one LLM call completes more than 10% of `AppWorld` queries at k=16. A set-level retriever trained on 75–90 in-domain queries reaches 0.33 with no LLM calls, while an LLM-navigated hierarchy reaches 0.30 at about five minutes per query. **Tasks with a complete retrieved tool set succeeded 21 of 21 times, versus 2 of 39 when the set was incomplete.**

papers.title: Structure-Aware Skill Retrieval and Arbitration for Optimization Modeling
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can turn natural-language optimization tasks into solver-checked answers, but current agents remain brittle under narrative rewrites and often store reusable experience at the instance level. We introduce \textsc{ArchOR}, an archetype-centric skill agent that builds on \textsc{OptSkills} by adding two retrieval-focused modules. \emph{Centroid-Aware Representation Learning} (CARL) refines the ordering of cached skill representations through a low-rank prototype residual. \emph{Signature-Guided Retrieval} (S\textsuperscript{3}R) attaches open-dimensional structural signatures to skills, prioritizes candidates by weighted Jaccard overlap, and bounds semantic re-ranking to a top-$K$ set. A baseline-preserving arbitration rule determines when the structural route should replace the original selector. With the same DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone and released skill library, \textsc{ArchOR} reaches 65.00\% Micro-Avg.\ Pass@1 across five benchmarks, improving over \textsc{OptSkills} by 1.64~pp Micro-Avg.\ and 2.68~pp Macro-Avg.
papers.summary: LLM agents can turn natural-language optimization problems into answers checked by a solver, but they break when a problem is reworded and they tend to store reusable experience per instance. `ArchOR` extends the `OptSkills` agent with two retrieval modules. `CARL` refines the ordering of cached skill representations, and `S3R` attaches structural signatures to skills, ranks candidates by weighted Jaccard overlap, and limits semantic re-ranking to a top-K set. A rule decides when this structural route should replace the original skill selector. Using the same `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` backbone and skill library, it reaches **65.00% micro-averaged Pass@1 across five benchmarks**, 1.64 points above `OptSkills`.

papers.title: Variance Reduction for Decentralized Stochastic Optimization with Multiple Local Updates
papers.abstract: Multiple local updates are widely used in decentralized optimization to enhance communication efficiency, often in conjunction with stochastic gradients when exact gradient computation is costly. However, such algorithms generally converge only to a neighborhood of the optimum, whose size depends on the stepsize and the variance of gradient noise. Variance reduction has been incorporated into ADMM-based methods to achieve exact convergence in expectation, but their stepsizes typically scale inversely with both the square root of the network size and the cube of the number of local updates, leading to slow convergence as the network size or the number of local updates increases. In this paper, we propose a novel primal-dual-based decentralized optimization algorithm that integrates variance reduction with multiple local updates, with a stepsize independent of the network size and inversely proportional to the number of local updates (rather than its cube), thereby enabling significantly larger stepsizes and faster convergence. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, we establish the first linear convergence guarantee in expectation for decentralized optimization with multiple local updates under stochastic gradients in the strongly convex setting. Beyond the theoretical guarantee, the proposed method exchanges only one variable per round, halving the communication cost compared with gradient-tracking-based methods. Numerical experiments further demonstrate its advantages in convergence speed and accuracy.
papers.summary: Decentralized optimization often runs several local stochastic-gradient updates between communication rounds, but this usually converges only to a neighborhood of the optimum. Earlier variance-reduced methods based on ADMM (alternating direction method of multipliers) need stepsizes that shrink with the network size and with the cube of the number of local updates. The authors propose a primal-dual algorithm whose stepsize does not depend on network size and scales only inversely with the number of local updates. They prove what they describe as **the first linear convergence guarantee in expectation for this setting under strong convexity**. The method exchanges only one variable per round, which halves communication compared with gradient-tracking methods.

papers.title: Binary Sparse Codes: Where are we on Energy Efficient Representations?
papers.abstract: Biological neural systems achieve impressive computational capabilities under tight metabolic constraints, relying on sparse cortical representations that minimise total neural activity. This combination of efficiency and representational power has motivated growing interest in sparse coding as a computational strategy for artificial systems. Artificial models designed to produce binary sparse codes span three broad paradigms, theoretical methods grounded in efficient coding, deep learning methods trained via backpropagation, and biologically plausible methods that learn through local Hebbian rules, each yielding codes whose quality depends not only on achieving low activation density but also on preserving the informational structure of the input. The latter property, however, lacks an agreed-upon quantitative definition, leaving the field without a principled basis for comparing methods. We propose a set of metrics that formalise information preservation as similarity preservation, measuring how faithfully a binary sparse code reproduces the relational geometry of the input space, and apply this framework to compare four representative methods under matched conditions. The results reveal a consistent trade-off in which models that achieve high information preservation do so at the cost of sparsity, while models approaching the uniformity of an optimal random sparse code tend to sacrifice it. Competitive Sparse Codes, a biologically plausible approach, is the only architecture to occupy a region of near-maximal sparsity while retaining meaningful information preservation. These findings frame the simultaneous satisfaction of both factors as an open challenge for the field and provide a reusable evaluation framework for measuring progress toward it.
papers.summary: Binary sparse codes, inspired by energy-efficient representations in the brain, should be both very sparse and faithful to the structure of the input, but there is no agreed way to measure that faithfulness. The authors propose metrics that define information preservation as similarity preservation, meaning how well the code reproduces the relationships between inputs, and compare four representative methods under matched conditions. They find a consistent trade-off between sparsity and information preservation, and **only `Competitive Sparse Codes`, a biologically plausible method, achieves near-maximal sparsity while still preserving meaningful information**.

papers.title: Observable-Specific Validity Tests for Scientific AI: Controlled Approximations and Intervention Response
papers.abstract: An approximation can reproduce an energy while missing its response, or satisfy an error tolerance without being certified by a given bound. We formulate observable-specific validity records for scientific artificial intelligence (AI) that link a reduction to its reference model, error measure, tolerance, parameter domain, and transformations or interventions. Explicit displacement and velocity certificates for a singularly perturbed oscillator recover distinct convergence orders and provide sufficient validity guarantees. Exact Hubbard dimer relations resolve the different coupling domains accepted by energy and response criteria. Across 16 repeated neural fits, imposing dimensional homogeneity reduces energy scale transfer error from 52.3% to 0.0768% and raises the median fraction jointly satisfying gap and response tolerances from zero to 100%. Paired transformations verify the protected scaling relation, while a coupling crossover identifies the additional information needed for response transfer. A causal model recovers a positive intervention response beneath a strong negative observational association. For two mechanisms observed with Gaussian noise whose responses first differ at order $x^k$, we derive an exact fixed control query requirement scaling as $x^{-2k}$ and verify its full success curve numerically. Together with a 256-task evaluation interface, these results provide independently checkable tests of controlled approximation, physical transfer, and mechanism discrimination in scientific AI.
papers.summary: An approximation can reproduce one observable, such as an energy, while getting another wrong, such as the system's response. The authors propose observable-specific validity records for scientific AI that tie an approximation to its reference model, error measure, tolerance, parameter domain, and permitted interventions. They test the framework on oscillators, the Hubbard dimer, neural fits, and causal models. Across 16 repeated neural fits, **imposing dimensional homogeneity cuts energy scale-transfer error from 52.3% to 0.0768%**. They also derive an exact query requirement for distinguishing two noisy mechanisms and release a 256-task evaluation interface.

papers.title: Sensorium: An Open-Source Multimodal Data Collection and Curation Library for Embodied Surgical AI
papers.abstract: Embodied surgical AI requires reliable multimodal data, yet surgical data collection remains costly, difficult to repeat, and strongly dependent on the hardware setup. We present Sensorium, an open-source Python library for recording, processing, annotating, and curating multimodal surgical data from configurable robot and sensor streams using the Robot Operating System (ROS) and ROS2 middleware. The library combines operator-facing data acquisition, configurable processing, semantic annotation, and episodic dataset generation. We evaluate Sensorium across 1516 recordings of phantom, ex vivo, and in vivo porcine experiments involving multiple surgical tasks and sensing configurations, and report preliminary usability feedback.
papers.summary: Collecting multimodal data for embodied surgical AI is expensive, hard to repeat, and tied to specific hardware. `Sensorium` is an open-source Python library for recording, processing, annotating, and curating synchronized surgical robot and sensor streams through the Robot Operating System (`ROS` and `ROS2`), producing episodic datasets. The authors evaluated it on **1,516 recordings from phantom, ex vivo, and in vivo porcine experiments** across several surgical tasks and sensor setups, and report preliminary usability feedback.

papers.title: Optimizing Stochastic Policy Geometry for Few-Step Flow Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Few-step flow models generate samples through a handful of large denoising transitions. Applying GRPO to such models requires introducing stochasticity into the denoising transitions, and when a single transition spans a wide range of noise levels, the choice of the resulting stochastic policy becomes a major factor in optimization. Recent constructions constrain the policy to preserve the target flow coefficients, but this constraint admits a family of policies and offers no criterion for choosing among them. We introduce Geo-FSRL (Geometry-Optimized Few-Step Reinforcement Learning), built on a selection principle: at a fixed conditioning state and timestep pair, choose the admissible policy that minimizes the conditional KL divergence induced by any given nonzero velocity-output update. Within a coefficient-preserving family of isotropic Gaussian transitions, this criterion reduces to minimizing a single scalar geometry factor that determines the conditional KL for every velocity-output update. The same factor governs velocity-space Fisher information and conditional transition log-likelihood-ratio variance. We derive the unique closed-form optimizer within this family, shared across all nonzero update magnitudes and directions, with transition coefficients determined by both the source and target noise levels. Because the minimized geometry factor still varies across timesteps, we further adopt gradient-scale matching from prior work and derive closed-form policy-gradient and KL weights that normalize explicit score scales and reference-KL curvature. Geo-FSRL trains on the original few-step schedule and retains the deterministic solver at inference. Our method achieves higher final reward scores than Flow-GRPO and Flow-CPS on both image generation and video generation models under the 4-step setting. Code is available at https://github.com/ModelTC/LightX2V/tree/main/lightx2v_rl
papers.summary: Applying `GRPO`-style reinforcement learning to few-step flow models requires adding randomness to a handful of large denoising steps, and how that randomness is shaped strongly affects optimization. `Geo-FSRL` chooses, among Gaussian policies that preserve the target flow coefficients, the one that minimizes the KL divergence caused by a given update. This reduces to a single scalar geometry factor with a unique closed-form optimum. The method also adds closed-form weights for the policy gradient and the KL term, trains on the original few-step schedule, and keeps deterministic sampling at inference. It **achieves higher final reward than `Flow-GRPO` and `Flow-CPS` on both image and video generation models with 4 steps**.

papers.title: Aligning MLLMs with the Latent Structure of Human Cognition via Behavior-Derived Semantic Dimensions
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations and decision criteria align with the latent structure of human cognition. In this work, we propose a novel framework to align MLLMs with the multidimensional mental representations underlying human similarity judgements. We build on a previously established behavior-derived semantic embedding space, in which objects are represented along 66 interpretable dimensions derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out (O1O) judgements. For each triplet, we infer the most salient decision dimension and convert it into a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale. This enables MLLMs to learn both the final choice and a justification consistent with the inferred behavioral criterion. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves model consistency with human similarity judgements while retaining competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. Furthermore, using searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we observe increased representational alignment between model and human. Ultimately, our findings point to a data-driven route for incorporating human cognitive structure into MLLMs alignment. The code is available \href{https://github.com/ening-open/cogalign}{here}.
papers.summary: The authors try to bring multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) closer to how humans judge similarity between objects. They use an existing embedding space of 66 interpretable dimensions derived from 4.70 million human odd-one-out judgements. For each triplet they infer the most important dimension behind the human choice and turn it into a written rationale, so that the model learns both the answer and a human-consistent justification. Fine-tuned models **agree more with human similarity judgements while staying competitive on standard multimodal benchmarks**, and searchlight representational similarity analysis (RSA) on the fMRI `Natural Scenes Dataset` shows closer alignment with human brain activity.

papers.title: Shock Loading Accesses Reaction Pathways beyond Accelerated Thermolysis
papers.abstract: Thermolysis and shock loading can produce similar major stable products in energetic materials, despite different chemical evolution and reaction pathways. Here, we develop EMFF-MACE, a reactive machine-learning potential for C/H/N/O energetic materials, enabling thermolysis simulations of 20 materials and shock simulations of 10 on a common potential energy surface. Comparisons at matched normalized reaction progress reveal divergent chemical states and local structural environments. Mean reaction-state similarity decreases from 94.0% at 20% progress to 25.9% at trajectory endpoints, while 47.1-92.6% of shock local environments lie outside corresponding material-specific thermolysis reference domains. Structural and reaction-network analyses reveal enhanced intermolecular reorganization and additional association and rearrangement branches under shock loading, despite partially shared early decomposition chemistry. These findings show that loading history influences the structural states and subsequent reaction pathways accessed during decomposition, rather than merely the rate of thermolysis.
papers.summary: Thermal decomposition and shock loading of energetic materials can yield similar final products, but it was unclear whether shock simply speeds up thermal decomposition. The authors build `EMFF-MACE`, a reactive machine-learning potential for C/H/N/O energetic materials, and simulate thermal decomposition of 20 materials and shock loading of 10 on the same potential energy surface. Compared at matched reaction progress, **average reaction-state similarity falls from 94.0% early on to 25.9% at the end of the trajectories**, and shock produces extra intermolecular reorganization and additional reaction branches. They conclude that loading history changes which reaction pathways are taken, not just how fast decomposition happens.

papers.title: Chronos-2: A foundation model for multivariate time series forecasting
papers.abstract: Accurate forecasting with uncertainty quantification is critical in a variety of scientific applications ranging from epidemiology and economics to energy systems and earth sciences. Yet most forecasting models still need to be developed and trained separately for each domain-specific dataset. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) aim to remove this limitation and enable the application of the same model across domains through large-scale pretraining. However, most existing TSFMs treat each time series independently and therefore cannot model interactions among time series and external drivers. Here, we introduce Chronos-2, a foundation model for zero-shot forecasting that models the interactions between multivariate time series and heterogeneous covariates, which commonly arise in scientific applications. The model infers relationships among time series directly from historical context and generates probabilistic forecasts without task-specific treatment. Across various benchmarks, Chronos-2 achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on average by improving skill scores by 5.2 percentage points relative to the strongest baselines and increasing win rates by 10 percentage points. Chronos-2 is also computationally efficient, generating forecasts for 100 time series in under one second on a single mid-range GPU, 50x and 1000x faster end-to-end than the best task-specific point and probabilistic forecasters, respectively. In addition, we demonstrate its effectiveness in diverse scientific settings -- including infectious-disease forecasting, macroeconomic modeling, carbon-flux prediction, and runoff simulation -- where the model matches or surpasses specialized methods developed for each domain. These results show that a single pretrained model can capture structure shared across temporal systems.
papers.summary: Most time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast each series on its own, so they cannot capture interactions between related series or external drivers. `Chronos-2` is a pretrained zero-shot forecaster that learns these relationships between multivariate series and mixed covariates directly from historical context, and it produces probabilistic forecasts without any task-specific setup. Across benchmarks it raises skill scores by **5.2 percentage points over the strongest baselines** and win rates by 10 points. It also forecasts 100 series in under a second on a mid-range GPU, and it matches or beats specialized methods for infectious-disease, macroeconomic, carbon-flux and runoff forecasting.
papers.highlight_summary:
Most time series foundation models forecast each series on its own, so they miss interactions between related series and external drivers. `Chronos-2` is a 120M-parameter encoder-only Transformer that learns those dependencies from the historical context at inference time, so it can forecast multivariate series with covariates zero-shot.

- The architecture alternates time attention, which works within each series, with a new **group attention** layer that pools information across an arbitrary set of related targets and known or past-only covariates at each patch, and it is pretrained on synthetic multivariate data built by linking univariate generators through random instantaneous (linear/MLP) and lagged (VAR/RNN) transformations.
- On `fev-bench` (100 tasks, 68 of them multivariate), it beats the strongest foundation models (`TimesFM-2.5`/`TiRex`) by **5.2 points in MASE skill score**, and **group attention alone adds 10.7 points of win rate** over univariate inference; it also leads on the mostly univariate `Chronos-Bench-II` and `GIFT-Eval`, and has the best calibration on 23 of 24 interval metrics.
- It is efficient: it forecasts **100 series in about 0.8 s on an A10G GPU**, which is **50× and 1000× faster end-to-end** than the best task-specific point (`CatBoost`) and probabilistic (`TFT`) forecasters, and it handles contexts up to 8,192 steps and horizons up to 1,024 in a single forward pass.
- Zero-shot scientific case studies show broad transfer: it beats the operational `RespiCast` Hub-Ensemble on ARI/ILI forecasts beyond a one-week horizon, outperforms `AutoETS` on German CPI components, beats supervised `XGBoost` on `FLUXNET` carbon and energy fluxes, and cuts hierarchical coherence error on `Tourism-M` from 15.2% to 4.4% without any reconciliation.
- Zero-shot results still lag specialized models in hydrology, with a median NSE of **0.68 versus 0.90** for the domain-specific LSTM ensemble on `CAMELS-DE`, and the gap closes only after fine-tuning; the model also cannot use static metadata such as catchment attributes.

papers.title: WASABI: Wasserstein Sampling via Bridge Interpolants
papers.abstract: Sampling from Boltzmann distributions is a fundamental problem in physics, chemistry, and biology. We introduce WAsserstein SAmpling via Bridge Interpolants (WASABI), a method that trains a diffusion model to generate samples from a target Boltzmann distribution given access only to the energy function. WASABI minimizes the KL divergence between the distribution generated by its diffusion model and the Boltzmann target using Wasserstein gradient flows. This approach builds on a principle underlying classical sampling methods such as Langevin dynamics. However, applying Wasserstein gradient flows to diffusion models is challenging because the updates require the gradient of the model's own log density, which is generally intractable. We derive a practical training algorithm that avoids computing this gradient. Once trained, WASABI can generate new samples without further evaluations of the energy or its gradient. On alanine dipeptide, WASABI outperforms the best reported baselines using an estimated 3.3 times fewer energy evaluations. It also achieves competitive performance on interacting particle system benchmarks.
papers.summary: Sampling from Boltzmann distributions when only the energy function is known is a core problem in physics, chemistry and biology. `WASABI` (Wasserstein Sampling via Bridge Interpolants) trains a diffusion model to minimize the KL divergence to the target using Wasserstein gradient flows, the principle behind Langevin dynamics. Its training algorithm avoids the usually intractable gradient of the model's own log density. On `alanine dipeptide` it beats the best reported baselines with an estimated **3.3 times fewer energy evaluations**, and it is competitive on interacting particle system benchmarks.

papers.title: Robust Learning of Multi-Index Models under Logconcave Distributions via Weak Partial Learners
papers.abstract:
We develop a new algorithmic framework for learning Boolean concept classes under logconcave distributions. Our framework applies to broad families of multi-index models and yields significantly faster robust learners than were previously known in these settings. It extends to partial classification and testable learning. Consequently, we obtain improved learners for several fundamental concept classes, including functions of halfspaces and multiclass linear classifiers, under logconcave marginals.
  Our starting point is a new boosting framework based on weak partial learners. Classical boosting approaches require often-intractable distribution-free weak learners or yield weak approximation guarantees. We show instead that weak learners for partial classification, where labels may be undefined on part of the domain, suffice for strong agnostic learning. The key challenge is that boosting requires a weak learner that succeeds under conditioned distributions that are not guaranteed to be logconcave. To address this, we develop a recursive moment-based partitioning procedure: given a logconcave distribution $X$ and a conditional version $X'$, we partition the space into polynomially many convex regions so that, on most regions, the low-degree moments of $X$ and $X'$ approximately agree. On each good region, a well-behaved multi-index model correlates with a low-degree polynomial, giving a weak hypothesis. Combining these hypotheses yields the required weak learner.
  A key ingredient of our approach is an efficient method for detecting moment discrepancy. Specifically, we show how to find a low-dimensional subspace that captures any non-trivial discrepancy between $X$ and $X'$, if one exists. Our approach combines spectral analysis of moment tensors with recent progress on isoperimetry for logconcave measures. This discrepancy-finding procedure may be of independent interest.
papers.summary: The authors give a faster algorithmic framework for robustly learning Boolean concept classes, including functions of halfspaces and multiclass linear classifiers, when the input distribution is logconcave. The framework rests on a new boosting result: **weak learners for partial classification, where labels may be undefined on part of the domain, are enough for strong agnostic learning**. Boosting creates conditioned distributions that may no longer be logconcave. To handle this, a recursive moment-based partitioning splits the space into convex regions where low-degree moments approximately match, and a spectral method finds the low-dimensional subspace that captures any moment discrepancy. The framework also extends to partial classification and testable learning.

papers.title: When Is a Game a Markov Decision Process? Correspondences Between Game Theory and Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning and game theory describe the same object from two sides. Game theory says what a rational outcome of a strategic interaction is; reinforcement learning says how an agent could reach one through experience. The two literatures nevertheless keep separate vocabularies for identical structures, and the treatments that bridge them present the correspondence as analogy rather than theorem. This monograph supplies the theorems. A game is a Markov decision process in three distinct senses, and every table entry is labelled with the one that applies: a definitional identity, an exact reduction carried by a value- and solution-preserving map, or a structural analogy that fails under identifiable conditions. We take every standard class of game, from normal-form through repeated, stochastic, partially observable, extensive-form with imperfect information, Bayesian, graphical, Stackelberg, potential, coalitional, mean-field and evolutionary games, and identify for each the decision-theoretic model that reinforcement learning already studies under another name. The same treatment is applied to solution concepts: Nash equilibrium and the fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator, quantal response equilibrium and the soft Bellman operator, the Shapley value and credit assignment, Blackwell approachability and no-regret learning. We map each model class onto the training procedures sound for it and record the complexity of the associated solution problems. A final part collects the correspondences that do not hold: the non-stationarity that invalidates the independent-learner reduction, the impossibility results that forbid uncoupled convergence to Nash equilibrium, and the gap between the coarse correlated equilibria that no-regret self-play reaches and the correlated equilibria it is credited with.
papers.summary: Game theory and reinforcement learning study the same structures under different vocabularies, and bridging treatments usually present the link only as analogy. This monograph turns the correspondences into theorems and labels each one as a definitional identity, an exact value- and solution-preserving reduction, or an analogy that fails under stated conditions. It covers every standard game class, from normal-form and stochastic games to Bayesian, Stackelberg, mean-field and evolutionary games, and links solution concepts such as Nash equilibrium to Bellman fixed points and quantal response equilibrium to the soft Bellman operator. It also maps each class to the training procedures that are sound for it and records the complexity of the associated solution problems. A final part catalogs the **correspondences that break**, including non-stationarity under independent learners, impossibility results for uncoupled convergence to Nash, and the fact that no-regret self-play reaches coarse correlated equilibria rather than correlated ones.

papers.title: Prune Gradually, Adapt Sparsely: Efficient Pruning of Large Language Models at Extreme Sparsity
papers.abstract: Weight pruning can reduce the storage and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), but preserving quality at high sparsity levels remains challenging. Existing methods face a quality-cost trade-off in this regime. One-shot pruning is cheap but degrades sharply as sparsity increases, even when followed by post-pruning recovery. A growing line of work instead optimizes the mask directly from the dense model under the end-to-end objective; among these methods, [Lee et al.,2026], the recent state of the art at extreme sparsity, reaches high quality but at the cost of model-sized optimizer state and auxiliary variables. To address this gap, we propose ETAPS, which prunes gradually and adapts sparsely: it tightens a global sparsity constraint in progressive stages while training a sparse delta with a small, fixed budget. Our key observation is that gradual weight removal keeps each pruning step small enough for sparse adaptation to compensate, allowing the adapted model to provide end-to-end gradients that guide the next pruning decision without model-sized optimizer state. Across six models from 125M to 13B parameters, ETAPS achieves lower perplexity than ELSA at every evaluated sparsity from 50% to 90%, with perplexity reductions of up to 42%. ETAPS is also far cheaper: at 90% sparsity, it prunes LLaMA2-7B on a single H200, where ELSA uses four, with $5.0\times$ smaller total persistent state and 49% fewer GPU-hours. Together, our findings point to a promising direction for achieving high quality in demanding regimes such as extreme sparsity at substantially lower cost.
papers.summary: Pruning large language models (LLMs) to extreme sparsity usually means a trade-off: one-shot pruning is cheap but degrades sharply, while end-to-end mask optimization such as `ELSA` gives high quality but needs optimizer state as large as the model. `ETAPS` tightens a global sparsity constraint in gradual stages while training a small, fixed-budget sparse delta. Because each pruning step is small, the sparse adaptation can compensate for it and supply end-to-end gradients to guide the next pruning decision. Across six models from 125M to 13B parameters, it reaches lower perplexity than `ELSA` at every sparsity from 50% to 90%, with reductions of up to 42%, and it **prunes `LLaMA2-7B` to 90% sparsity on a single H200 instead of four GPUs**, using 49% fewer GPU-hours.

papers.title: When Does Test-Time Search Help World Action Models? An Empirical Audit of Candidate Selection and Simulator Integrity
papers.abstract: World-action models increasingly apply test-time scaling, spending extra inference computation on candidate selection and adaptive allocation to improve control. Such gains are credible only when candidates carry exploitable signal, nominal compute savings become real speedup, and evaluation stays reliable. We audit all three on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa with a premise-first, pre-registered methodology. On clean data, a learned value selector is 1.66 pp worse than random; a hindsight oracle gains only 1.40 pp, with an episode-level interval spanning zero; and 82% of states show identical candidate outcomes, leaving little selection headroom. Token pruning cuts per-forward FLOPs by up to 47% but yields at most a measured 1.15$\times$ end-to-end speedup on the deployed path (1.25$\times$ on a decode-excluded path), short of a 1.5$\times$ target, and our adaptive-allocation experiment is inconclusive under a power gate. We further identify and fix a silent rendering corruption whose rate rises sharply along compute-heavy planning paths while leaving the official direct-policy result unaffected, and release a detector, fix, and scripts. These findings show why test-time scaling should be audited as a chain of premises (decision signal, realized efficiency, evaluationintegrity) rather than by success rate alone. Conclusions are scoped to the tested configuration.
papers.summary: World-action models increasingly spend extra inference compute on test-time search, and this pre-registered audit on `Cosmos Policy` and `RoboCasa` checks whether the conditions that would justify it actually hold. A learned value selector does 1.66 points worse than random selection, and a hindsight oracle gains only 1.40 points, because **82% of states yield identical outcomes across candidates**. Token pruning cuts per-forward FLOPs by up to 47% but delivers at most a 1.15x end-to-end speedup. The authors also find and fix a silent rendering corruption that grows along compute-heavy planning paths, and they argue that test-time scaling should be audited for decision signal, realized efficiency and evaluation integrity rather than judged by success rate alone.

papers.title: New Lower Bounds for Private PAC Learning
papers.abstract: We study realizable PAC learning under approximate differential privacy, and give a framework for proving lower bounds on its sample complexity. We construct classes with identical VC and Littlestone dimensions but different private sample complexities at common privacy and accuracy parameters, showing that these dimensions do not determine the sample complexity, even for improper learners. To address this we introduce the Independent Class Packing (ICP) parameter, the largest total sample complexity of classes in $\mathcal{G}$ that can be packed independently into a class $\mathcal{H}$, and prove that every $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP, $(\alpha, \beta)$-PAC learner for $\mathcal{H}$, possibly improper, uses $\Omega\left(\mathrm{ICP}(\mathcal{H}, \mathcal{G})/(\alpha\varepsilon)\right)$ examples. Using this framework we prove tight lower bounds for axis-aligned rectangles, union of intervals and linear subspaces and improved lower bounds for halfspaces and convex polygons. Finally we also show that for product classes, and more generally when the same classes pack into $\mathcal{H}$ and cover its domain so that target labels can be used directly, ICP characterizes private PAC sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.
papers.summary: For realizable PAC learning under approximate differential privacy, the authors build classes with identical VC and Littlestone dimensions but different private sample complexities, which shows that **those dimensions do not determine private sample complexity**, even for improper learners. They introduce the Independent Class Packing (`ICP`) parameter and prove that any private PAC learner needs a number of samples that grows with `ICP` divided by accuracy times the privacy parameter. The framework gives tight lower bounds for axis-aligned rectangles, unions of intervals and linear subspaces, and improved bounds for halfspaces and convex polygons. For product classes, `ICP` characterizes private sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.

papers.title: ID2Pattern: Pretraining Generalizable Identity Behavior Patterns for Transaction Risk Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Large-scale behavioral pretraining offers a promising route to generalizable representations in online payment systems. However, high-cardinality identity fields such as card, device, and account IDs, though rich in behavioral signals, remain underexploited. Their continually growing vocabularies and limited semantic meaning make existing vocabulary-based and semantics-based encodings ill-suited. Their generalizable signal lies not in specific values, but in the identity behavior patterns they exhibit across a transaction sequence. Building on this insight, we propose ID2Pattern, a pretraining framework that brings these patterns into transaction foundation models. ID2Pattern first encodes identity fields with a Local Anonymous ID (LAID) tokenizer, which captures how each identity appears and recurs within the sequence, independent of its specific value. It then pretrains a multi-scale pattern codebook on unlabeled sequences, which abstracts LAID sequences into discrete behavior patterns for downstream prediction. Experiments on an industrial dataset with over 100M sequences and six public datasets show that ID2Pattern consistently outperforms strong baselines, improving industrial by 4.13% and public datasets by 8.83% on average. Notably, ID2Pattern remains equally effective even when all identity values are unseen during training, highlighting its potential to generalize to new users and markets.
papers.summary: Identity fields in payment data, such as card, device and account IDs, carry strong behavioral signal, but their vocabularies keep growing and their values have little semantic meaning, so standard encodings handle them poorly. `ID2Pattern` encodes these fields with a Local Anonymous ID (`LAID`) tokenizer that records how each identity appears and recurs within a transaction sequence, independent of its actual value. It then pretrains a multi-scale codebook that abstracts these sequences into discrete behavior patterns for downstream risk prediction. It improves on strong baselines by 4.13% on an industrial dataset of more than 100M sequences and by 8.83% on average across six public datasets, and it **stays equally effective when all identity values are unseen during training**.

papers.title: DAMI: Dual-Axis Memory Initialization for Enhanced Long-Context Retrieval in Gated Linear Attention
papers.abstract: Linear attention scales linearly with sequence length, but its finite-state memory can limit long-context retrieval. In gated linear recurrences, memory retention depends on state decay, which is shaped jointly by gate parameters A_log and dt_bias and by input activations. In controlled Gated DeltaNet (GDN) experiments, both parameters remain highly correlated with their initial values after training, highlighting the importance of initialization. Therefore, we introduce Dual-Axis Memory Initialization (DAMI), which jointly configures these parameters before training. DAMI assigns geometric timescales across heads for varied retrieval distances and a low-high-low input-sensitivity profile across layers. A small activation sample calibrates the GDN-family implementation to match both behavioral targets without adding trainable parameters. Across GDN, KDA, GDN2, Mamba-2, and RWKV-7, DAMI improves average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29 to 16.71 percentage points over the corresponding random-initialization baselines. Performance on language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval remains broadly comparable to those baselines. Our code is available at https://speedai.com/research/dami.
papers.summary: Linear attention scales linearly with sequence length, but its fixed-size memory can hurt long-context retrieval, and in `Gated DeltaNet` (`GDN`) the decay-controlling gate parameters stay highly correlated with their initial values after training. Dual-Axis Memory Initialization (`DAMI`) sets these parameters before training. It assigns geometric timescales across heads so they cover different retrieval distances, and a low-high-low input-sensitivity profile across layers, calibrated on a small activation sample without adding trainable parameters. Across `GDN`, `KDA`, `GDN2`, `Mamba-2` and `RWKV-7`, it improves `RULER`-style retrieval accuracy by **5.29 to 16.71 percentage points** over random initialization, while language modeling and commonsense reasoning stay broadly comparable.

papers.title: SecPO: Principled Adversarial Training for Prompt Injection Security
papers.abstract: Recognized as a top threat to AI agents, prompt injection allows instructions from untrusted data (email, documents, websites) to manipulate the agent's operation. The existing best-defended LLM, Meta-SecAlign, is trained with the DPO loss but still suffers from attack success rates (ASRs) approaching 100% under adaptive prompt injections. One reason is that DPO anchors the model around the undefended reference model, which is insecure. We show an idealized reference model---an injection-invariant, utility-preserving oracle---can nevertheless be approximated, as its output distribution in training is interestingly accessible. This new observation motivates a theoretically principled SecPO loss. Another Meta-SecAlign shortcoming is that it trains on weak simulated attacks. We implement an efficient adversarial training (AT) pipeline that synthesizes strong injected inputs (best@240), and train the model on them. Our AT reduces ASRs by 1.5-14.5$\times$ across three SoTA adaptive attacks, compared with Meta-SecAlign; the SecPO loss reduces them by a further 2.4-4.6$\times$ compared with using DPO loss. In agentic workflows, our SecPO + AT Qwen3.6-27B is much more secure than Meta-SecAlign: 8.8% vs. 78.8% AgentDojo ASR@800 under the AttackerMovesSecond attack. Moreover, our defended model shows no noticeable reduction in benign utility in nine benchmarks covering agentic tool calling, instruction following, science, and math. We release our $\href{//github.com/Sizhe-Chen/SecPO}{\text{code}}$, $\href{//huggingface.co/datasets/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO-trainset}{\text{training data}}$ (with optimized injections from AT), and $\href{//huggingface.co/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO}{\text{model}}$.
papers.summary: Prompt injection lets untrusted data such as emails, documents or websites hijack an AI agent, and the best existing defense, `Meta-SecAlign`, still reaches attack success rates (ASRs) near 100% under adaptive attacks. The authors argue that its `DPO` loss anchors the model to an insecure reference model. Their `SecPO` loss instead approximates an idealized reference that ignores injections while preserving utility, and they pair it with adversarial training on strong synthesized injections. Adversarial training alone cuts ASRs by 1.5-14.5x, and `SecPO` cuts them by a further 2.4-4.6x. On `AgentDojo` the defended `Qwen3.6-27B` has an **8.8% ASR versus 78.8% for `Meta-SecAlign`**, with no noticeable utility loss across nine benchmarks, and the code, training data and model are released.

papers.title: Less Loss, Fixed Weights: Logit Corrections for Forgetting
papers.abstract: When a language model is fine-tuned to follow instructions, or further pretrained on a new subject, it often gets worse at predicting standard web text. This is known as "forgetting." We ask whether this loss can be undone by simple, fixed adjustments to the model's final token predictions. Across 14 pairs of base and derived models, from 1B to 7B parameters, we fitted a fixed bonus or penalty for each token (a vocabulary bias), alone or together with a temperature. On text held out from correction fitting, the largest top-4K bias recovery estimate is under 10%, with loss conditional on the retained vocabulary. Combining the bias with a temperature recovers up to 36%. Models further pretrained on math lose the most and recover almost nothing. Finally, in a controlled simulation where a model is damaged at random, with no planted bias or temperature change, the bias-plus-temperature fix still recovers 29%. Most of the real-model loss increase stays out of reach of our restricted fits.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning or continued pretraining often makes a language model worse at predicting ordinary web text, an effect known as forgetting. Across 14 pairs of base and derived models from 1B to 7B parameters, the authors test whether fixed per-token logit biases, with or without a temperature adjustment, can undo this loss. On held-out text, the largest bias-only recovery is under 10%, and **bias plus temperature recovers at most 36%**. Models further pretrained on math lose the most and recover almost nothing, so most of the forgetting cannot be fixed by such simple output corrections.

papers.title: AutoAnalysis: An automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration
papers.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more capable and widely used, understanding when and how humans should work with these systems is becoming increasingly important. However, the empirical evidence in this space offers conflicting recommendations, which leaves individuals and organizations without clear guidance on when to combine human and AI capabilities. Existing meta-analyses can help reconcile these findings, but they require substantial manual effort and cannot readily incorporate new evidence as it emerges. To address this challenge, we introduce AutoAnalysis: an automated, self-updating meta-analysis of when humans and AI work better together, and when they work better alone. AutoAnalysis' most recent run synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers. Across this body of work, we found that, on average, human-AI combinations performed significantly better than humans alone, but they performed significantly worse than the better of humans or AI alone. These findings highlight the important distinction between improving human performance and achieving human-AI synergy and underscore the need to evaluate collaboration against both human and AI performance alone. As new studies emerge, AutoAnalysis will integrate their findings into the meta-analysis, providing cumulative evidence about when humans and AI perform better together and how human-AI performance varies across AI agents, tasks, and processes.
papers.summary: Studies of whether humans and generative AI do better together give conflicting answers, and manual meta-analyses are slow and cannot absorb new evidence as it appears. `AutoAnalysis` is an automated meta-analysis that updates itself as new studies are published, and its latest run synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers. On average, human-AI combinations beat humans alone but **perform significantly worse than the better of humans or AI alone**. The authors conclude that collaboration should be evaluated against both human-only and AI-only baselines, not just against human performance.

papers.title: TradeWar: A Benchmark for Execution-Grounded Trade Negotiation with Adaptive LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Multi-turn negotiation remains a challenging problem for large language model (LLM) agents. While LLMs can conduct natural-language dialogue, existing benchmarks predominantly assess only agreement rates, overlooking whether negotiated commitments actually create value once executed. To address this gap, we introduce TradeWar, a multi-country simulation benchmark that translates negotiation dialogues into concrete tariff and trade-share policies, enforces capacity and network constraints during settlement, and evaluates outcomes via an Economic Health Index (EHI). To solve this execution-grounded task, we propose TACTIC (Trade-aware Adaptive Consolidation and Theory-of-mind for International Commerce), an agent that iteratively refines its negotiation strategy across episodes-without updating base LLM weights-by leveraging prior experience, opponent behavior, and past settlement outcomes. Despite using zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, PromptLLM attains a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 final EHI (*100), whereas TACTIC reaches 68.8. Across 20 sequential episodes and three seeds, TACTIC's final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, compared with 65.2 for an ablation without cross-episode updates. Under technology-controls and energy-crisis shocks, TACTIC also exhibits smaller performance degradation than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM. These results indicate that CoT deliberation and interaction memory alone do not fully address delayed execution feedback, whereas settlement-grounded adaptation improves long-horizon negotiation in TradeWar.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for large language model (LLM) negotiation agents mostly count agreements without checking whether the agreed terms create value once carried out. `TradeWar` is a multi-country simulation that turns negotiation dialogues into concrete tariff and trade-share policies, settles them under capacity and network constraints, and scores the results with an Economic Health Index (`EHI`). The proposed agent, `TACTIC`, refines its strategy across episodes using prior experience, opponent behavior and past settlement outcomes, without updating model weights. A zero-shot chain-of-thought baseline reaches a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 `EHI`, while **`TACTIC` reaches 68.8 and climbs from 58.2 to 73.2 over 20 episodes**, and it degrades less under simulated technology-control and energy-crisis shocks.

papers.title: TurnTurk-GPT: Text-Based Turn-Taking Prediction for Turkish
papers.abstract: This paper presents TurnTurk-GPT, a text-based turn-taking predictor for Turkish obtained by fine-tuning a Turkish GPT-2 model with the TurnGPT objective on synthetic and real dialogue, and evaluates it on real Turkish conversation against rule baselines, a zero-shot Turkish language model and a widely used multilingual end-of-turn detector. Evaluation uses word-level decision points on unpunctuated, lower-cased text approximating the output of streaming speech recognisers, recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint folds, nested threshold selection and paired cluster bootstrap tests. TurnTurk-GPT outperforms the multilingual detector under both recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation. It outperforms the zero-shot language model only when the test speakers occur in training; on unseen speakers the two are statistically indistinguishable. Removing the suffixes of the turn-final word reduces AP by up to 44%, against 2% for a sentence-internal word, locating the Turkish end-of-turn cue in verb-final morphology. Synthetic dialogue alone yields the weakest trained model, and when a speaker pauses the zero-shot and multilingual baselines remain close to chance. The model and the evaluation protocol are publicly released.
papers.summary: `TurnTurk-GPT` predicts when a speaker's turn ends in Turkish, using text alone. It fine-tunes a Turkish `GPT-2` with the `TurnGPT` objective on synthetic and real dialogue and is evaluated on unpunctuated, lower-cased text that mimics streaming speech-recognition output. It beats a widely used multilingual end-of-turn detector, but it beats a zero-shot Turkish language model only when the test speakers were seen in training. Removing the suffixes of the turn-final word reduces average precision (AP) by up to 44%, which shows that **the Turkish end-of-turn cue lies in verb-final morphology**.

papers.title: When Does Jacobian Fine-Tuning Stabilize Neural PDE Emulators?
papers.abstract: Neural emulators of chaotic PDEs are trained on one-step prediction but deployed autoregressively, where their errors compound. Jacobian-based regularisers aim to curb this growth, but in a chaotic system part of the growth is physical and cannot be trained away. We separate the two sources of this error with a first-order decomposition. We compare the emulator's error with a counterfactual that propagates the same one-step mistakes through the solver's Jacobian, giving an amplification ratio: the factor by which the model's own dynamics amplify its errors. We study 21 configurations across four PDEs, five architectures and two model sizes (8-10k and 33k parameters), with errors measured at one Lyapunov time. Jacobian fine-tuning reduced the error by more than 10% for 1 of 34 seeds whose amplification ratio was at most 1.25, and for all 20 seeds whose ratio was at least four; for the latter, the error fell by a factor of 8 (small models) and 55 (33k models) in geometric mean over seeds. The gain approximately equals the one-step accuracy cost of fine-tuning divided by the amplification ratio. Matching the solver's Jacobian along the model's own error direction (EDJM) outperformed random directions at the same cost on 28 of 35 seeds; input-noise injection performed comparably to EDJM.
papers.summary: Neural emulators of chaotic partial differential equations (PDEs) are trained on one-step prediction but run autoregressively, so their errors compound, and part of that growth is physical chaos that training cannot remove. The authors define an amplification ratio, the factor by which the model's own dynamics amplify its errors beyond what the true solver's Jacobian would. Across 21 configurations, Jacobian fine-tuning almost never helped when the ratio was at most 1.25 but helped every seed with a ratio of at least four, **cutting error by 8x to 55x** in geometric mean. Matching the solver's Jacobian along the model's own error direction (`EDJM`) beat random directions on 28 of 35 seeds, and simple input-noise injection performed comparably.

papers.title: Asynchronous Flow Map Language Models
papers.abstract: The order in which tokens are predicted in language modeling has a profound impact on the quality of generated sequences. Autoregressive and masked diffusion models iteratively fill in tokens and can exploit such orderings across generation steps, but how to leverage an ordering for one-step parallel language modeling is unclear. We introduce asynchronous flow map language models (aFMLMs), which incorporate prediction order into one-step modeling by learning the flow maps of asynchronous flows. These flows specify an ordering through a tokenwise time schedule that controls the relative denoising progress of tokens. We formulate a general class of asynchronous flows that admit both prescribed and learned, state-adaptive schedules, show that they define valid flow maps, and develop new methods for their flow map distillation. The resulting models can generate all tokens in a single forward pass by internalizing the ordering encoded in the flow into their hidden computations. On Sudoku solving and code generation for GSM8K math word problems, aFMLM establishes new state-of-the-art one-step performance.
papers.summary: Autoregressive and masked diffusion language models exploit token ordering across generation steps, but it has been unclear how to use an ordering when generating every token in one parallel step. Asynchronous flow map language models (`aFMLMs`) learn flow maps of asynchronous flows, in which a per-token time schedule controls how far each token has been denoised. Schedules can be fixed in advance or learned from the current state, and new distillation methods let the model generate all tokens in a single forward pass. The models set **new state-of-the-art one-step results** on `Sudoku` and on code generation for `GSM8K` math word problems.

papers.title: Know When the Equation Is Wrong: Structural Uncertainty for LLM-Guided Symbolic Regression under Extrapolation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can help discover mathematical equations from data, but most LLM-guided symbolic regression methods focus on a single best equation without quantifying uncertainty over alternative functional forms. This is challenging because distinct equations can fit the observed data similarly while producing substantially different extrapolations. Our experiments on the LLM-SRBench dataset show that standard conformal intervals achieve nominal in-distribution coverage but frequently fail under extrapolation. To tackle this challenge, we introduce LLM-SR-UQ, a framework that retains competing equation structures and uses their disagreement to characterize uncertainty about the underlying functional form. We extend the standard fixed-width conformal approach to quantify structural intervals, which measure disagreement among candidate equations and identify where prediction intervals should widen. Extensive experiments show our framework substantially improves coverage attainment by incorporating structural disagreement while preserving in-distribution coverage. Our approach also shows good generalizability when it is applied to other symbolic-regression methods.
papers.summary: Methods that use large language models (LLMs) to discover equations from data usually return a single best equation, even though different equations can fit the data equally well and still extrapolate very differently. On `LLM-SRBench`, standard conformal intervals reach their nominal coverage in-distribution but **frequently fail under extrapolation**. `LLM-SR-UQ` keeps several competing equation structures and widens prediction intervals where they disagree, extending fixed-width conformal prediction with these structural intervals. This substantially improves coverage under extrapolation while keeping in-distribution coverage, and it also works with other symbolic-regression methods.

papers.title: GhostPrefix: Synchronization-Free Universal Prefix Attacks for ASR Manipulation
papers.abstract: We present GhostPrefix, the first synchronization-free universal adversarial prefix attack against automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems.
