Unlike prior audio attacks, which are typically crafted per utterance, require synchronization with the victim waveform, or target narrow objectives, GhostPrefix learns a short, reusable audio segment prepended to arbitrary live speech to exert real-time control over ASR outputs without knowledge of the future utterance or temporal alignment. A key challenge is maintaining stable adversarial effects across unknown, evolving speech contexts. GhostPrefix combines token-level losses with a novel representation-level objective for stable, input-agnostic effects. GhostPrefix supports three attack modes: (i) prompted prefix attacks for semantic steering, (ii) targeted prefix attacks for transcript hijacking, and (iii) untargeted prefix attacks for transcription degradation. To remain perceptually inconspicuous, we regularize prefixes toward benign environmental-sound distributions and improve robustness against over-the-air distortions. We evaluate GhostPrefix across 13 open-source ASR models from four families. In digital settings, it achieves average attack success rates of 97.6% for prompted steering and 93.4% for targeted hijacking, while driving word error rate to 1.18 under untargeted attacks. Over the air, it achieves success rates of 91.5% and 89.5% for prompted and targeted modes, respectively. These manipulations propagate into downstream AI-assisted pipelines, including voice assistants and AI note-taking tools, causing systematic semantic misinterpretations. GhostPrefix exposes synchronization-free universal prefixes as a practical, under-explored threat to real-world ASR and downstream applications. Artifacts and demos are available at https://ghostprefix.github.io/.
papers.summary: `GhostPrefix` attacks automatic speech recognition (ASR) with a short, reusable audio segment prepended to arbitrary live speech, with no need to know the upcoming utterance or align with it in time. It combines token-level losses with a new representation-level objective, shapes the prefix to sound like ordinary environmental noise, and hardens it against over-the-air distortion. It supports semantic steering, transcript hijacking and transcription degradation. Across 13 open-source ASR models, it reaches **97.6% success for steering and 93.4% for hijacking** in digital settings, and about 90% over the air, and the manipulations carry through to voice assistants and AI note-taking tools.

papers.title: A Neural Network Approach towards Real-Time Knot Point Density Estimates for the Nonlinear Quadrotor
papers.abstract: Spline representations provide a compact way to approximate continuous trajectories using a finite number of parameters. When approximating trajectories generated by dynamical systems, the efficiency of a spline representation depends strongly on the placement of knot points. Uniform knot distributions often lead to inefficient representations, requiring either unnecessary control points or producing poor approximations in regions where the trajectory varies rapidly. In this work we propose a learning-based method for adaptive knot placement in B-spline approximations of trajectories generated by ordinary differential equations. A neural network learns a mapping from the initial condition of the system to quantities that characterize the local variation of the resulting trajectory. These estimates are used to construct nonuniform knot distributions that approximately equidistribute a local error indicator, reducing the number of control points needed to meet a prescribed accuracy.
papers.summary: B-spline approximations of trajectories need fewer control points when their knots are concentrated where the trajectory changes quickly, but uniform knot placement ignores this. A neural network learns to map a nonlinear quadrotor's initial condition to estimates of how much the resulting trajectory varies locally. These estimates are used to build nonuniform knot distributions that spread a local error indicator roughly evenly, which **reduces the number of control points needed to reach a given accuracy**.

papers.title: CausalXRL: Explainable Reinforcement Learning through Causal Graph Reasoning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning is a powerful paradigm for training autonomous agents and has achieved impressive performance in complex environments. However, this success often comes at the cost of interpretability, diminishing trust and complicating efforts to debug and improve agent behavior. To address these challenges, we introduce CausalXRL, a novel framework for explainable reinforcement learning (XRL). A key feature of CausalXRL is its use of causal graph reasoning, which provides transparent, structured, multi-level explanations of agent decision-making. We validate CausalXRL through comprehensive case studies and a two-part evaluation: (1) a quantitative analysis of explanation fidelity and causal-structure learning efficiency in benchmark RL environments, and (2) a qualitative expert study assessing explainability in the real-time strategy (RTS) benchmark MicroRTS. The quantitative results show that CausalXRL can provide faithful explanations while efficiently learning causal structures, and the qualitative expert study suggests that participants found CausalXRL useful for inspecting high-level RTS strategies.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning agents are hard to interpret, which reduces trust and makes them harder to debug. `CausalXRL` is an explainable reinforcement learning framework that uses causal graph reasoning to give structured explanations of agent decisions at several levels. In quantitative tests on benchmark environments it **produces faithful explanations while learning causal structure efficiently**. In a qualitative expert study on the real-time strategy (RTS) benchmark `MicroRTS`, participants found it useful for inspecting high-level strategies.

papers.title: Empirical Evaluation of Quantum Kernel Methods for Classification: A Comparative Study with Classical Kernels
papers.abstract: Quantum kernel methods are the most concrete near-term proposal for quantum machine learning on classical data, yet published benchmarks disagree on whether they outperform tuned classical kernels, and the disagreement cannot be resolved from the literature because the comparisons are not protocol-controlled. We argue that the obstacle is one of measurement, not theory: the usual setup fixes the quantum feature map's data scaling while grid-searching the classical kernel's hyperparameters, recomputes nothing per fold, and reports cost in simulator time. We therefore treat the comparison itself as the object of study and impose three controls. The bandwidth is tuned on the same grid budget as the classical $\gamma$, the kernel is recomputed inside every fold from fold-fitted preprocessing, and cost is counted in hardware circuit evaluations. On top of these we run a factorial design of 324 cells in which dimensionality, training size, class separability and data structure are explicit covariates, together with four standard datasets, a shots-versus-gate-noise ablation, and a cost sweep. The dominant effect we measure is not quantum: tuning the feature map's bandwidth is worth 0.120 accuracy on synthetic data and 0.339 on real data, exceeding every quantum-classical difference we observe. Tuned quantum kernels are then statistically indistinguishable from a tuned RBF on all four real datasets. The advantage on synthetic data is confined almost entirely to data generated by the feature map itself, and it shrinks with dimensionality (-0.0045 per qubit) while growing with sample size. Finite sampling costs an order of magnitude more accuracy than gate and readout noise, and a fidelity kernel needs $5\times10^{7}$ circuits at n = 10,000. Protocol variance is thus sufficient to explain the field's contradictory conclusions.
papers.summary: Published benchmarks disagree on whether quantum kernel methods beat tuned classical kernels for classification. The authors argue this is a measurement problem, not a theoretical one. They tune the quantum feature map's bandwidth on the same grid budget as the classical kernel, recompute kernels inside every cross-validation fold, and count cost in hardware circuit evaluations, then run a 324-cell factorial design plus four standard datasets. The largest effect is not quantum at all: tuning the bandwidth is worth up to **0.339 accuracy on real data**, more than any quantum-classical gap, and tuned quantum kernels are statistically indistinguishable from a tuned `RBF` kernel on all four real datasets. Any synthetic-data advantage appears mostly on data generated by the feature map itself, and finite sampling costs an order of magnitude more accuracy than gate and readout noise.

papers.title: There Is No Free Loop: When Does Looping a Trained Model Pay for Its Inference Compute?
papers.abstract: Looping re-applies a block of layers so that each token passes through the block more than once. Adding a loop to a trained model is attractive because it leaves the parameter count, and hence the disk size, the memory footprint and the training cost unchanged. Unfortunately, every generated token pays for the loop. Re-applying m of N layers makes each token about (N+m)/N times as expensive. Loops that a model learns during large-scale pretraining justify this price, but whether loops added after pretraining justify this cost remains unclear. We compare a looped model with two simple baselines. We first compare it with the same model trained identically without the loop (equal parameters). Secondly, we compare it with the best unlooped use of the same inference floating-point operations (equal FLOPs). Across Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 models from 0.8B to 9B parameters, only the looped 0.8B model beats both baselines. At 4B and 9B, the looped model does not beat the first baseline, i.e. the same model trained without the loop. This is not because the benchmarks are too easy, since on the same benchmarks the unlooped 9B model still scores up to 13 points higher than the 4B model, showing that there is ample room for improvement. Introducing loops in an already pretrained model therefore only pays for small models with a fixed parameter budget.
papers.summary: Looping re-applies a block of layers to each token, which raises inference cost without adding parameters. The question is whether adding loops to an already pretrained model pays for that extra compute. The authors compare looped `Qwen3` and `Qwen3.5` models from 0.8B to 9B parameters against two baselines: the same model trained identically without the loop, and the best unlooped use of the same inference FLOPs. **Only the looped 0.8B model beats both baselines**, and at 4B and 9B the looped model does not even beat its unlooped counterpart. Benchmark headroom remains, since the 9B model still scores up to 13 points above the 4B one, so the authors conclude that post-hoc looping only pays off for small models under a fixed parameter budget.

papers.title: Learning Clean Generative Processes from Noisy Measurements
papers.abstract: We study how to learn a generative model of clean images using only noisy observations. Diffusion processes and their generalizations to non-Gaussian noise require posterior predictions at every noise level. We first show that it is possible to learn these predictions from independent noisy views using Noise2Noise regression, but only at or above the noise level of the training data. To learn the predictions below that level, needed to generate clean images, we impose consistency: a prediction should equal its expectation after continuing the sampling process. We derive conditions under which consistency uniquely determines the continuation to the clean image distribution and verify them for Poisson, binomial, Gamma, and negative-binomial measurements. Experiments on CIFAR-10, photon-counting microscopy, and synthetic aperture radar show that the required posterior predictions can be learned from noisy views alone and that the consistency relation repairs the continuation beyond the noise level of the data, which severely deteriorates without consistency.
papers.summary: The goal is to train a generative model of clean images when only noisy observations are available. The authors show that `Noise2Noise` regression on independent noisy views can learn the posterior predictions diffusion-style samplers need, but only at or above the noise level of the training data. To get below that level, they impose a consistency condition: a prediction must equal its expectation after the sampling process continues. They prove this condition uniquely determines the continuation to the clean distribution for Poisson, binomial, Gamma, and negative-binomial noise. Experiments on `CIFAR-10`, photon-counting microscopy, and synthetic aperture radar show that **consistency repairs generation below the data's noise level**, which degrades severely without it.

papers.title: Same Question, Different Answers: Auditing Persona-Dependent Variation in Six LLMs on Smoking-Cessation Advice
papers.abstract: Hundreds of millions of people now ask large language model (LLM) chatbots for health advice, which raises a question that is simple to pose and hard to answer: does everyone get the same advice? We audit six widely deployed LLMs from four providers on smoking cessation, a domain with codified clini- cal guidance and substantial public-health stakes, by putting the same four cessation questions to twelve user personas that differ in life stage, self-described expertise, and smoking history, for a total of 2,880 responses. What the models say depends on who appears to be asking. Every model named FDA-approved prescription cessation medications less often to teen personas than to adult personas, by 32 to 67 percentage points, and in five of six models a persona presenting health- care expertise received fewer facts than a persona presenting none. We then evaluate one deployable intervention: a short system prompt specifying a factual floor, the set of core med- ical facts every user should receive when they are relevant, while leaving tone, vocabulary, and framing free to adapt. The prompt narrows persona differences in every model, but its effect on overall fact coverage varies in both magnitude and direction across models, so a prompt validated on one system cannot be assumed to transfer to another. Two cautions frame these results. Equal mention rates are not always the correct clinical target, because prescription cessation pharmacother- apy is not recommended for minors, so a defensible factual floor must be age-aware rather than uniform. And because our personas vary on several attributes at once, we report scenario- level differences rather than isolated effects of age or expertise. We release all 2,880 responses and the analysis code.
papers.summary: The authors audit six widely deployed large language model (LLM) chatbots from four providers on smoking-cessation advice. They pose the same four questions as twelve personas that differ in life stage, expertise, and smoking history, collecting 2,880 responses. Every model mentioned FDA-approved prescription cessation medications **32 to 67 percentage points less often to teen personas** than to adult personas, and in five of six models a persona claiming healthcare expertise received fewer facts than one claiming none. A short system prompt specifying a factual floor of core facts narrowed persona gaps in every model, but its effect on overall fact coverage varied in size and direction across models, so a prompt validated on one model cannot be assumed to transfer to another.

papers.title: Near-Optimal Second-Order Convex Finite-Sum Optimization under Individual Smoothness
papers.abstract: We study the stochastic second-order oracle complexity of solving smooth convex finite-sum optimization with $n$ components. Very recently, Tsedenov \& Kovalev (2026) showed that the minimax optimal complexity under averaged smoothness and convexity is $\tilde{\Theta}(n + n^{6/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$ by establishing nearly matching upper and lower bounds. In this paper, we show that individual smoothness and convexity provably enable further acceleration, where the lower complexity bound is $\Omega(n+ n^{5/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$ under this stronger assumption. Then, by establishing a novel second-order self-bounding inequality, we design a new Taylor-corrected lazy Newton method, which can lead to a better complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n + n^{5/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$ by applying the optimal Monteiro-Svaiter acceleration, matching our lower bound up to only logarithmic factors.
papers.summary: This work studies the stochastic second-order oracle complexity of smooth convex finite-sum optimization with n components. Under individual (per-component) smoothness and convexity, rather than the averaged assumption used in prior work, the authors prove a lower bound of Ω(n + n^{5/7} ε^{-2/7}). They then design a Taylor-corrected lazy Newton method, based on a new second-order self-bounding inequality and Monteiro-Svaiter acceleration, that **matches this lower bound up to logarithmic factors**, which shows that the stronger assumption provably enables faster rates.

papers.title: A richness-sensitive Acoustic Biodiversity Index from species-level detections: classifier benchmarking, false-positive control and validation against standard soundscape indices in an African savanna and an urban zoo
papers.abstract: Acoustic indices are widely used as rapid proxies for biodiversity, but they summarise the distribution of sound energy rather than the species producing it and often track richness poorly. We revise and test an Acoustic Biodiversity Index (ABI) built from species-level detections. Its primary form, ABI_E, is Shannon diversity of detections normalised by the regional species pool expected at the site and season (H / ln S_ref); temporal stability T is reported as a separate component. We first benchmarked four classifiers on a strongly labelled tropical dataset (1,216 calls, 24 classes) with recording-grouped cross-validation. BirdNET embeddings + logistic regression performed best (macro-F1 0.750 +/- 0.029), and random frame-level splits inflated accuracy from 0.41 to 0.70. We then applied BirdNET v2.4 with a location and season filter to recordings from a riverine savanna in the Zambezi Valley, Zimbabwe, and from three habitats at Emirates Park Zoo and Resort, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. A stricter post-hoc location filter removed 517 high-confidence detections of 9 implausible species, all at the zoo. After diel-matched rarefaction to equal effort (6 h), the savanna site held 21 species (Hill number 1D = 9.83; ABI_E = 0.38) against 1.3-13 species (ABI_E = 0.03-0.21) at the zoo sites. Across 149 recorded hours, ABI_E correlated strongly with richness (Spearman rho = 0.93), whereas six standard indices did not (best: ACI, rho = 0.48). The stability term was lower at the savanna site (0.39) than at the zoo (0.65-0.67), showing that it penalises the natural diel cycle of bird activity. Species-level indices with explicit false-positive control, a declared regional reference pool and effort standardisation provide a more interpretable biodiversity indicator than energy-based acoustic indices.
papers.summary: Standard acoustic indices summarize sound energy rather than the species producing it, so they often track species richness poorly. The authors revise an Acoustic Biodiversity Index (`ABI`) built from species-level detections, defined as Shannon diversity normalized by the expected regional species pool. They benchmark classifiers, finding that `BirdNET` embeddings with logistic regression perform best, and apply `BirdNET` with location filtering to recordings from a Zimbabwean savanna and an Abu Dhabi zoo. Across 149 recorded hours, the index **correlated strongly with richness (Spearman rho = 0.93)**, while six standard soundscape indices reached at best 0.48. A stricter location filter removed 517 high-confidence but implausible detections at the zoo.

papers.title: Exact Theory and Optimal Stepsizes for Stochastic Gradient Descent in Smooth Convex Minimization
papers.abstract: This work considers the design of stepsize schedules for stochastic gradient descent in smooth convex optimization. Throughout, we assume that gradient noise is conditionally zero-mean with bounded variance. Among problems with dimension $d\geq N+1$, we provide an exact worst-case analysis of the expected suboptimality of stochastic gradient descent's final iterate. Our analysis applies to any (potentially nonconstant) schedule of $N$ stepsizes in $[0,1.5]^N$. Here, exact means that we provide a matching objective function and noise distributions where our guarantee is attained. Whenever the variance bound is at least $\Omega(1/\sqrt{N})$, our theory provides the minimax optimal stepsize schedule for stochastic gradient descent and proves its uniqueness. These optimal stepsizes monotonically decrease, ruling out any accelerations in expected final suboptimality from fixed fractal schedules observed in the deterministic case.
papers.summary: The authors give an exact worst-case analysis of the expected suboptimality of the final iterate of stochastic gradient descent on smooth convex problems with bounded-variance gradient noise. The analysis covers any schedule of N stepsizes in [0, 1.5], and it is exact in the sense that a matching objective function and noise distribution attain the bound. When the noise variance is at least of order 1/√N, the theory yields the unique minimax-optimal stepsize schedule. **The optimal stepsizes decrease monotonically**, which rules out the accelerations that fractal stepsize schedules achieve in the deterministic setting.

papers.title: CRoS: Causality Reward on Scrambled CoTs Improves Accuracy and Reasoning Faithfulness
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become the standard method for training language models to reason. However, RLVR typically relies solely on outcome correctness, which does not guarantee that the CoT causally contributes to the final answer. Without this connection, outcome rewards may fail to reinforce high-quality reasoning. Existing causality metrics assess CoT causality by perturbing the CoT, such as deleting reasoning steps or injecting errors, and measuring changes in the final answer. However, these perturbations inevitably alter information in each step. Consequently, high causality scores may reflect sensitivity to information changes introduced by perturbation rather than true causality. Such confounding effects further induce undesirable reasoning behaviors when these metrics are used as training rewards, including generating less informative CoTs and reducing exploration and self-correction. To address this problem, we propose CRoS (Causality Reward on Scrambled CoTs), a novel CoT causality metric that perturbs the order of reasoning steps without altering content, thereby preserving information within each step. On Reasoning Gym with Gemma-3-4B, CRoS outperforms existing causality and outcome rewards in out-of-domain accuracy, CoT quality, and CoT faithfulness. Specifically, CRoS achieves 46.8% accuracy on five unseen logic and games datasets, outperforming the strongest baseline (43.8%). It also achieves better CoT quality, consistently outperforming baselines in CoT-Pass@K from K=1 to 128, averaging 43.4% vs. 41.4%. For CoT faithfulness, CRoS achieves a hint acknowledgment score of 34.0% vs. 20.2%.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) rewards only correct final answers, so it does not ensure that the chain of thought (CoT) actually drives the answer. Existing causality metrics perturb the CoT by deleting steps or injecting errors, which changes the information it contains and confounds the measurement. `CRoS` (Causality Reward on Scrambled CoTs) instead shuffles the order of reasoning steps without changing their content and uses the resulting causality score as a training reward. On `Reasoning Gym` with `Gemma-3-4B`, it reaches **46.8% out-of-domain accuracy versus 43.8%** for the strongest baseline, along with higher `CoT-Pass@K` and a hint-acknowledgment faithfulness score of 34.0% versus 20.2%.

papers.title: PersonaChatBench: Evaluating Chat Assistants with Diverse Simulated Users
papers.abstract: Conversational assistants are expected to help people with diverse backgrounds, preferences, and communication styles. Yet evaluations centered on a single cooperative user provide limited insight into how reliably an assistant serves users with different personas. We introduce PersonaChatBench, a framework for evaluating task competence and responsiveness to diverse user needs. PersonaChatBench pairs the same underlying task with multiple simulated users, each guided by a private persona card that specifies distinct needs, preferences, and interaction behaviors. By holding the task fixed while varying the user, the framework examines how assistant performance changes across user conditions. We evaluate 20 language models across six domains, separately assessing native task outcomes, fulfillment of expressed persona needs, and simulator fidelity. Our results show that task performance and need fulfillment vary across personas and domains. Strong task performance does not necessarily translate into satisfying individual needs, and models' relative strengths in meeting those needs are not consistent across domains. PersonaChatBench makes these differences measurable, revealing gaps obscured by aggregate scores and helping identify which users an assistant serves well and where adaptation is needed. It provides a basis for evaluating consistency across users and guiding the development of assistants that better accommodate diverse needs in everyday applications.
papers.summary: Most chat-assistant evaluations simulate a single cooperative user, which says little about how reliably an assistant serves people with different needs and communication styles. `PersonaChatBench` pairs each fixed task with multiple simulated users, each driven by a private persona card, and separately scores task outcomes, fulfillment of persona needs, and simulator fidelity. Evaluating 20 language models across six domains, the authors find that **strong task performance does not necessarily translate into meeting individual users' needs**, and that models' relative strengths at meeting those needs shift across domains, which aggregate scores hide.

papers.title: The Knowledge Layer Model (KLM): Evidence-Visible AI Output, Routing Diagnostics, and Negative Results
papers.abstract: AI answers require more than apparent correctness: reviewers need to inspect their recorded basis. We introduce the Knowledge Layer Model (KLM), an open, implementation-neutral specification for inference records with versioned epistemic assessments, evidence relations, and explicit unknowns. SEDIM, the knowledge and evidence architecture of Nage AI OS, is a reference implementation. We reference KLM v0.3 (repository tag v0.3.0). Empirical material consists of separate internal experiments, not end-to-end validation. A historical platform-domain routing benchmark reports 137/150 classifications across 15 classes (91.3%; nominal 95% Wilson interval 85.7-94.9%); the numerator is recovered from a rounded summary, and historical example membership is unverified. A native-model weight-path configuration yielded 0/15 successful answers in a corrected two-source test. A capacity-growth comparison could not establish a reliable effect because of a defective legacy scorer and missing original outputs. Lexical and scoped diagnostics each yielded AUC 0.008 for silent-versus-contradicted examples, below the registered minimum of 0.65. Legacy packing lost gold-containing text in 118/221 selected cases; repaired packing retained it in 221/221. These measure text presence, not answer quality. Python and TypeScript verifiers reportedly agreed on six checks per synthetic fixture; a separate production disclosure was not accepted. Restoration, re-derivation, human-rubric support, boundary isolation, and bounded-response evaluations remain proposed. Findings are internal and author-reported; historical observations are distinguished from later reproductions. Evidence visibility does not establish correctness, causal reliance, security, or regulatory compliance. Independent replication and a complete public audit package remain future work.
papers.summary: The Knowledge Layer Model (`KLM`) is an open, implementation-neutral specification for AI inference records with versioned epistemic assessments, evidence relations, and explicit unknowns, with `SEDIM` as a reference implementation. The empirical material consists of separate internal experiments rather than end-to-end validation. A historical routing benchmark reports 91.3% classification accuracy, but several other results are negative: lexical and scoped diagnostics reached an **AUC of 0.008**, far below the registered minimum of 0.65, and a capacity-growth comparison was inconclusive. The authors state that evidence visibility does not establish correctness and that independent replication is still needed.

papers.title: RAMA: Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Agent Routing with Episodic Memory for LEO Satellite Networks
papers.abstract: Low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks present a challenging routing environment due to rapidly changing topology, traffic, and link conditions. Existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) routing methods typically rely on current observations and information encoded in network weights, limiting their ability to exploit successful past experiences. We propose RAMA, a retrieval-augmented multi-agent DRL framework with Approximate Information State (AIS), in which each satellite combines its local observation, recent routing history, neighboring state information, and retrieved entries from a per-satellite episodic memory. Retrieved experiences are integrated through a Transformer-based decision network trained with AIS-based auxiliary objectives. With weights frozen in a 140-satellite Kepler constellation, RAMA reduces mean end-to-end latency by 13.4% and 99th-percentile latency by 66.7% relative to the state-of-theart double deep Q-network (DDQN) routing method, mainly by avoiding long detours. Updated online, RAMA remains stable while DDQN degrades. On the 1,584-satellite Starlink shell 1, the reduction in mean latency grows to 93.2%, and updating RAMA online lowers its mean latency by a further 25.5%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented memory for scalable decentralized routing in LEO satellite networks.
papers.summary: Routing in low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks is hard because topology, traffic, and link conditions change rapidly, and existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) routers rely only on current observations and their network weights. `RAMA` is a multi-agent DRL framework in which each satellite combines its local observation, recent routing history, and neighbor state with entries retrieved from its own episodic memory. A Transformer decision network trained with Approximate Information State (AIS) auxiliary objectives integrates these inputs. In a 140-satellite constellation, RAMA cuts mean latency by 13.4% and 99th-percentile latency by 66.7% versus a `DDQN` baseline, and on the 1,584-satellite `Starlink` shell 1 the **mean-latency reduction grows to 93.2%**.

papers.title: Differentially Private Synthetic Data from Sliced Chebyshev Moments
papers.abstract:
Research on practical differentially private (DP) synthetic data has largely focused on methods that approximately preserve low-dimensional marginals of a target distribution, and can thus only hope to preserve higher-dimensional, global structure as a lucky by-product. At the same time, existing methods that target global accuracy guarantees pay a price exponential in the data dimension, $d$.
  In this work, we address this ``curse of dimensionality'' by presenting a new DP synthetic data algorithm, SPLICE, that comes with a compelling global distributional guarantee, even in high-dimensions, and moreover, is practically state-of-the-art. Our algorithm is based on measuring noisy sliced Chebyshev polynomial moments of the target distribution and fitting a distribution to match, a twist on recent polynomial methods for 1-D synthetic data.
  We prove that, given a dataset of $n$ examples, SPLICE returns a private distribution with Sliced Wasserstein-1 distance $\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{n})$ from the target, for constant privacy parameters. Notably, this bound is independent of the data dimension, $d$. Along the way, we prove a moment matching result of independent interest: for a distribution on the unit ball, matching the first $O(1/\alpha)$ Chebyshev moments along $\tilde{O}(d/\alpha^2)$ random directions guarantees $\alpha$ Sliced Wasserstein error.
  Finally, we provide a practical implementation of the algorithm that borrows tools from the tensor decomposition literature and achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to prior DP synthetic data methods on an extensive benchmark.
papers.summary: Practical differentially private (DP) synthetic data methods usually preserve only low-dimensional marginals, while methods with global accuracy guarantees pay a cost exponential in the data dimension. `SPLICE` measures noisy sliced Chebyshev polynomial moments of the data along random directions and fits a distribution that matches them. The authors prove that it achieves **Sliced Wasserstein-1 error of Õ(1/√n), independent of the dimension d**, supported by a new moment-matching result. A practical implementation that uses tensor decomposition tools reaches state-of-the-art performance on an extensive DP synthetic data benchmark.

papers.title: RangeSWA: Training-Free Length Extrapolation for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models show promising potential in text generation tasks, but are prone to problems such as text repetition, semantic drift, and generation quality degradation when the generation length exceeds the training length. To address these challenges, we propose RangeSWA, a training-free length extrapolation method. The method combines local sliding-window attention, remote block summaries, and dynamic content retrieval to preserve local details and support long-range context access. In addition, generation degradation caused by length extrapolation is mitigated through positional remapping, conditioning attention correction, and denoising-stage-adaptive window scheduling. We conducted experiments on multiple continuous diffusion language models, and the results show that RangeSWA can effectively reduce generative perplexity and text repetition rates in long-text generation.
papers.summary: Continuous diffusion language models suffer repetition, semantic drift, and quality loss when generating text longer than their training length. `RangeSWA` is a training-free fix that combines local sliding-window attention, summaries of distant blocks, and dynamic content retrieval. It adds positional remapping, an attention correction for conditioning, and window sizes that adapt to the denoising stage. Across several continuous diffusion language models, it **reduces generative perplexity and repetition rates** in long-text generation.

papers.title: Cost-Aware Stopping for Freeze-Thaw Bayesian Optimization: When Does One-Step Lookahead Suffice?
papers.abstract: Freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization (BO) evaluates candidates in resumable increments but usually stops at a budget or convergence test. We maximize a budget-free utility, the best observed score minus a cost per increment, with a one-step lookahead: advance the candidate with the largest expected improvement (EI) under a fixed surrogate, and stop once no EI exceeds the cost. This rule, EI stopping, never falls below stopping immediately in expected utility, yet it can stop too early. We construct a certificate, a lower bound on the value of two-step lookahead, that proves such a stop premature, and repeating this correction never lowers expected utility under the surrogate. Under the surrogate, EI stops are premature on average at low costs and lose little at high costs. On three hyperparameter optimization benchmarks, a pre-registered test finds EI stopping noninferior to the correction in most high-cost settings, while the correction gains at low costs on two of the three; more information sharing in the surrogate raises EI stopping's utility. On the surrogates of two published methods, EI stopping trades lower scores for fewer training increments. EI stopping is a simple cost-aware reference whose utility depends on the surrogate.
papers.summary: Freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization (BO) trains candidates in resumable increments but usually stops at a fixed budget or a convergence test. The authors maximize a budget-free utility, the best observed score minus a cost per increment, with a one-step lookahead rule called EI stopping: advance the candidate with the largest expected improvement (EI) and stop once no EI exceeds the cost. They prove this rule can stop prematurely and construct a two-step lookahead certificate that corrects it without ever lowering expected utility. On three hyperparameter optimization benchmarks, **EI stopping is noninferior in most high-cost settings**, while the correction helps at low costs on two of the three.

papers.title: CausalWAM: Learning the Causes of Actions in World Action Models
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) learn latent variables from observations and use these to both predict the evolution of the scene and to generate actions. The prediction has to be of the whole scene, whereas only a portion of the scene causes actions. WAMs fitted to demonstrations do not, in general, guarantee that they will generate actions solely from the latent causes of the demonstrated actions (the action-relevant latent variables), as the model could just as well learn to imitate in this way whilst entangling the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance variables. We therefore separate out what causes action from what prediction depends on. We prove that under a sparsity constraint the latent variables used to generate actions are an invertible function of the action-relevant latent variables alone and the true structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables. This requires neither sufficient temporal dependence nor any assumptions on how the unobserved regimes evolve and holds even when the action-relevant latent variables are statistically dependent on the rest. We therefore propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which incorporates the constraint into a pretrained WAM by adding a sparse routing path to its action head, with the world modeling objective remaining unchanged. Experiments on both synthetic data and real-world robots validate the theory as well as showcase the improved efficiency in closed-loop success.
papers.summary: World action models (WAMs) learn latents that both predict the whole scene and generate actions, but nothing ensures that actions depend only on the action-relevant part of the scene rather than on entangled nuisance factors. The authors prove that under a sparsity constraint, the latents used for actions are an invertible function of the true action-relevant latents alone. This **identifiability result holds even when those latents are statistically dependent on the rest** and requires no assumptions about temporal dynamics. `CWAM` (Causal WAM) adds this constraint to a pretrained WAM through a sparse routing path in its action head, and it improves closed-loop success on synthetic data and real robots.
papers.highlight_summary:
World action models (WAMs) learn latents that must describe the whole scene for video prediction, but nothing forces their action heads to rely only on the variables that actually cause actions, so nuisance factors like a tablecloth can leak into control. The authors prove that a sparsity constraint on the latent-to-action dependency structure identifies the action-relevant latent block, and they build this into `Cosmos 3` as a sparse routing path to the action head, leaving the world-modeling objective unchanged.

- Without sparsity, fitting the demonstrations only guarantees that each action dimension depends on *at least* as many latents as the true mechanism; with a support-sparsity constraint, the dependency pattern is identified up to permutation, and the compact action state becomes an invertible function of the true action-relevant latents alone, with no need for interventions, temporal dependence, or assumptions on hidden regimes.
- `CWAM` adds an attention router from action hidden states over clean vision and task tokens, gated into the action head, plus a top-k attention-mass penalty (`λ = 0.01`) as a token-level surrogate for the sparsity constraint, while keeping the standard rectified-flow video-and-action co-training loss.
- On synthetic data with 20 latents, of which 4 drive the action, the sparse-head selection decodes the action-relevant latents with **R² = 0.996**, and its excess nuisance information is near zero (**0.039**, versus **0.646** for the dense readout and **0.316** for a standard VAE).
- Against a matched `Cosmos 3` baseline, `CWAM` improves closed-loop success in every `RoboCasa365` skill family (**nearly 2× average success** over 17 tasks), in every `LIBERO` suite (largest gain on `LIBERO-Goal`), and on a real Franka cube-stacking task, where it succeeds in a majority of 50 trials versus fewer than half for the baseline.
- Restricting the action queries to the routed tokens alone keeps **60.3%** success, versus 71.3% with full context and **24.5%** with an equal number of random tokens, but this test covers only CWAM's four best tasks, the deployed policy still keeps the dense visual path, and the theory does not identify individual latents, only the action-relevant block.

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Impact of Plasticity Loss on Reinforcement Learning in Stochastic Environments
papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful framework for sequential decision-making. Despite many high-profile successes in recent years, deep RL is known to be brittle. An emerging line of research attributes this brittleness to a loss of plasticity in neural networks. However, plasticity loss has so far been understudied in stochastic environments. We study this interplay systematically, training SAC agents on three DeepMind Control tasks augmented with controlled levels of observation and action noise. We find that plasticity-preserving methods increase learning robustness on the two harder tasks, with their advantage growing as observation noise increases, while combining resets with layer normalization underperforms resets alone at every observation noise level tested. Further, stochasticity can accelerate the loss of plasticity in harder environments, whereas in easier settings noise can act as a regularizer that sustains plasticity. Lastly, plasticity loss is most pronounced in the early stages of training. In the most challenging stochastic settings, TD instability rather than gradual plasticity loss becomes the dominant failure mode.
papers.summary: Plasticity loss, the gradual decline in a network's ability to keep learning, has been proposed as a cause of brittleness in deep reinforcement learning (RL), but it has rarely been studied in stochastic environments. The authors train `SAC` agents on three `DeepMind Control` tasks with controlled observation and action noise. On the two harder tasks, plasticity-preserving methods help more as observation noise increases, though combining resets with layer normalization underperforms resets alone. Noise accelerates plasticity loss on hard tasks but acts as a regularizer on easy ones, and **in the most stochastic settings, temporal-difference (TD) instability rather than plasticity loss becomes the dominant failure mode**.

papers.title: Hyperbolic Inverse Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) seeks to infer the reward function underlying observed behavior, but its predictive accuracy and interpretability depend on how that reward is computed from the underlying features. While prior IRL reward functions have been implemented through a variety of techniques including linear weights, neural networks, or other function approximators, none make assumptions about the geometry of the underlying feature space. Inspired by geometric organization observed in neural circuits, we introduce Hyperbolic inverse reinforcement learning (Hyperbolic IRL), which parameterizes reward as a function of Hyperbolic distance between the feature vector and a learned parameter vector, as well as its Euclidean distance variant. We tested our methods against a range of linear and nonlinear IRL baselines under both deterministic and stochastic policies. Our Hyperbolic approach achieved comparable performance to state-of-the-art models on established benchmarks and excelled in the low data limit and across dense environments. Applied to human navigation among multiple exhibits in a museum room, Hyperbolic IRL reveals reward structure that depends not only on individual exhibit-distance features, but also on non-separable conjunctions between them. Together, these results demonstrate that a Hyperbolic reward parameterization can improve both the predictive accuracy and interpretability of IRL, providing a framework for studying how non-separable, conjunctive structure can begin to explain behavior.
papers.summary: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) infers the reward function behind observed behavior, but existing reward parameterizations make no assumptions about the geometry of the feature space. `Hyperbolic IRL`, inspired by geometric organization observed in neural circuits, defines reward as a function of the hyperbolic (or, in a variant, Euclidean) distance between a feature vector and a learned parameter vector. It matches state-of-the-art IRL baselines on established benchmarks and **performs best when data is scarce** and in dense environments. Applied to human navigation in a museum room, it reveals reward that depends on non-separable conjunctions of exhibit-distance features.

papers.title: Hard Constraint Projection in a Physics Informed Neural Network (Burgers)
papers.abstract: Physics informed machine learning provides a framework to study and simulate fluid dynamics, potentially at a fraction of the computational cost of traditional numerical methods, with the goal of improving the explainability, accuracy and robustness of purely data driven machine learning methods. In this work, we extend the hard constraint projection (HCP) method developed by Chen et al. [Journal of Computational Physics, 445, 110624, 2021] from a linear partial differential equation (PDE) to a nonlinear PDE: the 1D Burgers' equation. To strictly impose a discrete approximation of the governing equation, the Burgers' equation is first locally discretised (using a finite difference stencil) then decomposed into a constraint matrix and a prediction matrix. Using tools from linear algebra, the constraint matrix is used to construct a projection matrix. A physics informed neural network (PINN) [Raissi et al. Journal of Computational Physics, 378, 686, 2019] is used to predict the velocity, and a final unlearnable layer projects the velocity prediction to the hyperplane of exact solutions to a discretised form of the Burgers' equation. Our initial results indicate that the HCP-PINN initially trains similarly to an equivalent PINN, and as the PINN loss plateaus, the HCP-PINN loss continues to decline. When tested on a previously unseen uniform grid of points covering the domain, the HCP-PINN exhibits higher accuracy, converging to a data error approximately an order of magnitude lower than the comparable PINN. We also observe that the inclusion of the HCP layer results in better observance of the governing PDE. Our findings suggest that the HCP-PINN can be more robust to the selection of physics collocation points, and less dependent on collocation point quantity.
papers.summary: The authors extend hard constraint projection (HCP) from a linear partial differential equation (PDE) to the nonlinear 1D Burgers' equation. The equation is discretized with a finite-difference stencil and split into constraint and prediction matrices, and a final non-learnable layer of a physics-informed neural network (`PINN`) projects predictions onto the space of exact discrete solutions. The `HCP-PINN` keeps improving after a standard PINN's loss plateaus and reaches **roughly an order of magnitude lower data error** on an unseen grid. It also satisfies the governing PDE better and appears less sensitive to how many collocation points are used and where they are placed.

papers.title: Regret-Optimal Wasserstein-Robust Linear Regression
papers.abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) minimizes worst-case risk under distributional uncertainty, but its decisions can be suboptimal in terms of their excess risk, or regret. We study this gap for multivariate least-squares regression, assuming that the observed source law and unknown target law differ by an adversarial 2-Wasserstein perturbation of size $\varepsilon$. We first identify the asymptotic complexity of robust decision-making in the $\varepsilon \to 0$ limit, characterized by a problem-specific condition number $\kappa$. Here, a wide spectrum of simple algorithms, including DRO, achieve the instance-optimal rate of $O(\kappa \varepsilon^2)$. For fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, we prove that DRO still achieves the minimax rate if the problem has bounded residual effective rank. On the other hand, we identify significant failure modes where DRO is provably suboptimal by dimension-dependent factors. Fortunately, we prove that two alternative procedures, minimax regret optimization (MRO) and spectral-norm regularization (SNR), attain the minimax rate. We derive an exact convex reformulation of MRO and an accelerated proximal algorithm for SNR, along with high-probability finite-sample guarantees. We support these theoretical results with numerical experiments separating the performance of MRO and SNR from DRO.
papers.summary: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) minimizes worst-case risk but can be suboptimal in excess risk, or regret. The authors study this gap for multivariate least-squares regression in which the target distribution is a 2-Wasserstein perturbation of the source distribution. As the perturbation size goes to zero, many simple methods, including DRO, achieve the instance-optimal rate. At fixed perturbation sizes, however, **DRO can be suboptimal by dimension-dependent factors**, while minimax regret optimization (MRO) and spectral-norm regularization (SNR) provably attain the minimax rate, with a convex reformulation and an accelerated algorithm provided for each.

papers.title: SATFRONT: Detecting Atmospheric Fronts with Satellite Data using Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Atmospheric fronts are associated with much of the high-impact weather in the mid-latitudes, yet their identification and classification remain largely manual and subjective. Existing deep learning approaches rely primarily on gridded reanalysis or forecast data, limiting their applicability to satellite observations available for time-critical applications. We introduce SATFRONT, a machine learning framework for detecting cold, warm, and occluded fronts over Europe from geostationary satellite observations, with reanalysis data as an optional additional input. The model is trained on frontal analyses from five European national meteorological services and evaluated against UK Met Office analyses for 2024. Using satellite observations alone, SATFRONT achieves a Critical Success Index (CSI) of 0.428 at a 150 km tolerance, within the range of agreement between analyses from different meteorological services (0.277-0.501) and higher than that of an operational rule-based front detector that uses satellite data (0.133). Adding ERA5 reanalysis increases the CSI to 0.591. ERA5 substantially improves the placement of individual fronts, although its effect on their annual spatial distribution varies by front type. These results demonstrate that cold, warm, and occluded fronts can be detected directly from geostationary satellite observations, providing a basis for automated frontal analyses at the high temporal frequency required for time-critical applications.
papers.summary: Atmospheric fronts drive much of mid-latitude high-impact weather, but identifying them is still largely manual, and existing deep learning approaches depend on gridded reanalysis or forecast data. `SATFRONT` detects cold, warm, and occluded fronts over Europe directly from geostationary satellite observations, trained on analyses from five national meteorological services. Using satellite data alone, it reaches a Critical Success Index (CSI) of 0.428, within the range of agreement between human forecasters and well above an operational rule-based detector's 0.133. **Adding `ERA5` reanalysis data raises the CSI to 0.591.**

papers.title: Subquadratic Attention with a Hierarchical Tree-Structured Indexer
papers.abstract: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). In this paper, we derive an asymptotically subquadratic sparse attention method based on a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer, which we call Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA). ZHA constructs a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which future queries traverse from the top down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Crucially, by iteratively growing the tree's depth, the total cost including routing and final attention grows sublinearly in sequence length, resulting in overall subquadratic (but superlinear) scaling for attention. We demonstrate that ZHA can be cheaply applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation training stage over a few billion tokens, and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical, and agentic coding evaluation tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is highly robust to tree geometry including very deep trees of up to 6 levels. Finally, we develop a detailed performance model and show that our approach scales subquadratically, dramatically outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million context, and ultimately has the potential to extend effective context windows to the hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.
papers.summary: Attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, which limits long context in large language models (LLMs). Existing workarounds either lose expressiveness, as with sliding-window or linear attention, or only give constant-factor speedups because their indexers still scale quadratically. `Zyphra Hierarchical Attention` (`ZHA`) builds a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, and each query walks the tree from the top down to fetch a sparse set of keys. As the tree grows deeper, routing plus attention cost grows sublinearly per query, so **overall attention scales subquadratically**. Existing pretrained models can be converted with a short KL-distillation stage over a few billion tokens while keeping performance on long-context retrieval, reasoning, math and agentic coding tasks. The authors' performance model suggests the method beats competing approaches beyond 1M tokens and could extend context windows to hundreds of millions of tokens.

papers.title: ACCT: Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer
papers.abstract: In real-world deployments, large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly evolving from single-model invocation toward heterogeneous deployments in which different models are dynamically invoked for inference. When the same context is reused across models, however, each newly selected target model typically has to process it again, repeatedly incurring substantial computational costs. Therefore, we propose ACCT (Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer), which targets KV cache transfer between models of different scales within the same model family. ACCT transforms the KV cache produced by a source model into sparse KV states that can be directly consumed by a target model, thereby enabling cross-model reuse of context computation and decoupling context computation from downstream inference. ACCT consists of three lightweight components: the Cartographer identifies query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head; the Allocator determines how many context tokens each target layer and KV head retains under a shared total KV budget; and the Compiler transforms selected source KV into sparse target KV. The target model can therefore perform inference using the transferred KV without reprocessing the original context. We evaluate ACCT in two complementary settings comprising five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks. Experiments show that ACCT matches or exceeds the target model's original inference performance even when reducing the KV cache size by 75%. At a context length of approximately 19K tokens, ACCT's KV conversion achieves a 6.5-21.2 times speedup over target context prefill. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring context computation across models under a limited KV budget.
papers.summary: When a system routes the same context to different LLMs, each newly selected model usually has to reprocess that context from scratch. `ACCT` (Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer) converts the KV cache from a source model into sparse KV states that a differently sized model in the same family can use directly. It has three lightweight parts: a Cartographer that picks query-relevant tokens for each target layer and head, an Allocator that splits a shared KV budget across them, and a Compiler that maps the selected source KV into the target's format. Across five general benchmarks and six context-heavy tasks, `ACCT` matches or beats the target model's own performance **while cutting KV cache size by 75%**. At about 19K tokens, the conversion runs 6.5 to 21.2 times faster than having the target model prefill the context itself.

papers.title: Fast Privacy Loss Accounting for Random Allocation via Multiscale FFT
papers.abstract: In the random allocation sampling scheme each user's data is used in $k$ steps chosen randomly and uniformly from a sequence of $t$ steps. This scheme is known to improve on Poisson sampling in private optimization and in communication-efficient aggregation. The existing privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant for this scheme runs in time quadratic in the inverse of the accuracy parameter $\alpha$ (Feldman and Shenfeld, 2026). We give an algorithm, \emph{multiscale FFT}, that represents likelihood ratios on a grid that is uniform within each dyadic interval and computes the exact rounding of every pairwise sum using FFTs within each interval. It keeps the guarantees of the accountant and improves the dependence of its running time on $\alpha$ from $O(\alpha^{-2})$ to $O(\alpha^{-1}\log(1/\alpha))$. In addition, we demonstrate that rounding can be performed via the mean-preserving connect-the-dots projection of (Doroshenko et al., 2026). This reduces the errors that rounding introduces in the mean of the privacy loss and in the $\chi^2$ divergence of the computed pair from the order of $\alpha$ to $O(\alpha^2/\log(t))$. In our experiments, our algorithm achieves speedups of several orders of magnitude at high accuracy and gives improved privacy bounds for DP-SGD with PREAMBLE.
papers.summary: In random allocation sampling, each user's data is used in k steps chosen uniformly at random out of t training steps, and this scheme can give better differential-privacy guarantees than Poisson sampling. The existing privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant for it runs in time quadratic in the inverse accuracy parameter α. A new algorithm, `multiscale FFT`, represents likelihood ratios on a grid that is uniform within each dyadic interval and uses FFTs to compute every pairwise sum with exact rounding, **cutting running time from O(α⁻²) to O(α⁻¹ log(1/α))** with the same guarantees. Rounding with a mean-preserving connect-the-dots projection also shrinks the rounding error. In experiments the method is several orders of magnitude faster at high accuracy and gives tighter privacy bounds for `DP-SGD` with `PREAMBLE`.

papers.title: Gradient Descent on Two ReLU Neurons: Global Landscape and Bifurcation Dynamics
papers.abstract: Understanding how gradient descent learns features remains a central challenge in neural network theory. We study this question in a minimal multi-index setting that already exhibits rich multi-phase gradient dynamics: a well-specified two-neuron ReLU teacher-student model under isotropic Gaussian inputs, trained by population gradient flow from small initialization. We show that the dynamics are organized by two directions: the "easy" bisector direction, which carries the leading signal, and the "hard" splitting direction, which governs specialization. To characterize the loss structure and learning behavior, we analyze the population squared-loss landscape and show that every critical point with both student weights nonzero is either a global minimum or a saddle. We then track the gradient-flow trajectory, showing that student neurons first collapse toward a bisector saddle before escaping and specializing to teacher neurons. Our results provide both a landscape and dynamics account of the multi-phase symmetry-breaking behavior that arises in a simple multi-index model and under standard algorithmic and architectural choices.
papers.summary: To study how gradient descent learns features, the authors analyze a minimal teacher-student setup: two ReLU neurons, Gaussian inputs, and population gradient flow from small initialization. The dynamics turn out to be governed by an "easy" bisector direction that carries the leading signal and a "hard" splitting direction that drives specialization. The authors prove that **every critical point with both student weights nonzero is either a global minimum or a saddle**. They then follow the trajectory: the student neurons first collapse toward a bisector saddle, then escape and each specialize to one teacher neuron. Together these results account for the multi-phase symmetry-breaking seen in this simple multi-index model.

papers.title: Physiological Trajectories and Observation Patterns in ICU Mortality Prediction: Transportability Under Changing Measurement Conditions
papers.abstract:
Objective: To distinguish the transferable predictive value of physiological trajectories from that of observation patterns in ICU mortality prediction, and to assess whether measurement timing affects performance independently of observation quantity.
  Materials and Methods: In-hospital mortality was predicted at 48 hours using MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU. Nested representations progressively integrated latest-value snapshots (R1), longitudinal physiological summaries (R2), and measurement frequency and timing features (R3). Models fitted on 7,762 MetaVision patients were evaluated on 21,682 MIMIC-IV patients and 43,878 eICU patients across 204 hospitals. The effect of measurement timing was assessed while holding the number of retained observations constant.
  Results: Physiological trajectories improved external prediction in eICU (R2-R1 log-loss difference -0.00922, 95% CI -0.01148 to -0.00704). Observation-pattern features improved locally developed eICU models (R3-R2 -0.00257, 95% CI -0.00370 to -0.00146), but not clearly after transfer from MetaVision (-0.00012, 95% CI -0.00206 to +0.00208). R3 was favoured in 10 of 30 source bootstrap refits. At matched observation counts, retaining measurements spread throughout the window reduced log loss relative to random retention by 0.03280 for R3 versus 0.00703 for R2. Removing the final 12 hours increased log loss relative to count-matched random removal by 0.01947 for R3 versus 0.00822 for R2. Under reduced availability, the local R3 increment changed from beneficial to harmful.
  Discussion: Physiological trajectories transferred more consistently, while observation-pattern features were particularly sensitive to the timing and availability of measurements.
  Conclusion: Clinical prediction models should be evaluated not only in new patient populations but also under the measurement conditions that supply their inputs.
papers.summary: Intensive care unit (ICU) mortality models can draw on two kinds of signal: how a patient's vital signs evolve over time, and how often and when clinicians take measurements. The authors test which kind holds up in new settings. Using nested feature sets on `MIMIC-III`, `MIMIC-IV` and `eICU`, they train on 7,762 patients and evaluate on more than 65,000 patients from 204 hospitals. **Physiological trajectories transferred consistently, while observation-pattern features helped only in locally trained models** and were sensitive to when measurements were taken and how many were available; under reduced data availability their benefit turned harmful. The authors conclude that clinical models should be evaluated under the measurement conditions that will supply their inputs, not only on new patient populations.

papers.title: DecisionRank: On-Policy Distillation for Decision-Model Rerankers
papers.abstract: Decision models target structured tasks by directly predicting choices or scores, avoiding autoregressive decoding latency. However, transferring a generative LLM's ranking knowledge to a decision model remains challenging: the teacher expresses preferences through a ranked list of document ID sequences, while the student determines the ranking using scores from the first-token position. To bridge this gap, we introduce DecisionRank, a decision model trained through item-space on-policy distillation (OPD). Item-space OPD constructs the student's rollout by sorting its document scores into a ranked sequence. A generative teacher takes the resulting ranking list as inputs and provides conditional feedback to directly supervise those scores. Combined with offline ranking supervision, DecisionRank achieves state-of-the-art performance on both general and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks such as TREC DL, BEIR, and BRIGHT. Across four benchmarks, item-space OPD consistently outperforms alternative training objectives. Even at 1.7B parameters, DecisionRank surpasses its 27B generative teacher on TREC DL19--23. At 8B, it outperforms its generative listwise counterpart while running $24.5\times$ faster on TREC DL and $16.7\times$ faster on BRIGHT.
papers.summary: Decision-model rerankers score documents in a single forward pass rather than generating a ranked list, which avoids slow autoregressive decoding. That makes it hard to distill ranking knowledge from a generative LLM teacher, whose output is a sequence of document IDs. `DecisionRank` uses item-space on-policy distillation (`OPD`): the student's scores are sorted into a ranking, which the generative teacher critiques to supervise those scores directly, alongside offline ranking supervision. It reaches state-of-the-art results on `TREC DL`, `BEIR` and `BRIGHT`, and **a 1.7B student beats its 27B generative teacher on TREC DL19–23**. At 8B it outperforms its generative listwise counterpart while running 24.5 times faster on `TREC DL` and 16.7 times faster on `BRIGHT`.

papers.title: Instance-dependent sequential limits as an exact information ledger
papers.abstract: Instance-dependent limits for bandit regret, sequential tests, best-arm identification and Markov decision processes are proved by one chain. It runs from a divergence decomposition through data processing to a statistic, a testing step that turns a class guarantee into a requirement on the history, and optimization over alternatives and allocations. Only the first step is an identity. This work writes the chain as an exact ledger. By the chain rule, data processing loses exactly a conditional divergence, which vanishes for arms in natural exponential families at the per-arm counts and reward sums. A one-parameter family of martingale identities extends the decomposition to every tilt between two instances. The classical limits follow by relaxations with named defects. All defects but the asymptotic step's can be computed from an algorithm's own runs, the uniform quantification's only when the class guarantee is a number. On seven published sources, from movie ratings to engine replacement, the ledger locates the difference between standard algorithms and the classical limits. For identification among trained models and for Wald's test the largest term is usually the uniform quantification's.
papers.summary: Lower bounds on performance that depend on the specific problem instance, for bandit regret, sequential tests, best-arm identification and Markov decision processes, are usually proved through the same chain of steps, but only the first step is an exact identity. The authors rewrite that chain as an exact "ledger" in which each relaxation leaves a named, quantifiable gap. These gaps include the conditional divergence lost to data processing and a family of martingale identities covering every tilt between two instances. **All gaps except the asymptotic step can be computed from an algorithm's own runs**. Applied to seven published datasets, from movie ratings to engine replacement, the ledger pinpoints where standard algorithms fall short of the classical limits, with the uniform-quantification step usually the largest term.

papers.title: A Better Critic Matters for Distribution Matching Distillation
papers.abstract: Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) trains a few-step student using the difference between a teacher's score and an online critic's estimate of the student distribution's score. We investigate what the critic needs, in capacity and in information, to provide a reliable training signal. On the capacity side, controlled experiments across seven SiT model sizes on ImageNet show that increasing teacher size while keeping a small critic fixed can degrade student quality and cause training collapse. Scaling the critic alongside the teacher, a strategy we call joint scaling, prevents collapse in our experiments and allows the student to benefit from larger teachers. On the information side, rather than forcing the critic to model a step-agnostic mixture of student outputs, we introduce a step-aware critic (STAC) that conditions on the student's generation step to estimate step-specific scores. Together, joint scaling and STAC consistently improve few-step distillation across class-conditional ImageNet generation, text-to-image generation with SDXL and FLUX.2, and text-to-video generation with Wan2.1.
papers.summary: `Distribution Matching Distillation` (`DMD`) trains a few-step image generator using the difference between a teacher's score and an online critic's estimate of the student's score. Experiments across seven `SiT` model sizes on `ImageNet` show that **growing the teacher while keeping the critic small can degrade the student and even collapse training**. Scaling the critic along with the teacher ("joint scaling") prevents this. The authors also introduce a step-aware critic (`STAC`) that conditions on the student's generation step instead of modeling a mixture over all steps. Together, the two changes consistently improve few-step distillation for `ImageNet`, text-to-image with `SDXL` and `FLUX.2`, and text-to-video with `Wan2.1`.

papers.title: Counting on Dummies: Privacy Amplification with Observable Counts and Truncated Batches
papers.abstract: In many practical deployments of Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), the server processes data in batches. Randomly sampling these batches allows for better privacy bounds via privacy amplification results. Most sampling schemes with provable privacy amplification, including Poisson sampling and random allocation, result in variable batch sizes. The privacy guarantee of these schemes requires that the batch sizes are not revealed. In distributed settings, the server performing the aggregation or any party observing the communication traffic may learn these batch sizes. Furthermore, in both centralized and distributed settings, memory and computation constraints may require each batch to be of some maximum size $s$, necessitating truncation of the batch when it exceeds this limit. It is known that this truncation can result in a significant increase in privacy loss. In this work, we address both of these challenges via a simple mechanism that uses a random number of \emph{dummy points} to privatize the batch size and maintain the privacy guarantee even under truncation. We demonstrate that our mechanism is easy to implement in a distributed setting, and provide a general analysis of this mechanism for both Poisson sampling and random allocation. Our analysis is designed to support efficient and relatively tight privacy accounting. It also effectively amplifies the privacy of the count releases by subsampling, making the expected number of dummy points asymptotically smaller than what is needed to directly privatize the (sensitivity-one) batch sizes with non-negative noise. For Poisson sampling with truncated batches, we demonstrate empirically that our mechanism achieves better privacy--efficiency tradeoffs than the direct accounting for truncation recently given by (Ganesh, 2025).
papers.summary: Sampling schemes that amplify privacy in Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (`DP-SGD`), such as Poisson sampling and random allocation, produce variable batch sizes that must stay hidden. In practice those sizes can leak, for example to observers of network traffic in distributed training, and memory limits often force large batches to be truncated, which raises privacy loss. The proposed mechanism pads each batch with a random number of dummy points, which **hides the batch size and keeps the privacy guarantee even when batches are truncated**. It is easy to implement in distributed settings and comes with accounting for both Poisson sampling and random allocation. Because subsampling also amplifies the privacy of the released counts, fewer dummy points are needed than for adding noise to batch sizes directly, and the method beats prior truncation accounting on privacy–efficiency tradeoffs.

papers.title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
papers.abstract: Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In RoboArchitect, a coding model observes a robot's rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy. The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks. Without updating any model weights, RoboArchitect raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5x) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2x), across multiple benchmarks and policies. The gains are largest where the benchmark is far from the policy's training data: wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness yields a specialist that often outperforms even the finetuned version. Intuitive control strategies are automatically designed, such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in horizontally when an obstacle blocks the way from above. The harness also evolves its own persistent memory, carrying learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions. These results suggest that substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and its design can be effectively automated and optimized without weight updates.
papers.summary: Frozen robot policies work much better inside an agent harness, which is control code that decides when to call the policy, use vision tools, or move the arm directly, but these harnesses are currently written by hand for each robot and benchmark. In `RoboArchitect`, a coding model watches rollouts, diagnoses failures and iteratively rewrites the harness around the frozen policy, then the result is tested on held-out scenes and tasks. Without any weight updates, **average success rises from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks**, across several benchmarks and policies. The evolved harnesses discover intuitive strategies, such as lifting a jammed arm clear, and build their own persistent memory of lessons like effective grasp depths. Around a general-purpose policy, they often beat a version finetuned for the task.
papers.highlight_summary:
Hand-built agent harnesses can make a frozen robot policy perform much better, but engineers currently redesign them for every new robot and benchmark. `RoboArchitect` automates that work: a coding model watches rollouts, works out why they failed, and rewrites the control code around the policy without updating any weights.

- The harness starts as a simple pass-through of the `VLA` policy, and over up to 5 iterations `claude-opus-5` reads the full execution traces and proposes revisions that can follow the policy, call auxiliary tools (`Grounding-DINO`, `SAM 3`, `Molmo2` pointing, `GraspGen`) or command the arm directly; a revision is kept only if it raises training-episode success.
- Across five simulated benchmarks and seven policies, mean held-out success rises from **9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5×)** and from **12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2×)**, and iterative refinement roughly doubles the one-shot design on unseen scenes (**21.4% vs. 43.3%**).
- Wrapping the general `X-VLA` checkpoint often beats the same model finetuned on the target benchmark, for example **52.6% vs. 35.2%** (unseen scenes) and **72.5% vs. 32.1%** (unseen tasks) on `VLABench`, and **87.5% vs. 70.8%** on `SimplerEnv WidowX` unseen scenes.
- Useful behaviors emerge without being specified: the harness drops a useless policy entirely and becomes a code-as-policy agent, and it learns targeted routines such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in sideways under a shelf; it also builds its own persistent memories (such as grasp depths that worked), which held-out episodes consult 3–13 times each, with **over 90% of reads** finding a stored entry.
